News.title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' detained for UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about Â£21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

News.title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
News.content:
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.

"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.

But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

Video editor: Serene Khalifeh

News.title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development.

"Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.

This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.

She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".

In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".

She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.

This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.

She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.

A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project.

"This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess.

"We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing.

"My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."

Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."

The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.

There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".

The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

News.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
News.content:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

News.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
News.content:
The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

News.title: We must save water as drought becomes new normal, says minister
News.content:
The government has warned action is needed to prevent water shortages becoming "the norm" after severe drought was declared across parts of southern England.

Water and flooding minister Emma Hardy told MPs current drought conditions were "something we have not experienced for decades" and urged people to "think about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks".

Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England on Thursday after months of low rainfall, with around 50 million people now impacted.

Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are all affected by the move announced by the Environment Agency.

The government said supplies would not be interrupted but declaring severe drought would ensure "proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Hardy said the measures were down to "exceptionally low rainfall" and depleted reservoir levels.

News.title: Police officer who raped two women jailed for 12 years
News.content:
A former police sergeant who was found guilty of a catalogue of sex crimes, including raping two women, has been jailed for 12 years.

Campbell Petrie had been convicted of eight charges involving physical and sexual abuse towards the women in Glasgow over a 17-year period between 2006 and 2023.

Petrie, who had denied the allegations, will be supervised and monitored in the community for a further three years after his release.

He is one of four serving or former Police Scotland officers who have been exposed as rapists in the space of five months.

It has also emerged that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

News.title: The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day
News.content:
Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.

"I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says.

"But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out."

She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom.

Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.

A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.

This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions.

"It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything.

"I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise."

For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests.

She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself.

British Athletics doctors ran tests that gave no answers, so she carried on, assuming it was lingering glandular fever that would eventually pass.

She qualified for that year's World Championships, Commonwealth Games and European Championships in what was an unusually condensed season owing to the backlog from the pandemic.

Her health progressively deteriorated. At the Worlds, she struggled with a painful throat and was waking at unusual times in the night. At the Commonwealths, she was dizzy while running and her body was more sore than normal.

At the Europeans, she false-started after losing all feeling in her legs while in the blocks. She spoke of her "year of hell" in an emotional interview with BBC Sport after that race.

News.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around Â£2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see âthem as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future â prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to Â£3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

News.title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
News.content:
The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm.

In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected.

She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform.

More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of Â£120,000.

The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive".

It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines.

In its response to the report, the government says, external it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively."

Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families.

News.title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
News.content:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments.

Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks during undercover filming for an ITV News investigation, external in the run up to council elections in May.

Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".

He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable".

In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison".

Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year.

In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites".

He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Friday, Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

He added that all parties had "bad apples" and denied it was any more of a problem in Reform than other parties.

On Thursday, the party told the BBC that Feeney had "mutually agreed" to resign from the party.

News.title: Wildlife park reopens after man killed by tiger
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened for the first time since a man was killed by a tiger in an enclosure.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday. The public were evacuated after the incident with the attraction closed since then.

An inquest that opened into Chapman's death on Thursday heard of his history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia. His family expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services leading up to his death.

City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the inquest was told.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park confirmed on Thursday it would reopen following "engagement with the relevant authorities".

In a previous statement on social media, the park said "many, many people" had contacted it about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident, and it confirmed he was "safe and well" and would not be euthanised.

A spokesperson said its "Land of the Tiger" area, where Saturday's incident took place in front of staff and members of the public, was also open.

News.title: Doctor regrets not going to police earlier about Lucy Letby
News.content:
A senior doctor who raised suspicions about Lucy Letby has said he should have gone to police sooner.

Dr Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital when the nurse murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others.

In his first interview since the publication of the Thirlwall Inquiry report into what happened, Brearey reflected on the effect on staff and said he had "naively" assumed senior managers would respond to suspicions about the nurse's involvement in a series of baby deaths.

The inquiry found a "toxic negativity" within the NHS that continued to discourage staff from speaking out, despite stronger whistleblowing guidance, and said regulation was lacking.

Brearey claimed his warnings about Letby were repeatedly ignored by bosses at the hospital, which is now under new management - and also fears cultural change at the NHS will take time to implement.

"I was naively thinking that raising concerns with senior managers, they had the same values that I did and, once they got it, they would be thinking the same way," he said.

The doctor led a group of seven consultants who shared the same concerns about Letby.

Hospital bosses carried out a series of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but Cheshire Police was not asked to investigate until May 2017.

Letby remained employed at the hospital until her arrest more than a year later.

"I think one of the reasons we got through this and ended up picking up a police investigation is that the seven of us stuck together," he said, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"But obviously in retrospect, clearly, if we'd known what was ahead of us, we would have gone to the police earlier."

News.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
News.content:
Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16 in England and Wales.

The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".

Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, Baroness Bertin said porn showing strangulation had "absolutely sort of normalised this kind of sexual violence".

"That has to come to an end and I hope this law change will be the beginning of that," she said - adding that it aimed to "marry up" differences in the law about what was acceptable online and offline.

Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent, but its depiction online is currently not illegal.

Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.

Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.

"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.

"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."

News.title: 'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
News.content:
Donaldson represents a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service", Acheson added.

"There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor," he said.

But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit.

"The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme.

"Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community.

"I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background.

"So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found.

"I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal."

News.title: Ten-year-old Willow among children to benefit from pioneering same-day test to spot infections
News.content:
"The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey.

"It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.

With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital.

She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.

During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.

The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.

Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens.

By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.

Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.

Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.

A man killed by a tiger may have had his medical records breached by NHS staff, an ambulance trust has said.

William Chapman was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster on Saturday.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service Trust said that two members of its staff may have accessed or attempted to access medical information "without a legitimate reason" and it has launched an investigation,

In a statement, the trust said: “First and foremost, our thoughts are with William Chapman’s family at this distressing time.

“The Trust has identified an information governance concern in relation to this tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park and William’s family has been informed of our ongoing investigation into this.

“We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.

“We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.

“The Trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals. We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) and we will continue to keep William’s family informed as our investigation progresses.”

Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on 10 October when Mr Chapman, 23, who police said was visiting the park alone, entered the enclosure of a rare Amur tiger called Altai. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

On Friday, the park opened its doors for the first time since the tragedy, including to Land of the Tigers enclosure.

News.title: Plan unforgettable family adventures in the UK and abroad
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Long journeys tend to create a lot of unspent energy among little ones. Discover kid-friendly activities and thrilling experiences, abroad or at home.

Head to Durham for the ideal UK getaway

( The Bowes Museum )

If you’re after an autumn staycation with character, Durham delivers an irresistible mix of heritage, adventure, culture and countryside. There’s certainly no shortage of museums. Step aboard a vintage tram at Beamish – The Living Museum of the North or discover the story of rail at Locomotion in Shildon, the world’s first railway town. Plus, marvel at the enchanting 200-year-old Silver Swan automaton at The Bowes Museum

Meanwhile, at Raby Castle, Park and Gardens, uncover centuries of history at one of England’s most dramatic medieval castles. You can also discover unexpected treasures and glorious grounds at Ushaw Historic House, Chapels and Gardens.

For a stay to remember, unwind like medieval royalty at Lumley Castle Hotel. From city to countryside and coast, make Durham your next stop this autumn.

Follow Hertfordshire’s largest Christmas light trail

( Ashridge House )

Experience the brand-new Illuminated experience at Ashridge House. Inspired by the beloved Christmas poem A Visit from St Nicholas, by Clement Clarke Moore, follow a reimagined trail through the historic Hertfordshire estate, where enchanting light, sound and storytelling provide festive wonder at every turn.

Illuminated 2026 features new installations and spectacular projections that will transform the house. Plus, there are immersive moments designed to delight all ages. Before or after your journey, explore the Christmas market, featuring seasonal treats, warming drinks and festive shopping. With free parking, dog-friendly evenings and free entry for children under four years old, it’s a magical festive experience for the whole family.

Illuminated 2026 is open from 20 November 2026 to 2 January 2027.

Explore history and science in Florence

The breathtaking 16th-century armillary sphere ( Museo Galileo )

Florence’s Museo Galileo offers an extraordinary journey into the history of science in the birthplace of the Renaissance. Home to more than 1,000 scientific treasures once owned by the infamous Medici and Lorraine families, the museum is bound to fascinate adults and children alike. One of the many highlights is the extensive collection of Galileo’s own instruments, including the only two telescopes he ever built.

Elsewhere, you can trace scientific inventions from the Middle Ages, marvel at the breathtaking 16th-century armillary sphere and discover what is thought to be the world’s oldest Arab celestial globe. Interactive 3D screens and a free app further bring the museum to life for visitors of all ages.

Experience art, nature and architecture in Portugal

( SAGG Napoli )

Based in Porto, the Serralves Foundation is one of Portugal’s leading cultural institutions, bringing together several cultural sites at which families can experience art, architecture and nature. Explore the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art, designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Álvaro Siza; the Manoel de Oliveira Cinema House; the Álvaro Siza Wing or the striking Art Deco Serralves Villa.

Whether you decide to take a refreshing stroll in the park or admire the impressive architecture, Serralves offers families the freedom to experience the sites at their own pace. Plus, you can enjoy a cultural and educational programme combining contemporary art, architecture, cinema and activities connected with nature.

Marvel at gravity-defying shows and thrilling rides

( Zippos Circus )

News.title: Jimmy Kimmel’s latest Katie Zacharia lawyer joke had even Kim Kardashian laughing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kim Kardashian couldn’t control her laughter when Jimmy Kimmel made a joke that her legal training made her more qualified than the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia.

The reality TV star appeared Thursday night on Jimmy Kimmel Live, and discussed her progress toward becoming a lawyer in the state of California. Kardashian explained that she had passed a preliminary exam, known as the “baby bar,” but hadn’t yet passed the final bar exam.

“So, I’ve made it all the way through except for the final one,” she told Kimmel.

“So you are technically, uh, more a lawyer than the White House press secretary,” Kimmel replied in reference to Zacharia, whose legal qualifications have been questioned after she came into the role this week.

In response, Kardashian burst into laughter, and Kimmel inquired if she would consider applying for the press secretary position.

open image in gallery Jimmy Kimmel joked about the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, in the latest installment of his late night show ( ABC / Getty Images )

“Um, do you have any interest in that? I could put in a word if you like,” Kimmel asked. “[Trump] watches the show.”

“No interest,” Kardashian said with a smile.

Kardashian began a four-year law apprenticeship in 2019 and passed the California “baby bar” preliminary exam on her fourth attempt in 2021. Last year, she announced she failed the main California bar exam but said she would continue trying “until I get there.”

Meanwhile, Zacharia, who touted herself as an attorney before landing the press secretary gig, fended off questions about her legal credentials and acknowledged that she failed California’s bar exam in 2011.

When a reporter outside the White House asked which state she had passed the bar in, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.” She later told The New York Times that she had misheard the question over the noise of Marine One.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she told the newspaper.

open image in gallery Kardashian began a four-year law apprenticeship in 2019 and passed the California ‘baby bar’ exam on her fourth attempt in 2021 ( ABC/Jimmy Kimmel Live )

Kimmel’s latest barb comes days after he wasted no time critiquing Zacharia after her rocky first briefing.

“It was the first day of kindergarten for the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia,” Kimmel said during Tuesday night’s show. “You know, Trump’s been president for quite a long time now. I think it’s been about what 50-60 years? And in order to keep him awake and interested, every six months they bring in a new fawning blonde dolt to add to the rotation.”

He continued: “Things did not get off to a great start for Malibu Katie today. Her first briefing was brief. It was only 14 minutes long, but even in that short time, she accomplished exactly what she was brought in to do, which is slobber a whole tube of lip gloss all over the president’s behind.”

After playing a clip of Zacharia’s remarks in which she read hesitantly and looked down at her script, Kimmel laughed: “Her reading is good for an 11 year-old. He hired a fourth grader to be press secretary.”

Despite her bumpy start, the White House has rallied to support Zacharia.

“She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.

News.title: South African rugby player dies on tour after fall at team hotel
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

South Africa Rugby has paid tribute to “gifted” Hyron Andrews after the Lions lock forward’s tragic death after falling at the team’s hotel during a tour to France.

The 31-year-old, who played for KZN Sharks and Sale Sharks in England, has passed away following an accident at the team’s hotel in La Rochelle.

Andrews leaves behind his wife, Maiglin, and young sons, with his Lions teammates set to play their European Champions Cup match against Stade Rochelais on Saturday.

The squad decided to play the match “in honour of their teammate,” with a moment’s silence to be held ahead of every Investec Champions Cup and EPCR Challenge Cup match this weekend. While former team Sale will pay tribute to Andrews before their Champions Cup fixture against Glasgow Warriors.

The Lions stated Andrews’ loss was “felt profoundly by his teammates, coaches, supporters and all who had the privilege of knowing him.

While a statement from Mark Alexander, president of SA Rugby, read: “This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron’s family and the whole Lions rugby community.

“There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, teammates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.

“Hyron was a respected member of the rugby community whose contribution to the game and impact on those around him will be remembered with great fondness.

open image in gallery Hyron Andrews of Sale Sharks prior to the Gallagher Premiership Rugby match between Sale Sharks and Saracens ( Getty )

“His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him.

“The thoughts and prayers of the entire South African rugby family are with Maighlin and all those mourning his loss. May they find strength, comfort and peace in the memories they shared with him and in the support of those around them.”

While Rudolf Straeuli, Chief Executive Officer of the Lions Rugby Company, added: “We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron. He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family having recently joined us this season.

open image in gallery Hyron Andrews of Sale Sharks makes a break past Josh Hodge of Exeter Chiefs in 2025 ( Getty )

"On behalf of our Chairman, Mr Altmann Allers, the board and everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to Maiglin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family. We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect.”

Andrews was born in Paarl and attended Hoërskool Garsfontein in Pretoria and also represented the Junior Springboks in 2015, though his presence was felt in Greater Manchester during his time with Sale, making 45 appearances in total.

Sharks Director of Rugby Alex Sanderson said: “Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant teammate. He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with.

“He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him.

“It was a big move for Hyron and his Maighlin to come to England but he truly made a second home in Manchester and it was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.

open image in gallery Hyron Andrews of the Sharks against the Reds in Brisbane in 2020 ( Getty )

“Most importantly, he was a loving husband to Maighlin and a doting father to his two gorgeous boys. It was an absolute privilege to get to know him and it’s just absolutely devastating for everyone.”

And EPCR Chairman Dominic McKay added: “The thoughts of everyone at EPCR and the wider international rugby community are with Hyron’s wife Maiglin, his young sons, wider family, friends, teammates, the 10bet Lions and all those who knew and loved him at this incredibly difficult time.”

News.title: British father avoids jail for causing son’s death in Cyprus hotel fall
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A British father has avoided a prison sentence for causing the death of his toddler son, who fell from a window in Cyprus.

Joshua Foster appeared at Paphos District Court on Friday for sentencing, where he was fined €3,000 (£2,500).

The 37-year-old, a senior accountant at KPMG, had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.

The two-year-old boy fell nearly 40 feet from the fourth-floor window of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July.

Prosecutor Chryso Perganti earlier said that the toddler was pronounced dead in hospital a couple of hours after his fall, having suffered multiple skull and bone fractures and damage to his vital organs.

Foster wore a light blue shirt and held back tears as his sentence was read out on Friday by District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.

open image in gallery Foster’s son died after falling from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort ( PA )

After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.

The court previously heard that Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view and “lost control” of him.

“That fraction of a second will haunt him for the rest of his life,” his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told judge Froso Christodoulidou during mitigation proceedings.

“This is punishment he and his family will carry with them for the rest of their lives.”

Foster, his wife, two children, and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of 12 July.

After spending the day doing activities, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.

Foster, his father-in-law and son left their rooms and walked towards the elevator at around 6pm.

open image in gallery Joshua Foster, right, with his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou ( PA )

As they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside, Mr Alexandrou told an earlier hearing.

Foster pushed the elevator button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” happened before Foster had a chance to react, the court was told.

After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos General Hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.

It was said that during the time of the incident – by this point around six hours earlier – the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.

The alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against the defendant, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.

The lawyer told the court that Foster has no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.

He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving his child, he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.

News.title: Meta launches new ‘open’ AI model – and it comes with a big surprise
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Meta has launched a powerful new “open” model, which contains at least one surprise.

The company says that the system, named Meta Spark Open, is the most powerful open weight model made by a US company. Open weight models are so-called because their developers make public the “weights” that decide how a system will respond to a request.

That means that they are available for anyone to download to their own devices, as well as to adjust. It means that they can be used on a device itself, rather than on a company’s servers, as well as allowing them to be adapted to different purposes.

It was that particular characteristic that led to a surprise perhaps even bigger than Meta’s announcement.

As Meta announced the new model, it also said that it had been working with Apple to ensure that it ran well on its Mac Studio computer. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg wrote in a post on X that Muse Spark Open “runs great” on Apple’s hardware, because of work with Apple and its new chief executive, John Ternus.

“Congrats to the team!” Mr Ternus wrote in reply. “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk.”

The collaboration represents an unexpected peace among the two companies, which have long had a complicated and sometimes antagonistic relationship. The two have repeatedly clashed over a variety of issues, most notably conflicts between Apple’s commitment to privacy and Meta’s use of advertising in its business model.

But the release of the new system seemingly shows how the race to build and embrace AI features is bringing unexpected collaborators together. It also demonstrates how some in the technology industry including Apple and Meta are looking to move beyond AI systems that rely on controversial data centres and difficult-to-acquire chips, and instead move towards running artificial intelligence on people’s own devices.

That is made more possible with the release of open weight models, since they can be downloaded and installed on users’ own computers. Meta’s release of Muse Spark Open follows the launch of a number of open weight models in recent days, including from competitors such as Nvidia and Mistral.

Despite the positives of open weight models, however, many US companies including Meta have chosen to release most or all of their systems in ways that ensure they control the whole experience. They have argued that doing so keeps the models safer because the companies can more effectively ensure they are not used for dangerous purposes, but it also means that they can increase revenue by requiring customers to pay for monthly subscriptions or show advertising.

That resistance to open weight models among US companies has meant that much of the development of the technology has been undertaken by Chinese competitors. Many of the most popular and powerful Chinese AI companies – including DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai – have launched highly capable open weight systems of their own, and Meta and other US companies have yet to catch up to their performance.

News.title: Sleeping Tesla driver using self-driving mode crashes into police car injuring officers
News.content:
A Tesla driver claimed he was asleep at the wheel when his vehicle, in Full Self-Driving mode, plowed into a California Highway Patrol (CHP) vehicle, injuring two officers.

The CHP car’s dashcam recorded the incident on October 13 on Interstate 80 in the Bay Area, where officers had sealed off a lane while they investigated a crash.

The Tesla, driven by a 22-year-old from Sacramento, entered the closed area, marked by flares, cones and emergency vehicle flashing lights. It then hit the occupied CHP vehicle.

CHP warned drivers that “despite its name, Full Self-Driving is not fully autonomous” and must be monitored at all times. Authorities have not yet announced what charges the driver could face.

News.title: UK could rejoin EU ‘within months’ with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, MEP says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A senior MEP has said the UK could rejoin the EU within months if it strikes a deal similar to Switzerland’s agreement, as Andy Burnham seeks closer ties with the bloc.

German MEP Bernard Lange, who was involved in the initial Brexit negotiations, said he would “love to see the UK come back” and lay out a potential speedy route for Britain to rejoin the EU.

He told The Guardian that the UK could follow a similar path to Switzerland, which is not a full member state of the EU but has access to the European single market.

However, Switzerland has agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£317m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds to gain access.

open image in gallery The prime minister announced at Labour’s annual conference last month that he would look at options that would take Britain closer to the bloc and suggested that re-entry into the EU could be included in Labour’s next election manifesto ( PA Wire )

Mr Lange said the framework could also work as a model for the UK, but warned it was “passive”.

“As a step-by-step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged,” he said.

“So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.”

The prime minister announced at Labour’s annual conference last month that he would look at options that would take Britain closer to the bloc and suggested that re-entry into the EU could be included in Labour’s next election manifesto.

open image in gallery In a statement to parliament on Monday, the prime minister said he would use a key UK-EU summit in Brussels next month to push for a Brexit reset aimed at improving relations with the bloc with a focus on growth, immigration and security ( PA Wire )

His announcement was welcomed by a number of EU leaders, including France’s president Emmanuel Macron and Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sanchez.

In a statement to parliament on Monday, the prime minister said he would use a key UK-EU summit in Brussels next month to push for a Brexit reset aimed at improving relations with the bloc with a focus on growth, immigration and security.

As part of The Independent’s campaign ‘Europe: The Way Back’, polling guru professor Sir John Curtice recently said that support for rejoining the EU was now at its highest level since the Brexit vote, at 61 per cent.

open image in gallery ( The Independent )

As prime minister Andy Burnham looks at the way ahead for Britain’s relationship with Europe, The Independent has been leading the charge, campaigning to secure the absolute best deal for Britain. News.title: Bank tax would raise mortgage costs, warns UBS
News.content:
Bank stocks have fallen on fears that John Healey will launch a tax raid on the sector in the Budget.

NatWest and Lloyds Banking Group shares were both down more than 2pc in early trading on the London Stock Exchange as investors responded to news the Chancellor is poised to raise taxes on the industry.

The banking sector has come into Mr Healey’s focus after their earnings were boosted by higher interest rates caused by the Iran war.

He is understood to be planning to target lenders despite praising banks at an International Monetary Fund (IMF) event in Bangkok on Thursday.

He said: “They’re a big contributor to the economy.

“They’re an important part of our business. They’re a part of the jewel, if you like, in the British economic crown.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey poised to launch raid on banks | Chancellor prepares to target lenders despite playing down fears of higher levies in the Budget

2) UAE bid for Telegraph threatened press freedom, Ofcom found | Media watchdog concluded takeover by RedBird IMI was contrary to the public interest

3) John Lewis puts Snowdonia hotel up for sale | Retail group makes ‘tough decision’ to offload historic staff retreat amid high running costs

4) Britain prepares to hand military satellite contract to US defence giant | US move to curtail Ukraine’s access to Starlink triggers ‘kill switch’ fears around Lockheed Martin’s Skynet bid

5) Cult London cinema beloved by Tarantino saved from closure | The Prince Charles Cinema secures its future with 25-year lease after bitter landlord dispute

What happened overnight

Asian shares mostly rose a day after a tech sell-off dragged stocks lower.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index jumped 3.6pc, after tumbling 7.6pc on Thursday. Samsung Electronics was up 4.2pc, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix added 3.5pc.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.9pc to 65,658.59, after falling 4.9pc a day earlier. OpenAI investor SoftBank climbed 1.7pc. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron was 2.8pc higher and memory chipmaker Kioxia advanced 3.2pc.

The Asian technology stocks traded higher after losses in AI shares moderated in the US.

Kevin Warsh, the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, said Friday at the IMF and World Bank gathering in ⁠Bangkok that AI could bring about positive impacts to global economies.

He said: “I’d say, the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime.

“There really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, the US economy, over the horizon.”

Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI frenzy, was up 0.6pc. But shares of TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, were 0.4pc lower even as it posted record quarterly profits on Thursday and said AI demand remained very strong.

In Indonesia, the Jakarta Composite index fell more than 10pc, the lowest in years, after MSCI said Indonesia’s continued classification as an emerging market would be “no longer appropriate.”

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 1.2pc to 24,353.69. The Shanghai Composite index rose 1pc to 3,742.66.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 1.1pc higher at 8,812.90.

India’s Sensex edged up 0.2pc.

News.title: Are my smart home devices always watching me? How to stay safe (and private) in a connected house
News.content:
The past decade has seen a huge rise in the number of smart devices in the home, from video doorbells to robot vacuum cleaners.

Smart connectivity offers many useful upsides, from letting us keep an eye on package deliveries to streamlining household chores. However, concerns remain about whether these devices are safe from hackers and how they might impinge on our privacy.

As a technology journalist for almost 20 years, I have reviewed many smart appliances and have lots of connected devices in my own home, so I’m an experienced user. To find out more about their potential downsides, and how to keep yourself protected, I’ve also spoken to an expert from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, a board member at the Connected Standards Alliance (CSA) – which promotes openness and safety within smart-device networks – as well as other leading brands in the space.

What is a smart appliance?

A smart appliance connects to your home network, often via Wi-Fi, to allow for a wider range of interactions. That might be a washing machine that notifies you when it’s finished, or a fridge-freezer such as the Samsung Family Hub with a screen and voice controls.

But smart appliances don’t have to be huge: connected lightbulbs, baby monitors, smart plugs and more can all link up with your home network, in many cases integrating with voice assistants such as Amazon’s Alexa or Apple’s Siri.

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”

News.title: Ukrainian Vampire drones drop food on town besieged by Russian army
News.content:
On Ukraine’s front lines, drones are the deadliest weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal, hunting Russian soldiers one by one with chilling precision.

But across the Dnipro River, the same machines have been given a very different mission: keeping trapped civilians from dying of starvation.

Since March, Ukrainian drones have been flying food and medicine into occupied Oleshky, on the river’s left bank, where residents are surviving on grass and weeds.

The town is less than three miles from Kherson, a city battered by Russian drones and shelling.

Since December, Oleshky has been under an effective blockade. Its roads are mined and shops have closed, with no food arriving by road since late May. Humanitarian agencies are blocked from entering, and the health system has all but collapsed.

Only around 2,000 of its 24,000 pre-war residents remain. For them, the drones are now their only lifeline.

“With the onset of winter, the situation is only getting worse,” said Elvina Osmanova of the Kherson regional military administration. “Food supplies are running out. People are facing a life-threatening choice: risk their lives trying to find food outside the city or remain without food.”

News.title: Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle
News.content:
When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

News.title: Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six
News.content:
Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Full team news on the way shortly.

Sports.title: Barcelona workers ready to go on strike for El Clasico as they reach ‘last resort’ in huge contracts row

BARCELONA are facing major disruption ahead of their El Clasico showdown with Real Madrid after club workers threatened to go on strike.

Around 60 permanent seasonal employees are planning a three-day walkout over pay, staff shortages and alleged contractual irregularities.



And the proposed industrial action is set to coincide with the Spanish giants’ blockbuster clash against their bitter rivals on October 25.

According to Spanish outlet SPORT, the strike will begin at midnight on October 23 and run until 6am on October 26.



Workers have accused Barcelona of failing to honour agreements and allowing working conditions to deteriorate.

They have also raised concerns over alleged discrimination between male and female employees and the club’s increasing reliance on outsourcing.

The strike committee warned that the situation was affecting the quality of services provided to supporters.

In a statement, they said: “We warn that this situation is undermining service standards, reducing the ability to respond to incidents and harming the service provided to members and supporters.”

They added: “We consider this industrial action to be a last resort in the face of a lack of progress and concrete commitments.”

The employees are demanding a pay rise and a 50 per cent increase in staffing levels, taking their workforce from around 60 to 90.

And the planned walkout could cause headaches for Barcelona as they prepare to welcome Real Madrid to the Spotify Camp Nou.

But the disruption could extend beyond El Clasico.

Workers are also planning action at the Johan Cruyff Stadium, Palau Blaugrana and Joan Gamper Training Centre.



That means Barcelona’s women’s team, basketball and handball sides, as well as youth-team activities, could also be affected.

Sports.title: Carrick and Wilcox are approaching the end but Man Utd’s biggest problem is Ratcliffe making same mistake as the Glazers
Sports.content:
Next

MICHAEL CARRICK is approaching the endgame and the game should be up for Jason Wilcox. But the biggest problem at Manchester United remains the ownership.

That now extends beyond the reclusive Glazer family. For all of Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s braggadocio, history has repeated itself on his watch.



United’s tendency to rein in spending after they have qualified for the Champions League has continued during the Ineos era. It has been a hallmark of the Glazers dating back to their first summer managing the purse strings in 2005.

United’s two senior signings were Edwin van der Sar for £2.5million and Ji-sung Park for £4m. Two bargains.



The previous summer, United forked out £7m for Alan Smith, £6.9m for Gabriel Heinze and £27m for Wayne Rooney. Heinze cost more than Van der Sar and Park combined.

In 2006, the overrated chief executive David Gill promised “two world-class signings”. United bought Carrick and Tomasz Kuszczak. Neither ever were world-class.



It was the Glazers’ good fortune that a genius of a manager was building his third great United side. Nemanja Vidic and Patrice Evra joined for a combined £12.5m in January 2006.

The 2007 title – Sir Alex Ferguson’s greatest against Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea juggernaut – a first Champions League semi-final in five years and flawlessly frugal spending gave Ferguson credit in the bank.

United bought Nani, Anderson, Owen Hargreaves and Carlos Tevez for around £47m in up-front fees in 2007, their best-ever window.

But after the club-record £30.75m arrival of Dimitar Berbatov in 2008, United did not break the £30m barrier for a signing until Juan Mata in January 2014.



Ferguson’s hit rate in the market dwindled in his latter years yet United still had enough serial winners and quality to either win or compete for the league.

After the purse strings were tightened in 2009 (Michael Owen on a free, Antonio Valencia and Gabriel Obertan), United came second by a point, first, second on goal difference (an asterisk can now be added to that) and first.

Without Ferguson to mask the Glazers’ thriftiness, United have been exposed time and again, despite spending more than £2bn in 13 years.

Almost all of United’s biggest summer outlays have come when they have not qualified for the Champions League: £155.5m in 2014, £145.3m in 2016, £145m in 2019, £228.8m in 2022, £206.06m in 2024 and £225.22m in 2025).

They have never shelled out £200m whilst in the Champions League. United’s recent summer strategy, which ended with a £155m spent on incomings, suggested they never had any intention of hitting the £200m mark.



United wanted Lewis Hall but there was more chance of the Glazers putting their hands in their own pockets than United submitting an offer considered acceptable by Newcastle.

The Glazers are unashamedly complacent. Champions League revenue to line their wallets is their main objective and United achieved that last season. It is always cash over glory.

There was a breathtaking lack of ambition in the 2018 summer (two release-clause buys and Lee Grant) and in 2023 (refusing to move for Harry Kane over the Daniel Levy factor). United tumbled to sixth and eighth those seasons.



It even happened in 2015, albeit that was marred by Ed Woodward’s incompetence. United failed to sign a centre back or an established striker and Woodward took an easyJet flight to Barcelona under the delusion that a deal for Neymar was doable.

Woodward had the gall to veto Jose Mourinho’s recommendations for a centre back in 2018. On Ineos’s watch, United still have an underqualified football administrator in Wilcox.

Carrick warrants criticism for the umpteen mistakes he has made this season. There are three with Ayden Heaven alone: starting him at centre back against Hull, at centre back against Brighton and left back against Atletico Madrid. Three defeats.

Patrick Dorgu on the wing at Hull, Mateus Cunha through the middle, hooking Marcus Rashford at Everton, sending on two defenders unenforced in the same game, not sending Benjamin Sesko on sooner against City, eight changes against Brighton, reverting to a tried and tested XI at Fulham. The selection cock-ups are closing in on two dozen nine games in.

Wilcox came from Southampton and does not have the credentials for a United ‘head coach’ to answer to him. Whether it is one who was at Middlesbrough or Sporting Lisbon before they were allocated an office at Carrington.



But Wilcox does not control the club’s finances. United have a debt of £1.15bn and their majority owners have never invested a cent into the club.

United’s reputation has preceded them where they have overspent on misfits time and again. Ajax were adamant Antony would not go for less than £51m. United agreed to pay £85.5m.

Casemiro commanded a £70m fee even though he was already in his 30s. Chelsea held out for £60m for Mason Mount, who played 16 minutes in their final 13 league games in 2022-23. Andre Onana joined for £47.2m a year after he was a free agent. Senior United figures insisted they would not pay more than £60m for a striker in 2023. They ended up agreeing to pay £72m.



That’s not the punchline. It was Rasmus Hojlund.

Ratcliffe named Antony, Casemiro, Onana and Hojlund as signings Ineos “inherited”. All four arrived across two windows.

Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada had to try to abolish the United tax. There was logic in baulking at the asking price of some midfielders. £85m for a talent in Mateus Fernandes relegated in consecutive seasons is not sensible spending.

Yet United know they fell short. They have squandered the momentum from the 12 wins in 17 matches between January and May and compromised the culture. Look at how unfussily United have welcomed Marcus Rashford back into the fold.

Rashford does not want to be at United and United wanted rid of him. He has still not scored this season.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

United could not give him away for £26m. If Ruben Amorim was around, Rashford wouldn’t be.

It was Wilcox who saw off Amorim.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso reveals Chelsea transfer plan with crocked Reece James to miss up to 22 games over next three months
Sports.content:
Next

XABI ALONSO has revealed Chelsea will NOT panic in the January transfer window following Reece James’ injury.

Skipper James underwent knee surgery and is set to be out for 22 games.



Despite missing out on midfield reinforcements at the end of the summer window, Alonso stressed that James’ injury does not affect the Blues’ plans, if any, in the January transfer window.

Alonso said: “No I don’t think so because we expect by that time he’s back, maybe some weeks before maybe after, it’s not exact, so it doesn’t affect [January transfer window].”



On the injury Alonso said: “We are all disappointed, especially for him. He wanted to have a good start after the international break but in the last training he had an injury.

“We wanted to wait to know the result of the tests, but the surgery has been successful.

“He keeps reporting here. He is close to the team and a great influence even when he is not available. We don’t set timelines, but he will be out for several weeks. It is not going to be short.

“After Christmas, time will tell. Things must be done properly. Get that knee in the best possible condition. It is a disappointment for everyone, for him, but we have the squad to deal with it.”

Chelsea fans have become accustomed to seeing their team struggle during the December months, following multiple turbulent Christmas-times in recent years.

So while Blues fans might be optimistic about ending their tendency to flop during the winter time under new boss Xabi Alonso, they will have to make amends on previous years without one of their best players in James.

Despite almost every game being a test in the modern Premier League, James will miss a host of huge clashes across multiple competitions.

Having already missed Chelsea’s thrashing of Bournemouth on Sunday, James will miss matches against the likes of Tottenham, Liverpool twice, Manchester United and Maresca’s Man City.

Earlier this week, FK Viagem Ústí nad Labem boss David Olehla went to great effort to avoid looking in the wrong direction as busty club presenter Sabina Jaksova quizzed him following a 3-2 win.



Talking to SunSport, Sabina, 30, praised Olehla’s “willpower” to stay professional in the moment.

She also said the coach’s wife, Lucie Hloupa keeps a close eye on their interviews.



Speaking about the clip, Sabina admits she was surprised by the reaction the video got globally.

She said: “I’m used to attention, because FK Viagem Ústí nad Labem are one of the most followed clubs in the Czech Republic.

“People recognise me in my own country, and I am a popular presenter.

“But I was pleasantly surprised that it spread like this beyond our borders.”

‘Awkward’ moment

Many fans online joked that football manager Olehla looked awkward during the post-match chat.

One fan on social media said: “Call the VAR here too to see if he looked or didn’t look!! The guy was fighting for his life.”



A second said: “Admirable, the warrior’s effort!”
