'Every Saturday, between the age of six and 12, I would go racing to Wolverhampton with my dad and I would be distraught if he didn't have a runner!

'When I started dealing with the horses more at home, I didn't go racing as much as I was working in the yard then.

'My dad's work ethic is second to none – he works so hard every day and growing up alongside him and working with him, that was instilled in me from an early age.

'Wolverhampton and Ascot are my two favourite courses, but Wolves will always have a special place in my heart for obvious reasons.'

While parallels have understandably been drawn with Dettori, Loughnane's infectious manner, professionalism and joyous personality are arguably more in keeping with the legendary rider whose record he may strive to hunt down this year.

Sir Gordon Richards was born within hailing distance of Loughnane's beloved Dunstall Park at Donnington Wood in Telford, Shropshire, overcoming tuberculosis as a 22-year-old just months after becoming Champion Jockey for the first time.

Loughnane, who has been compared to Frankie Dettori, was Champion Apprentice in 2023

In a career which stretched from 1920 until his retirement following a fall at Sandown in 1954, Richards partnered 4,870 winners and was crowned Champion Jockey a staggering 26 times.

The son of a miner, Richards was not only a colossus in the saddle but earned a reputation as a rider of integrity and professionalism while those who knew him well described him as a warm, generous and modest man.

Humility and Dettori were not always comfortable bedfellows, but Loughnane's effervescent demeanour has quickly earned a sincere affection from the British racing public who welcomed him back to the winner's enclosures of Newmarket, Ascot and Goodwood this summer with the fervour reserved for champions.

'I love my job and I love riding horses – it's all I've ever wanted to do,' enthuses Loughnane with an endearing simplicity.

'It's amazing I've found something that is a passion of mine and I'm able to do it as a job. It's all I have ever wanted to do, and I've never looked another way.'

Referring to the fact Richards was Champion Jockey an incredible 26 times, he quips: 'I don't think I'll be riding in 26 years' time to be honest!

'It (the record) is in my sights. I'm just going to take the rest of this month and November (as normal) and then assess in December to see if it's possible.'

The last word goes to mother Clare, arguably the most important cog in the family training business, to whom her son credits his meticulous attention to detail and professionalism.

Loughnane rode the golden trio of elite successes aboard Bow Echo (yellow silks) this season

'I think the day it all changed was on Champions Day three years ago,' revealed Clare.

'Billy had enjoyed a fairly smooth year winning the Apprentice Jockey's Championship and when we turned up at Ascot that day and saw a giant poster of him hanging there, we said to ourselves "wow, this is a big thing".

'It was then that we said to him, well done, you've had a brilliant year, but now the hard work starts for real.

'We helped him when he was starting at the lower level, but we couldn't prepare him for what was to come at the top level.

'He has had to deal with that himself and he has changed from a young boy to a young man since.

'As parents, we couldn't be any prouder of him as he's been exceptional in his conduct from day one and has maintained the same persona throughout.

'He even comes home occasionally!'

Sports.title: Adam Wharton's family embroiled in clash with French football fans ahead of Crystal Palace's defeat in Lyon - with England star's mum and dad playing peacemakers
Sports.content:
Adam Wharton’s family were caught up in an altercation before Crystal Palace’s defeat by Lyon on Thursday night.

In a video posted on X, a group of Lyon supporters chanted La Marseillaise, the French national anthem, at Palace fans on a metro platform while station staff tried to keep them apart.

One Palace fan called it on, urging the provocative Lyon crew to square up to him before being dragged away. Meanwhile, the Wharton clan were front and centre with Adam’s brother, Simon, hurling abuse while pointing and probing at rival fans.

Wharton’s mum and dad, Helen and John - who are regulars in the Palace away end and even have their own chant - played peacemakers during the trouble.

Helen, a PE teacher, drew on her playground conflict-resolution tactics, restraining Simon and urging the other Palace fan to calm down as she tried to stop the skirmish.

The account that posted the video on X suggested the clip was the ‘start of a fight’ in the Metro but ‘everyone was quickly separated by security and law enforcement ’, with the incident beginning with someone ‘barrelling down the stairs’.

Adam Wharton's family were caught up in an altercation with rival fans on Thursday night

Crystal Palace have been contacted for comment.

Palace lost 3-2 in Lyon, where Wharton captained the side, and his parents were spotted drinking with fans on the afternoon of the game.

Wharton joined Palace from Blackburn Rovers in 2024 for £18 million and has made 105 appearances for the Eagles, winning three trophies.

The 22-year-old has been capped four times by England and was in the Euro 2024 squad but has been named in just two squads during Thomas Tuchel’s reign.

Sports.title: Morgan Gibbs-White a doubt for Arsenal clash, under-pressure Alvaro Arbeloa remains defiant - and Enzo Maresca insists Man City have been galvanised by guilty verdict: Premier League press conference round-up
Sports.content:
Morgan Gibbs-White a doubt for Arsenal clash, under-pressure Alvaro Arbeloa remains defiant - and Enzo Maresca insists Man City have been galvanised by guilty verdict: Premier League press conference round-up

Managers up and down the country will be speaking to the press ahead of the latest weekend of Premier League action.

Daily Mail Sport will bring you all the key news here...

Maresca: City galvanised by guilty verdict

Enzo Maresca believes the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City for serious breaches of financial rules have galvanised the whole club.

City are three points clear at the top of the Premier League going into Saturday's home game against Ipswich Town and possess a 100 per cent domestic record this season.

Their case with the league is going to appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of all substantive charges, with calls for the leaders to be expelled from the division.

Enzo Maresca believes the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City for serious breaches of financial rules have galvanised the whole club

City have won at Anfield and lost a Champions League classic against Paris Saint-Germain since the judgment and Maresca has seen a change in his players.

And it appears that the squad are leaning into the idea that the majority of top-flight followers want them to lose – something Ruben Dias recently suggested has spurred them on for some time.

'Ruben said that people don't like City winning,' Maresca said. 'But we like to win. I think that is a good message for everyone. Since the noise, I can see from my personal point of view the fans, the club, the team more together for sure.

'From my point of view, the wise way to judge a situation is always to wait for the final words. But I can understand that now people need to speak about this situation. I don't need people from outside the club to (help) understand the situation.

'I don't feel any kind of stress about the outside situation, because it's something that I don't control.'

Daily Mail Sport revealed last week that in a meeting ahead of Liverpool, Maresca's motivational address was focused on how they have a title to battle for. The Italian has reiterated publicly that they must 'make their own noise'.

City maintain their innocence and insist they will prevail on appeal, with ex-manager Pep Guardiola's attendance in midweek a show of support for his former employers.

Guardiola is thought to have entered the dressing room but Maresca said he didn't speak to the players.

And Guardiola's successor has been fascinated by the influx of inflatable bananas brought to matches by supporters over recent days in a throwback to a craze first introduced in the 1980s.

'I didn't know the history behind the banana,' Maresca added. 'I hope tomorrow I can see many bananas in the stadium.

'I think it creates a nice environment for the fans and for everyone that is in the stadium. I have four kids and they already asked me about them. Tomorrow they're going to be at the stadium and we'll see.'

By Jack Gaughan

Arbeloa not distracted by sack talk

Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa maintains he cannot allow speculation over his job to distract him from keeping everyone focused on beating Hull.

The Spaniard's position has come under the spotlight with his side bottom of the Premier League table and only having secured two points from six games following last weekend's late defeat at Ipswich, where they had been 1-0 up with three minutes left.

Former Real Madrid boss Arbeloa, who took over at Craven Cottage in the summer, insists his only focus has to be on Saturday's showdown with newly promoted Hull – a game which he had previously described as a 'final'.

Arbeloa said at a press conference: 'I am focused on tomorrow's game, on my players, on my team. That for me is the most important thing.

Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa won't let speculation over his future distract him from beating Hull

'It is not about me. It is about the club, it is about the players. It is about the supporters. And like I said before, we are waiting for the game where the performance turns into a result.'

Despite reports he would be sacked if Fulham do not beat Hull, Arbeloa again stressed it was business as usual. 'For me, it has been a normal week where we have been working hard, where we were preparing a difficult match against a very difficult team,' he said.

'They (players) did (execute the game plan) for many minutes against Ipswich. We did against Man United, we did against Liverpool, so for me, we need to try to keep that level for 90 minutes.

'I saw the commitment of the players this week, how they have been training, and they are so focused on tomorrow's game. I saw them how they can play and for me, it is the most important thing: the performance of my players.'

Gibbs-White a doubt for Forest's clash with Arsenal

Nottingham Forest are sweating on the fitness of Morgan Gibbs-White ahead of Sunday's clash with Arsenal.

The England international picked up a calf injury in last weekend's defeat at Crystal Palace and has not trained all week.

He is expected to train with the squad on Saturday and will be assessed before the visit of the champions.

Nottingham Forest are sweating on the fitness of Morgan Gibbs-White ahead of Sunday's clash with Arsenal

'Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt, he couldn't train the entire week with us,' boss Oliver Glasner said. 'But it looks like he can join tomorrow's session.

'He had an individual session today with our rehab coaches, and he suffered a minor muscle injury at Palace. Then we have to see how he reacts today and how he deals with tomorrow's session, and then how we take the final decision.'

Forest will also assess Nikola Milenkovic, who has returned to training after a bone bruise.

'Milenkovic trained for the first time today,' Glasner said. 'Let's see now how he reacts.

'He could be in the matchday squad, but let's see, because he's been out now for several weeks.'

Sports.title: Reece James set for THREE months on the sidelines after knee surgery in major blow to Chelsea - as club give update on injured captain after he missed 5-1 win over Bournemouth
Sports.content:
Reece James set for THREE months on the sidelines after knee surgery in major blow to Chelsea - as club give update on injured captain after he missed 5-1 win over Bournemouth

Reece James is set to be out of action for around three months after having surgery on a knee injury sustained in training.

James, 26, missed his side’s 5-1 Premier League win over Bournemouth after the international break.

While he usually still travels with the squad on the team coach when injured, he did not do so for that victory, sparking concerns that there was more to his latest setback.

Now, Chelsea have confirmed that James has had a ‘successful minor’ operation, and will be without him for their league trip to Everton on Saturday and beyond.

In a statement, Chelsea said: ‘Captain Reece James has undergone successful minor knee surgery.

'The 26-year-old was absent from Saturday’s 5-1 victory over Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge while medical assessments took place following the injury suffered in training.

Reece James has undergone knee surgery after missing Chelsea's 5-1 win over Bournemouth

‘Those assessments confirmed surgery would be the required course of action. Reece has already begun his road to recovery and will be supported by the club's medical department at Cobham during this rehabilitation phase.

‘Everyone at Chelsea wishes Reece a speedy recovery and will support him on his road to return.’

Levi Colwill captained Chelsea against Bournemouth in James’ absence.

Xabi Alonso said on James: 'It's not going to be short. It's not going to be two or three weeks. It's going to be longer. We will see. Before Christmas, after Christmas, time will tell.

'But things have to be done properly, so that he feels right, and that means in the best possible condition. Yes, is it a disappointment for everyone, for him. But we have a squad for that to deal with injuries.'

On whether James' injury will force Chelsea to use the January window, Alonso added: 'No, I don't think so. We expect for that time that he is back. It doesn't affect (transfer business).'

James has an unfortunate history of injuries, largely due to hamstring issues. With that, Alonso had been morphing him into a midfielder rather than a right back.

In fact, James has missed 842 days of action, as per Transfermarkt, since he broke into Chelsea's first team during the 2019-20 season. That is the equivalent of 2.31 years or 99 games for club and country.

Given that record, Daily Mail Sport understands that Chelsea won't rush the 26-year-old back prematurely and will ensure he recovers fully before returning to action.

James suffered the injury in training and is set to miss around three months of action

James’ new problem robs Alonso of another midfield option, at a time when there were already concerns surrounding numbers in that central area.

Moises Caicedo is now back from being sidelined, which should help until January, when Chelsea are likely to try to add at least one reinforcement.

They are known to admire Alex Scott, though Bournemouth say they want more than £100million to sell him this winter.

Other midfield options for Alonso include the injury-prone Romeo Lavia, Valentin Barco, Jordan Henderson, full-back Malo Gusto and youngster Reggie Watson.

The Blues face Everton on Saturday lunchtime, before league games against Tottenham, Man United and Sunderland ahead of next month's international break.

Sports.title: 'Brendan Venter would get involved in training and whack players harder than anyone': Untold stories of Saracens coach from devout Christian and GP to a referee's nightmare, his golf-course plan that beat England and why 'intense doesn't do him justice'
Sports.content:
'Brendan Venter would get involved in training and whack players harder than anyone': Untold stories of Saracens coach from devout Christian and GP to a referee's nightmare, his golf-course plan that beat England and why 'intense doesn't do him justice'

The door was always open to Nick Mallett’s coaching office at the 1999 Rugby World Cup. His Springbok players were encouraged to pop in to give feedback on the team's game plan and there were two who were particularly forthcoming: Rassie Erasmus and Brendan Venter.

‘Generally speaking, the South African psyche in the post-Apartheid era was that you took orders,’ Mallett tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Whatever the headmaster, coach or preacher said, you did it. I wanted players to question the way we played and Rassie and Brendan were the best at it by a long way.’

At the time, Erasmus was a young flanker who spent time with the military and sold office equipment. He is now the double World Cup-winning coach of the Springboks.

Venter was a seasoned centre who trained as a GP, treating patients around Cape Town. Rugby was secondary but he is now back in the hot seat for his second coaching stint with Saracens.

And he is already making waves – having been fined for refusing to do post-match media duties, explaining that away by saying he had actually resigned as director of rugby a month earlier to become 'head of rugby culture and wine consultant'. Then, last week he railed against media obligations as 'autocratic', in a strident speech that took in Gaza and Ukraine.

‘They were different personalities,’ adds Mallett. ‘Brendan was married and very religious. Rassie was a single guy who partied quite a lot. They weren’t bosom buddies but they respected each other. They were brilliant rugby minds.

Brendan Venter has already made his mark on his return to Saracens, being fined for refusing to do post-match media media and claiming it was because he was the club's 'wine consultant'

Venter represented the Stormers in his homeland and won 17 caps for South Africa, including as a substitute in the 1995 World Cup final win

Springboks coach Nick Mallett told his 1999 World Cup squad to be more outspoken and challenge their game plan - the best two at that were Venter and Rassie Erasmus

‘Brendan was a strong personality who was very confident in his own opinions, so it didn’t bother him at all to challenge the coach. He was very self-confident and said what he thought with no filter.

'Rassie didn’t come from such an academic background but he did a hell of a lot of rugby research. He was more self-deprecating. He would come to me and say, “Listen, I’ve seen this, I don’t know if you would like to use it?” Whereas Brendan would come and say, “Listen Nick, I’ve seen this, we HAVE to do this”.

According to Mallett, Venter’s input was central to South Africa’s quarter-final victory over England in that World Cup, when Springbok No10 Jannie de Beer kicked five drop-goals in a 44-21 win at the Stade de France. The drop-goal plan was concocted on the golf course.

‘I was on a golf cart with Brendan on the Wednesday before the game,’ says Mallett. ‘On the other cart were Jannie and Joost van der Westhuizen. I said to Brendan, “Jeez, I’m getting very frustrated with Jannie because he’s sitting too deep and giving metres back to the opposition”.

'Brendan said, “Listen, Jannie will always play like that. He sits in the pocket and has a very good kicking game. Do you know he kicks drop-goals?” Jannie had never mentioned drop-goals to me. That’s where the plan started. Brendan was like a player-coach.’

In 2001, Venter moved to London, where he worked as a locum in local hospitals and played for London Irish. There, he formed a centre partnership with Mark McCall, unaware that a few years later they would become central figures behind Saracens’ golden era of domestic and European dominance. Venter was initially hired as a defence coach at the London club by Eddie Jones in 2008.

‘I knew Brendan from South Africa and I brought him in as a defence consultant,’ Jones tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘History shows that most really good defence coaches have come from South Africa. It’s almost part of their DNA. They prefer not to have the ball.

‘He introduced this touch game called Sonny Bill Williams. It was basically shoulder charging, because Williams was pretty good at shoulder charging. He'd participate and he'd whack the players harder than anyone. It set the tone for Saracens to become a great defensive team.

Jannie de Beer (right) celebrates with Joost van der Westhuizen as the fly-half's five drop-goals - a plan concocted by Venter - knocked England out of the 1999 World Cup

Venter joined London Irish as a player-coach in 2001 and won the Powergen Cup the following year at Twickenham

Eddie Jones brought Venter in at Saracens as a defence coach, before recommending him as his replacement a year later

‘I was brought in at Saracens by the old Brumbies chief executive, Mark Sinderberry. Three months into it, the South Africans took over and I didn’t get on with the new chief executive, Edward Griffiths. For me, the director of rugby has to have the authority. We couldn’t see eye to eye at all.

‘When I decided to leave, the most obvious person to take over was Brendan. If I look at the success of Saracens, the two people who drove them into a really high performing team were Brendan and his captain, Steve Borthwick. Brendan brought that hardness. He brought a winning style of play: kick a lot, defend hard, good set piece. He’s a really charismatic, intelligent, forceful guy.’

Venter and Griffiths remain close confidants, while the South African influence at Saracens remains, with countryman Ed Coetzee now CEO. Venter’s no-nonsense approach to media duties has historically landed him in trouble.

He has publicly criticised referees – earning a £21,000 fine (£13,000 of which was suspended) for comments following a defeat by Leinster in November 2010 – and he was one of the first to publicly defend Erasmus when he released a video criticising officials during the 2021 British & Irish Lions series.

His most notorious incident came after a Heineken Cup defeat by Racing Metro in December 2010, giving extremely short answers to every question in Sky Sports' post-match interview – and later admitting it was inspired by Mike Bassett: England Manager.

‘The first time I came across Brendan was on South Africa’s 1994 tour to Wales, Scotland, and Ireland,’ says Griffiths. ‘I was the team’s media liaison guy on that tour. There wasn't much call for Brendan from the media at that time because Francois Pienaar was captain, but we spent quite a lot of time together. He had strong views on the game but he was relentlessly positive and that’s his USP.

‘He’s a very dedicated Christian and his faith is at the heart of everything. There are a lot of Christians who talk the talk but Brendan walks the walk in the way he leads his life.

'Around 2014, my son was in Cape Town with a friend and they had a car accident in the early hours of the morning. They were in their early 20s. They couldn't drive away from the situation and people were gathering around them in a less-than-ideal location.

'If I look at the success of Saracens, the two people who drove them into a really high performing team were Brendan and his captain, Steve Borthwick,' says Jones

Venter has publicly criticised referees in the past, landing a £21,000 fine in 2010 after a defeat by Leinster in the Heineken Cup

'In the middle of the night, I called Brendan, explained the situation, and within 25 minutes, he got up, got dressed, drove out, and picked them up. There's not many people who would do that without thinking twice.

'He has a very clear sense of what he believes is right and wrong and he’s unafraid to live according to those judgments, regardless of the outcome. He was always honest in his opinions – sometimes too honest. Because of that, dealing with the media was something he'd rather not do.

'Some people might say he was difficult, but I never found him difficult, except in the sense that he would have an opinion and he would stick to it. He doesn’t stop at uncertainty.’

In my experience, Venter has always been happy to pick up the phone to contribute to research about Saracens or South Africa.

The ‘wine consultant’ incident landed badly, but the club’s executives have since worked to build positive relationships with journalists. Venter has sent an open invite to the media to join him next week for a wine-tasting evening at StoneX Stadium.

The club moved quickly to sack academy player Totoa Auvaa this week, with Venter and Coetzee telling the squad of the decision less than 48 hours after the Samoan youngster punched a man in a St Albans street, having been given a formal warning for a nightclub incident involving England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson this summer.

‘Take the incident that happened over the weekend,' says Saracens and England hooker Jamie George. 'He just gets it out in the open, has an adult conversation with people. That's the end of it. “Now we move on”.

‘Having not worked with him for 12 years, he took me by surprise in terms of what he emphasises. He’s brought some things to the club that maybe we let slip over the last couple of years – how we are with referees, discipline, how we are with each other.

The ‘wine consultant’ incident landed badly, but the club’s executives have since worked to build positive relationships with journalists

‘The word intense doesn't do him justice,' says Jamie George. 'He demands intensity and passion in terms of rugby, but what comes first is caring about people and their families'

'You put it down on a piece of paper and you want a confrontational, physical rugby team. But he wants us to be able to marry it up with being calm and clear and respectful.

‘With Brendan, the word intense doesn't do him justice. When I first came in, I was 18 and I was always blown away by how close he will stand to you when he's talking to you. He's a massive space invader.

‘He demands intensity and passion in terms of rugby, but always what comes first is caring about people and their families. During pre-season, he spoke almost as much about tactics as how we can make the players’ lounge at the stadium better for families, wives and girlfriends. People often don't give him credit for that side because you probably get the finger-wagging side.

‘The wine consultant thing was a bit of fun. I hope people get to see the character and the funny side to him because he's got that too. Honestly, I think he's brilliant. I think he's a breath of fresh air.’

Sports.title: Burn down the mission: Inside the Watford 'circus' as Elton John leads irate fans in revolt - 'crazy' meddling from on high, players turning on executives, staff leaving 'unrecognisable' club and why Gino Pozzo is struggling to sell
Sports.content:
'Burn down the mission. Burn it down to stay alive. It's our only chance of living' -Elton John, Burn Down The Mission. The pitchforks are out at Watford. The torches are lit. There’s no turning back now as they march to Vicarage Road. The mission is in their sights and they are, figuratively speaking, ready to burn it to the ground. For them, now, it’s their only chance to survive. Over the past few days, Watford have come to discover that when it comes to his beloved football club, if Sir Elton John speaks out, soon does everyone else. They rise up and make their voices heard. After the Hornets’ 4-0 defeat by Burnley at Vicarage Road, a team previously 241 days without a win, the legendary singer and former Watford chairman made his feelings known. ‘As a lifetime supporter of Watford FC, I am very upset and disappointed at the decline over the past few weeks,’ wrote Elton in a now-deleted comment to a club post on Instagram. ‘I really feel for the other supporters who have to watch this.’ In doing so, he lit the fire. Elton made no reference to the club’s ownership in his comment – and Daily Mail Sport understands he has been in contact with chairman Scott Duxbury since making it – but, suddenly, a fanbase that had long been simmering with malaise and discontent towards Gino Pozzo and the Watford board heard the rallying call they needed. Sir Elton John lit a fire around his former club Watford this week, after another damaging defeat saw the Hornets slip into the Championship relegation zone Watford have lost four games in a row, conceding 12 goals in the process and raising the heat on their owner Gino Pozzo

Your browser does not support iframes.

Out they came. Former captain Troy Deeney said the ‘writing was on the wall’. The Watford Supporters Board called for owners to give ‘urgent attention’ to the ‘deep concern’ fans had about their leadership. The club’s Supporters Trust backed their statement. Even the mayor got involved. The 1881 Movement, the supporters’ group behind the singing section in the Rookery Stand, issued an open letter of no confidence in Pozzo. ‘For too long now, Watford has been treated as a revolving door of managers, a testing ground for short-term decisions, and a vehicle for constant upheaval,’ it read. ‘The endless cycle of appointments and dismissals has reduced a once-proud club to a source of ridicule.’ Pozzo is due to meet Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement at the training ground today after the Watford owner became aware of the open letter and reached out via the club. Moore agreed on the proviso he could report back to supporters what was said. ‘Full transparency was the price of acceptance,’ he said. Only three days earlier, Watford lost 5-1 to Cardiff, a fourth straight defeat that dropped them into the Championship relegation zone. By then, the supporters were already in full revolt. In response to every club post on X, hundreds of fans replied with bright yellow squares with the words ‘Pozzo Out’ emblazoned across them. Streams and streams of them, forming their own yellow brick road. Supporters in the ground sung anti-Pozzo chants. They will do so again at Vicarage Road on Saturday against Charlton, turning their backs and raising their scarves in the 14th minute in protest against 14 years of Pozzo ownership. They feel it is the only way to save the club, in the words of the final track of Elton's 1970 album Tumbleweed Connection, about a settler starting a revolt against the wealthy establishment, is to Burn Down The Mission. The defeat in South Wales looked as if it might prompt that managerial door to revolve once more. Reports emerged mid-match that Alessio Dionisi, who only arrived in the summer, was for the chop and the Hornets would be looking for a 24th manager since Pozzo bought the club in June 2012 and their 14th since 2021. Their former manager Tom Cleverley, by the way, is currently top of League One with Plymouth. As it happens, the club are sticking by Dionisi for now and he will take charge against Charlton on Saturday. The owners are said to recognise they have been too hasty with hirings and firings in the past and so will give the Italian more time. That’s always the thing with Watford, though, you never know quite how much time that will be. It’s believed Pozzo was scouting out potential replacements over the weekend. Two days after a supporter group published an open letter of no confidence in Pozzo, Watford lost 5-1 to Cardiff Reports emerged mid-match that manager Alessio Dionisi was for the chop but Watford are sticking by the Italian... for now

Your browser does not support iframes.

Daily Mail Sport understands players and staff held a big meeting on the Sunday after the Burnley defeat at the club’s training ground to air their frustrations. While club sources were keen to play down the idea of ‘showdown’ talks, it’s understood senior players led by captain Mattie Pollock spoke up about the current form and launched a staunch defence of their manager. Dionisi is well-liked around the dressing room. There were believed to be pointed comments made, too, towards Duxbury about his glowing remarks on Watford’s official podcast about young midfielder Jack Grieves – despite the 21-year-old only making a single matchday squad all season. Grieves’ brother Ben even called into a phone-in on Watford fan podcast Do Not Scratch Your Eyes after the Cardiff defeat to complain about his lack of match action and to add his voice to calls for change. ‘Some players care, some players don’t,’ he said. ‘There is something seriously, seriously wrong with our football club at the minute and there has got to be something that changes.’ For the fans, it is clear what should change – the owner. Pozzo, who took over the club with his father in 2012 before having sole ownership two years later, has enjoyed great success in his time with six seasons in the Premier League and four trips to Wembley, including an FA Cup final. It was the club’s best run of success since the days of Graham Taylor, under Elton’s stewardship, in the 1980s. And yet, since that historic day against Manchester City in 2019, the cracks have begun to appear and widen. The player trading model on which Watford is based, and previously led to huge profits on players like Richarlison and Joao Pedro, has gone stale. Recent signings from Udinese, Pozzo’s other club, haven’t fired as they once did. The constant churn of players and managers leaves a place that describes itself as ‘the original family club’ feeling more like a hotel lobby which bodies merely pass through. Members of staff have left, with a heavy heart, a club they no longer recognise. Gino Pozzo at the 2019 FA Cup final, which Watford lost 6-0 to Manchester City. Since that day the club has been on a gradual decline The club’s summer business was described by recently departed midfielder Tom Ince as ‘soulless’ Watford's summer business, described by recently departed midfielder Tom Ince as ‘soulless’ in another incendiary interview by a former player, saw players arrive late in the window, miss chunks of pre-season, and soon pick up injuries. The club barely spent a penny on their 12 summer transfers as they look to tighten the purse strings even more now that the parachute payments have dried up. The most recent accounts for 2024-25 showed Watford to be spending more on wages (£28m) than revenue (£26m), though the club are now understood to have one of the lowest wage bills in the Championship at around £14m. Watford were in talks with former West Ham striker Michail Antonio throughout the summer but felt they couldn’t do a deal due to wage demands, only to bring him in on September 11. Antonio is yet to play a single minute. The signing of former Monaco defender Krepin Diatta was seen as a huge coup for the club – ‘our point of difference, which other clubs don’t have, is our scouting network,’ said Duxbury on the club’s official podcast – only for the player's agent to suggest he’d had to settle for the Hornets after being rejected by clubs all summer for asking for excessive wages. Ince’s comments poured yet more fuel on an already raging furnace. ‘From the outside you see Watford is a circus, but when you’re in it you kind of feel it too,’ he said on the BBC’s 72+ podcast. 'Circus' was the word used by another former player to Daily Mail Sport this week. ‘Players knew the manager wasn’t important,’ added Ince. ‘They would almost bypass the manager (and speak directly to the owner) as we knew he had no control. ‘Watford is built to be a Premier League team but they need to think, "Are we more bothered about profit or building a successful football team?" and not hire yes men who are told who to play, what systems to play, how training goes.’ There’s always been stories like that around Watford, of envelopes slipped under hotel room doors with team changes sent from on high. One source close to a former manager recalled players being signed without their knowledge. Daily Mail Sport heard a perhaps far-fetched tale this week of senior players receiving WhatsApp messages in the dressing room at half-time with substitute recommendations to pass on to the coach. ‘It’s crazy at that place,’ another former player told Daily Mail Sport this week. ‘I only expect it to get worse, sadly.’ Krepin Diatta was seen as a huge coup for the club, only for the player's agent to suggets he’d had to settle for the Hornets after being rejected by clubs all summer over wage demands Burnley had not won all season when they turned up at Vicarage Road last week. They ran out 4-0 winners As always with clubs in a downward spiral, it’s issues off the pitch that trickle on to the grass. The club's ownership are understood to be open to offers. They have sold the women’s team to a US investment firm. The academy has been downgraded to Category 3 and its director, club legend Richard Johnson, has just left. One agent told Daily Mail Sport they had been approached multiple times by interested parties asking for the best way in. However, the £175m valuation placed on the club, when it sought out £17.5m for a 10 per cent share a few years ago, seemed far too high. As the club is in a worse position now than it was then, such a figure is surely unrealistic now. According to football finance analyst Swiss Ramble, Watford have repaid a Championship-high net £34m to their owners in the six years to 2024-25. The £53m still owed to them carries interest of up to 8.75 per cent, with £7.7m built up so far. The club's available cash appears to come almost entirely from player sales. Watford were forced to pay out to a stewarding company in the summer, who had hit them with a winding-up petition. The club is also understood to have recently threatened legal action after questions were raised about its finances. There’s still the uncomfortable relationship Watford has with agent Mogi Bayat, who they continue to do business with despite him awaiting trial in Belgium over charges including money laundering and fraud. Bayat denies all wrongdoing. And then there’s Pozzo’s own court case in Spain next month, where he stands accused of evading more than £7.5m in tax on transfers while at Granada. A guilty verdict would see him fall foul of the Football League’s owners regulations. Pozzo's lawyers have said he 'refutes in the strongest possible terms that he has breached Spanish tax laws in any way'. The message from the club is that patience is required and there’s no need to panic. Results will come and they always change the mood. For supporters, it’s too late for that. For them, they only have one way left to stay alive. Their only chance of living.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
