World.title: Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
World.content:
Russia has close ties with the Taliban and is courting Islamabad, but analysts say its leverage remains uncertain.

Share Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan? on social media

Islamabad, Pakistan – Sitting with his elbows on his knees, Russia’s Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev leaned towards Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for talks in Rawalpindi on October 14.

While Kolokoltsev was in Pakistan, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), flew into Kabul to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq.

Officially, Russia, Pakistan and Afghanistan have issued little beyond standard statements about the meetings. But the signs are clear: Pakistan and Afghanistan have spent the past year exchanging fire and public threats. Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire in Doha last October and China hosted talks in Urumqi in April, but attacks inside Pakistan continued. Islamabad again struck Afghan territory in June, September and this month.

Russia now appears to be stepping in as a mediator.

Moscow’s special representative for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, told Russia’s TASS news agency earlier this month that his country was ready to play peace broker between Kabul and Islamabad if both sides requested it.

Pakistan’s ambassador to Russia, Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, said in March that Islamabad had approached Moscow. The Taliban, though, have not publicly requested Russian mediation, raising questions about how much and in what capacity Moscow can push Pakistan and Afghanistan to talks when other mediators have struggled.

A complicated history adds to the challenge Russia faces.

A diplomatic opening

Pakistan’s military media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said the Rawalpindi meeting discussed issues of “mutual interest and the regional security environment, with particular emphasis on strengthening bilateral security cooperation.”



The statement did not mention Afghanistan and neither Russian officials nor the Taliban have disclosed what the intelligence chiefs discussed. Moscow has, however, voiced concern about the fighting.

“We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children,” the Russian embassy in Kabul posted on X earlier this month.

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said Pakistani strikes between September 30 and October 1 killed at least 10 civilians, mostly children.

In decades past, the idea of Russia mediating between Pakistan and the Taliban might have been unthinkable. Throughout the Cold War and even after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia was – and remains in many ways – one of the closest strategic and military partners of India, the neighbour Pakistan has fought multiple wars against. While in Afghanistan, Russia backed the Northern Alliance against the Taliban throughout the 1990s.

But in recent years, Russia has significantly strengthened relations with both Pakistan and the Taliban. Then Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was in Moscow when Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022. Last year, Russia became the first country in the world to officially recognise the Taliban government in Afghanistan.

Those shifts have been driven by Russia’s desire to broaden its options in South Asia, at a time when India has embraced the United States and to counter the rise of the Afghan branch of ISIL, also known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or ISKP. While the Taliban are concerned with ruling Afghanistan, ISKP has broader territorial ambitions and carried out an attack in Moscow in 2024 that killed nearly 150 people. The Taliban and the ISKP are sworn enemies.

Fighting between Pakistan and the Taliban created regional instability and Moscow was worried that could make it easier for armed groups to spill into Central Asia, said Taimur Khan, a research associate at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI).

“Mediation also helps Moscow preserve its regional influence and avoid a vacuum that could invite renewed extra-regional involvement,” he told Al Jazeera.

Why mediation stalled

Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban in Doha last October, but talks in Istanbul collapsed the following month and skirmishes resumed. Islamabad also launched air raids inside Afghanistan. China hosted talks in Urumqi in April.

In mid-September, Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, met Taliban officials in Kabul and Kandahar before travelling to Islamabad.



An attack in Kohat followed on September 18, with Pakistan striking Afghanistan on September 24 and October 1.

“Other actors have so far achieved more tangible mediation results in this conflict,” Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Central Asia analyst and head of research at the geopolitical foresight agency, Nightingale Int, told Al Jazeera.

Russia’s own effort stalled at a Moscow meeting on October 5.

Kabulov told TASS that the Afghan delegation objected to Afghanistan being mentioned too often in connection with “terrorism”.

“For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said on October 9 at a weekly media briefing.

Kabul-based security analyst Tameem Bahiss said the objection reflected Kabul’s longstanding position.

“Accepting language that repeatedly associates Afghanistan with terrorism could be seen as an acknowledgement of the very allegations Kabul has consistently denied,” he told Al Jazeera.

The TTP problem

At the Moscow meeting, Pakistan’s special representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, said “terrorism” remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems.

Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said the two countries’ problems could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, according to Afghan media.

Pakistan says the Pakistani Taliban and other armed groups shelter in Afghanistan.

Kabul rejects the allegation, saying it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries and that Pakistan’s security problems are largely internal, Bahiss said.

Moscow’s public warnings have focused on the ISKP.

“There is no visible public pressure from Russia on the Taliban over Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and Moscow is unlikely to exert such pressure,” Gusseinov said. TTP is the official name of the Pakistani Taliban, which is behind dozens of the deadliest attacks Pakistan has suffered in recent years.

He argued that pressing the Taliban hard on Pakistan’s behalf would undermine Moscow’s standing as a neutral mediator and its partnership with the Taliban against ISKP.

“Russia’s primary concern is ISKP and it appears satisfied with the Taliban’s efforts to counter the group,” Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based analyst specialising in armed groups and security dynamics in Afghanistan and Pakistan, told Al Jazeera.

What Moscow brings

Still, Russia has something earlier mediators did not. In July 2025, it became the only country to recognise the Taliban government.

Taimur Khan said that could give Moscow another source of influence.

“The Taliban authorities’ interest in preserving that recognition and expanding cooperation with Moscow could give Russia additional influence in seeking action against the TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan,” he said.

In May, the two sides signed an unpublished military-technical agreement covering, according to Kabulov, the repair and maintenance of equipment the Taliban already hold, mostly Soviet and Russian-made.



Three days after the signing, the Taliban’s Defence Minister, Mohammad Yaqoob, said Pakistan would soon no longer dare to launch strikes.

On June 9 and 10, Pakistani aircraft struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika provinces, killing 13 civilians, according to the Afghan government.

“Russia has greater access to the Taliban than any other major power, but its actual leverage is considerably more limited than is often assumed,” analyst Gusseinov said.

Sayed said senior Taliban leaders continued visiting Russia and India as fighting escalated, seemingly signalling they could offset Pakistan’s military superiority through new alignments.

“While the military and political significance of these ties remains unclear, the Taliban present such diplomatic developments to the Afghan public, particularly their supporters, as political achievements that reinforce their image of strength,” he said.

Why the SCO matters

Pakistan chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) for 2026-27 and will host the 10-member bloc’s summit in Islamabad next year.

The Taliban were not invited to this year’s summit in Bishkek, where members called for an inclusive government in Kabul.

On July 16, then-Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Afghanistan first needed diplomatic relations with member states, when asked whether Pakistan was blocking its inclusion in the SCO.

In September, Tirmizi, the Pakistani envoy in Moscow, said he did not see full SCO membership for Afghanistan as an option under the current Taliban government.

“The chairmanship strengthens Moscow’s reasons to invest in its relationship with Pakistan and manage differences over Afghanistan constructively,” Taimur Khan said.

The Foreign Office did not answer Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the Taliban would be invited next year.

“I cannot recall an instance where Kabul has explicitly requested Moscow to mediate between the two countries,” Bahiss said. “Nevertheless, Kabul’s repeated calls for diplomacy and its relatively close relations with Russia suggest that it would likely welcome Russian mediation if Moscow offered to play such a role.”

World.title: Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
World.content:
Ethiopia has announced that an interim government will take control of the state of Tigray, after its armed forces retook control of the northern region.

The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday. He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state.

The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Tigray’s main political party had launched the insurrection after announcing in April that it was retaking control of the region, effectively ending a peace deal with Ethiopia’s federal government.

The government promised that the interim government would create “a stable political situation” in Tigray so that free elections could be held. It has appointed five officials to run the state, including the mayor of the capital, Mekelle.

The officials will carry out “directives and instructions” delivered directly from the federal government.

The TPLF has yet to respond to the announcement. The rebel group launched an ambitious offensive in September in alliance with several other armed groups aimed at toppling the Abiy government. The Ethiopian government has accused the breakaway state of Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, accusations that Eritrea has denied.

After some early gains in the Afar region, its fighters were defeated and lost Tigray’s major cities. They surrendered in Mekelle in early October. Eritrean troops who had entered Tigray withdrew after heavy drone strikes from the Ethiopian armed forces.



The TPLF governed Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until 2018, when Abiy’s party came to power. Tigray, in response, boycotted national elections and rejected the central government, creating a severe rift.

The region remains scarred by the 2020-2022 war between federal forces, backed at that time by Eritrea, and the TPLF, which resulted in the killing of almost 600,000 people.

A peace deal ended the fighting, but key promises were not kept, including the return of displaced people and the disarmament of the TPLF.

Since the recent escalation, Ethiopia and Eritrea have accused each other of inciting war, raising fears of a wider conflict.

On Wednesday, the United States urged both sides to “de-escalate” during a phone call between Abiy and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

World.title: Jerusalem Daily: Israeli settlers burn Palestinian olive groves
World.content:
NewsFeed Jerusalem Daily: Israeli settlers burn Palestinian olive groves

Israeli settlers carry out violent pogroms on Palestinian olive groves in the towns of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya, near Ramallah. Several Palestinians and journalists were injured. Al Jazeera’s Mohammad Saleh reports.

World.title: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
World.content:
Share Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know on social media

Israeli settlers brutally attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a photojournalist working for The Washington Post in the occupied West Bank on Friday, beating villagers and setting olive groves ablaze.

The attack was among several targeting Palestinians trying to gather their olive harvest, with further assaults and arson reported in nearby communities as well.

These incidents are just the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms on local communities in the West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.

Veteran journalist Heidi Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault on Friday in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. A Palestinian man was also shot in the thigh by Israeli soldiers, according to a witness who spoke to Al Jazeera and the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

Here is what we know.

What happened during the attack?

Dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.

Levine, an American freelance photojournalist who works for The Washington Post, fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.

Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.



Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported.

Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said.

As they helped her towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. Levine was eventually taken to hospital in Ramallah.

Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said.

“They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the man was eventually taken away in an ambulance.

“We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of The Washington Post, said in a statement.

Wafa also reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added.

Where else have olive pickers been attacked?

There was violence in other parts of the occupied West Bank on Friday, as well. In Burqa, east of Ramallah, four Palestinians were reported to have been injured in a settler attack on olive pickers. In nearby Turmus Aya, settlers assaulted farmers and burned vehicles and olive trees. A civil defence volunteer was also injured, according to Wafa.

The attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians gathering olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.

Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted. On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.

How widespread are attacks?

The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks, and have stepped up as the seasonal Palestinian olive harvest gets under way.



The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has recorded at least 170 pogroms since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, Reuters reported.

The violence threatens Palestinian livelihoods and access to their land. Farmers endure assaults, the destruction of trees and the theft of crops, while settlers have also begun stealing olives from Palestinian-owned groves themselves.

Al Jazeera correspondent Tareq Abu Azzoum reported that the intimidation extends beyond agricultural land to Palestinian homes and vehicles, creating pressure on communities to leave.

“People there are still living under threat of attack, not just on their agricultural lands, but also on their properties,” he said.

“Vehicles and houses have been repeatedly hit by settler attacks, which have been used by the Israeli military, apparently, to create a deterrent environment with Palestinians expected to leave these areas so they can later turn them into Israeli settlements.”

World.title: Spain punished by FIFA for Islamophobic chants during Egypt friendly
World.content:
Spain sanctioned by FIFA after incidents at Espanyol’s stadium in Barcelona, which staged the friendly with Egypt.

Share Spain punished by FIFA for Islamophobic chants during Egypt friendly on social media

Spain have ‌‌‌‌been fined $20,000 and ordered to partially close their stadium ⁠⁠⁠⁠for their ⁠⁠⁠⁠next friendly after supporters twice chanted Islamophobic slogans during the game against Egypt in March, FIFA said ⁠⁠⁠⁠in a statement.

The sanctions relate to incidents at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona, home of LaLiga club Espanyol, ⁠⁠⁠⁠where some Spain fans chanted, “Who doesn’t jump is a Muslim” during a World Cup warm-up match which ended in a 0-0 draw.

After the second occurrence of the chant, the stadium announcer ‌‌‌‌issued a warning and the scoreboard displayed a message against discriminatory behaviour.

Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants at the time, describing them as disrespectful and intolerable and calling those responsible “ignorant and racist”.

Spanish police launched an investigation the following day, while world governing ⁠⁠⁠⁠body FIFA later started disciplinary proceedings against ⁠⁠⁠⁠the Spanish football federation (RFEF).

It argued that the word ‘Muslim’ was “neither insulting nor pejorative”, adding that the fans’ conduct should be assessed under FIFA’s Article 17, ⁠⁠⁠⁠which covers political, ideological, religious or offensive messages, rather than Article 15, which deals ⁠⁠⁠⁠with discrimination and racist abuse.

However, FIFA’s disciplinary ⁠⁠⁠⁠committee rejected that argument, saying Article 15 does not require the explicit use of a slur and that a term can be discriminatory when ‌‌‌‌used in context as “an insult, taunt, or marker of inferiority”.



FIFA fined the RFEF and ordered the closure of at least ‌‌‌‌15% ‌‌‌‌of available seats for Spain’s next friendly.

Al Jazeera has contacted the RFEF for comment.

World.title: Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
World.content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he is "only standing up for Ukraine's interests" after scathing criticism from Donald Trump, who said Kyiv's new wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries was a "disgrace".

The US president, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import diesel, also said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".

Zelensky, who has been angered by the diesel deal, said he could not accept it, because a gas agreement could come next. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" he said at an EU summit in Brussels.

Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated over the diesel deal and curbs on Ukraine's battlefield satellite network.

Zelensky's trip to Brussels, following a visit to London, has come at the end of a bruising week. As he arrived at the summit on Friday, where EU leaders rallied around him in support, Zelensky said it was good to be back among allies. "Leaders, real leaders," he said, in a possible slight to the US president.

At the summit, funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the agenda.

The war will cost â¬155bn (Â£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least â¬70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.

Zelensky said that while Ukraine could produce up to three times more drones, it "simply [doesn't] have enough money for that".

A fundamental problem for Kyiv - which cannot be easily fixed - is the chronic lack of US-made Patriot missiles to defend its towns and cities.

Zelensky said he believed Europe did possess all the interceptors his country would need this winter but described them as being scooped up in a piecemeal fashion.

It has been reported some EU countries are refusing to send extra supplies beyond those needed for their own defence and required to be kept under their Nato obligations.

World.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
World.content:
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.

The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.

"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.

Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own.

"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

World.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
World.content:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

World.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.

Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.

World.title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
World.content:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.

"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

World.title: US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions
World.content:
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it had unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection.

In the letter, sent to the US defence department inspector general, the senators express "grave concern" about reports of speed curbs between 12 and 14 October.

Asked whether the US might have had a role in the slowdown, a US official told the BBC "no such request was ever made by the president [Donald Trump]".

The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors.

It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure".

Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.

On Friday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told a news conference in Brussels that Starlink services were still being restored in his country.

"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," he said.

The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine.

"We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says.

"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add.

The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats.

World.title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
World.content:
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.

They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.

But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.

The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.

Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.

Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."

Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."

An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.

After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.

World.title: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
World.content:
A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.

The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.

Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".

Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.

Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.

Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg.

A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre.

World.title: Fintech firm Onafriq to close Nigeria agent banking business
World.content:
Fintech firm Onafriq Nigeria Payments Limited has announced it will wind down its Nigerian agent banking business, Baxi, and refocus on pan-African payments.

In a statement on Friday, the company cited macroeconomic headwinds such as inflation and currency depreciation as key factors affecting trading volumes and operating costs and undermining the sustainability of its offline agent banking model.

South Africa-based Onafriq, with a footprint in Morocco, Mali, Kenya, and Tanzania among others, entered the Nigerian agent banking market in 2021 when it acquired the Baxi business (also known as Capricorn Digital Limited) and invested heavily through 2023 to strengthen and scale its agent network.

Operating conditions changed significantly for the firm beginning in 2024, with a sharp depreciation of the naira and broader macroeconomic pressures dramatically impacting its operations.

A rapid growth of instant account-to-account payments simultaneously changed the mix of transactions at agents’ POS.

According to Onafriq, increased competition in this segment, coupled with associated margin compression, further strained the business.

After reviewing its long-term strategy and the business’s sustainability, the group concluded that winding down the agent banking operation is the way to go.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We entered Nigeria with conviction and commitment, but did not achieve the outcome we set out for. Closing this business was a difficult decision to arrive at, one that affects colleagues, agents, and business partners across Nigeria who poured their hearts and soul into building out the Baxi network,” Dare Okoudjou, founder and CEO of Onafriq, said

“We are committed to honesty, fairness, and a well-managed transition for everyone impacted. Nigeria remains central to our mission, and we will continue to serve the market as a Payment Solution Service Provider through the Onafriq payments network and our card issuing services,” he added.

The closure will only affect employees whose roles are connected to the agent banking business. The company said every affected employee will be consulted, treated fairly, and supported through the transition.

Onafriq said agents onboarded via the Baxi payments platform have been transitioned to another principal bank, and it has asked them to transfer their funds to their preferred principal bank within 30 days.

“Onafriq’s teams are available to provide support and guidance throughout the process. The company will continue to honour its commitments to affected stakeholders and communicate openly during the transition,” the company said.

It added that the decision affects only its agent banking business in Nigeria and does not represent an exit from the Nigerian market.

“Onafriq Group remains strong, with continued growth across its cross-border payments network and card issuing services,” it said.

World.title: Bola Ahmed Tinubu: The most consequential president, By Jibrin Ibrahim
World.content:
This morning, we are at the public presentation of the book – Tinubu: From Renewed Hope to Despair; written by Abubakar Siddique Mohammed, Aliyu Sanusi, Alkasum Abba and Massoud Omar. The event was supposed to have taken place yesterday at Arewa House, Kaduna, a research institute run by Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. Due to “pressures from above”, the university cancelled the booking. The organisers then went around other hotels in Kaduna but they shut their doors claiming they had been warned. That is the state of our democracy today as civic space is closed down. Undaunted, the organisers decided to “bombard the headquarters”. As they closed doors in the provinces, they opted to go to the headquarters and have the event in Yar’Adua Centre. They have an important story to tell about our President, Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Bola Ahmed Tinubu is in a keen contest with Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida (IBB) in the race as the most consequential president in Nigeria’s post-independence history. He is in a keen contrast with his predecessor Muhammadu Buhari, the General that lived in Aso Rock for eight years but did not even try to govern the country. As I said on many occasions under the Buhari Presidency, when the president refuses to govern, others govern in his name because as we all know, there is no vacuum in politics. IBB had a profound effect on the culture of politics and statecraft in Nigeria but I doubt that his impact could have been as deep and profound as Tinubu’s. Do not take me up on my words, read the book that is being presented to the Nigerian public today and as the saying goes, one reading will convince you.

Tinubu’s claim, (and please don’t ask me the justification), is that it was his turn to govern Nigeria and many people assumed that he wanted to enjoy the excellent cuisine and soothing spirits of Aso Rock. I am an Ahmadu Bello University trained materialist in my methodology training so I know nothing about the world of sprits. For more on this matter of spirits, ask my good friend Dr Rueben Abati. Nigerians erroneously assumed he was there to enjoy his turn. What the country is realising today is that he came to change Nigeria by dismantling its democracy, disbanding federalism and establishing one-man rule. He did not start the process but he is working very hard to complete the job.

The Fourth Republic has been in place since 1999. Over that period, the country’s democratic process has been emptied of its essence. One way of understanding what happened to our democracy is to review how reckless political cabals have created a situation in which Nigeria faces a grave threat to its foundational constitutional principle of the separation of powers. Checks and balances between the branches of government have been imperilled. The separation of powers divides government responsibilities into three distinct branches—legislative (makes laws), executive (enforces laws), and judicial (interprets laws). This constitutional framework ensures a system of “checks and balances” that prevents tyranny, preserves individual liberties, and promotes governmental accountability.

Under President Tinubu, the legislative branch has been placed under near total control of the executive branch. The judiciary has lost both its independence and its integrity. The checks on the powers of the executive have been dismantled and he runs the government as he pleases without accountability or respect for the people’s welfare. Institutions have been compromised, weakened, and subordinated to the interests of the executive arm of government. This erosion of institutional independence has fuelled public distrust to its highest level in our history creating a crisis of political exclusion and impunity that is pushing violent extremism, organized crime, and communal conflict to a tipping point.

As Tinubu struggles to secure a second term to conclude his agenda of deepening the transition from “Hope to Despair”, it is important to understand his assets and skill set. While presidents from Shagari to Buhari had to rely on financiers and godfathers to finance their campaigns, Tinubu had the resources to fully fund his 2023 campaign himself and therefore had no stakeholders with voice in the system. Now that he owns the treasury, there is no cabal to bring some diversity and multiple voices to the table. There are only people who work for him at his pleasure. Our arrogance as democracy defenders that even the military dictatorships of Babangida and Abacha were stopped in their tracks of seeking to establish one-man rule is shattered by the reality of the iron-grip of the Tinubu control. I had written numerous articles in the past on how the National Assembly successfully fought off and gained its independence from the attempt to control them. Today, we have a National Assembly that is proud that it does not even discuss executive bills, it simply passes them without debate. Its only expectation is that it is well compensated financially.

The situation with the judiciary is worse. It has been undermined through corruption and for matters of no political relevance, the highest bidder wins automatically. When however, there is a political stake in a matter, the government position is the automatic winner. The Judiciary is complicit in dismantling the democratic process by its disregard for the rule of law. The Nigerian Bar Association that has a solid history in defending human rights and the rule of law has today lost its voice and raison d’etre.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The most serious problem confronting Nigerian democracy today is the active way the Tinubu Administration is using the powers of incumbency to ensure that there is no level playing ground for political parties. President Tinubu knows something about how opposition parties can come together, overcome their differences, create synergy around a single candidate, mobilise and defeat an incumbent president. He was a key player between 2013 and 2015, when opposition parties came together, negotiated, agreed on how the candidate would emerge and then went ahead to agree on a consensus candidate. The outcome of the consensus position that emerged was that for the first time in the history of this country, a sitting President was defeated at the polls and handed over power peacefully in 2015. Precisely because he knows the script, he has decided he is not going to sit and allow what he had done to another person be done to him.

The Tinubu political strategy since 2023 has been to apply slash-and-absorb tactics to opposition parties by actively encouraging factional crises within them and enticing key members to abandon ship and join the ruling party. This was not a sustainable tactic because there were limited positions within the ruling party, and giving the new entrants many goodies would mean depriving those within the party of these, which would become a crisis generating mechanism for the ruling party itself. This was indeed the context that encouraged opposition parties to strategize towards the establishment of a unified mega opposition platform to face the APC in the 2027 elections, the African Democratic Congress (ADC). By making opposition parties ungovernable, the ruling party assumes it can maintain its control until the elections. This cannot be guaranteed because there is a campaign and Tinubu is discovering today that there are too many negatives in his governance record so selling a second term might be impossible for the people who might abandon their leaders who had sold out.

The consequential impact of Tinubu rule is not only on our democracy. The book on Tinubu: From Renewed Hope to Despair provides detailed empirical analysis on destruction of our federal arrangement, national cohesion, lopsided infrastructural development, economic crisis and deepening poverty. Reading the book produces a constant chilling effect that there are no positives in Tinubu’s governing narratives, there are only negatives. Insecurity around the country has been spreading and deepening and the government’s only perspective seems to be to beg the Americans to come and solve our problems of insecurity. As security deteriorates, what is on offer is lopsided development. I had always been indignant at Buhari’s clannish approach to rule and ethnic favouritism.

The authors provide statistics showing federal appointments have today become the most lopsided in our country’s history. It does not stop there. Infrastructural projects are today concentrated in Lagos and the South West. Federal institutions are transferring key aspects of their organisational work to Lagos. The official policy appears to be to tear Nigeria at the seams. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s debt burden has been built to an unmanageable level. The numbers they provide tells the sad story of the policy reform that has multiplied levels of poverty and malnutrition in the country. While the government speaks of successful policy reform, what the people experience is the highest level of the development of misery. The authors draw attention to credible data sources that show universal policy reform failures.

Another consequence of Tinubu’s rule is the complete subordination of Nigeria’s interests to American hegemony. Since his inauguration, the President has been actively soliciting close ties and collaboration with the Americans. He has taken the option of succumbing to American imperialism at a historical moment when that crumbling hegemon is declining, indeed collapsing before our very eyes. We are becoming close friends with a country that recently acted as a brigand, sending a military force to kidnap President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and his wife. Why are we so close to a country that decided to completely wipe out the leadership of Iran to impose regime change only to find out that the Iranians do not tolerate hegemons but give them a sound beating.

A professor of Political Science and development consultant/expert, Jibrin Ibrahim is a Senior Fellow of the Centre for Democracy and Development, and Chair of the Editorial Board of PREMIUM TIMES.

World.title: From reform to prosperity: The work to reelect the president starts now, By Ima Niboro
World.content:
The coming elections should provide Nigerians with the opportunity to examine records, policy choices, consequences, and alternatives. And President Tinubu will have to defend his record before Nigerians, as every incumbent seeking re-election should. His challengers will equally have to explain not only what they would do differently, but how they would do it, what it would cost, and what consequences would follow.

Yesterday, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu formally inaugurated the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council. With that ceremony, the work of presenting the case for his re-election to Nigerians begins in earnest.

For those of us in the Media and Strategic Communications Directorate, however, the work did not begin today. We have been at it since August, putting together the structures, strategy, and communications architecture required for what will undoubtedly be an intense national campaign. Today was the formal inauguration by Mr President and the signal for the machinery to move into full campaign mode.

Within the APC PCC Media and Strategic Communications Directorate are six subcommittees. I have the privilege of serving on three of them: the Committee of Campaign Spokespersons, the Strategy Committee, and the Committee on the Screening of Media and Advertising Agencies that will work with the Presidential Campaign Council.

These are responsibilities I have taken on with a clear understanding of what lies ahead.

I have always been unequivocal about my support for the Tinubu administration. That support does not mean I delude myself that everything is perfect. Far from it — because tough but completely unavoidable decisions have been made that have had real and sometimes difficult consequences for many Nigerians.

Indeed, I have always made the point that, in terms of sheer numbers, we members (and supporters) of APC are at the top demographic of those living through these economic realities. Our NIN-verified membership stands at about 12.8 million (PDP – 2.4 million, ADC – 1.6 million, NDC – 700,000). Our members and supporters are traders, civil servants, farmers, transporters, professionals, artisans, and businesspeople. We buy from the same markets, pay the same transport fares, and confront the same economic pressures as everybody else. But despite these, we remain focused and confident, because joy comes in the morning — and that morning is here!

So, this campaign cannot be built on denying the obvious. It must be built on explaining why difficult decisions were taken, what they have achieved, where they are taking the country, and, most importantly, when and how those gains translate into better lives for ordinary Nigerians.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This is the central conversation of this campaign; and it is called: from reform to prosperity!

When President Tinubu assumed office in 2023, Nigeria faced deep fiscal and monetary distortions that had accumulated over several years. Central Bank financing of government deficits through Ways and Means advances (meaning printing cash, Zimbabwe Style, backed by nothing) had risen to about ₦30 trillion.

The foreign exchange system had become fragmented across multiple windows. By May 2023, the official NAFEX rate was about ₦465 to the dollar, while the parallel market rate was about ₦763 — a differential of roughly 63 per cent. That enormous gulf created opportunities for arbitrage and rent-seeking, while businesses without privileged access to official foreign exchange were forced into a much more expensive, arbitrary, and unsustainable parallel market.

The president could have continued the pillage and made humongous gains for himself and his allies, like was going on before he took power. But he said no. Nigeria first! This country must respect that.

Then there was the petrol subsidy regime, which consumed enormous public resources. while encouraging distortions, arbitrage, and heavy smuggling. Government revenues were under severe pressure, debt-service obligations were at almost 98 per cent of the budget, investors were voting with their feet due to economic uncertainty, and the country faced what the World Bank described as the danger of a “fiscal cliff.”

Obviously, something had to give. The country was collapsing under the weight of its own contradictions, and the choice before Tinubu was clear: Continue the arbitrariness, reinforce the slide, and supervise Nigeria’s final collapse, or execute a course correction, block the leakages, stop the haemorrhage, and return the country to a path of sustainable growth and economic stability.

Because he chose the latter, history will be kind to him!

So, petrol subsidy was removed. Multiple foreign-exchange windows were unified, and the exchange rate moved towards a market-determined system. The Central Bank tightened monetary policy, began rebuilding reserves, addressed outstanding foreign exchange obligations, and stopped merely printing money (who still does that in the 21st century!) to finance fiscal deficits.

His administration simultaneously embarked on tax, oil and gas, power, infrastructure, and credit reforms intended to rebuild the foundations of the economy.

The first phase was painful, no doubt. Fuel prices rose. The naira underwent a severe adjustment. Inflation impacted household incomes. Interest rates increased as the monetary authorities fought inflation. Businesses and families carried a heavy burden.

But three years later, the evidence increasingly shows that Nigeria has moved beyond the most difficult stage of that adjustment. The numbers are now telling a different story.

Foreign reserves have climbed above $54 billion, compared with about $32 billion in mid-April 2024. Nigeria’s external position has strengthened considerably. The World Bank says real GDP grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 3.9 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025 and 3.5 per cent in 2024.

The same World Bank report says that stronger growth stabilised Nigeria’s poverty rate for the first time since 2019. That does not mean poverty has disappeared, but it represents an important change in direction that leads to a bright new future for our great country.

Hand-in-hand, Nigeria’s current account position has also strengthened, as rising reserves provide a bigger buffer against external shocks. We all remember when foreign airlines were leaving Nigeria in droves because they had rooms full of naira notes and no dollars to convert it to? Or when you couldn’t use your naira card for any international transaction, whether locally or abroad?

Those days are gone!

And the international financial community is noticing.

In May, S&P Global Ratings raised Nigeria’s long-term sovereign credit rating from B- to B, citing an improving macroeconomic profile, stronger oil production, increased domestic refining capacity, and the liberalisation of the foreign exchange regime.

In August, Moody’s revised Nigeria’s outlook to Positive from Stable, while retaining its B3 rating, citing stronger external resilience, higher foreign exchange reserves, and economic growth.

Then, last week, Fitch revised Nigeria’s sovereign outlook from Stable to Positive, while affirming its B rating. Among the factors Fitch identified were stronger external buffers, greater exchange rate flexibility, disinflation, and increased confidence in the continuity of the reform framework.

JP Morgan has now included Nigeria among the countries in its new GBI-EM Edge frontier local currency bond index, another avenue through which global investors can assess exposure to Nigeria’s domestic debt market. And its banking arm, JP Morgan Chase, is bringing a brand new investment bank to Nigeria.

Clearly, the world knows that Nigeria has not solved all its problems. Neither should we, back home here, pretend that credit ratings put food on anybody’s table.

But what these developments state unequivocally is that institutions whose business it is to assess sovereign risk increasingly see powerful changes in Nigeria’s economic fundamentals. And lower sovereign risk, if sustained, means lower costs, greater investment, more businesses, more jobs, greater resources to develop our country, and ultimately money in the pocket and food on the table.

The next phase is therefore the most important one: converting economic stabilisation into prosperity.

That means bringing inflation down further so that wages recover more and more purchasing power. It means maintaining foreign exchange stability so businesses can plan and price their products with greater certainty. It means increasing food production and attacking the structural problems driving up food prices.

It also means ensuring that higher federation revenues continue to translate into better roads, hospitals, schools, water, security, and social services at federal, state, and local government levels.

It means expanding conditional cash transfers to the poorest of the poor among us; it means increasing consumer and business credit so that Nigerians can finance homes, vehicles, education, and enterprises without having to possess the entire purchase price in cash.

It means deepening the CNG programme and electric-powered transport interventions to reduce the cost of mobility. It also means expanding domestic refining so that Nigeria can put a final stop to importing petroleum products and the foreign-exchange pressures associated with that.

Moving from Reform to Prosperity means attracting the investment required to create millions of productive jobs. But above all, it means making sure that the macroeconomic recovery moves from the computer screens, the big and sometimes confusing numbers on the spreadsheets, rating reports, and government statistics into Nigerian pockets, kitchens, and dining tables.

That, in my view, is the great assignment of the next phase, and there’s no one better positioned to accomplish this task than the chief visioner of the reform programme, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu himself.

Our national economic foundations have been reset. Now the Nigerian people are about to see and feel the full benefits of the house built upon these structures.

So much has been done already. At the heart of the Tinubu administration’s interventions have been programmes designed to put money in people’s pockets, ease the cost of living, and widen access to opportunity. The national minimum wage has been increased, while conditional cash transfers are providing support to vulnerable households. Students who might otherwise be unable to afford higher education are benefiting from the Students Loan Scheme through NELFUND, while consumer credit, YouthCred, the Nigeria Youth Investment Fund, and loans and grants for MSMEs are expanding access to finance for workers, young people, entrepreneurs, and small businesses.

The administration has also targeted the everyday pressures Nigerians feel most directly — food, healthcare, transportation, and jobs. Agricultural programmes, including dry-season farming support, tractor deployment, and the National Agricultural Growth Scheme, are increasing food production and strengthening farmers. Primary healthcare revitalisation and expanded cancer-treatment infrastructure are improving access to essential healthcare, while the CNG initiative is providing a cheaper transportation alternative. Programmes such as 3MTT, digital youth training, and the Creative Economy Development Fund are equipping young Nigerians with skills and opening new pathways to employment and enterprise.

Beyond these immediate interventions, major investments are being made in security, electricity, roads, rail, ports, and other infrastructure that affect daily life and economic opportunity. Counterterrorism operations are daily strengthening security, while power-sector reforms, grid expansion, the Zungeru hydropower project, national road rehabilitation, the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Highway, and revitalised Abuja Metro are improving the foundations for growth. The broader reforms in taxation, foreign exchange, public revenue, debt management, and the petroleum sector are all parts of the machinery required to sustainably finance a more secure country, improve decrepit public services, create more jobs, and improve living standards for our people.

This is why the work to reelect the president shifts into high gear effective today.

The coming elections should provide Nigerians with the opportunity to examine records, policy choices, consequences, and alternatives. And President Tinubu will have to defend his record before Nigerians, as every incumbent seeking re-election should. His challengers will equally have to explain not only what they would do differently, but how they would do it, what it would cost, and what consequences would follow.

For those of us entrusted with communicating the president’s case, our responsibility is therefore substantial.

We will explain without insulting the intelligence of Nigerians; defend without denying obvious difficulties; persuade with facts. We will celebrate the successes and acknowledge where more work remains to be done. And we will demonstrate why continuity of the reforms offers the country a path towards stronger and more broadly shared prosperity.

I have seen before what happens when an incumbent government is unable to persuade Nigerians that its work deserves to continue.

I served President Goodluck Ebele Jonathan and watched his administration lose re-election in 2015. That experience taught me a permanent lesson about politics: performance alone is never enough. A government must continuously explain what it is doing, why it is doing it, and where it intends to take the country.

That lesson remains branded on my mind, and I carry its weight with me always.

In this election, we will make the case vigorously, respectfully, and factually. Nigerians will ultimately make their choice, as is their democratic right. For us, however, there can be no complacency.

The campaign has begun. The work begins in earnest.

And we shall win!

Ima Niboro is one of the spokespersons of the Tinubu Presidential Campaign.

World.title: Court upholds appointment of receiver/manager in debt recovery suit against Stallion Group
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Lagos has ruled in favour of United Bank for Africa (UBA) in a N156 billion debt recovery suit against Stallion Group and its subsidiaries and upheld the appointment of the receiver/manager, Romeo Ese, by the bank as valid.

In a judgment delivered by Justice Daniel Osiagor on Friday, the court granted all the reliefs sought by the bank and affirmed its jurisdiction to hear the case.

It also affirmed the right of the receiver/manager to take possession of the mortgaged property, with the receiver/manager declared to be entitled to seek protective orders,

It also affirmed the right of the receiver/manager to take possession of the mortgaged property, the enforceability of the mortgage security and the liability of the guarantors.

The court also declared that the receiver/manager is entitled to seek protective orders and noted that the defendants did not dispute their indebtedness, even though they challenged the amount claimed.

According to the court, the reconciliation of accounts between the parties did not negate the underlying indebtedness.

In his ruling, Justice Osiagor dismissed the objections raised by Barbedos Ventures Limited, the 12th Defendant, holding that it failed to establish any proprietary rights over the mortgaged property.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

On that score, its consent was not required for the creation of the mortgage, and its objections were declined.

The court forbade the defendants from diverting the receivables due to them from government agencies, reinforcing the bank’s ability to protect its recovery interests.

The ruling affirmed the liability of the guarantors, boosting the legal position of UBA to seek recovery of the outstanding obligations.

The ruling is crucial for enforcing creditors’ rights in Nigeria, underscoring the validity of properly constituted security arrangements and the authority of duly appointed receivers to enforce creditors’ interests.

Background

According to UBA, the bank granted several credit facilities to Stallion Nigeria Limited in 2014 on the agreement that the credit facilities could be utilised by other companies within the Stallion Group in accordance with the terms of the offer letter.

The bank said the defendants pledged assets in Kano, Port Harcourt and Lagos as security for the loans.

According to an affidavit deposed to by Anthony Chilaka, the group head, Recovery and Remedial Management Department of UBA, on 18 October 2023, Sunil Vaswani, the chairman of Stallion Group, made a personal guarantee in respect of the facilities.

Stallion Motors was awarded a contract by the Federal Government in 2014 to supply 700 Ashok Leyland trucks/Stallion troop carrying vehicles and 50 Falcon seater buses to be used by the military on the agreement that the receivables from the government would be paid into Stallion’s account with UBA, the bank claimed.

On delivering the vehicles, Stallion Motors allegedly asked the government to make the first payment of $50 million into its Dubai account and received N8.2 billion into its offshore account instead of the UBA account, contrary to the earlier understanding between the parties.

UBA said the defendants failed to settle its debts totalling N156 billion.

Acting on an order of the Federal High Court, Lagos, in November 2023, UBA took over Stallion Group’s assets and those of its subsidiaries in Lagos, Kano, and Port Harcourt as part of the debt recovery push.

The assets comprised mortgaged property known as “all that piece or parcel of land together with any building thereon” at Plot 371, Trans Amadi Industrial Layout, Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

“Plot 353, Trans Amadi Industrial Layout, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Plot 370, Trans Amadi Industrial Layout, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, KM17, Lagos-Badagry Expressway, Lagos State and No. 54, Challawa Industrial Estate, Kano State, Nigeria.”

World.title: Nigeria’s metering rate jumps to 63% as unmetered electricity customers drop to 4.7 million
World.content:
Nigeria’s electricity metering rate rose marginally to 63.1 per cent in August 2026 from 62.4 per cent in the preceding month, helping reduce customers without meters to 4.7 million, according to metering factsheet data published by the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) on Wednesday.

Metered customers in Nigeria rose from 7,903,819 in July to 8,045,565 in August, a 1.8 per cent increase, the data showed.

However, newly metered customers declined during the period, falling from 159,980 in July to 141,746 in August.

The figures indicate that although metered customers continued to grow, the pace of new installations slowed in August.

The data implies the total number of active electricity customers in the country increased from 12,671,795 in July to 12,749,789 in August.

This represents an increase of 0.6 per cent, or 77,994 customers, in the month.

Arbitrary estimated billing due to metering gaps has been a major challenge in electricity billing in Nigeria over the years.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A significant portion of registered electricity customers in Nigeria lack access to prepaid meters, forcing distribution companies to rely on estimates rather than actual consumption when calculating their bills.

Similarly, poor power supply, driven by infrastructure constraints and frequent grid collapse, continues to undermine reliable electricity supply in the country.

Joseph Tegbe, the Minister of Power, vowed, following his appointment in June, to identify power distribution, metering, transparency, and sub-national participation as key areas of intervention in the industry.

Eko and Ikeja DisCos lead metering performance

A breakdown of the 11 electricity distribution companies’ (DisCos) performance showed considerable differences in their metering rates.

Eko Electricity Distribution Company recorded the highest metering rate at 89.6 per cent in August, up from 89.3 per cent in July.

Ikeja Electric followed with a metering rate of 87.7 per cent, slightly below the 87.9 per cent reported in July.

Abuja Electricity Distribution Company recorded a metering rate of 82.6 per cent, up from 82 per cent the previous month.

Port Harcourt Electricity Distribution Company also improved its metering rate to 71 per cent in August from 69.6 per cent in July.

Benin DisCo’s metering rate rose from 63.2 per cent to 64.4 per cent, while Ibadan DisCo improved from 58.6 per cent to 59.2 per cent.

Enugu DisCo recorded a metering rate of 52.4 per cent, slightly up from 52.1 per cent in July.

Northern DisCos record lowest rates

The factsheet showed that Jos DisCo had the lowest metering rate in August at 37.6 per cent, up from 36.5 per cent in July.

Yola DisCo followed at 39.2 per cent, up from 37.8 per cent.

Kaduna DisCo recorded 42.3 per cent, relative to 41.3 per cent in July, while Kano DisCo’s metering rate increased from 41.6 per cent to 42.8 per cent.

READ ALSO: Electricity firm explains why some customers are now paying higher bills

The relatively low rates mean many customers served by these companies remain without meters.

The August figures indicate that Nigeria’s electricity metering coverage continues to improve, but progress varies across distribution companies.

While Eko, Ikeja and Abuja have metered more than 80 per cent of their active customers, Jos, Yola, Kaduna and Kano remain below 43 per cent.

The overall increase in metered customers also came alongside a rise in the number of active customers, highlighting the need for distribution companies to sustain and accelerate installations to reduce the metering gap.

World.title: Tinubu celebrates aide Basheer Lado at 60
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Basheer Lado, his special adviser on National Assembly Matters (Senate), on his 60th birthday on 16 October.

The president described Mr Lado, a former senator, as a dependable public servant and accomplished legislator who served in the Senate for four years before becoming his liaison officer in the National Assembly’s Upper Chamber.

President Tinubu said Mr Lado’s experience in lawmaking and public administration has continued to benefit the nation, particularly by fostering cordial relations between the Executive and the Senate.

The presidential aide represented Kano Central Senatorial District in the 7th National Assembly from 2011 to 2015. In the Senate, he served as vice chairman of the Senate Committee on Works.

President Tinubu remarked: “In the several capacities he has found himself, Senator Lado has been very impactful. As Senator, Lado facilitated the Kundila Bridge, popularly known as Gadar Lado, among other projects for his constituents in Kano.

“As Federal Commissioner at the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons and as Director-General of the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), Lado helped protect vulnerable Nigerians, confronting human trafficking and advancing the welfare and rehabilitation of displaced persons.

“His humanitarian gesture is further reflected in his Ladon Alheri Foundation, particularly in education, healthcare, women’s economic empowerment, rural water supply and support for disadvantaged communities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“As Senator Lado attains 60, I commend his commitment to public service, loyalty to our Renewed Hope administration and invaluable contributions to strengthening democratic governance in Nigeria.

“I congratulate him on this milestone and wish him good health, wisdom and strength as he continues to serve our nation.”

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President

(Information & Strategy)

October 15, 2026

World.title: How Bakassi Boys arrested ‘Issakaba’ distributor, accosted Sam Dede — Lancelot Imasuen
World.content:
Nollywood filmmaker Lancelot Oduwa Imasuen revealed that the Bakassi Boys arrested the distributor of his 2001 film, Issakaba, in Aba, Abia State, and confronted its lead actor, Sam Dede, over its portrayal of the vigilante group.

Mr Imasuen said the group took issue with the film’s portrayal of its activities and questioned how the filmmakers obtained details of its operations.

The filmmaker recalled the incidents in an interview with Channels Television while discussing Issakaba Returns, the forthcoming sequel to the action franchise.

“That was one of the most unbelievable moments of my life. The distributor in Aba was then arrested by them, the Bakassi Boys,” he said.

“They were dealt with, and they felt like the film went too far. They were asking, how did we know about them? Sam Dede was accosted in Aba while travelling to Port Harcourt.”

Mr Dede played Ebube, the leader of the fictional Isakaba Boys, whose campaign against criminals formed the centre of the film’s story.

Mr Imasuen said the production drew directly from events unfolding in southeastern Nigeria at the time, adding that he and his collaborators followed the vigilante group’s activities before its operations became increasingly entangled in political interests.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“They were not fallacy; they were true. Before the infiltration of the actual people that created that, we followed the story tenaciously as it was played in real time. We were making the movie,” he said.

The filmmaker said the team understood the risks of dramatising the activities of a group known for confronting suspected criminals through methods that attracted both public support and controversy.

“When political actors started taking advantage of them, we could have localised it and said, ‘Oh, it’s just chiefs’, but we knew what we were talking about at that time,” he said.

“Our fears then were real. We feared they might come to us. ‘ But the success that trailed the release of that film then, we couldn’t just stop.”

He said the decision to continue making the film was driven by more than its commercial prospects.

“The success was not about, ‘Oh, there was money to be made.’ It was about the reality that was with us,” he said.

The 2001 film was produced by Chukwuka Emelionwu and Moses Nnam.

The real-life story behind ‘Issakaba’

The controversy surrounding Issakaba reflected the film’s connection to one of southeastern Nigeria’s most contentious security developments in the late 1990s: the emergence of the Bakassi Boys.

The vigilante group emerged in Aba in 1998 amid growing concerns about armed robbery and insecurity. It subsequently expanded its influence across parts of the South-east, earning support from residents who viewed it as a response to violent crime.

However, its methods, including the treatment and killing of suspected criminals without due judicial process, also attracted criticism over allegations of extrajudicial killings and human rights abuses.

The group’s activities provided the backdrop for Issakaba, which transformed the real-life security crisis into a supernatural action thriller built around vigilante justice, traditional beliefs and the fight against criminal gangs.

Mr Imasuen said the film’s idea followed the success of his earlier production, The Last Burial, produced by the late Chukwuka Emelionwu of Kas-Vid International.

Issakaba

The original film featured several actors who were prominent in Nollywood during the home-video era.

The cast included Sam Dede as Ebube, Chiwetalu Agu as Odiwe, Pete Eneh as Mbanefo, Amaechi Muonagor as Igwe, Susan Obi as Lolo, Mike Ogundu as Nwoke, John Okafor as Amazuru, Andy Chukwu as Danga, Zulu Adigwe as Akuku, Diewait Ikpechukwu as Odogwu, Tom Njemanze as Idoko and Uche Ndigwe as Osita.

Other actors included Emeka Nwachukwu, Emeka Ani, Remmy Ohajianya, Fabian Adibe, Steve Eboh, Cynthia Okereke and Stella Ikwuegbe.

Several original cast members, including Pete Eneh, Amaechi Muonagor, John Okafor, and Zulu Adigwe, have since died.

Released as Nigeria’s home-video industry expanded rapidly, Issakaba drew on public anxieties about armed robbery, insecurity, and the perceived limits of conventional policing.

‘Issakaba Returns’: Ebube’s comeback

More than two decades after the original film, Mr Imasuen is returning to the franchise with Issakaba Returns, which is scheduled for nationwide cinema release on 13 November 2026.

Production began in 2024, with principal photography completed in Asaba, Delta State. Mr Dede returns as Ebube.

Mr Imasuen returns as director, and the sequel brings together veterans of the original production with a new generation of Nollywood actors.

The announced cast includes Chidi Mokeme, Nosa Rex, Iyabo Ojo, Regina Daniels, Alex Osifo, Charles Okafor, Mark Angel, Phyna, Francis Onwochei, Ben Olaye, Chudi Kashimawo, Yekini “Itele” Ibrahim and Sanni Danger.

Returning cast members include Mr Dede, Mr Agu, and Mr Ogundu.

World.title: Fans threaten to boycott Davido’s December concerts over Adeleke’s support for Tinubu
World.content:
Some Nigerians on social media have threatened to boycott Davido’s three December concerts in Lagos after Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke endorsed President Bola Tinubu for a second term.

The backlash followed Mr Adeleke’s appointment as the Osun coordinator of Mr Tinubu’s 2027 presidential campaign, a development that surprised some supporters because the governor belongs to the Accord Party.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Mr Adeleke pledged his support for the president during the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council inauguration at the State House in Abuja on Wednesday.

The governor said Mr Tinubu needed another four years to consolidate his administration’s economic reforms.

Three-night residency

Davido announced on X on Thursday that he would perform for three consecutive nights at the National Theatre in Lagos from 17 to 19 December.

The concerts, tagged Oriadè: The Residency, will mark the singer’s return home and commemorate his 15 years in the music industry.

According to the singer, the performances will feature songs from his latest album, Oriadè, alongside selections from his earlier projects.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the announcement attracted criticism from some social-media users opposed to his uncle’s support for Mr Tinubu.

Some vowed not to buy tickets for the concerts, while others sarcastically urged the singer to rely on family members and the APC to fill the venue.

Old post resurfaces

The controversy also revived discussions about Davido’s previous remarks against the APC during the Osun governorship election.

In an earlier post on X, the singer described APC supporters in the state as “enemies of progress”.

Some users cited the post while questioning the apparent difference between Davido’s earlier political stance and his uncle’s decision to support the APC president.

Others accused the singer of hypocrisy for remaining silent while Mr Adeleke openly rallied support for Mr Tinubu.

Several users also criticised the Adeleke family, arguing that the governor’s decision disregarded the sacrifices supporters made during the campaign that brought him to office.

They recalled the violence, hardship, and losses some residents allegedly experienced during the struggle for Mr Adeleke’s electoral victory, saying his support for Mr Tinubu undermined those sacrifices.

However, other users urged the public to separate Davido from his uncle’s political choices, arguing that the singer should not be punished for a decision he did not make.

As of press time, Davido had not publicly responded to the boycott calls.
