World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria's Hunger Crisis Takes an Emotional Toll on Caregivers #WorldFoodDay
World.content:
Fatima Ibrahimâs 23-month-old daughter, Aisha, was admitted to the Nilefa Kiji nutrition facility in Maiduguri after battling meningitis and repeated convulsions. The three weeks spent in hospital were filled with conflicting emotions. While grateful to see her daughter improve, Fatima could not stop thinking about the eight children she had left at home.

As millions of people across northern Nigeria face severe food insecurity, children continue to bear the consequences of a deepening malnutrition crisis. But the impact is far beyond the children in treatment. This can be a source of significant anxiety, exhaustion, and emotional distress for parents and caregivers, particularly those who spend weeks in the hospital when a child is severely malnourished and are concerned about starving children at home.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 34.7 million people in Nigeria are in crisis levels of food insecurity during the lean season, while more than 5.4 million children are acutely malnourished. In northern Nigeria in 2025, MSF teams provided treatment to 425,634 children who were suffering from acute malnutrition.

The food crisis has particularly affected Nigeria's northeastern states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe. It is estimated that by 2026 nearly 5.8 million people will be severely food insecure. In Borno State, conflicts, climate shocks and displacement are interfering with people's means of livelihood and damaging local food production, putting about 15,000 people at risk of suffering from catastrophic hunger.

The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that ongoing insecurity is worsening hunger by forcing communities to flee their homes, preventing farmers from accessing their land and restricting the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

Monica Genya, Association Director at Doctors Without Borders (MSF) Southern Africa, described the "situation as critical," with medical teams treating children suffering from severe acute malnutrition and related illnesses.

In MSF nutrition facilities such as Nilefa Kiji in Maiduguri, she said, teams see intensive care units full of children fighting severe acute malnutrition. Many arrive severely wasted, and because malnutrition weakens their immunity, many also have illnesses such as measles, diphtheria and malaria, she said.

"It is severe, and it is life-threatening for many children," said Genya.

In 2025, MSF treated 353,989 children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 90,723 for moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). She said that SAM is the most dangerous form that continues to claim young lives in the region. Children are severely wasted, and their immune systems are weakened. Some arrive at treatment facilities already suffering from diseases such as measles, diphtheria and malaria. Treatment can last anywhere from a week to more than a month, leaving caregivers facing prolonged separation from the rest of their families.

Genya said MSF treated 41.8 per cent more children for acute malnutrition in 2025 than in the previous year, reflecting a worsening crisis. Admissions have risen steadily since 2022, driven by insecurity, displacement, food shortages, disease outbreaks, economic hardship and cuts to humanitarian funding.

"These pressures compound one another, so more families are pushed to the edge each year," she said.

The rising number of children requiring treatment also raises questions about whether humanitarian resources are keeping pace with the need. MSF supports the state Ministries of Health in Zamfara, Katsina, Kebbi, Borno, Bauchi, Sokoto and Kano.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF Inside a ward of MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Here, MSF provides care for children suffering from malnutrition.

Supporting caregivers as part of treatment

Genya said that the emotional burden carried by caregivers is often overlooked in discussions about child malnutrition, where attention tends to focus on medical treatment, admissions and recovery rates.

"Medical statistics capture admissions and recovery rates, but they cannot measure the emotional burden carried by the person at the bedside, who is most often the mother," she said. Caregivers endure fear, anxiety, guilt, uncertainty and emotional exhaustion, and some develop symptoms of depression."

The consequences extend beyond their own wellbeing. This matters for the child's recovery too. A caregiver's emotional wellbeing influences how engaged they stay in treatment, whether they follow medical advice and how well they can care for the child after discharge.

"Caring for the caregiver is part of caring for the child," she said.

The competing demands on caregivers are evident in the experiences MSF counsellors encounter at its nutrition facilities in northern Nigeria. "Caregivers are pulled in two directions," said Genya. "Many arrive with a critically ill child while having left other children at home, sometimes with no one to look after them and little to eat."

Their worry does not stop when treatment begins. Genya recalled the experience of a mother in Maiduguri.

"One mother in Maiduguri told us she had left eight children at home, and when she heard one had a fever and there was no money for treatment, she cried and could not eat. Another was asked by her eldest son when she was coming home, because the children were hungry without her," she said. In another case, counsellors met a mother of six who had to leave the hospital because her husband had left the children with neighbours and she could not bear to stay.

"These stories show how guilt, worry and separation can put a child's treatment at risk, which is why we listen and respond," she said.

Recognising the emotional toll of malnutrition, MSF incorporates mental health and psychosocial support into its nutrition programmes.

At Nilefa Kiji, caregivers receive psychological first aid on arrival, followed by individual counselling and group sessions where they can share experiences, express their fears and learn coping strategies. Caregiver education helps families understand and manage the emotional and behavioural challenges that can arise during and after treatment. Children take part in structured play activities that help restore a sense of normalcy during recovery.

"The support is also practical," she said.

Counsellors help distressed caregivers reach relatives by phone, and in some cases supervised home visits let a caregiver briefly check on their family before returning to finish their child's treatment. She said that this helps caregivers cope, builds their confidence, supports treatment adherence and contributes to better recovery. "Many regain hope as they watch their children get better, and some come back after discharge just to show how healthy their children have become," said Genya.

Beyond treating malnutrition

For MSF, addressing the crisis requires more than treating children after they have become severely malnourished. Families must also be reached earlier, before food insecurity and other pressures push children into life-threatening conditions.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF MSF counsellor-educator Keturah John engages Adamaâs daughter, Fatima, in a play therapy session at MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Fatima is an inpatient and has been receiving treatment for malnutrition.

"Treating children once they are already severely malnourished saves lives, but we also need to reach families before they get to that point," she said.

Insecurity and displacement, disease outbreaks and economic hardship continue to undermine families' ability to provide adequate food and care. Genya said prevention and treatment must go hand in hand, alongside support for caregivers who bear much of the responsibility for children's recovery.

She added that the pressures pushing children into malnutrition, including insecurity and displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks and the economic crisis, are not easing. Sustained funding is needed not only for nutrition services but also for mental health and psychosocial support, she said. Governments and humanitarian organisations must work to ensure families can access essential assistance before children reach the point of severe malnutrition.

"This is why MSF's work focuses on both prevention and treatment, and why we care for the whole family, including the caregivers at the bedside, through counselling and psychosocial support. This work depends on public support," she said. "Donating to MSF's humanitarian efforts helps our teams keep reaching children across northern Nigeria, treating them early and supporting the families who care for them."

With over 5.4 million children acutely malnourished this year, every contribution makes a difference, she said.

As the world marks World Food Day, the experiences of families in northern Nigeria underline the need to recognise the human cost of food insecurity beyond the physical effects of hunger.

Genya said that addressing the crisis requires supporting caregivers alongside treating children. She said that there is a need to support caregivers through mental health and psychosocial services. She said that behind every child in our facilities is a caregiver, most often a mother, living with fear, anxiety, guilt and exhaustion. Many are worried sick about children left at home without enough food. Their emotional wellbeing shapes whether they can stay engaged in treatment, follow medical advice and keep caring for their child after discharge.

"Recognising and supporting caregivers is therefore key to ending this crisis, not a side issue," she said.

She urged donors to reconsider humanitarian funding cuts and sustain investment in nutrition care, including mental health and psychosocial support, to ensure children and their caregivers receive the help they need. "Behind every statistic is a caregiver's mental health impacted by malnutrition," said Genya.

The fear of losing a sick child, combined with guilt over being separated from other family members, can take a significant toll on their mental well-being. "A mother sits at a hospital bedside, grateful that her child is improving, while worrying that her other children at home have nothing to eat. She is afraid of losing the child in front of her, and guilty about those she can't be with," she said. "These are people showing extraordinary resilience under immense strain, and their stories rarely get told."

"Healing is not only about restoring a child's weight," said Genya. "It is also about restoring hope and resilience to the person who sits at the bedside every day."

World.title: South Africa: Lions Player Dies From Suspected Cardiac Arrest in French Hotel
World.content:
A Lions player has apparently died in a hotel room in France, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

French media are reporting that a Lions player has died in a hotel room on the Île de Ré, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

Île de Ré is an island off the western coast of France, and connected via a bridge to the mainland city of La Rochelle.

According to media reports in France, the player was found unresponsive in a shower cubicle.

Paramedics attempted to resuscitate him but were unsuccessful. He was pronounced dead. The player, in his thirties, was in cardiac arrest when emergency services arrived shortly before 10.30am.

Sources have independently confirmed the news to Daily Maverick, but the player's family have yet to be informed, so his name cannot be released.

It is unclear at this stage whether the Champions Cup match against two-time champions La Rochelle will go ahead, originally scheduled for Saturday, 17 October 2026. DM

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Establishes Six-Month Caretaker Administration in Tigray
World.content:
New admin tasked with restoring security, rebuilding institutions and preparing for elections

Ethiopia's federal government has established a six-month caretaker administration for the Tigray region, assigning it responsibility for restoring security, rebuilding damaged infrastructure and organizing elections intended to return the region to an elected government.

The Council of Ministers established the administration under a regulation following a decision by the House of Federation, which cited Article 62(9) of the Constitution and Article 14(2)(b) of Proclamation No. 359/1995 as the legal basis for establishing an interim administration in the region.



The government said repeated efforts to resolve the conflict in Tigray under the Pretoria peace agreement had failed, blaming the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) for obstructing implementation. It also accused the TPLF leadership of initiating renewed fighting, which it described as the group's fourth failed attempt to wage war.

The government said the new administration was intended to help Tigray emerge from prolonged conflict, restore peace and enable residents to exercise self-government and benefit from development.

Under its mandate, the caretaker administration will work to restore stability, rebuild government institutions and damaged infrastructure, resume interrupted social services and facilitate the return of displaced residents to their homes.

It will also coordinate with federal defense, police and security institutions, as well as regional security forces, to establish stability across the region, including at the local administrative level. Its responsibilities include facilitating the disarmament and reintegration of armed groups and restructuring the region's security apparatus.

A central objective is to establish conditions for free and transparent elections within six months, allowing Tigray to resume its place as a regular component of Ethiopia's federal system under an elected government.

The administration will also coordinate media activities, organize public forums and undertake measures intended to promote reconciliation, rebuild public confidence and prepare residents for reconstruction and development.

The government said the caretaker administration must base its activities on Ethiopia's national interests and territorial integrity, as well as the fundamental interests of the people of Tigray.

Its authority will be limited to providing routine regional services and creating conditions for the next election. It will not undertake matters with longer-term strategic implications, the government said, and will operate under the direction and supervision of the federal government.

The administration's senior officials are Asefa Abraha Hagos, chief executive for administration and public services; Tewodros Aregay Woldeselassie (PhD), chief executive for the economy and reconstruction; Gebre Egziabher Beyene Hailu (Brig. Gen.), chief executive for security and peace; and Redae Hailuom Woldeselassie, chief executive for political affairs and public organization.

Shishay Amare (PhD) was appointed mayor of Mekele, the regional capital.

The federal government will provide direction, support and oversight for the officials' activities, according to the announcement.

World.title: Malawi: Gold Rush or Gold Bust? Malawi's Smuggling Crackdown Faces Credibility Test
World.content:
Malawi's latest bid to turn gold into a lifeline for its struggling economy is facing uncomfortable questions about the evidence on which it has been built.

A state-backed scheme designed to intercept gold before it is smuggled out of the country rests on a headline-grabbing claim that $100 million worth of the precious metal is lost annually through illegal trade. Yet, according to an analysis by Collins Mtika for the Mail & Guardian and the Centre for Investigative Journalism Malawi, the figure has never been publicly explained.

The programme, spearheaded by the Malawi Mining Investment Company (Mamico), aims to buy gold from artisanal miners operating at roughly 100 sites nationwide, funnel it through buying centres in Lilongwe, Kasungu and Nkhotakota, and ultimately sell it to the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM).



But a closer examination of the numbers reveals a troubling inconsistency.

Earlier this year, Mamico reported findings from a month-long assessment which estimated that more than $700 million worth of gold was being lost each year through illicit activity and identified 81 illegal mining sites.

The latest estimate is seven times lower. At the same time, the number of mining locations linked to the programme has increased to around 100.

The analysis asks a simple question: which number is accurate?

Without a published methodology, there is no way to test either claim. For a project requiring hundreds of billions of kwacha in public and private financing, that gap matters.

Mamico says it will need K85 billion to fund its first three months of operations and around K300 billion annually thereafter. The company has enlisted FDH Bank and NBS Bank as partners, but key parts of the commercial framework are still unresolved.

Most notably, the arrangement depends on an offtake agreement with the RBM that has yet to be concluded.

The uncertainty extends beyond the figures.

The analysis points to potential duplication between Mamico's planned operations and an existing RBM gold-purchasing initiative run through the Export Development Fund.

By September, that programme had already acquired about 1.63 tonnes of gold, raising questions about whether the government is creating parallel structures within the same market.

There is also a more fundamental challenge. Artisanal miners will only sell through official channels if they can secure competitive prices and prompt payment.

If unofficial traders offer better deals, the incentive to bypass the formal system remains intact, regardless of how many buying centres are established.

Close 

Yet the pressure to make the project work is immense.

Malawi's foreign exchange position remains fragile. Official reserves stood at $600.6 million in September, enough to cover just 2.4 months of imports, below the internationally recognised three-month benchmark.

Gold has emerged as one of the few commodities capable of generating substantial foreign currency earnings. In April alone, the RBM exported 589.95 kilogrammes of locally purchased gold valued at $75.09 million.

For ministers and policymakers, the allure is obvious: bring more gold into formal channels and bolster dwindling reserves.

But as Mtika's analysis suggests, the success of the strategy may hinge less on ambition than on transparency.

Until Mamico discloses how it calculated its smuggling estimates, clarifies how it will coexist with existing state-run gold programmes, and produces verifiable data on production, purchases and exports, the initiative will continue to face a credibility problem.

For now, the government's gold rush is asking the public to trust numbers it has yet to prove.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia's Govt Welcomes Election Timetable and Urges Political Dialogue
World.content:
Mogadishu — Somalia's federal government on Thursday welcomed an election timetable announced by the Independent National Electoral and Boundaries Commission, covering elections for both houses of parliament and the president.

In a statement dated October 15, 2026, the government described the timetable as an important step towards implementing the electoral process and strengthening democracy in the country.

The government said it had spent the past 18 months offering opportunities for consultation and negotiations aimed at helping Somali political stakeholders reach agreement on key national issues, particularly the electoral process.

It said the consultations would continue, adding that it remained committed to securing a broad-based understanding among the country's political actors.

The government described its support for the election timetable and its continued commitment to dialogue as complementary efforts that would help preserve stability, strengthen national unity and safeguard citizens' constitutional rights.

It called on all political stakeholders to engage in consultations in good faith and with a sense of national responsibility, urging them to work together to ensure peaceful elections that strengthen public confidence and Somalia's state institutions.

The statement comes amid political differences over Somalia's electoral process, including disagreements over the proposed arrangements and calls for an inclusive political agreement.

World.title: South Africa: Masemola Back As Police Commissioner After Ramaphosa Lifts Suspension
World.content:
Masemola was placed on precautionary suspension in April 2026 after appearing in court on charges linked to a R360-million police health services tender.

Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane has served as acting National Police Commissioner, and Ramaphosa says she served with distinction.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has lifted the suspension of National Police Commissioner General Fannie Masemola, who will resume his full duties on Monday, 19 October.

The Presidency made the announcement on Friday.

Ramaphosa and Masemola agreed in April 2026 that Masemola would be deemed to be on precautionary suspension. This followed his appearance in the Pretoria Magistrate's Court on charges of contravening the Public Finance Management Act. The charges were linked to a R360-million police health services tender awarded to Medicare24.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

National Director of Public Prosecutions Andy Mothibi ordered the charges to be withdrawn after a review found no reasonable prospects of a successful prosecution on 15 September. The Pretoria Magistrate's Court formally withdrew the charges on 22 September.

Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane, the police's chief financial officer, was appointed acting National Police Commissioner when Masemola was suspended.

Ramaphosa thanked her and said she served with distinction in the interim.

"The President welcomes the National Police Commissioner on his return to his full duties," presidential spokesperson Vincent Magwenya said.

The South African Policing Union had urged Ramaphosa to lift the suspension after the charges were withdrawn. After the withdrawal, Masemola told the media that he had not heard from the president.

The National Prosecuting Authority has also referred the case to the oversight judge of the Investigating Directorate Against Corruption, to look into whether there was any malice behind the original charges.

World.title: Jerry Seinfeld turns tables on radical anti-Israel agitators after chaotic Chicago stunt backfires

Comedian Jerry Seinfeld turned the tables on anti-Israel hecklers who attempted to derail his Chicago performance last Friday, mocking the protesters as security removed them from the venue.

Viral video from the confrontation shows activists shouting at Seinfeld at the Chicago Theatre, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza and alleging that American taxpayer dollars are funding the deaths of thousands of civilians.

"Twenty-two thousand Palestinians who are children now are killed with our taxpayer money, and you’re making jokes!" a woman shouted in clips posted online.

JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE'

Seinfeld then dances on stage and mocks the protesters with sarcastic remarks, calling himself "racist" and saying, "It’s a genocide. I’m into it." He also joked that he would find out how much the protesters paid for their tickets and send the money directly to Israel.

As security personnel escorted the demonstrators out of the auditorium, one audience member shouted, "Rough her up!"

The Anti-War Committee Chicago and the Chicago branch of the US Palestinian Community Network have taken credit for organizing the disruption, writing on Instagram, "Friday’s disruption sent a clear message: Those who defend Israel’s genocide and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and throughout Palestine will be met with protest and are not welcome on Chicago’s stages without opposition."

COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT

Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team for comment but did not hear back.

The altercation is the latest in a string of protests targeting the 72-year-old Jewish comedian over his staunch defense of Israel.

ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTERS LABEL MAMDANI A 'TRAITOR,' ACCUSE HIM OF 'GENOCIDE' OUTSIDE OCT 7 VIGIL

Comedian and media analyst Tim Young told Fox News Digital he believes protesters are paying top dollar to hijack comedy shows for viral attention rather than political discourse.

"They know that once they start yelling, everyone will whip their cameras out, and it is a very direct interaction and maybe one of the only direct interactions protesters get to have with celebrities and with the internet," Young said.

"If you are in a very intimate environment where everyone is quiet, listening to one person, you will be heard. And, so, that's what they're taking advantage of here."

Young compared the disruptions at Seinfeld's shows to protests at political rallies, arguing that some activists are willing to pay steep ticket prices to confront the comedian.

"It seems like people are going to Jerry Seinfeld's shows like they're going to a Trump rally to protest," Young said. "They wanted to get Jerry's attention. They want to, for some reason, they're very, very adamant on getting him to react to the Israel-Palestine conflict."

Young also linked the disruptions to Seinfeld's past criticism of performing at universities.

30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS

"It's why Jerry doesn't like to go and perform at college campuses. And he said he hates performing at college campuses specifically for that reason," Young said.

"He doesn't want to get into the political thing. He doesn't want to have protesters yelling back and forth with him. It's a waste of the rest of the audience's time, and he knows that."

In May 2024, dozens of students walked out during Seinfeld's commencement address at Duke University, some holding Palestinian flags.

Seinfeld returned to the university in September 2025 to introduce freed Israeli hostage Omer Shem Tov at a campus event, where he addressed anti-Israel protests, saying, "Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews."

QUIET PART OUT LOUD: ANTI-ISRAEL MOBS WANT ONE STATE CALLED 'PALESTINE,' ERASING ISRAEL

"By saying ‘Free Palestine,’ you’re not admitting what you really think," he said. "So, it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest."

Seinfeld also faced controversy overseas last month when several European acts withdrew from the inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Lisbon, Portugal, where he is scheduled to headline later this year.

The acts did not name Seinfeld directly in their withdrawal statements, but some cited concerns about the Israel-Gaza conflict. One performer said someone involved in the festival defended ideas they considered indefensible.

Young, who previously dismissed efforts to cancel Seinfeld over his support for Israel, argued that protesters target the billionaire comedian because of his influence and celebrity status.

World.title: I lost half my right lung to cancer. Pope Leo's diagnosis gives me hope
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

When Pope Leo told the crowd in St. Peter's Square on Sunday that doctors had found "a small, localized nodule" in his lung, the reassurances came fast. Most nodules are benign, media medical experts quickly said. Probably nothing to worry about.

I heard the same reassurances about my own lung not long ago. They were wrong then, and on Tuesday the Vatican confirmed they were wrong now. The nodule was adenocarcinoma, lung cancer. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Holy Father's right lung through a few small incisions, guided by a camera rather than an open chest, and he was back in his room the same afternoon.

POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS

That is almost exactly what happened to me. Half of my right lung was removed just 12 months ago, and I was running just four weeks after that. So, my first reaction when I heard the pope's diagnosis was not dread. It was hope.

I was 43, a mother of four, a daily runner, and the daughter of a lung doctor. The morning I learned I had lung cancer, I had already completed a six-mile run without a hint that anything was wrong. I had no symptoms. Under current guidelines, I was not supposed to be at risk, and I did not qualify for screening.

POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS

My diagnosis came from a scan I chose, not from a symptom. My husband and I have always leaned toward proactive testing, and at his urging I scheduled what I assumed would be a baseline full-body scan, paid for out of pocket. It showed a 3.8-centimeter nodule on my right lung. Initial advice from the reading radiologist recommended to follow-up if symptoms occurred. But with a father as a lung doctor and a friend as a lung radiologist, they pushed me to follow up sooner. The new low dose CT of my chest showed the mass had grown in just two months. But that scan led to a diagnosis of stage 1B lung cancer and, like the pope, to surgery to remove it. Still, no symptoms ever appeared.

Four weeks to the day after my operation, I was on a plane. I was running again within weeks. Caught early and handled by a skilled medical team and a surgeon who does this every day, lung cancer is not a death sentence. It is a survivable disease, a fixable problem. If the pope keeps his November trip to South America, he will board that plane about as far out from surgery as I was.

DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH

So the gloom I see in my text threads with Catholic friends this week is misplaced. What should worry Americans is something else entirely. The pope's cancer was found during a routine checkup. Mine was found because I paid for a scan no one recommended. Most Americans get neither.

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States and one of the most expensive cancers to treat, because it is usually found late. Current guidelines recommend screening only for adults ages 50 to 80 with a heavy smoking history. Fewer than one in five people who qualify ever get the scan. And nearly two-thirds of people diagnosed with lung cancer would not have qualified at all. I am one of them.

POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS

Stage at diagnosis is the strongest predictor of both survival and cost. Found at stage I, five-year survival can exceed 90%. Yet most cases are still found after the disease has spread, when curative treatment becomes unlikely.

There is a fix on the table. The Saving Health by Identifying Risk for Americans (SHIRA) Act, a draft bill now circulating in the White House, HHS and Congress, would make lung cancer screening free to the patient under Medicare — no copay, no deductible. It would cover veterans exposed to burn pits, guarantee a first scan to cancer survivors and those with a family history, and require Medicare to modernize who counts as "high risk" so that never-smokers, like me, stop being invisible. It builds a path toward age-based screening after 40, the way we already screen for breast and colorectal cancer.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

I was fortunate. A preventive scan, a persistent friend and father, and an early diagnosis gave me a future I might not otherwise have had. The pope was fortunate too: a routine check found his cancer before he felt a thing. Luck should not decide who survives lung cancer. Screening policy should.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I am praying for the pope this week, and I am confident. I would like every American to have the same reason for confidence he does.

World.title: Josh Jacobs sues police to permanently seal video evidence in battery case against him
World.content:
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs filed a lawsuit against the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department, seeking to have evidence in his battery case permanently sealed.

According to the criminal complaint, Jacobs was accused of throwing his ex-girlfriend onto the ground and damaging her phone, and video would show the portion that occurred in the garage. The NFL is attempting to obtain the video as part of its own investigation, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport.

Jacobs' complaint says the police should be prohibited from publicly releasing "descriptions, images, audio recordings, video recordings, statements, communications, or other materials" whose disclosure might threaten the woman’s "privacy, dignity, safety, emotional well-being, or ability to obtain closure."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The complaint also notes that public sports figures have recently been targeted for robberies and other related property crimes, and that releasing the video would reveal details of the garage’s interior that might put Jacobs at risk.

"The public availability of (Jacobs’) schedule or travel information increases the risk that persons could identify periods when (Jacobs) is away from home and use released information concerning the residence, garage, access points, security arrangements, or property to target the property," the complaint says. "Widespread public dissemination of those details would materially increase (Jacobs’) vulnerability to theft, burglary, robbery, trespass, or other targeted criminal conduct."

Jacobs pleaded no contest to battery and criminal damage to property from the May 23 incident, which were both misdemeanors. Jacobs was also ordered to have no contact with the woman involved, pay restitution, attend counseling and be under supervision for one year.

DAN ORLOVSKY ANNOUNCES 'UNIMAGINABLE TRAGEDY' AS BROTHER-IN-LAW DIES SUDDENLY AT AGE 43

That video hasn’t been released, and lawyers representing the woman filed a motion last month asking that the evidence be sealed.

The veteran running back remains on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, though time spent there would count toward a suspension. The matter remains under review by the league's personal conduct policy and there's no timeline for a decision.

The NFL’s baseline suspension for a first-time domestic violence offense is six games without pay as part of its conduct policy. The suspension could increase depending on factors including the involvement of a weapon, repeated striking and more.

World.title: Controversy over Abdul El-Sayed's family ties to Muslim Brotherhood ignored, downplayed by liberal media
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Several legacy news organizations have not covered allegations involving the family of Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

El-Sayed's denial of having any family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood has drawn questions after several social media posts from his half-sister suggested that members of their family, including their mother, were active in the Islamist group.

ABC and CBS had not mentioned the allegations on their morning or evening news broadcasts as of Thursday, Oct. 15, according to a Fox News Digital review of Grabien transcripts.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

The allegations were finally mentioned on CBS’ morning show on Friday, but simply to note that El-Sayed has denied claims by his Republican opponent Mike Rogers.

CNN and MS NOW have similarly not aired dedicated news reports about the allegations as of Thursday, despite several hours of daily programming per transcripts. A conservative panelist made a brief reference to the controversy on Monday's "CNN This Morning," which went without acknowledgment by host Audie Cornish. On Thursday night, CNN's Abby Phillip disputed concerns raised by another conservative guest, arguing that the allegations did not establish a connection between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood.

"Abdul was not raised by his biological mother," Phillip said. "His parents divorced when he was 3. He doesn't have that kind of relationship with her. So the idea that he would be tarred and feathered for a Muslim Brotherhood connection that frankly A. is not verified, and B., does not actually say anything about how he was raised here in Michigan."

"He said to his knowledge, he is not aware of any connections with the Muslim Brotherhood. And you know what? You can take that up with him, but the insinuation is that he is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood," she later added.

On Friday morning, conservative guest Jesse Arm told CNN viewers that El-Sayed’s family had "deep ties" to the Muslim Brotherhood in a comment that was met with pushback.

"We should really point out there’s also a lot of CNN fact checking, and specifically on the mother and brother, what he has responded to," anchor Erica Hill said. "There is so much for all candidates that is in their past and needs fact-checking."

MS NOW's most direct reference to the allegations came Monday night when guest host Jacob Soboroff knocked El-Sayed's Republican opponent for focusing on the "smears" against the Muslim Democrat, including tying El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.

The New York Times, widely dubbed "The Paper of Record," has not published a single report on the subject this week, according to search results on its website.

NBC was the only broadcast network identified in the review as having covered the allegations, having questioned El-Sayed directly in two interviews.

ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

During an interview that aired on Sunday's "Meet the Press," NBC's Kristen Welker asked El-Sayed if he could "set the record straight" on allegations that he and his family had connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. He firmly replied, "No," before suggesting his GOP rival was using Islamophobic attacks against him and his family.

However, according to social media posts made by his half-sister Eman Abdelhadi, members of their family, including their mother, had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college #respect," Abdelhadi wrote in a 2012 X post, as first reported by the Washington Free Beacon.

Their mother, Fatten Elkomy, had attended Egypt's Alexandria University, which, according to a report from the Brookings Institution, had strong Muslim Brotherhood activity back in the 1970s.

EL-SAYED’S HALF SISTER OFFERED OCT 7 ‘BLESSING,’ ONE YEAR AFTER HAMAS ATTACK: ‘ALLAHU AKBAR’

In another 2012 post, Abdelhadi, a professor at the University of Chicago, wrote: "My family has long been MB, but I've always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively."

In a third post from 2013, she wrote, "Praying for all my family that supports the #MB in #Egypt. Lie low, stay safe."

On Wednesday's "NBC Nightly News," El-Sayed was confronted by NBC's Tom Llamas about how Abdelhadi's posts appear to contradict his own denial to Welker.

"It's funny to me," El-Sayed responded. "I was born in 1984 down the street in Rochester Hills. I was raised here in Michigan, went to the University of Michigan, rebuilt the health department in this city, led the health department in this county — and you want to ask me about what's happening in Egypt in 1970? Are you serious?"

"I get it, but you were asked a question, and you gave an answer," Llamas responded.

"I have no ties, we have no ties," El-Sayed said, reiterating his denial.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

The Democratic hopeful told Llamas he hadn't had conversations with his mother about her alleged Muslim Brotherhood activity and accused the anchor of using "hearsay evidence from a tweet."

"That's just not serious," El-Sayed said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"But you've also gone after the president for truthfulness and when people ask you a question, do you expect the truth?" Llamas then asked.

"Are you insinuating that somehow I was lying?" El-Sayed fired back.

"I don't know, that's why I'm asking," Llamas responded.

"And I'm telling you that I was not," El-Sayed told him.

Representatives for ABC, CBS, CNN, MS NOW and The New York Times did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: Amazon About You may know you a little too well
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Amazon knows what you buy, what you search for and even what you tell its shopping assistant. Now, the company is giving you a look at the personality profile it has built from all that information. When I checked my own Amazon About You profile, I found 81 results, including a reference to my mother that caught me off guard. The feature brings together details about your shopping habits and preferences. Some are helpful. Others might make you wonder how Amazon reached those conclusions in the first place.

Shoppers are now sharing screenshots of descriptions that range from funny to completely inaccurate. Amazon says the feature helps improve shopping recommendations. However, it also raises an interesting privacy question. How much should a retailer know about you, and how much control do you really have over that information?

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

What is Amazon About You?

Amazon introduced About You in May 2026, although the feature has recently attracted widespread attention as shoppers share their profiles on social media. Amazon has personalized shopping recommendations for years. If you bought a coffee maker, you probably noticed suggestions for filters or other accessories soon afterward. That kind of recommendation has become familiar to anyone who shops online. Now, Amazon is taking personalization further with About You, a section that shows shoppers what the company believes about their interests and preferences.

According to Amazon's announcement, the feature draws on information from several sources, including your purchase history, product reviews and items saved to Lists. Searches and conversations with Alexa for Shopping can also influence what Amazon learns.

For example, someone who regularly buys dairy-free milk might receive recommendations for other dairy-free products. A shopper researching gardening supplies could start seeing suggestions for fertilizer or companion plants. That sounds useful enough. However, Amazon can also develop assumptions about your personal preferences from individual purchases or short-lived interests. That's where things can get awkward.

Amazon's About You feature is already amusing shoppers

Some shoppers have started sharing screenshots of their Amazon profiles on social media. The results range from remarkably accurate to unintentionally hilarious. One Threads user discovered that Amazon had included the description "flat buttocks" in her profile. "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I'm literally speechless," she wrote.

She even acknowledged that the assessment wasn't entirely wrong. Still, it's hard to imagine anyone asking an online retailer for that particular evaluation. Meanwhile, another shopper shared a profile describing an obsession with minimalist, one-bag travel and a preference for Anker charging products. The shopper confirmed that Amazon had accurately identified those interests. A different user discovered that Amazon had recorded a "one-time specialty cheese exploration." The response was simple: "guilty."

Other shoppers have shared descriptions such as "has no friends" and "cannot keep real plants alive." One woman even reported that Amazon had described her as a "fifty-year-old man." These are the kinds of assumptions that can leave you wondering whether Amazon knows you at all.

My own profile included some remarkably specific observations. Amazon said I "do not like scary movies," "value professional grade audio equipment," "prefer dark chocolate treats" and "enjoy swimming." It even noted my regular fresh flower purchases. But one entry really surprised me. Amazon claimed my mother had stayed at a hotel with another person, whom it identified by name, and had a negative experience. I certainly didn't expect to find that kind of information about a family member in my shopping profile.

These examples show how an algorithm can turn shopping activity into surprisingly specific personal descriptions. Of course, Amazon's conclusions may be incomplete or inaccurate. Buying something for a friend, for example, doesn't necessarily mean you have any personal interest in that product.

YOUR PHONE MAY REVEAL DOCTOR, CHURCH AND PHARMACY VISITS

Why Amazon knows so much about your shopping habits

Every time you interact with Amazon, you potentially give the company another clue about your preferences. A product search can suggest an interest, while a purchase provides a stronger signal about something you wanted at that moment. Amazon also uses information from its AI shopping assistant. If you tell Alexa for Shopping that your cat prefers a particular flavor of food, Amazon can use that detail to recommend similar products later.

According to the company, these interactions help make recommendations more relevant. However, a single purchase might reflect a temporary need rather than a lasting preference. Think about buying an unusual gift for a relative. You might suddenly find Amazon treating that purchase as evidence of a personal hobby. That raises another concern. Some purchases can indicate sensitive interests involving health, relationships or other aspects of your private life. Even when Amazon draws an incorrect conclusion, you may still want to remove it from your shopping profile.

How to see what Amazon knows about you

Amazon makes About You available through its Shopping app, mobile website and desktop website. You can review the information the company has associated with your profile and make changes.

On the Amazon Shopping app or mobile website

Open the Amazon Shopping app or visit Amazon.com on your phone.

Sign in to your Amazon account.

Tap the Me tab.

Select your name.

Tap About You.

Review the details Amazon has collected or inferred about your preferences.

If you don't see About You using those steps, try this alternate route in the Amazon Shopping app:

Tap You or the person icon at the bottom of the app.

Select Account.

Under Account Settings, look for Shopping preferences.

Tap About You.

Select Manage your information if that option appears.

On Amazon's desktop website

Visit Amazon.com and sign in.

Move your cursor over your name above Account & Lists in the upper-right corner.

Click your name or choose Who's shopping? Select a profile.

Select About You.

Review the information displayed in your profile.

How to remove personal information from Amazon About You

Here's where I would spend a few minutes if you use Amazon regularly. The company says About You lets you correct preferences, provide feedback and remove information you don't want used for personalization.

Review and delete unwanted preferences

Open About You using the steps above.

Select a category to review the details Amazon has recorded or inferred about you.

Find an entry you want to delete.

Select Remove for that entry.

When the confirmation prompt appears, select Remove again. You don't need to provide a reason.

Repeat these steps for other unwanted entries.

If you want to correct a detail instead of removing it, open the entry and look for an edit or feedback option. Make your changes and follow the prompts to save them. Amazon hasn't established that every account will show identical editing controls. The available options may depend on the information displayed. Removing a detail from About You changes how Amazon uses that preference for personalization. It does not necessarily erase the original purchase, search or conversation from every Amazon system.

How to reduce what Amazon uses for recommendations

Editing your About You profile is a useful starting point. However, you should also review the activity that influences Amazon's suggestions.

Remove items from your Amazon browsing history

Amazon provides browsing history controls that can help reduce recommendations based on products you've viewed.

Sign in to Amazon.com.

Open Browsing History from your account or browsing history controls.

Review recently viewed products.

Choose Remove from view for items you don't want included in your visible browsing history, when that option appears.

Look for Manage history if you want to adjust additional browsing history settings.

Removing a product from the browsing history display should not be treated as confirmation that Amazon has deleted every record of the interaction.

Adjust Amazon's shopping recommendations

Amazon also provides controls for managing recommendations associated with past purchases.

Sign in to your Amazon account.

Visit Amazon's recommendation preferences help page.

Follow the available links to your recommendation settings.

Review purchases or other activity that may influence your recommendations.

Exclude eligible items from recommendations when Amazon provides that option.

This can be particularly helpful when you've purchased gifts or products that have nothing to do with your interests.

Review Alexa shopping interactions

If you regularly use Alexa for Shopping, consider what you share during those conversations. Amazon says the assistant can remember details you provide and use them to improve future shopping experiences. Ask "What do you know about me?" to review the preferences Alexa can describe. Then use About You to correct or remove unwanted details. For additional privacy controls, review your Alexa privacy settings and voice history in the Alexa app or your Amazon account. Deleting voice recordings and removing shopping preferences are separate actions, so check both.

Can you completely delete your Amazon shopping profile?

Amazon provides ways to edit preferences and manage certain recommendation signals. However, the company hasn't established that removing everything displayed in About You permanently deletes all underlying information. Your purchase history, for example, can remain associated with your account even after you exclude an item from recommendations. Amazon may retain certain transaction records for operational or legal reasons. Also, About You is only one part of Amazon's broader personalization system. Correcting an assumption doesn't necessarily stop Amazon from generating new recommendations based on future shopping activity. If privacy is your priority, review your browsing history, recommendation settings and Alexa privacy controls rather than relying exclusively on the new profile page.

Kurt's key takeaways

I've always found Amazon's recommendations fascinating, but seeing 81 personal details in my own profile was an eye-opener. Some were surprisingly accurate. Others, including information about my mother, left me wondering how Amazon reached those conclusions. I appreciate being able to review and remove these details, but I'd like more transparency about what happens to that information afterward. My advice? Take a few minutes to check your own Amazon About You profile. You might be surprised by what the company thinks it knows about you.

Would you be comfortable with Amazon building a personality profile from everything you buy and search for, or has online shopping personalization gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: The College Football Playoff is sacrificing its soul to be an ATM for conferences with expansion to 24 teams
World.content:
INDIANAPOLIS - We are on the cusp of the college football playoff once again undergoing a drastic change in teams allowed into the postseason, and there are plenty of fans across the sport asking why it's needed.

That question, along with plenty of others, is the catalyst of the most impactful kerfuffle we have seen in recent memory involving the college football universe.

But, the answer to said argument is pretty simple when you peel through the layers of talking points each conference commissioner will recite over the next few weeks.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF PREPARING EXPANSION TO 24 TEAMS IN 2027, WITH MORE GAMES COMING TO CAMPUSES ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Money.

This entire ordeal can be traced back to the infamous BCS formula, which captivated audiences with computer rankings that led to fans essentially yelling at computers at seasons end.

INSIDE CFP EXPANSION BATTLE AS SEC, BIG TEN AND TV NETWORKS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S NEXT BIG MOVE

Fast forward to 2026, college football fans are vastly united in their stance that a jump from 12 to 24 teams is just not warranted during this current era of the sport. Sure, we are watching schools across the country make tough decisions about the ramifications that have come with increased spending within the sport.

Because schools are now spending a large amount of money on piecing together rosters, with college football being the main driving force in universities paying their athletic department bills, conference officials have decided that they will use the College Football Playoff as their own line of credit to help pay the bills that keep accumulating.

College Athletics has a spending problem, and CFP is the ATM

If you haven’t noticed over the past five years, we are now living in a professional sports model, within what was once described as amateur sports. The amount of money that is needed to keep up with rival schools has shot through the perceived roof, with some programs spending upwards of $50 million this season to compete for a CFP title.

The thinking behind the closed doors of universities mostly centers around the idea that if they are going to spend that amount of money for a roster, they need more assurances that they will also receive a spot in the postseason, or at least in some way justify this thinking.

COACHES PUSH FOR 24-TEAM CFP, AS COLLEGE FOOTBALL HEADS TOWARDS PARTICIPATION TROPHY TERRITORY

Now, when a team finishes the regular season with an 8-4 record, they'll be able to hang a banner inside the football facility that reads 'College Football Playoff First Round', which they know is not the flex that it has been over the past two seasons.

Yes, remember that we are only two years into the already expanded playoff system, after starting at four teams.

Now, with a straight face, those in favor of expanding the playoff want you to think it's anything other than a money grab, or justification, during an era in which schools are having to find different ways to raise capital.

On Thursday, after 34 days of negotiating, ESPN formally presented CFP committee members a formal offer of how much it is willing to spend for the extra games that would come from increasing the amount of teams by 12.

Yes, this move would also be the end of conference title weekend across college football, though I could see this move actually opening up an avenue for Group of Six leagues to continue putting on a show for fans, if they chose to.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S MEGA ROSTERS AREN’T DELIVERING A RETURN ON INVESTMENT AS LSU, TEXAS A&M AND OREGON PROVE

According to sources, there was no vote taken on Thursday by members of the committee that are made up of conference commissioners and Notre Dame. And, there were some questions raised by those same committee members about whether they should take this to the open market, even though they essentially know how much other networks would be willing to offer.

"Constructive discussions with ESPN continued this week," the CFP said in a statement. "We have enjoyed a strong partnership with ESPN since our inception and are appreciative of the productive dialogue we have had throughout the negotiating period and continuing over the last several days.

"We will provide additional updates on the matters of future format and media rights when appropriate."

What's really on the line with future expansion?

It's simple: the regular season.

Three weeks ago, I watched Ohio State lose to Texas in what was a thrilling game in Austin, with the Longhorns providing themselves with some cushion in case they were to drop two games over the remainder of this season.

Last weekend, even though folks wanted to proclaim loudly that this game did not really mean much in terms of punishment pertaining to the regular season, Alabama and Georgia battled until the final seconds of what turned into a heavyweight fight in Tuscaloosa.

Sure, Alabama can afford another loss this season and still make the playoff. But, two losses? Nope, the Crimson Tide would most likely be on the outside looking in, while someone else from the SEC grabs their spot in the postseason.

What if Texas were to lose on Saturday to a Florida team that will be heading to Austin with consecutive losses? Well, we'd be having a serious conversation about Steve Sarkisian missing the CFP with a roster that costs more than $40 million this season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In the eyes of the conferences, and CFP committee, the allure of a postseason bid is the carrot that would dangle in front of them so that fans would look the other way at the nonsense this creates for the football played in September or October.

Sure, fans will continue to show up, but the sport will have officially lowered the stakes of the intense showdowns we witness on a weekly basis across the sport during a regular season.

The point is that in this new format, games that take place in September, or even early October, will feel more meaningless than ever. Showdowns this weekend, like Missouri versus Ole Miss or Notre Dame versus BYU, will be looked upon with a different eye by those attending or watching at home.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Any team with a 9-3 record, or maybe even 8-4, who calls the SEC or Big Ten home will no longer feel the tension that comes with sitting at home to watch the CFP selection show in hopes of pulling off a miracle and being selected by the committee.

We have officially lost the plot to what made college football so great, with every dollar that this new deal creates for every conference that makes up the sport.

If they actually cared about what is best for college football, those in charge of helping the sport grow would have read the room and kept this playoff at 12 teams, or 16 at most.



But, since everyone deserves an trophy to justify the amount of money they are spending to field a football team, we are now just waiting on CFP members to sign off on creating 12 more spots so everyone can feel like they accomplished something.

Hang that banner. I hope that 8-5 season made you feel better, and paid off when the check clears.

World.title: Lindsey Vonn kicks off birthday weekend with a European bikini beach day, my Bob Dylan memory & money
World.content:
Welcome to Screencaps, "America's Best Daily Column," as named by the readers. Screencaps, which publishes seven-days-a-week, is a mix of sports, pop culture, and emails from sane readers from around the world. This column isn't for the coastal elites. Give us a week to steal your heart. Our track record is pretty good. Let's have some fun.

I have to give Lindsey Vonn credit...she's not skipping days in the gym

At 41, Vonn could say screw it. She could start a podcast, sit on her ass all day yapping about random topics while crushing red wine. Instead, she's been in the gym staying fit. Instead of using her platform to sit around her house yelling about politics and everything else that these losers do with their platforms, she's doing exactly what multi-millionaires should be doing — she's having fun in Europe blowing some money.

It just happens that this weekend, Lindsey turns 42. Hell yeah, girl, go have fun with the new boyfriend. Live life.

Why I don't think a 24-team playoff will increase the chances schools schedule tough out-of-conference games during the regular season

What incentive do schools have unless ESPN is going to throw a massive pile of cash at them? This year, Indiana's football season didn't begin until Oct. 10 when it faced its first road test at Nebraska. Yes, there was the home game against Northwestern that was way closer than it should've been, but let's not act like facing Northwestern, in this era, is considered a massive game.

These schools don't have the depth to get through these seasons as is, why make it any tougher? Cignetti knows the formula. Treat the first 3-4 games as the preseason. Get your transfer NIL quarterback acquainted. Build continuity with the playoff as the target. Indiana had to win three games to win the title in January. With the 24-game tournament, it would now need to win four games.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS IN 2027, WITH MORE GAMES COMING TO CAMPUSES ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Why play harder early games? That's more chances for injuries. More chances to lose your quarterback. More wear and tear on bodies. More travel (maybe, if your team actually leaves home). Unless we go to two super conferences and ban games against the MAC, Conference USA, etc., Indiana isn't changing a thing.

Quick thoughts:

I don't want to hear college football complain when it turns itself into college basketball. There is absolutely no reason, unless you're a degenerate, to get worked up over a regular-season college basketball game. 8-4 Iowa would've made the tournament last year. Let that sink in. CFB wants to own that open weekend between AFC/NFC weekend and the Super Bowl – badly. Personally, I don't need college football in late January. Enough already. This year, the championship will be played on Jan. 25. I love college football, but by then, I'm burnt out. Now I'm left wondering how CFB will fill conference championship weekend because there's ZERO chance they don't play games the weekend after Thanksgiving. Do they move rivalry week into December? I don't see that happening. What sells more Thanksgiving weekend advertising: Random SEC games or Bama-Auburn or Ohio State-Michigan? If you're a top-level college talent who might be a first round draft pick, how are you going to feel about being required to play more high-level games and risk more wear on your body?

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANSION IS NOTHING MORE THAN A DESPERATE FINANCIAL BAILOUT DISGUISED AS PROGRESS

World.title: Trump looms as tensions flare in final Maine Senate debate
World.content:
BANGOR, Maine — The marathon of debates in the Maine Senate race has ended, but there is still one unanswered question: Just how large will President Donald Trump loom in November?

That question was at the center of the clashes between Democrat Troy Jackson and longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins as they faced off in four debates over the last two weeks, including a finale Thursday hosted by Maine Public Broadcasting Network, the Portland Press Herald and NBC affiliate WCSH of Portland.

Jackson is betting voters’ views of Trump, who has never won Maine, will dominate their views of this Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.

He repeatedly tied Collins to Trump throughout all four debates. Collins, meanwhile, tried to appeal to Mainers who want a senator willing to break with his or her party.

“I voted against my own party more often than any other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said during the final debate. “That is not something that Troy could ever say. He’s going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position, no matter what. We have lost a lot of the centrists, and one reason I’m running again is we need people who will work across party lines.”

Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate Thursday in Bangor. Gregory Rec / Portland Press Herald via Getty

Jackson countered: “The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there. That has happened time and time again.”

Trump’s policies were intertwined with the major topics covered in all four debates, including high costs, the war in Iran, immigration enforcement and an ongoing trade war with Canada, which Maine borders.

On Thursday, Collins was also pressed about her support for some Trump Cabinet officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She said she didn’t regret having voted to confirm him while noting that she disagrees with Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism. Collins said Kennedy has helped release more funds from a program to help low-income Mainers buy heating oil amid soaring prices.

Jackson, meanwhile, said he would vote to convict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on impeachment charges.

“But that’s not my focus,” he quickly added. “My focus is delivering healthcare, prescription drugs, child care, the things that Mainers need right now more than ever, and getting out of the Iran war so we can stabilize prices.”

Tensions were high after four debates in rapid succession. This one was the first in front of a live audience, with roughly 200 people gathered in a theater at Husson University.

Around 20 minutes into the debate, a young man stood and shouted about his concerns about data centers, exclaiming that he was scared for the future.

“Thirty years for what?” the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the theater, referring to Collins’ time in the Senate.

Collins claimed the protester was a Jackson supporter, and Jackson remarked, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”

While the protester questioned her decades in the Senate, Collins has argued that her seniority makes her an effective advocate for Maine. She often touts her role as chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, arguing she has helped bring home huge sums of federal money to fund projects in the state.

Collins stressed that she has broken with Trump on some key issues, noting she voted against Trump’s sweeping “big, beautiful” tax and spending law last year, though she did vote to allow the measure to proceed on the floor.

“I nevertheless voted against the bill, even though it was the president’s top legislative priority. I’ve also voted nine times against the president on the Iran war,” she said.

Jackson has argued that Collins could have done more to oppose the military action.

Asked where he would break with his own party, Jackson pointed to his pledge not to accept donations from corporate political action committees.

“I think the Democrats are still too close to that,” Jackson said. “I don’t accept corporate PACs. I don’t accept corporate money. This is a campaign about fighting for everyday working-class people, and that’s one thing that I’ve been consistent on.”

Collins tried to undermine that argument, using her one question to ask Jackson about ads run in coordination with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which does accept corporate PAC money.

Jackson countered that he doesn’t approve those ads. While he acknowledged he has had some support from billionaires, he said his campaign is powered by small-dollar donors.

Jackson raised more than $20 million from July through September, according to a fundraising report filed Thursday. That is nearly four times Collins’ $5.2 million haul over the same period.

Jackson, a former state Senate president and logger, then pressed Collins about her claims that he couldn’t be effective in the Senate.

“I have the experience fighting for working-class people, and they deserve a senator that respects them. Is it just me that you look down on, or is it working-class people overall?” he asked.

“Troy, I do not look down on you or on anyone. I grew up in Caribou. My first job was picking potatoes,” Collins countered, saying she has “literally” worked since she was 10 years old.

“I have supported all the social safety net programs,” she said later.

Collins’ experience in the Senate is a major reason her supporters are backing her for a sixth term.

“He is just not strong on the mechanics of government,” Collins supporter Mary Ann Lynch said of Jackson. Lynch is a lifelong Democrat but is backing Collins. And she said in a phone interview Wednesday that the debates hadn’t changed her mind.

“Just watching the debates, it’s hard for me to say that if we sent Troy Jackson to Washington, he would ever be able to cut a path of leadership,” said Lynch, 71, a former member of the Cape Elizabeth Town Council.

But Jackson’s push to tie Collins to Trump does resonate with voters leaning toward supporting him, like Dan Tremble.

Tremble, a Penobscot County commissioner, said he was “pretty solid” in his decision to support Jackson as he entered the theater in Bangor on Thursday night.

“Susan Collins has done a lot for the state of Maine,” Tremble, 61, a Democrat, said when he was asked why he wasn’t certain he’d support Jackson. “But I think having her in the Senate, I think, would still leave a majority for the president in the United States Senate, and that’s very worrisome with this president.”

“He says, ‘Vote like I’m on the ballot,’” Tremble added, referring to Trump. “I will.”

CORRECTION (Oct. 15, 2026, 10:17 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified the Cabinet secretary Troy Jackson said he’d vote to convict on impeachment charges. It was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, not Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

World.title: Oregon mom says she ran to son's school when co-worker heard gunshots
World.content:
Kayla Major was at work Thursday afternoon just steps from her son's elementary school in Bend, Oregon, when her co-worker said she heard gunshots and employees started locking the doors.

"I don't think I even had a first thought," Major told "CBS Mornings" on Friday. "I think I stood up, they were locking the doors, and I kind of was figuring out what was going on and why they were locking the doors, and then I heard 'active shooter' and then I said, 'Where?' and they said, 'the school behind us.'"

"I don't know if my co-workers understood that I had a child that went to school there, and so I kind of fell back into my seat for a second, and then paced for a minute, and I stood up and I unlocked the doors and I just started running over to the school," she said.

Major's son was uninjured, but three students — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and one teacher were killed in the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, police said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported to St. Charles Bend Hospital with critical injuries, according to police.

The alleged shooter, a 16-year-old male, was shot and killed by a bystander who entered the school.

Kayla's ex-husband, Tyler, said their son didn't really understand what was going on during the incident.

"I mean, they're children and, you know, he didn't even understand that anybody had died until after we picked him up," Tyler Major said. "So we talked to him about that."

Kayla and Tyler Major are the parents of a child at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. Kayla ran to the school to find her child unharmed after a shooting that killed four people. CBS News

Tyler Major said he was standing back from the large group of people who had gathered outside the school in the wake of the shooting when he saw another parent be told their child had been shot.

"I just saw an older lady come out and I could tell she was looking for somebody who was going to get some bad news," he said. "It was heart-wrenching. I had to go take a break and sit down and, I don't know, grieve for her and for the other families that aren't going to have their loved ones anymore ever again."

Police received a 911 call just before 1 p.m. local time from a person who said their truck had been shot several times by a suspect with a long gun.

The shooter then forced his way into the school by "shooting at locked doors," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a press conference Thursday. A motive for the shooting has not been released.

World.title: New guidelines support hormone therapy for menopause symptoms
World.content:
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has released new guidance for the treatment of common menopause and perimenopause symptoms, including recommending hormone replacement therapy for many women with hot flashes and night sweats.

It's the first time in more than a decade that the group, which is the leading OB-GYN professional organization in the United States, is changing its advice on the use of hormone therapy for menopause and perimenopause.

"Hormone replacement therapy is now the first line" for vasomotor symptoms including hot flashes, night sweats and sleep issues, said Dr. Kameelah Phillips, an OB-GYN and menopause specialist.

"Before, we used to say, 'Here's an antidepressant. Make sure you work out. Why don't you try a glass of wine?' All of those were not helpful," Phillips said in an interview on "CBS Mornings." "We're using hormones mainstream now."

How hormone replacement therapy for menopause works

Most menopause symptoms are caused by steep drops in the hormones estrogen and progesterone, typically in a woman's late 40s or early 50s. Those hormone drops result in hot flashes, night sweats and other symptoms. Low levels of estrogen and progesterone can also lead to reduced bone density, increasing the risk of osteoporosis or fractures.

Hormone replacement therapy can help "eliminate these symptoms," Phillips said.

Hormone replacement therapy can be delivered in a number of ways, including options like pills, patches, sprays or gels, or a vaginal ring that can deliver doses of hormones directly into the bloodstream. Some women also benefit from low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy.

"Menopause is a normal and natural stage of life, but that doesn't mean that women must suffer through the symptoms without help," ACOG said in a statement about the new recommendations.

Who is eligible for hormone replacement therapy?

Not every person going through menopause is eligible for hormone replacement therapies. Women with a history of blood clots, stroke and liver disease should not use them. People with a personal history of breast cancer should also avoid these therapies, according to ACOG.

A 2002 long-term study on women's health raised concerns that the use of hormones could be linked to an increase in breast cancer. But that study was focused on older patients who may not have started hormone replacement therapy until about a decade after undergoing menopause, explained Dr. Céline Gounder, CBS News medical contributor and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News.

Newer research shows that factors like age and dosing can make treatment safe for many patients. It may also help slow biological aging, according to a 2024 study of over 10,000 women.

The ACOG recommendations say women should begin hormone replacement therapy before the age of 60 or within 10 years of starting menopause.

Women who are not eligible for hormone replacement therapy may be able to benefit from other treatment options. Phillips recommended consulting with a menopause trained specialist.

"There are really good options that are non-hormonal for these women," Phillips said. "But that's why this requires conversation with your healthcare provider."
