World.title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
World.content:
Houston — Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.

Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.

Tesla unveiled its long-delayed new Roadster — which took flight using high-pressure gas boosters — at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. Tesla/Handout via REUTERS

"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."

Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.

The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.

The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.

Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

Turns out the future does have flying cars pic.twitter.com/6fexPp6SXI — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 16, 2026

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."

"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

World.title: American journalist injured in West Bank clashes
World.content:
Several Palestinians and an American photojournalist working for the Washington Post were injured after a group of masked Israeli men attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eyewitnesses and Palestinian authorities.

Video of the incident obtained by CBS News showed a group of around 20 masked men clad in black or gray clothes descending a hill from the area of an Israeli settlement outpost into an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.

Another video from the incident showed two vehicles set on fire and a Palestinian man with a bloodied face being escorted away from the area by a woman and a man.

Among the injured was Heidi Levine, a veteran American photojournalist working with the Washington Post.

Video shared by the Israel-based Foreign Press Association showed Levine was surrounded by masked men, pushed to the ground and beaten, and her camera equipment taken from her.

While Levine was on the ground, the video showed the masked men throwing stones and firing slingshots at Palestinians, who then responded by throwing stones themselves.

Levine was taken to a hospital in Ramallah for medical treatment. Footage of Levine in her hospital bed showed she had a large wound on one of her legs and one of her hands had been bandaged.

Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post, speaks to journalists at the hospital after sustaining multiple injuries during an attack by Israeli militant settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives, in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Oct. 16, 2026. Ali Sawafta / REUTERS

"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me," Levine said from her hospital bed.

In a statement, the Washington Post confirmed the attack, saying Levine "was knocked to the ground, repeatedly kicked and robbed of her cameras and phone despite wearing a protective vest marked 'PRESS' and a helmet."

Israel's police and military said they had opened investigations into the incident.

The Israeli military said its forces used riot control measures to disperse the confrontation. The military added that soldiers fired warning shots in the air and also fired toward a suspect who ran toward soldiers holding "a sharp object and posed a threat to them."

"The Israel Defense Forces strongly condemns this incident and views any manifestation of violence with utmost severity. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the Israeli military said.

A U.S. Embassy spokesperson said they are monitoring the situation and talk regularly with partners about improving security in the area.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the U.S. Embassy's statement said.

The Binyamin Regional Council, an Israeli governmental body responsible for settlements in the area of the clashes, said the Palestinian Authority had sent activists to deliberately provoke residents of the Israeli settlement outpost near Abu Falah.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it treated three Palestinians for injuries at Abu Falah. The wounded included a man who had been shot in the thigh, according to WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority.

Clashes between Israeli settlers and Palestinian olive pickers also took place on Friday near the villages of Burqa and Turmus Ayya, which are located in the central West Bank, WAFA reported. The Palestine Red Crescent treated four people for injuries sustained at the clashes near Burqa, WAFA said.

Attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank have surged in recent years, particularly after the establishment of Israel's current hard-right government in late 2022, according to statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.

Despite those public promises by Netanyahu, the violence has continued in recent weeks.

Human rights groups and critics say the government is complicit in the attacks and that Netanyahu's condemnation appears to be posturing since the Israeli military often intervenes on the settlers' side and the perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.

Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, last month condemned Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, calling the behavior an "act of terror" as he visited with Palestinian American residents shaken by months of attacks.

Over the past 18 days, Yesh Din, an Israeli settlement monitoring group, says it has documented 486 violent incidents against Palestinians across 181 different Palestinian localities, and that 234 of these incidents were related to the olive harvest.

In August, three journalists from NBC and a Palestinian woman they were interviewing were attacked by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

World.title: Photos show pope celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
World.content:
The Vatican released new photos of Pope Leo XIV — the first since his lung cancer surgery — showing him celebrating Mass at the hospital in Rome.

The photos, released Friday, show the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital.

Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome, where he is recovering after having cancer removed from his right lung. Vatican Media via AP

Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that the pontiff presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.

In his homily, Leo thanked the medical personnel for their service and their closeness to those who are fragile, and for the way they have taken care of him.

The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. He is expected to remain at Gemelli Hospital until Oct. 20.

On Thursday, he resumed "a little bit of work activity," including reading documents, and co-celebrated Mass, Vatican officials said. He also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state.

Pope Leo XIV, flanked by his personal secretary, Monsignor Edgard Iván Rimaycuna Inga, celebrates Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome. Vatican Media via AP

Doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement" in his recovery.

"His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Leo's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.

The Vatican said Leo will make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer. Past popes who have been hospitalized have recited the Angelus from the balcony on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital.

Trip to South America appears still on

Leo is scheduled to travel to South America next month. His ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time.

However, on Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the pope's plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Posting the media list signaled that, at least organizationally, the trip was going ahead.

Cancer patients send well-wishing notes to Leo

The Vatican also released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli's pediatric oncology ward.

One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. "My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon," he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom.

A drawing sent to Pope Leo from children in the pediatric oncology department at the Gemelli Hospital. Vatican Media

Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language.

"When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we're going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you," she wrote. "I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too."

World.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
World.content:
Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests

toggle caption i Vipin/AP

NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

toggle caption i Prabhat Mehrotra/AP

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Sponsor Message

Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.

The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

toggle caption i Channi Anand/AP Photo/Channi Anand/AP

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.

"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

Sponsor Message

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

World.title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
World.content:
Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained:

"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

Sponsor Message

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.

Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media , Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

toggle caption i Richard Shotwell/Invision/ AP

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

Sponsor Message

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."

Free speech concerns

But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.

U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.

Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."

Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.

For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.

But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."

Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

Sponsor Message

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.

World.title: Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens
World.content:
Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A teenager opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher, officials confirmed. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander killed the 16-year-old suspected shooter after following him into Silver Rail Elementary School, according to local officials. The suspected shooter has not been identified. Officials say he was a resident of Bend. He used a "long gun," which is similar to a rifle or shotgun, during the attack. His connection to the school — if any — remains unclear.

toggle caption i Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images

🎧 The teenage suspected shooter was able to enter the school by firing at locked doors, according to the Bend Police Department. NPR's Arezou Rezvani tells Up First that something she found interesting on the Bend-La Pine Schools website was its emphasis on security protocols. They said they have secure vestibules for sign-in, ID checks for visitors and electronic buzz-in systems, but none of these measures stopped the gunman. Rezvani says police arrived at the school within minutes after the shooting started, but an unidentified community member shot the alleged shooter soon after the officer arrived.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department is suing California to stop the state from counting ballots that the government claims are from noncitizens. Three weeks before Election Day, the DOJ provided a flash drive containing the names of 20,000 people it suspected of being noncitizens on California's voter rolls to Los Angeles County's top voting official. The DOJ gave him 48 hours to investigate the names or face a lawsuit, which was filed yesterday.



🎧 California and many election experts doubt the administration's noncitizen voting claims, citing President Trump's history of misinformation around the topic and flawed data analysis that can produce false positives, NPR's Miles Parks says. With vote-by-mail ballots already sent out for upcoming elections, the DOJ is seeking to segregate ballots linked to these claims for investigation so they don't get counted. Parks says it would be surprising if the DOJ succeeds in this lawsuit, as the Constitution clearly states that states manage elections.

Trump administration lawyers will argue today at a federal appeals court that White House papers belong to Trump rather than the American people. The case could end up in front of the conservative-leaning Supreme Court. The White House's claim comes after a series of actions during Trump's second term that challenged the limits put on the president after the Watergate scandal. For some 200 years, presidents could personally decide what to do with the papers they created in office. Then, Congress established the Presidential Records Act following disputes with Richard Nixon. Until this year, every president has followed this records law. Six months ago, the Trump administration moved to invalidate it. The move came after Trump was indicted on obstruction-of-justice charges for allegedly possessing classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, although a federal judge dismissed the case for technical reasons and the Justice Department later dropped it after Trump won reelection.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Monika Evstatieva, senior producer on NPR's Investigations team

toggle caption i Collage by Jackie Lay/NPR

It all began with a tip. A colleague of mine had a friend in Ann Arbor who needed help. When I called her, she told me her elderly mom had been walking through a mall when a salesperson approached her with an eye cream sample. She went into a store called Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Mich., and came out with $5,000 in skincare products she didn't want, tried to refuse, and couldn't return. But, she said, it wasn't an isolated incident. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. She asked me to look into it.

And so began an investigation that took place over more than a year. My reporting partner, Caley Fox Shannon, and I found similar complaints all over the country. We followed the trail, and found a network of mall skincare stores that systematically targeted older adults and people with disabilities across the United States. There was a link between them: one company, the California-based Mazal Group.

Over the past year, we spoke with more than 50 people, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. We looked at state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints we got through Freedom of Information Act requests. We went to stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.

You can read about what we found in NPR Investigations' whole report here, watch our documentary or listen on Consider This.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Nintendo

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Other Mommy, starring Jessica Chastain, follows a 7-year-old who is visited by a mysterious entity that takes the form of her mother. Pop Culture Happy Hour describes it as an intense horror film filled with dark family secrets.

Sponsor Message

📺 TV: The Lowdown is back for its second season, featuring Ethan Hawke as a freelance investigative reporter entangled with a prominent Tulsa family.

📚 Books: The Two Saddest Kitchens is a comic conversation between cartoonists Roz Chast and Jason Adam Katzenstein about their fear and shame over their apartment kitchens and their disinterest in cooking.

🎵 Music: Remi Wolf's new album, Mud, emerged from a period of significant personal change, including a breakup and becoming sober. Watch her talk about it and perform some songs on World Cafe.

🎮 Gaming: NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino got to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time early, ahead of its Nov. 5 release. He says, "The game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players."

❓ Quiz: This week featured changes at the White House, a child reality star's comeback and Elon Musk. If you kept up, you might score perfectly.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating suspicious mailings, some of which contained a white powdery substance, to state election officials and congressional offices. Trump has canceled the livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution. The former Army psychiatrist killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas. The Smithsonian National Zoo welcomed five cheetah cubs this month. You can watch them grow and snuggle with their mom on a 24-hour livestream cheetah cam.

World.title: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups
World.content:
What this bankruptcy says about AI startups

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

After you win the economics Nobel, what would your first act be? Buy a Corvette? Gloat to your childhood bully? For co-winner Michael Woodford, his first act was … proctor an exam. The DAY that Columbia professor Michael Woodford found out that he and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel, he returned to his class with the pithy title "Cognitive Mechanisms and Economic Behavior" to administer an exam. He was welcomed to the classroom with cheers and applause. He held up his arms in triumph.

toggle caption i Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Coming up:



Character.ai is going through bankruptcy. What can we learn from the AI startup's decline?

Why President Trump wants to import diesel fuel from Russia

Why stagflation was John Maynard Keynes' Achilles' heel

News We're Watching

When AI startups get vacuumed up, what's left behind?

What to know: Character.ai is a company that allows you to speak with a "companion" — an AI-powered fictional character, historical figure, or whatever you decide to build. It came out just before ChatGPT and quickly went viral in part thanks to its adoption on TikTok. It hit 28 million monthly active users at its peak.

Sponsor Message

Character.ai had a lot of engagement, a big customer base, lots of talent … and Google promptly picked 'em up for $2.7 billion back in 2024. But Google didn't buy the company and absorb it! No, that traditional "acquihire" model would require all sorts of legal and regulatory approvals. Instead, they hired away the founders (and other big hitters on the team) and bought the nonexclusive license to the technology, leaving the company itself behind. That's called a "reverse acquihire," and it's happened at least six times in the past two years with AI startups. Now this week, Character.ai is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

toggle caption i Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Why it matters: A "reverse acquihire" doesn't leave a company in the greatest position. After the Google deal, Character.ai had to change its business model away from the quite costly LLM training and toward developing AI characters. Its founders were gone. Sure, the shrunken company had $2.7 billion in the bank, but leadership was still looking to raise money as they struggled to monetize their user base.

So is the "reverse acquihire" what caused the pain? Or was it a symptom of a larger issue? Character.ai faced a mountain of litigation over alleged harm to minors plus copyright concerns from Disney. So what's left behind? A once very promising company, which Disney is very excited to pick over for parts of it for $20 million.

Sponsor Message

Will this Russian diesel deal affect price?

What's going on: President Trump signed a deal last week to get diesel from Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Two weeks ago, we talked in the newsletter about the potential of a diesel export ban to lower prices. It didn't happen. One week ago, we talked again about Trump issuing an executive order to defer a tax from diesel. Now, this!

It's safe to say people were surprised by the move, given Trump signed a Russian sanctions law just last month that looked to tamp down on their energy revenues. Beyond surprise, a bipartisan group of senators is openly calling for the president to rescind the deal. They said it gives Putin the funds to power his war machine and "enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

Will this do anything? The same bipartisan group of senators said this deal will mean "limited to no relief to Americans." Goldman Sachs estimated the release of Russian oil would affect wholesale prices by $1 to $2 per barrel. The price of a barrel of diesel is around $200. So a $1 to $2 impact? Neil Atkinson, an independent energy analyst, says, "Frankly, [it's] a rounding error. It makes no fundamental difference to the global diesel market."

What's weirder to Atkinson, though … Russia hasn't really been exporting diesel. Its refineries have been damaged, and it's literally been importing diesel to make up for shortfalls. " So where these barrels of Russian diesel are going to come from to go either to the United States or elsewhere in the global market is a bit of a mystery," said Atkinson.

Today's Indicator

The Nobel Prize that wasn't

If you HAVEN'T listened: Reporter Greg Rosalsky opens the piece describing WHAT exactly Michael Woodford and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel for. They helped shape what's known as NEW Keynesian economics by bringing microeconomic principles to the traditional models of John Maynard Keynes. BUT THEN, Greg goes on to explain that the Nobel Prize did not initially include an economics award. No, that changed when the Swedish Central Bank, the oldest central bank in the world, wanted to celebrate its 300th anniversary with a bang. They would fund a new award for economics. It's a fascinating story which you can listen to below.

Sponsor Message

If you HAVE listened: A leading philosophy of John Maynard Keynes is that governments could fight recessions by boosting spending, and deal with inflation by holding spending back. In the initial draft that didn't make it into the final episode, Greg touched on how STAGFLATION was a central thorn in the side of this concept. Specifically, back in the 1970s, during the Arab oil embargo, the U.S. dealt with the one-two punch of high unemployment and high inflation, bringing about stagflation. It challenged the Keynesian idea that when lots of people are out of work and spending less, inflation comes down. Because at that point, unemployment and inflation rose together. Isn't that nice? Greg Rosalsky writes Planet Money's newsletter … you can catch that here.

Rest of the week



In Our Spare Time

Producer Cooper Katz McKim is reading The AGI Chronicles

Man oh man, this is the page-turniest nonfiction book I've read in a while. Kevin Roose, co-host of the upcoming NPR podcast Machine Gods, formerly The New York Times' Hard Fork, tracks the handful of characters racing to make AI a commercial reality. It is far from a clear-cut story. There's no one character who came up with the idea and executed it … the existence of AI today comes down to many papers, many individual discoveries, and a whole lot of obsession. I didn't realize how much progress had been made in AI prior to 2020 and how concerned many industry leaders were about even creating AI (looking at you, Amodei) for fear of creating a super-intelligence that moves outside of human control. It's gossip-y, it's matter of fact … I would recommend.

World.title: Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in
World.content:
Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in

toggle caption i Alon Skuy/Getty Images

President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House.



In arguments Friday before a federal appeals court in Washington, administration lawyers will make an especially bold claim: that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The move comes amid a series of actions under Trump's second term to test the limits put in place after the Watergate scandal, and could be another case that ends up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the Presidential Records Act, a federal law in place since 1978. Conservative lawyer Michael Edney cast the move in a long line of other attempts to pare back statutes from that era.

Sponsor Message

"This is a story about a post-Watergate, overbroad statutory incursion into the prerogatives of the executive branch," Edney said in a recent webinar sponsored by the Federalist Society.

For some 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office, until disputes with Richard Nixon prompted Congress to weigh in. Every president since then has complied with the records law, until this year.

"The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The White House's reinterpretation of the act comes after Trump was indicted on obstruction of justice charges for allegedly stockpiling classified documents in a bathroom, ballroom and office at his Mar-a-Lago resort. A federal judge threw out the case for technical reasons, related to the appointment of the prosecutor, and the Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after Trump won reelection.

Question about the public's right to papers

Nikhel Sus is chief counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group that sued over the Trump move.

"If the courts were to accept it, and we are hopeful that they will not, it would mean the people really have no right of access to the president's papers and that would be a major loss for archivists, historians and to the American people writ large," Sus said.

Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, ruled against the Trump White House this year, in a decision that opened with a passage from George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past," the judge wrote.

Sponsor Message

Three judges from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit will consider the issue on Friday.

The Trump administration said in court papers that keeping all those records imposes a burden on the White House and that it could chill advisers from having honest conversations with the president.

Continuity of government

But former government officials say being able to consult these papers is essential.

"Access to the records on national security issues of former presidents is really vital for the continuity of our government," said John Bellinger, who served as legal adviser to the National Security Council under George W. Bush.

Bellinger said he and other members of Bush's staff sometimes requested the papers of President Bill Clinton, to understand conversations Clinton had with world leaders and members of Congress.

"Often the only record of what a president has said to a foreign leader — or perhaps even more important, what a foreign leader, friend or foe, has said to the president of the United States — is in a written document," Bellinger said.

To not be able to see those papers, he said, will leave future presidents at a "terrible disadvantage."

Edney, who also worked for Bush's National Security Council and Justice Department, said he believed that Congress could probably pass a "thoughtful" records preservation statute. He said parts of the current Presidential Records Act that provide Congress with automatic access and presume the records will be publicly disclosed are "constitutionally problematic."

Edney said he has some doubts about whether the watchdog groups suing to challenge Trump's move actually have legal standing to proceed.

But the Trump administration appears to have breezed past those concerns, because they have a higher goal in mind.

"They want this to go to the Supreme Court," Edney said. "I think they want this resolved at a time of their choosing, with arguments of their choosing, and a court of their choosing, and with the Solicitor General's office that's making their arguments, as opposed to a subsequent administration."

World.title: 'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote
World.content:
'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote

toggle caption i Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App.

Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.

That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.

The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research, a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio, are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate.

Sponsor Message

For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.

"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)

John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.

"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."

Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed Navigator polling released in August, which found that nearly a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.

Sponsor Message

Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.

Shifting toward Democrats, or not

While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.

Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.

"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."

He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.

But enthusiasm is a different question.

Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.

"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.

That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.

"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.

Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling, which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."

"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

World.title: Former student says someone hid a webcam in her Royal Military College dorm. No one was ever charged
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kelly Stewart was plugging in her phone in her dorm room, planning to let it charge while she was in class at the Royal Military College of Canada (RMC), when she found a cord she didn't recognize — one she would later trace to a web camera hidden inside the heater in her wall.

"My whole body just went completely cold," she said during a recent interview at her home in Kingston, N.S.

Documents obtained by Stewart through Access to Information legislation, and shared with CBC News, show the Canadian Forces Military Police launched an investigation into voyeurism and breaking and entering offences on Oct. 31, 2018 — the same day Stewart discovered the webcam in her Kingston, Ont., dorm room and reported it to her superiors.

The following day, the National Investigation Service — a specialized unit that investigates serious matters — took over her case. According to the documents, no charges were ever laid due to insufficient evidence.

Eight years after the alarming discovery — and five years after a firestorm of sexual misconduct allegations in the Canadian Armed Forces prompted a federal review — Stewart is sharing her story publicly for the first time, emboldened by the support for a woman who alleges she was gang raped at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.

Stewart posted on social media on Oct. 3, writing that recent events out of Cornell had brought back painful memories.

"For 8 years I have carried the weight of other people's disgusting actions, failures and systemic sexism. I owe it to my 20-year-old self to pass that weight off to the men who failed."

WATCH | The moment Stewart found the camera: Woman describes the moment she discovered the hidden webcam | Duration closed caption 1:39 Kelly Stewart was plugging in her phone in her dorm room, planning to let it charge while she was in class at the Royal Military College of Canada, when she found a cord she didn’t recognize — one she would later trace to a web camera hidden inside the heater in her wall.

Stewart files official complaint

Stewart, now 28, believes the investigation into her case was flawed, and though she believes the webcam was put in her room by another student, she says her superiors didn't support her, told her to "toughen up" and suggested her career could be affected by accessing mental health support.

She says her health suffered so much that she ultimately requested a voluntary release, which was granted in September 2019 on compassionate grounds, meaning she was not required to reimburse the government for the cost of her schooling.

In her social media post, Stewart named four people: her former superiors and a military police investigator. CBC News is choosing not to name them as there is no suggestion of any legal wrongdoing on their part.

The Department of National Defence (DND) has confirmed to CBC News that two of the four individuals have since retired. DND declined an interview, but in a statement said it is aware of claims, but for privacy and legal reasons it doesn't comment on matters involving identifiable individuals.

Stewart also filed a formal complaint on May 11, 2025, about the investigating officer. The Military Police Complaints Commission confirmed to CBC News that the complaint is being processed.

The 2018 RMC investigation

The 335-page military police report is heavily redacted but contains photos of the webcam, handwritten police notes and officer activity logs that shed some light on the investigation.

Stewart said she initially thought the investigation would reach a successful conclusion quickly. She felt her immediate, lower-level superiors took her seriously and there was a physical piece of evidence, the camera.

"I found myself a year later with nothing having been actioned," she said.

The documents show it took a month to access surveillance footage from the hallway outside Stewart's room, and that there was some confusion around whether an officer had even requested it.

Stewart said it took more than four months for the police to seize the suspect's laptop, which she said she witnessed herself. She believes it was the first time his laptop was taken.

Investigative photos that show the inside of Stewart’s dorm room at the RMC. Stewart says she found the webcam in the heater. (Canadian Forces National Investigation Service)

The documents show the investigation was formally closed on Aug 14, 2020 because it did not yield enough information to substantiate the elements of the offence.

The documents list one "person of interest." All the information about them is redacted.

Stewart said around three months after she discovered the webcam, and after she had moved back into her dorm, a staff member at the college told her that her superiors knew who the suspect was and that he was living a few doors down from her. She said the staff member told her he had been told not to give her this information.

Having to continue living alongside the man she believed violated her was incredibly difficult, she said.

She said she repeatedly asked her superiors to move the suspect to another building but was told it was not possible — that she could move instead. She felt that was unfair.

Stewart said she quit going to class, was afraid to go to the dining hall for fear of running into the suspect and lost a lot of weight.

She said a superior told her: "If you want a career in the military, you'll have to get used to being uncomfortable and not getting along with everybody."

Stewart's release records, which she provided to CBC News, state she performed well in all aspects at the college, up until her last semester, when she failed three courses.

Her release records state she was a victim of harmful and inappropriate sexual behaviour and that her release was directly related to that incident.

Sexual harassment not uncommon: former RMC student

CBC News has spoken with a male friend of Stewart's, who lived in the same dorm.

CBC News is withholding his name because he remains a serving member of the military and fears disciplinary repercussions that could affect his career progression.

He said he believes it was possible for RMC to move the suspect to another building to make things easier for Stewart.

"I just don't think they were thinking hard enough because they could have just moved a handful of people into different positions at the beginning of the next year."

He also said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there.

"I don't think I know a single one that didn't have something happen."

A friend of Stewart's said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

During her interview with CBC News, Stewart also disclosed that she had previously been sexually assaulted while she was a student at the French military college in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Que., before transferring to RMC.

She said she did not include that incident in her social media post because she did not report it. "At the end of the day, nobody failed me because I didn't do anything about it."

A 2023 survey of women attending Canadian military colleges, administered by the colleges, found that five per cent of women canvassed said they were sexually attacked during the previous 12 months.

Everyone deserves 'dignity and respect,' DND says

DND declined an interview, but called Stewart's assault allegations "very concerning," in a statement, stressing there is no time limit for making a report.

"Every Defence Team member has the right to serve in an environment where they are safe and treated with dignity and respect," the statement reads. "We know this standard has not always been met."

The statement goes on to say that in recent years DND and the CAF have taken steps to strengthen support for those affected by sexual misconduct, improve how incidents are reported, reinforce leadership accountability and create a safer culture.

On June 18, the Military Justice System Modernization Act received Royal Assent.

The new law means cases of sexual misconduct in the military will be transferred to the civilian justice system. It includes prohibiting military police from investigating voyeurism. There will be a mandatory external review in three years to determine whether the law should be repealed.

WATCH | The federal government's apology in 2024: Anand issues apology to victims of sexual assault in Canadian Armed Forces | Duration 2:35 Canada's Minister of National Defence Anita Anand said the government acknowledges the pain and trauma members of the Canadian Armed Forces experienced.

Only the passage of time will tell whether there has been meaningful change, said Megan MacKenzie, an expert in gender and the military at Simon Fraser University in B.C.

"We definitely have seen a commitment from many leaders, from many senior people to make changes," she said.

"Whether that is executed on a day-to-day basis for individual leaders and the people that they are responsible for, it's hard to know."

Stewart said she has been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder and complex post traumatic stress as a result of her experience.

She wants the higher chain of command to know her story.

"I want the colonels, the generals to hear this," she said. "I want them to wake up in the morning and go, 'What can I do differently to protect my subordinates?'"

World.title: Montreal police suspend 2 officers following report officer urinated on unhoused person
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours.

In a statement to CBC News, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) confirmed that it has launched an internal investigation into two officers from Station 21, which covers downtown Montreal.

The police response comes after a report published Friday by La Presse detailing the alleged incident, which reportedly disgusted colleagues who then reported the behaviour to superiors.

The SPVM declined to provide further details on the investigation, citing privacy obligations under provincial law.

"Be assured that the SPVM takes any allegation against one of its members seriously," police said in its statement. "Regardless of the nature of an internal investigation, we are determined to get to the bottom of things and take the required actions."

Another officer from the same station was also suspended in recent weeks in connection with a separate case. According to La Presse, the officer allegegedly appeared to be posing and mocking a suspect placed in a humiliating position during an arrest.

The officers have not yet formally presented a defence.

Advocate denounces 'degrading' act

Annie Savage, executive director of the advocacy group RAPSIM (Réseau d'aide aux personnes seules et itinérantes de Montréal), said she was "extremely shocked" but not surprised by the allegations, citing what she regularly hears from people living on the streets.

"It's hard to imagine a more degrading or violent act," Savage told Radio-Canada's Tout un matin.

Savage added that relations between police and unhoused residents have deteriorated as the city's homelessness crisis has deepened. She warned that police should not treat the incident as an isolated case.

Last June, RAPSIM released a joint report with legal aid organization Clinique Droits Devant that outlined tension between unhoused Montrealers and law enforcement, including Montreal police officers and special constables patrolling the city's transit network.

The study found that 40 per cent of unhoused individuals surveyed felt heavily ticketed or targeted, while 66 per cent reported rarely or never being treated like other members of the public. None of the respondents expressed high confidence in police during an emergency, with many saying they avoid calling 911 out of fear of being treated as suspects.

The report documented cases of physical and verbal abuse, unjustified searches, an increased reliance on private security guards in public spaces, and heightened surveillance across the Metro system.

The allegations come as Montreal prepares for La Nuit des sans-abri, an annual event held across Quebec to raise awareness about homelessness.

In a statement to CBC, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the allegations are "extremely serious and undermine the dignity every person deserves."

She added: "I applaud the police officers who spoke up to report this situation. The investigation must now run its course so the full truth can come to light."

The Montreal police brotherhood, the union representing SPVM officers, said in a statement it "firmly condemns" any behaviour that violates human dignity or breaches professional standards.

While declining to comment on the specific allegations, the brotherhood called the reported conduct contrary to the values of Montreal police officers.

The SPVM is in the midst of another scandal involving its officers. A patrol unit at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord was disbanded last June after officers allegedly racially profiled residents.

World.title: Alberta separatism question puts strain, tension on relationships
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For years, Katrina Dodge and her mother Gabriele have been able to talk about anything and everything, but recently there has been some strain in their relationship over the issue of separatism.

Katrina, who grew up in Nanton and now lives in Calgary, is a proponent of Alberta remaining in Canada. But the majority of her family, including her mother Gabriele, is voting for a second, binding referendum on independence to be held.

“It’s a little bit isolating, obviously. It’s a bit anxiety-inducing at times,” Katrina said.

While Katrina said it doesn’t make family dinners or gatherings awkward, she said it can sometimes be tense, adding it can be tricky to navigate conversations with her family.

Katrina Dodge is in favour of Alberta staying in Canada. (Peter Evans/CBC)

“Sometimes there’s taking pause and really listening to find a point where I can interject with an opposing view or try to lend some other ways to look at things, to sort of foster more understanding,” she said.

Mom Gabriele said she and Katrina have come to an understanding.

“She knows how I feel and I know how she feels so we try not to get into each other’s … spaces where she feels uncomfortable or I feel uncomfortable,” Gabriele said.

Guardrails often play an important role in their relationship.

“We have learned to say that ‘This is too personal’ or ‘This bothers me. Can we change the subject?’ And we usually do,” she said.

Gabriele Dodge is voting for Alberta to hold a second, binding referendum on independence. (Peter Evans/CBC)

While Katrina said her family is kind and respectful of their political differences, she admits it can be trying.

“I definitely try to check in with my body and ask, ‘Do I have the emotional, mental capacity for this? Am I super tired and cranky? Do I need a snack before I have a deep sort of debate?” she said.

Whereas mom Gabriele said a healthy respect goes a long way.

“She has a right to her feelings and opinions and I feel I have a right to mine … If we get too close to what we know hurts the other, we kind of give a sign or we say, ‘Okay you’re now saying something that’s not fair’ and we stop,” she said.

Impact on relationships

Separatism has dominated conversations in Alberta for months and recent data shows it is affecting relationships.

Numbers from Abacus Data from September show 23 per cent of those surveyed said conversations about separatism have strained relationships while 38 per cent say they have avoided bringing up the issue over worries it would lead to an argument.

One thousand Albertans were surveyed between Sept. 4 to 7. The report has a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3.1% points, 19 times out of 20.

CEO David Coletto said it’s clear there are deep divides over the issue and calls the numbers “concerning.”

David Coletto is the CEO of Abacus Data. (Olivier Hyland/CBC)

“I think they reflect the reality of a moment that’s highly emotionally charged on both sides and what can happen when that gets in between a relationship,” he said.

While focus has been on the lead-up to referendum day, there is some worry over what happens in its aftermath.

“Most Albertans also believe that no matter what happens on October 19th, that this debate and this tension and this divide is going to continue for some time. There’s not a lot of hope that, if there is a clear majority who want to stay in Canada, that this is going to go away the next day,” Coletto said.

Recommendations from psychologists

Vanessa Goodchild, a registered psychologist with Solace Psychology and Wellness, said separatism’s impact on relationships is presenting itself more often during sessions with clients.

“There can be resentment and frustration if your family members don’t agree with you and with your viewpoint,” she said.

Vanessa Goodchild is a registered psychologist and owner of Solace Psychology and Wellness. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

Goodchild said it should be less about trying to change their mind and more about learning how to agree to disagree, adding that open communication and setting boundaries can be key.

“It’s not about stepping away from your family or cutting them off. It’s just about protecting your relationship with your family and not doing something that you may regret later,” she said.

Goodchild suggests families should focus on doing activities everyone enjoys, such as family walks or family dinners, and having conversations about other day-to-day things.

“Don’t let any kind of political disagreement really define your relationship because there’s other things that you value with this person or within this relationship,” she said.

Family over politics

Even though family dynamics have been affected, Katrina said she doesn’t believe the debate over Alberta independence has pulled her family apart.

"I know that we still love each other at the end of the day. We can have conversations, which I think is so important," she said, adding that engagement with diverse opinion is important.

“That’s the only way we can really learn and grow and move forward and you can’t really change minds but you can … use your mind."

For Gabriele, family will always trump politics.

“Politicians change and political parties change but my family doesn’t. My children are my children and they’re going to stay my children and I love them dearly,” she said.

World.title: Tesla unveils Roadster that can flip in the air and land using thrusters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first ‌showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.

The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event, it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the manoeuvre.

Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he ​has explored by discussing their overlap.

Tesla shares were up five per cent in pre-market trading on Friday.

The reveal ​gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.

'An engineering flex'

"It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers," Gene Munster, ​managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X.

"The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can't wait to bring [Tesla] ��⁠and [SpaceX] together," Munster said.

Musk has played down ⁠the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move ‌the needle in a major way financially."

But the car still carries symbolic weight.

"Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.

Viewers and witnesses gushed over the spectacle of the launch.

"That was the most insane product demo I've ever seen," Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. "I just saw this in person, and ⁠I'm still asking how this wasn't AI."

$50K US deposit needed

Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday's event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000 US for the vehicle.

Tesla's reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday's event showed a "Performance" version of the vehicle requiring a $50,000 US deposit and a "Thrust" version with "acceleration thrusters" requiring a $250,000 US deposit. A "Rocket" variant, which Tesla says is "invite only," is described as a ‌single-seat model with a "full flight system."

The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown.

"This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven't seen in any movie," Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors.

Zero to 97 km/h in under a second

The Roadster can ​accelerate from zero to 97 km/h in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 370 km/h, Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said.

"Definitely much faster than that," an excited Musk said. "I think you've got to crack ⁠halfway to the speed of sound."

The Roadster can also travel over 480 kilometres on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla ⁠first revealled a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020.

The Roadster, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, comes in for a landing at the unveilling on Thursday. (Tesla/Reuters)

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever electric vehicle ⁠and used a ⁠Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world's view of what an ​EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.

The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp ​shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and ⁠robotics from manufacturing cars for human drivers.

This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab — a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.

Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Sales of Tesla's aging lineup of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high gas prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter of 2026.

"The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at ⁠trading platform eToro.

World.title: Nova Scotia to host massive data centre to power artificial intelligence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under construction just outside Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels said it will build the facility in two stages, with the first phase to come online by the end of 2027 and the second in 2028.

The company, headed by Australian-American private equity veteran Trent Vichie, had previously confirmed it has data centre ambitions, but said little else.

On Friday, EverWind released more information about its plans.

The company is building the facility and has signed an agreement with an as-yet unnamed AI company to lease the first phase for a term of at least 20 years.

The first phase would have a capacity of 95 megawatts and the second, 325 megawatts, for a total of 420 megawatts. Nova Scotia’s current electrical generating capacity is close to 3,000 megawatts.

EverWind raising $8 billion for project

EverWind said it will pay for any required upgrades to Nova Scotia’s electricity system.

“Nova Scotians should expect us to demonstrate that we can protect ratepayers, safeguard local resources and deliver lasting community benefits, and we intend to be accountable for those commitments,” Vichie said in a news release.

EverWind said it is raising $8 billion in private capital to fund the project and an additional $2 billion for four of the onshore wind farms it is planning to build.

It said those wind farms would eventually support the data centre’s electricity needs, but existing generation on the provincial grid would be the primary supply to begin. Company officials said the provincial grid operator has done a system-impact study that indicates the grid can support the first phase.

EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

EverWind has been trying to develop renewable energy projects in Nova Scotia for several years. It says those plans remain unchanged.

The data centre is to be built at the same site as one of EverWind’s other proposed projects — a green hydrogen and ammonia facility — in the industrial park at Point Tupper, Cape Breton.

Data centre controversies

Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling. Concerns about AI’s potential impacts on jobs and dire warnings about risks to human existence also have some people pushing back.

There are some proposed data centres that would dwarf this one in size, including the Wonder Valley data centre in Alberta — the first phase of which is meant to be more than a gigawatt — but this project is still on the larger end of facilities that have been recently announced in Canada .

EverWind said it has signed on to Ottawa’s responsible data centre development principles — a set of non-binding guidelines the federal government released last month .

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston recently laid out similar guidelines. Both levels of government say they expect any data centre to have local benefits, minimal environmental impact and minimal water use, and for there to be no resulting power rate spikes.

“We applaud the federal and provincial governments for setting high standards for responsible development,” Vichie said in the release. “And we will continue to work with communities to ensure that our work meets their expectations.”

Community benefit program

EverWind said it will use a closed-loop water-glycol system. The company’s preliminary estimate for water usage is an average of 100,000 litres per day for the first phase and 500,000 litres of water per day including both phases.

Water would be drawn from nearby Landrie Lake. The provincial regulator has approved the Landrie Lake Water Utility to withdraw 34 million litres from the lake each day, which would make EverWind’s daily requirements about one per cent of the total safe withdrawal volume.

The company promised the data centre would come with a community benefit program worth tens of millions of dollars. A specific dollar figure was not provided. Local communities and the data centre’s unnamed customer would consult on how to spend the money.

A consortium of Mi’kmaw communities, fronted by Membertou First Nation, is negotiating a nine per cent equity stake in the project.
