Royal Media Services (RMS) was established in 1996 by Dr S.K. Macharia, its website says. It runs three TV stations, Citizen TV, Inooro TV and Ramogi TV, and 13 radio stations.

RSF says RMS dominates the market and that Citizen TV is among the most popular channels. The Reuters Institute’s 2025 survey found Citizen TV reached 68% of an online sample weekly, down from 76%.

NMG runs the TV channels NTV and QTV and the radio station Easy FM, the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development says. The Standard Group’s 2024 annual report lists KTN Home, KTN News, Btv, KTN Farmers TV and three radio stations.

RSF says three of the Standard Group’s four TV channels and Radio Vybez were forced to close in 2024. It names KTN News, KTN Burudani and KTN Farmers TV, two of which the company’s 2024 report also lists.

K24 is a Mediamax Network station, Kenyans.co.ke said in 2021, citing Communications Authority registration documents. A public shareholder register for Mediamax was not found.

Paid television is small, the CA’s figures show. At 30 June 2026 it counted 874,777 digital terrestrial, 643,947 satellite and 30,240 cable subscriptions.

The CA blames a 1.8% quarterly drop on viewers moving to internet TV and on higher decoder costs. Rising global chipset prices have made set-top boxes more expensive, it says.

Digital Outlets and Online Audiences

NMG says its digital footprint grew to 64.7 million users in 2025 from 62.5 million in 2024, and digital revenue rose 5%. Its website also lists 60 million monthly pageviews and 62.4 million social media followers in October 2026.

Citizen Digital calls itself the online home of all RMS brands, and Standard Digital carries the Standard Group’s news. Other sites such as Tuko.co.ke, named in the 2025 survey, add further competition.

The Digital News Report 2026, published on 16 June 2026, puts trust in Kenyan news at 68%. That compares with a global average of 37%, though the sample is urban, English-speaking and not representative.

Money pressures reach digital outlets too, and RSF says state bodies were urged to place advertising online while media debts went unpaid. NMG laid off 180 staff in June 2024, it adds.

The Standard Group’s first-half 2025 revenue fell 24% to KES 789 million (about US$6.1 million), its filing shows. It blamed slower government contracts and lower advertising.

Who Owns Kenya Media

On Tuesday, 10 March 2026, the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development (AKFED) agreed to sell its Nation Media Group holding company. Buyer Taarifa Ltd is owned by Tanzanian businessman Rostam Azizi, and the holding company controls 54.08% of NMG.

By Saturday, 29 August 2026, Taarifa had completed the purchase and NMG had named six new directors, Kenyans.co.ke reported. One of them, Georgia Mutagahywa, is chief of staff to the chairman of Azizi’s Taifa Group, and NMG’s board page lists her.

NMG’s website now lists Joe Muganda as chairman and Geoffrey Odundo as group managing director and chief executive. The group’s audited 2025 results, dated Friday, 24 April 2026, show a pre-tax loss of KES 321 million (about US$2.5 million).

NMG is listed on the NSE under the symbol NMG. Its board did not recommend a final dividend for 2025.

At 31 December 2024 the Standard Group’s largest shareholder was S.N.G Holdings Limited (Surrey, United Kingdom), with 69.03%. Trade World Kenya Limited held 10.90% and Miller Trustees Limited 10.53%, its 2024 annual report shows.

The report does not name the people behind S.N.G Holdings. The Standard Group added three independent directors on 15 October 2026, its filing shows.

Chaacha Mwita became chief executive on 1 April 2026, a Standard Group filing shows. Kenyans.co.ke reported on 16 October 2026 that he will leave on 1 November, with no successor named.

Royal Media Services names its founder, Dr S.K. Macharia, but no public shareholder list for it was found. Lists for Mediamax and Radio Africa Group were not found either, so exact stakes cannot be confirmed.

The state owns KBC as a state corporation and shapes the wider sector through the regulator. RSF says the authorities can influence media appointments and the regulator’s leadership, which depends on government in practice.

Who Regulates the Media

The Communications Authority of Kenya is the regulatory authority for the information and communications sector, its website says. David Mugonyi is director general, and Charles Karondo chairs a board that includes three government principal secretaries.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy sets policy under Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo. Stephen Isaboke is principal secretary for broadcasting and telecommunications.

The Media Council of Kenya (MCK) was created by the Media Council Act, which gives effect to Article 34 of the Constitution. It accredits journalists and sets media standards, while the Act also created a separate Complaints Commission.

The Code of Conduct for Media Practice, 2025 in the Act covers accuracy, privacy, hate speech and the use of artificial intelligence. David Omwoyo is MCK’s chief executive, and its website says a Media Council Bill went to public participation in October 2026.

Press Freedom and the Courts

RSF ranks Kenya 106th of 180 countries in 2026 with a score of 50.51, up from 117th and 49.41 in 2025. Its weakest indicator is economic, where Kenya ranks 133rd with 34.40 points.

Kenya ranks 107th on politics, 103rd on the legal framework, 104th on security and 95th on the social context. RSF’s barometer showed no journalists killed in 2026 and none detained as of 16 October 2026.

Police attacked or obstructed four journalists covering demonstrations in eastern Nairobi on Wednesday, 5 March 2025, RSF says. It calls arbitrary arrests and police violence against reporters common, especially during anti-government protests.

On Wednesday, 25 June 2025, CA Director General David Mugonyi ordered TV and radio stations to stop live protest coverage. His directive cited Articles 33(2) and 34(1) of the Constitution and threatened licence revocation and suspension of transmission.

NTV, Citizen TV and K24 said their signals were cut after CA officials allegedly accessed transmission equipment in Limuru. The Law Society of Kenya (LSK), the lawyers’ body, went to the High Court the same day, Capital FM reported.

Justice Chacha Mwita issued a conservatory order that day suspending the directive and ordering any switched-off signals restored immediately. He warned that disobedience would bring penal consequences.

In a judgment reported on Thursday, 27 November 2025, Justice John Chigiti quashed the directive and barred the CA from implementing it. The Katiba Institute, a rights group, had argued the CA acted outside its mandate and restricted press freedom unlawfully.

The pressure continued in 2026. RSF says at least eight journalists were assaulted covering an opposition rally in Homa Bay on Sunday, 16 August 2026.

Media vehicles were also vandalised, and police said they arrested 37 suspected gang members. RSF warned that such hostility, less than a year before the vote, is incompatible with a free election.

On Wednesday, 2 September 2026, MCK said armed people abducted Standard Group associate editor Alex Kiprotich the night before. He was taken on the Gilgil-Nakuru road and left in Machakos, and police said Inspector General Douglas Kanja ordered an inquiry.

Police denied any role, Citizen Digital reported, and MCK said no one was arrested after an earlier attempt in Nakuru County. RSF says electoral campaigns often bring sharp rises in abuses against journalists, and perpetrators usually go unpunished.

The Cybercrimes Act and Online Speech

The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act of 2018 is the main law used against online speech. Section 23 punishes knowingly publishing false information that causes panic, chaos or violence, with up to ten years in prison.

Under the text in force until 3 November 2025, the Section 23 fine is up to KES 5 million (about US$38,500). Section 22 carries up to two years, and Section 27 on cyber harassment fines up to KES 20 million (about US$154,000).

RSF says about twenty laws regulating journalism in Kenya contain provisions that challenge press freedom. It cites the 2018 Act’s prison terms of up to ten years for spreading fake news likely to incite violence.

The 2025 amendment to the Act drew challenges from activists who said it could silence critics, journalists and bloggers. On 22 October 2025 a judge suspended several provisions in a case by activist Reuben Kigame and the Kenya Human Rights Commission.

On Thursday, 2 July 2026, the High Court struck down parts of the 2025 amendment as unconstitutional, Capital FM reported. It voided a state committee’s power to order websites blocked without court approval, which the judge said amounted to prior censorship.

The court also struck down part of the cyber harassment offence as vague and overly broad. It upheld the rest of the law and found that public participation had been sufficient.

A separate Supreme Court petition by media and rights groups targets the 2018 Act’s interception provisions, Kenyans.co.ke reported. Whether the state will appeal the July 2026 ruling is not known.

Social Media and the Phone Boom

The CA counted 87,999,998 mobile SIM subscriptions and 54,925,257 mobile broadband subscriptions at 30 June 2026. SIM cards are not people, since one person can hold several.

Smartphones numbered 52,262,565 against 27,420,856 feature phones, and mobile money subscriptions reached 54,005,800. The CA’s population base is 53.3 million, taken from the Economic Survey 2026.

DataReportal counted 23.4 million internet users in Kenya at the end of 2025, or 40.5% of the population. It counted 18.4 million social media user identities, equal to 31.8%.

Advertising tools reached 18.4 million adults on TikTok, 17.0 million on Facebook and 12.1 million on YouTube in late 2025. Instagram reached 3.95 million and X 2.09 million, though these are advertising estimates, not counts of active users.

WhatsApp has no official Kenyan user count in the sources reviewed. The Digital News Report 2026 nonetheless calls it influential for circulating political information and mobilisation.

X is where creators have a visible political influence, the same report says, despite its small user base. TikTok and YouTube are central entry points for younger audiences.

US platform companies are directly affected, because the 2025 amendment’s blocking power would have let a state committee restrict apps and websites. The July 2026 judgment removed that power for now.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors in Meta and Alphabet should note that a Kenyan court voided a power to block sites without court approval. An appeal or a new law could revive that risk before the August 2027 election.

Travelers and business visitors should follow several outlets across ownership camps, such as Citizen Digital, Nation.Africa, The Standard and The Star. NMG has a new controlling owner, so readers should watch for any change in its coverage.

Journalists and researchers working in Kenya may need accreditation from MCK, which accredits journalists and foreign journalists under the Media Council Act. Legal advice before publishing allegations is prudent given the cybercrimes law.

Visitors can find practical advice in the Rio Times Nairobi city guide and wider coverage on the Kenya news hub. Related explainers cover Kenya security and crime, Kenya politics and key players, Kenya culture and Kenya natural resources.

Conversions in this guide use the open.er-api.com rate of 129.73 Kenyan shillings per US$1 on 15 October 2026. Amounts from earlier years are converted at that rate for comparison only.

What Is Not Known

Audited circulation and audience figures for most Kenyan newspapers, channels and sites are not published in one reliable public source. Market shares by company can therefore only be estimated.

The owners behind S.N.G Holdings and exact stakes in Royal Media Services, Mediamax and Radio Africa could not be confirmed. The price of the NMG sale, its regulatory approvals, any minority offer and any editorial change are also not known.

Standard Group’s 2025 results and a reported 1 November chief executive exit were not on its investor page on 16 October 2026. Which of its TV channels remain on air is unclear.

The contents of the Media Council Bill and any appeal against the 2025 and 2026 court rulings are not known. It is not known who abducted Alex Kiprotich or whether anyone will be charged.

No official count of WhatsApp users in Kenya was found. DataReportal and the Communications Authority also use different population bases, 57.8 million and 53.3 million.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the main newspapers in Kenya?

Nation Media Group publishes the Daily Nation, Taifa Leo and Business Daily, and Standard Group publishes The Standard. The Star is part of Radio Africa Group, and RSF says the Daily Nation is the most-read of four dailies.

Who owns Nation Media Group?

The Aga Khan Fund agreed on 10 March 2026 to sell its 54.08% stake to Taarifa Ltd, owned by Rostam Azizi. NMG is listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, and the sale would end 66 years of Aga Khan ownership.

Which TV channels are most watched in Kenya?

RSF names Citizen TV, owned by Royal Media Services, among the most popular channels. A 2025 survey of online news users found it reached 68% weekly, but the sample is not representative.

How free is the press in Kenya?

Kenya ranks 106th of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, up from 117th in 2025. RSF says police violence and self-censorship remain problems, especially around protests and elections.

What happened to Kenyan TV stations during the June 2025 protests?

The Communications Authority ordered stations on 25 June 2025 to stop live protest coverage, and three channels said signals were cut. The High Court suspended the order that day and quashed it in November 2025.

Which social media platforms are biggest in Kenya?

In late 2025 advertising tools reached 18.4 million adults on TikTok, 17.0 million on Facebook and 12.1 million on YouTube. DataReportal gives these as advertising estimates, and WhatsApp has no official Kenyan user count.

Who regulates the media in Kenya?

The Communications Authority licenses broadcasters and regulates telecoms, while the Media Council of Kenya accredits journalists and sets media standards. The Media Council Act also created a Complaints Commission.

Sources: Reporters Without Borders, Kenya country profile, 2026 index and barometer; RSF, Homa Bay attack on journalists (18 August 2026); Communications Authority of Kenya, Sector Statistics Report Q4 2025/26; Communications Authority, board of directors; Communications Authority, management committee; Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, leadership; Media Council of Kenya, statement on the abduction (2 September 2026); Media Council of Kenya; Kenya Law, Media Council Act; Kenya Law, Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act (2018); Nation Media Group, audited results for 2025 (Nairobi Securities Exchange); Nation Media Group website; Nation Media Group, board of directors; Nairobi Securities Exchange, listed companies; Standard Group, annual report 2024; Standard Group, half-year results 2025; Standard Group, appointment of chief executive (1 April 2026); Standard Group, changes in the board (13 October 2026); Standard Group, about us; Royal Media Services; Kenya Broadcasting Corporation, about us; Aga Khan Development Network, media services; DataReportal, Digital 2026 Kenya; Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026 and 2025, Kenya; The Standard, Aga Khan Fund sale of NMG stake (10 March 2026); Kenyans.co.ke, NMG board changes (29 August 2026); Capital FM, High Court order on the CA directive (June 2025); The Star, High Court suspends broadcast ban (25 June 2025); Citizen Digital, High Court judgment on the directive (November 2025); Bloggers Association of Kenya, High Court suspends sections (October 2025); Capital FM, cybercrimes judgment (2 July 2026); The Star, cybercrimes judgment (2 July 2026); Kenyans.co.ke, cybercrimes judgment (2 July 2026); Citizen Digital, police statement on the abduction (2 September 2026); Radio Africa Group; Kenyans.co.ke, Standard Group chief executive notice (16 October 2026); Kenyans.co.ke, Mediamax stations (2021); Rio Times Kenya explainers (all accessed 16 October 2026).

World.title: Bolivia in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances
World.content:
BOLIVIA · LATIN AMERICA

Key Facts — The basics Bolivia is a landlocked Andean republic of about 11.4 million people, a full Mercosur member since August 2024 and a member of the Andean Community, the OAS and CELAC, whose ALBA membership was suspended in October 2025.

— Why it matters Bolivia holds an estimated 23 million tonnes of lithium resources, the third largest national figure in the world, while its gas exports are shrinking, so its alliances shape regional energy and minerals.

— The numbers The IMF’s October 2026 outlook forecasts a 3.0% contraction in 2026 for an economy of US$53.8 billion, income of US$4,223 per person, the lowest in South America, and public debt near 100% of output.

— Who is who President Rodrigo Paz of the Christian Democratic Party took office on 8 November 2025, Héctor Huanca has been foreign minister since 3 August 2026, and Vice President Edmand Lara broke publicly with the government in November 2025.

— What to watch Chile’s President José Antonio Kast is due in La Paz on Friday, 16 October 2026 for talks on trade, fuel and the sea claim, and the fate of two lithium contracts with Chinese and Russian partners is open.

— Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US investors face a shrinking economy but a US$1.9 billion IMF programme, US travellers face a Level 2 advisory with sudden road blockades, and Washington has promised to restore ambassadors after 17 years.

The Bolivia continent story is a landlocked, mineral-rich country with a shrinking economy and falling gas exports. This guide explains its weight, its regional seats, its disputes and its allies, as of October 2026.

The central question is how a landlocked Andean republic of about 11.4 million people fits into Latin America. The short answer is that Bolivia is small in money, large in minerals and busy in diplomacy.

For US readers, Bolivia matters because it holds the world’s third-largest national lithium estimate and is courting Washington. It also matters because Brazil buys its gas, Chile and Argentina share its lithium region, and Chile holds the coast Bolivia claims.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Figures come from the IMF’s World Economic Outlook of October 2026, the national statistics institute INE and Bolivian ministries. All money is given in US$, using the IMF’s own dollar series.

Daily news is in the Rio Times Bolivia section, and the pillar Bolivia in 2026 explained covers the fuel crisis. The lithium explainer and the profile of President Rodrigo Paz go deeper on two themes below.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “IMF sees Brazil as 8th-largest economy by 2027” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The Bolivia Continent Story in Numbers

INE counted 11,365,333 people in the census of Saturday, 23 March 2024. The IMF projects 12.75 million for 2026, about 1.4 million above the census, and its per-person figures use that higher number.

The IMF forecasts an economy of US$53.8 billion in 2026, shrinking 3.0%, with a further fall of 1.5% in 2027. Income per person is about US$4,223, the lowest of South America’s 12 countries.

Prices rose fast, with average inflation of 19.5% in 2025 and a projected 12.7% in 2026. The IMF also puts gross public debt at 100.2% of output in 2026, up from 83.3% in 2025.

The IMF and Bolivia agreed on 29 July 2026, at staff level, on a 36-month programme worth about US$1.9 billion. Press reports say the IMF board approved it in early October 2026, releasing about US$214 million at once.

The IMF said the authorities plan a more flexible, market-based exchange rate and an end to distortions in the currency market. The programme also aims to rebuild reserves and strengthen social safety nets.

The COB, Bolivia’s main union body, and peasant groups blocked roads for seven weeks in May and June 2026, demanding Paz resign. A state of exception followed on Saturday, 20 June 2026, with losses estimated unofficially at about US$3 billion.

Mercosur and the Andean Community, Bolivia in Both

Bolivia handed over its accession instrument at the Mercosur summit in Asunción on Monday, 8 July 2024. Under the protocol, full membership took effect 30 days later, on Wednesday, 7 August 2024.

Mercosur is the customs union of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, with Venezuela suspended. Mercosur says Bolivia has up to four years to adopt the bloc’s rules, and the accession protocol dates from 2015.

President Paz attended the 68th summit in Paraguay on Tuesday, 30 June 2026. Leaders pledged there to speed up the protocol’s implementation.

The leaders also backed respect for Bolivia’s constitutional government. They welcomed the interim trade agreement with the European Union, in provisional application since Friday, 1 May 2026.

Mercosur lists Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru among its associated states, so Bolivia sits where two blocs overlap. Bolivia is also a founding member of the Andean Community, created by the Cartagena Agreement of Monday, 26 May 1969.

The community has four members today, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, and its secretariat sits in Lima. Peru took over its rotating presidency from Ecuador on Wednesday, 30 September 2026, in Quito.

Where Bolivia Sits in the OAS, CELAC, ALBA and BRICS

Bolivia belongs to the Organization of American States, the Washington-based political body of the Americas. In June 2026 its General Assembly in Panama passed a resolution backing Bolivia’s elected government, ABC Color reported.

OAS Secretary General Albert Ramdin led a mission to La Paz and Santa Cruz from Wednesday, 29 July 2026. The mission praised its frank talks with Bolivian sectors and will report to the Permanent Council in Washington.

Bolivia is one of 33 members of CELAC, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, constituted in 2011. Uruguay’s President Yamandú Orsi took over its rotating presidency at the Bogotá summit in March 2026.

ALBA, the leftist alliance founded by Venezuela and Cuba, suspended Bolivia on Friday, 24 October 2025. It cited statements by the incoming Paz government against Cuba, Venezuela and Nicaragua, and spoke of a suspension, not an expulsion.

Bolivia had announced its withdrawal from ALBA once before, in November 2019, under its interim government. Its status after the October 2025 suspension could not be confirmed, and no formal withdrawal notice was found.

BRICS, the group of emerging powers chaired by India in 2026, lists Bolivia as a partner country since Wednesday, 1 January 2025. Partner status is a step below full membership.

The Shield of the Americas is a US-led security grouping that began at a Doral, Florida, summit in March 2026. Bolivia took part, and on Friday, 5 June 2026 its foreign ministry thanked the grouping’s member countries for their support.

Chile, the Sea and 48 Years Without Ambassadors

Bolivia has no coastline, and its claim to sea access has shaped relations with Chile for generations. On Monday, 1 October 2018, the International Court of Justice found that Chile never undertook a legal obligation to negotiate sovereign access.

The two countries have kept only consular relations since Friday, 17 March 1978. On Tuesday, 10 March 2026, the Bolivian presidency announced that ambassadors would be restored.

The Chilean daily Emol still described relations as consular, without ambassadors, on 2 October 2026. Chile’s conservative President José Antonio Kast took office on Wednesday, 11 March 2026.

Kast is due in La Paz on Friday, 16 October 2026, with an 11-point agenda on trade, security, fuel and critical minerals. The Chilean outlet Pauta calls it the first official visit by a Chilean president to La Paz since August 1955.

Officials plan to sign terms of reference to modernise ACE 22, the bilateral trade agreement. La Paz also wants faster fuel transport from the Chilean port of Arica to Sica-Sica in Bolivia.

Bolivia also raised timber shipments investigated in Chilean ports, and the foreign ministries had agreed to convene a free-transit working group. Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo said the sea claim stays on the agenda.

Aramayo added that Bolivia has never abandoned the path of its maritime claim. The Rio Times has followed the oil and minerals talks, and the pillar on Chile and its neighbours covers the Chilean side.

Lithium, Gas and the Resource Disputes

The US Geological Survey puts Bolivia’s lithium resources at 23 million tonnes, behind Argentina’s 28 million and ahead of Chile’s 13 million. The three countries form the “lithium triangle” of the high Andes, which the Rio Times lithium guide maps.

YLB, Bolivia’s state lithium company, signed two contracts in late 2024 with CBC of China and Uranium One Group of Russia. Both cover industrial plants in the Salar de Uyuni, and YLB confirmed in February 2026 that they went to the Legislative Assembly.

There they must follow the procedure for a law, and the Assembly’s final decision could not be confirmed in October 2026. The contract values reported in 2025 differ between outlets, so none is given here.

YLB said in February 2026 that no industrial contract was signed under Paz, only a talks deal with Australian-German group EAU Lithium. It added that the 2024 and 2025 agreements will be subject to a new lithium law, whose passage could not be confirmed.

In a presidency note dated 16 October 2026, Aramayo said lithium calls for coordinated action among Chile, Argentina and Bolivia. The 2024 contracts, by contrast, went to partners from China and Russia.

Gas export revenue fell to US$283.8 million in January to May 2026 from US$471.3 million a year earlier, INE data show. YPFB, the state oil and gas company, calls the picture very worrying.

YPFB projects a 30% fall in gas exports in 2026, the Brazilian outlet eixos said in May. Exports average 9.11 million cubic metres a day, and YPFB sees export capacity ending in 2030 on current reserves.

Proven reserves are 3.7 trillion cubic feet, against 8.95 trillion in 2018, Correo del Sur wrote in July 2026. Argentina ended its Bolivian gas purchases in 2024, after the supply contract expired on 31 July and extra volumes ran through September.

GTB, the pipeline operator, expects under 0.5 million cubic metres a day of Argentine gas through Bolivia in 2026, eixos reported. Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva met Paz on 30 June 2026, saying Bolivia should stay Brazil’s top gas supplier.

Lula and Paz agreed to speed up talks between Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, and YPFB on gas extraction. The earlier Rio Times pillar on Bolivia in 2026 covers the fuel side of the crisis.

Washington, Brasília, Buenos Aires and Beijing

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Paz announced on Saturday, 8 November 2025 that ambassadors would return after 17 years. Ties were downgraded in 2008, when Evo Morales expelled the US ambassador and Washington reciprocated.

China took 21.6% of Bolivia’s goods trade in 2025, against 4.6% for the United States. Those IMF trade shares feed The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, which also lists Bolivia as a Belt and Road partner.

Argentine President Javier Milei attended Paz’s inauguration and met him in La Paz on Saturday, 8 November 2025. Both pledged a common agenda, and Paz stressed cooperation across Bolivia’s five borders.

Paz repeated the point in October 2026, saying his government is working across all five borders, Chile included. Correo del Sur reported his remarks on 12 October 2026, and added that Bolivia has already held dialogue with Brazil.

Where Bolivia Ranks in the Power Index

The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, October 2026 edition, puts Bolivia 12th of 14 countries with 28.4 points. It scores Bolivia highest on military means (54.6) and state capacity (49.4), and lowest on influence (13.0) and economic weight (13.2).

The index puts Bolivia in its hedging group: a BRICS partner that also takes part in the Shield of the Americas. Only Brazil, Mexico and Uruguay share that middle group.

Who Leads Bolivia in October 2026

Rodrigo Paz Pereira of the Christian Democratic Party won the runoff on Sunday, 19 October 2025, with 54.96% of valid votes. He beat former president Jorge “Tuto” Quiroga, who took 45.04%, and took office on Saturday, 8 November 2025.

Vice President Edmand Lara, elected on Paz’s ticket, said on 25 November 2025 that he was no longer part of the government. On Monday, 5 October 2026, as president of the Assembly, he swore in José Armando Urioste as interim attorney general.

Foreign Minister Héctor Huanca, a former official of the foreign-trade vice-ministry, was sworn in on Monday, 3 August 2026. He replaced Fernando Aramayo, who became Minister of the Presidency.

How Bolivia Compares With Its Peers

Bolivia’s peers in Mercosur and the Andean Community are mostly richer and faster growing. The IMF’s October 2026 forecasts for 2026 give the following picture.

Bolivia: about 12.75 million people, an economy of US$53.8 billion, about US$4,223 per person and a contraction of 3.0%.

Paraguay, the other landlocked state in Mercosur, has half of Bolivia’s population but a larger economy. Brazil’s economy is about 49 times the size of Bolivia’s.

Bolivia is the only one of these six countries the IMF expects to shrink in 2026. It forecasts a smaller contraction of 1.5% in 2027 and public debt of 95.1% of output.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors face an economy in contraction, average inflation of 12.7% and public debt near 100% of output. The US$1.9 billion IMF programme gives Bolivia fresh financing, but its reviews will set the pace.

US policy has moved from confrontation to courtship, with ambassadors promised and Bolivia taking part in the Shield of the Americas. The two 2024 lithium contracts went to Chinese and Russian partners, and the Assembly’s final decision on them could not be confirmed.

US travellers face a Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, issued on Tuesday, 18 August 2026, citing crime, unrest and health. Blockades can close roads quickly, so flexible plans matter.

Lithium buyers and Brazilian gas importers watch the same two files. Those are the Assembly’s decision on the lithium contracts and the talks between Petrobras and YPFB.

Readers planning a stay can start with the guide to the cost of living in La Paz. Daily developments appear in the Bolivia section linked above.

What Is Not Known

The outcome of the Kast visit on 16 October 2026 was not public when this guide was finalised. That includes whether ambassadors will be restored, and the full list of the 11 agenda points was not found.

Whether Bolivia’s new lithium law has passed, and whether the Assembly has voted on the two contracts, could not be confirmed. Nor is it clear what ALBA’s status is after the suspension or whether La Paz plans a formal exit.

It is unclear whether Bolivia is covered by the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement. Nor is it known whether either capital has named an ambassador since November 2025.

The exact date of the IMF board approval, reported for early October 2026, could not be confirmed on the IMF’s own site. The same applies to the exact launch day of the Shield of the Americas, which was in March 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Bolivia a member of Mercosur?

Yes, Bolivia deposited its accession instrument on 8 July 2024, and full membership took effect on 7 August 2024. It has up to four years to adopt the bloc’s rules.

Does Bolivia have access to the sea?

No, Bolivia is landlocked. The International Court of Justice ruled in 2018 that Chile has no legal obligation to negotiate sovereign sea access.

Which regional bodies does Bolivia belong to?

Bolivia is a member of Mercosur, the Andean Community, the OAS and CELAC, and a BRICS partner country. Its ALBA membership was suspended on 24 October 2025, and its current status could not be confirmed.

How much lithium does Bolivia have?

The US Geological Survey estimates 23 million tonnes of resources, second in Latin America after Argentina’s 28 million. No industrial plant is confirmed as approved, because the Assembly’s decision on two 2024 contracts could not be confirmed.

Who is the president of Bolivia?

Rodrigo Paz Pereira of the Christian Democratic Party has been president since 8 November 2025. His vice president, Edmand Lara, said in November 2025 that he was no longer part of the government.

Does Bolivia still export gas to Argentina and Brazil?

Exports to Argentina ended in 2024, while Brazil remains a gas buyer. Gas export revenue fell to US$283.8 million in January to May 2026 from US$471.3 million a year earlier.

World.title: South Africa Media Landscape Explained
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · MEDIA

Key Facts — The basics South Africa media mixes the state broadcaster SABC, the commercial channel e.tv, the pay TV giant DStv, now owned by Canal+, and private newspapers and news sites led by News24.

— Why it matters South Africa ranks 21st of 180 countries in the 2026 press freedom index, up from 27th, so US investors, diplomats and travellers have access to open, critical local coverage.

— The numbers Broadcasting revenue fell 4.6% to R33.0 billion (about US$2.0 billion) in 2025, pay TV subscribers dropped 9.6% to 6.7 million, and social media had 29.1 million user identities in October 2025.

— Who is who Naspers owns Media24 and News24, Canal+ owns MultiChoice and DStv, Arena Holdings publishes the Sunday Times, eMedia owns e.tv, and ICASA, the communications regulator, licenses broadcasters.

— What to watch A revised SABC Bill with a new funding model is still to be tabled in Parliament, and the future of the former Independent Media newspapers remains unsettled as of October 2026.

— What it means for you US readers can follow credible English coverage on News24, Daily Maverick and TimesLIVE, but should weigh paywalls, shrinking newsrooms and ownership disputes when choosing sources.

South Africa media mixes a struggling public broadcaster, Canal+ pay TV and a press ranked 21st of 180 for freedom. This guide maps the outlets, owners, rules and platforms as of October 2026.

South Africa media is diverse, sturdy and dynamic, according to the 2026 World Press Freedom Index of Reporters Without Borders (RSF). The index puts the country 21st of 180, but newsrooms are shrinking and owners are changing as of October 2026.

For US readers, this matters because these outlets set the facts on South African elections, markets and security. This guide covers newspapers, broadcasters, digital outlets, owners, regulation, press freedom and social media as of October 2026.

Newspapers and Digital News Sites

RSF says the Sunday Times is still the best-selling newspaper and calls News24 very popular. The Digital News Report 2026 names News24 as the largest news site.

Arena Holdings publishes the Sunday Times, Business Day, Sowetan, Financial Mail, The Herald and the Daily Dispatch in print. Its websites, led by TimesLIVE, serve more than 10 million readers a month, the company says, without dating that figure.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Sudan's army chief sends Trump a message on peace” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Media24, owned by the Naspers group, publishes News24 and Netwerk24 and has closed much of its print business since 2024. News24 has added a paywall, which RSF says increasingly limits access for readers who cannot afford to pay.

Caxton and CTP, founded in 1980, owns The Citizen daily. It also publishes regional community newspapers and says it employs about 5,500 people, a figure its website does not date.

Daily Maverick keeps its content free, RSF says, and made its first cuts in December 2024, the Digital News Report 2025 says. The Digital News Report 2026 says the Mail & Guardian is cutting 12 of its 25 permanent newsroom staff.

Newer digital voices are growing, including the Debrief Network, founded in 2025 and anchored by former News24 editor Qaanitah Hunter. Trust in news fell to 50% in 2026, down 5 points, though still above the 37% global average.

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Broadcasters, From the SABC to DStv

The SABC is the public broadcaster, and the regulator ICASA counts three public television and 18 public radio licences in 2026. The SABC gets R234 million (about US$14 million) from the 2026/27 budget and has won two straight unqualified audit opinions.

The TV licence costs R265 a year (about US$16), BusinessTech and IOL report. Both outlets say most households that must pay do not, and the SABC’s funding model is under review.

e.tv is a commercial free-to-air channel owned by eMedia Holdings, which also runs eNCA and Openview. The group’s results for the year to March 2026 describe an 8.7% contraction in the broader TV advertising market.

In August 2026, Business Day and IOL reported 171 of eNCA’s 309 staff at risk in a shift to a digital-first newsroom. The parent company, eMedia Holdings, is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) under the code EMNE.

MultiChoice, owner of DStv, came under Canal+ control on 22 September 2025 in a deal worth about US$3.0 billion. MultiChoice left the JSE in December 2025, and Canal+, a French media group, plans a secondary JSE listing.

Canal+ reported 22.6 million Africa and Asia subscribers on 30 June 2026, up 7.2% on a combined basis. It said June 2026 was its best month for new South African subscribers in a decade, and Showmax closed in April.

ICASA counted 6.7 million pay TV subscribers at 30 September 2025, down 9.6% in a year as streaming grew. Broadcasting revenue fell 4.6% to R33.0 billion (about US$2.0 billion) in 2025, and subscriptions brought in R24.5 billion (about US$1.5 billion).

Radio is mostly community-run, with 206 community radio licences, 24 commercial and 18 public radio licences in ICASA’s 2026 report. Six community television licences also exist, alongside the three public TV licences.

The Rio Times has covered the new DStv packages that MultiChoice introduced in September 2026. They show how the pay TV leader is trying to win back viewers.

How South Africa Media Is Owned

Ownership sits with a few groups: Naspers, Arena Holdings, Sekunjalo, Caxton, eMedia and now Canal+. Media24, Independent Media and eNCA have each restructured since 2024 as print revenue shrank and platforms took advertising.

Naspers, a JSE-listed technology group, owns Media24, whose revenue fell 28% to US$102 million in the year to March 2026. TimesLIVE and IOL reported its adjusted loss before interest and tax at US$16 million, up from US$10 million, with 1,194 employees.

In 2024 Media24 announced it would close the print editions of five newspapers, three of them moving to digital-only brands. On 27 February 2026 Media24 began consultations on closing the City Press newsroom, and the final outcome was not confirmed.

Lebashe Investment Group launched Arena Holdings in 2019 by buying Tiso Blackstar’s media assets for R1.05 billion (about US$63 million). Arena’s current shareholders were not confirmed for this guide, and the company’s website does not list them.

Independent Media’s mastheads include The Star, Cape Times and The Mercury, which Sekunjalo says it owns and had licensed to Independent Media. Sekunjalo said on 21 July 2026 it would stop funding the loss-making company, with the licence due to end 31 July.

National Media Group, a new publisher, was unveiled on 31 July 2026 for former Independent titles such as the Cape Times. Sekunjalo says it holds a financial stake in the group, but its full ownership has not been disclosed.

Sekunjalo says it invested more than R5.2 billion (about US$314 million) in Independent Media and related businesses over a decade. IOL says it has been independent since 2014 and announced a R200 million (about US$12 million) expansion in May 2026.

Daily Maverick says part of that claim was spending on broader media operations, not direct investment in Independent Media. The Press Council expelled the Independent Media group on 23 October 2024 for refusing to obey its rulings.

Rand conversions use 16.58 rand per US$1, the rate of 15 October 2026. Amounts that sources gave in US$, such as Media24’s results, are shown as published.

Press Freedom and the Rule Book

RSF ranked South Africa 21st of 180 countries in 2026 with a score of 77.95, up from 27th in 2025. It placed the country 17th on the legal indicator and 15th on the social indicator, but only 49th on safety.

RSF says the 1996 Constitution protects press freedom. It adds that apartheid-era and anti-terrorism laws are used to limit reporting on institutions deemed in the national interest.

Journalists are rarely arrested, RSF says, but Thomo Nkgadima was held for more than 48 hours in December 2023. RSF also cites surveillance of investigative reporters and smear campaigns, with the opposition Economic Freedom Fighters party the most virulent.

RSF says high costs hamper small independent outlets, and the government is accused of steering advertising to favoured titles. In 2021 the Constitutional Court ordered changes to the interception law to better protect journalists’ confidential sources.

The Press Council of South Africa, a voluntary body, applies a Press Code to member titles through a Press Ombud. Its recent rulings, published between 8 and 14 October 2026, involve News24 and the Oudtshoorn Courant.

On 23 October 2024 the council expelled the Independent Media group for refusing to obey its rulings. It was only the second expulsion, after The Jewish Report in May 2022.

ICASA, the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa, regulates broadcasting, telecoms and postal services. It receives R505 million (about US$30 million) from the 2026/27 budget, the communications minister said on 12 May 2026.

The Film and Publication Board, another content regulator in the same portfolio, gets R112 million (about US$7 million). ICASA’s March 2026 report says a Draft White Paper on Audio and Audiovisual Media Services and Online Safety proposed rules for streaming.

The SABC Bill and Public Broadcaster Funding

Communications Minister Solly Malatsi withdrew the SABC Bill (B32-2023) on 10 November 2024, before its second reading. He said it delayed a funding model by three years and gave the minister influence over board appointments.

On 12 May 2026 Malatsi told Parliament the SABC had won a second straight unqualified audit opinion. He added that a funding model study was complete and that talks with National Treasury were under way.

IOL quoted Malatsi in January 2026 saying the revised bill is envisaged for tabling in the 2026/27 financial year. BusinessTech wrote in July 2026 that the draft was incomplete and could reach Parliament only within the 2028 financial year.

Funding is the sticking point, as Malatsi said Treasury did not approve the SABC’s R4.7 billion (about US$283 million) request for 2026/27. IOL reported on 14 October 2026 that the department plans a funding model for Cabinet by the end of 2026/27.

Social Media and Messaging Apps

DataReportal counted 29.1 million social media user identities in South Africa in October 2025, equal to 44.9% of the population. It counted 51.7 million internet users, or 79.6% of the population, in the same month.

Facebook’s advertising tools reached 27.9 million South Africans in late 2025, or 42.9% of the population, DataReportal found. YouTube reached 26.9 million and Instagram 8.60 million, while X reached 2.96 million, or 4.6% of the population.

TikTok’s ad tools reached 29.1 million adults in late 2025, equal to 64.8% of all South Africans aged 18 and above. These are advertising reach estimates, not counts of active users, so they overlap and cannot be added together.

A 2024 Competition Commission survey of 1,182 people found 77% used social media as their main online source of news. Among social media news users, 84% put Facebook in their top three, with TikTok at 47% and WhatsApp at 46%.

ICASA says prepaid mobile messaging revenue fell 49.2% in 2025 as WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal replaced text messages. Statistics South Africa’s 2024 household survey found 82.1% of households had internet access from any location.

Only 17.4% of households had a fixed internet connection at home, the same ICASA report says. Prepaid mobile data revenue rose 7.7% in 2025 as customers relied on smartphones for social media and streaming.

Forbidden Stories reported payments for pro-Russian content, and OpenAI found a user who generated at least 38 pro-Kremlin articles. Most of the articles appeared on South African news sites, and the Digital News Report says foreign incursions are eroding trust.

Money, Platforms and the Future of News

On 13 November 2025 the Competition Commission released the final report of its Media and Digital Platforms Market Inquiry. It announced a R688 million (about US$41 million) media support package agreed with Google and YouTube for national, community and vernacular media.

Meta, TikTok and X agreed to expand monetisation support for publishers, and AI firms agreed to offer content controls. It also urged the communications department to develop content-moderation rules and set up an independent Social Media Ombud.

A first fund, run with the Association of Independent Publishers, gave R10.7 million (about US$645,000) to 23 digital news projects. The Digital News Report says it is too early to judge whether such money brings lasting recovery or a brief respite.

The Digital News Report says news creators are drawing audiences away from legacy outlets toward personality-driven channels. It adds that some creators, including conservative commentators copying United States techniques, are less invested in ethical journalism.

News24 appointed a head of AI strategy and rolled out an AI newsroom assistant, the Digital News Report says. A Stellenbosch University study found most journalists use AI cautiously and often check its output by hand.

What It Means for US Readers

US readers can follow South African politics and business in English through News24, Daily Maverick, TimesLIVE, Business Day and the SABC. Some of these sites sit behind paywalls, so check which stories are free before relying on one source.

Investors tracking Naspers, eMedia or Canal+ should note that South African television advertising fell 8.7% in the year to March 2026. Canal+ says its MultiChoice turnaround is under way, while Media24 and eNCA are cutting jobs.

Expats in Cape Town and Johannesburg use local news for safety, traffic and protest alerts, so a mix of sources helps. Visitors can also read the Rio Times guide to South African culture and key figures before they travel.

Washington watchers should note that foreign information campaigns have reached South African news sites, as the Digital News Report documents. For wider context, see the Rio Times guides to who runs South Africa and foreign powers and investors in South Africa.

Audience and language context is in the guide to South Africa’s population and ethnic groups. Daily news from the country is collected on the Rio Times South Africa page.

What Is Not Known

No official count of WhatsApp users in South Africa was found in the sources opened for this guide. DataReportal’s platform figures are advertising reach estimates, not active users.

Union Sactwu’s liquidation bid against the Independent Media Consortium was set for hearing on 19 August 2026; its outcome was not confirmed. The final ownership of National Media Group and the future of the former Independent titles are also undisclosed.

It is not confirmed whether the Independent Media group has rejoined the Press Council since its expulsion in October 2024. Arena Holdings’ current shareholders were not found on the company’s website.

The date for tabling a revised SABC Bill is unclear, because reports give both the 2026/27 and 2028 financial years. The Digital News Report survey sample is mostly English-speaking and online, so its trust figures do not represent all South Africans.

Current circulation figures for newspapers were not found in an open primary source. Brand-level weekly reach figures appear only as charts in the Digital News Report and could not be read as text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the main newspapers in South Africa?

Leading titles include the Sunday Times, Business Day, Sowetan and The Citizen, alongside the digital outlets News24 and Daily Maverick. RSF names the Sunday Times as the best-selling newspaper in its 2026 index.

Who owns the SABC, e.tv and DStv?

The SABC is the state-owned public broadcaster, e.tv belongs to eMedia Holdings and DStv’s owner MultiChoice now belongs to Canal+. Canal+ took control of MultiChoice on 22 September 2025.

How free is the press in South Africa?

RSF ranked South Africa 21st of 180 countries in 2026, up from 27th in 2025. The Constitution protects press freedom, but journalists face smear campaigns and surveillance.

Who regulates the media in South Africa?

ICASA regulates broadcasting, while the voluntary Press Council handles complaints about print and online news through its Press Code. The Competition Commission also shapes the market through its 2025 inquiry into digital platforms.

Is TV licensing ending in South Africa?

Not yet: the licence costs R265 a year (about US$16) and the SABC Bill that proposed changes was withdrawn in 2024. A revised bill with a new funding model has not yet been tabled.

Which social media platforms are most used in South Africa?

TikTok reached 29.1 million adults, Facebook 27.9 million and YouTube 26.9 million in late 2025, DataReportal says. X reached only 2.96 million, and no official WhatsApp user count was found.

Where can I read trusted South African news in English?

News24, Daily Maverick, TimesLIVE, Business Day and the SABC all publish in English. The Digital News Report puts overall trust in South African news at 50% in 2026, above the 37% global average.

World.title: Religion in Nigeria Explained
World.content:
NIGERIA · RELIGION

Key Facts — The basics As of October 2026, Nigeria has no census count of religion, and survey estimates put Muslims at about 56% and Christians at about 43%, with traditional faiths and other groups under 1%.

— Why it matters Faith and region overlap in Africa’s most populous country, so religion shapes party tickets, security debates and US policy, including a Country of Particular Concern designation by President Donald Trump on 31 October 2025.

— The numbers The 2023-24 national health survey found 57.6% of women and 58.2% of men aged 15 to 49 were Muslim, and 41.9% of women and 40.8% of men were Christian. Twelve northern states run sharia penal codes.

— Who is who The Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs, led by the Sultan of Sokoto, and the Christian Association of Nigeria, led by Archbishop Daniel Okoh, are the two main bodies speaking for Muslims and Christians.

— What to watch Watch the presidential election on Saturday, 16 January 2027, where the faith of tickets, campaign language and insecurity in the north and Middle Belt will test the country’s religious balance.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Bola Tinubu a 73.5% chance of winning the Nigerian presidential election and Peter Obi 20% (16 October, 10:50 a.m. ET).

— What it means for you Visitors and investors should expect public holidays for Eid, Easter and Christmas, sharia penal rules for Muslims in 12 northern states, and security conditions that differ sharply from region to region.

This guide to Nigeria religion explains the main groups, their political weight, the festivals and the tensions, using dated surveys. Nigeria is split almost evenly between Muslims and Christians, with traditional beliefs woven into both faiths.

Nigeria religion is split almost evenly between Islam and Christianity, with Muslims holding a narrow majority in recent survey estimates. No census has published a religion count since 1963, so every figure below is an estimate from dated surveys.

That matters in the United States because Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and religion now features in US policy toward it. On 31 October 2025 President Donald Trump named Nigeria a Country of Particular Concern, citing claims the Nigerian government disputes.

Nigeria Religion by the Numbers

Nigeria’s 2006 census did not ask about religion, and the last published count dates from 1963. On Wednesday, 29 March 2023, the National Population Commission said its planned census would also leave out religion and ethnicity.

The commission called both topics sensitive within Nigerian politics. Researchers therefore rely on household surveys, above all the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS).

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Sudan's army chief sends Trump a message on peace” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Fieldwork for the 2023-24 DHS ran from 1 December 2023 to 7 May 2024. It asked women and men aged 15 to 49 about their religion.

It found 57.6% of women and 58.2% of men were Muslim, against 41.9% of women and 40.8% of men who were Christian. Catholics made up 8.2% of women and 7.6% of men, and traditionalists 0.4% and 0.9%.

Pew Research Center, using DHS data, estimated that Muslims were 56.1% of all Nigerians in 2020 and Christians 43.4%. It put all other groups at 0.6%.

Pew estimated that Muslims grew 32% to about 120 million between 2010 and 2020, and Christians 25% to about 93 million. Because half of Nigerians are under 18, Pew noted in 2025, studies of adults alone can show a different balance.

Earlier surveys differ because of method, timing and who is counted. A 2009 Pew survey found 52% Muslim and 46% Christian, and the 2018 DHS found 53.5% of women Muslim.

Religion follows geography and ethnicity to a large degree. The Middle Belt separates a largely Muslim north from a heavily Christian south, Pew says.

In Pew’s 2009 survey, 96% of Igbo respondents were Christian and 96% of Hausa respondents were Muslim. The Yoruba of the south-west were split, with 54% Muslim and 45% Christian.

The Rio Times guides to Nigeria history and Nigeria population give the longer background to these regional and religious divides. One runs from the Nok culture to the 2027 election, and the other covers ethnic groups and languages.

Islam in Nigeria, Sunni, Sufi and Shia

In Pew’s 2009 survey of Nigerian Muslims, 38% called themselves Sunni and 42% said they were just Muslim. The US State Department says most Sunnis follow the Maliki school of law.

Sufi brotherhoods are a major strand, with 19% of Muslims in the Tijaniyya and 9% in the Qadiriyya in Pew’s 2009 survey. Salafi groups known as Izala form another current, the State Department says.

Pew’s 2009 survey found 12% of Muslims described themselves as Shia, a figure that no census can confirm. The government has proscribed the Islamic Movement in Nigeria, whose members hold Ashura processions.

The Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA) is the apex Islamic body, set up in 1973 at a conference in Kaduna. It announces the start and end of Ramadan after moon sighting.

As of October 2026 its president-general is the Sultan of Sokoto, Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar, and its secretary-general is Prof. Is-haq Oloyede. The Sultan of Sokoto traditionally leads the council.

The council scheduled a national prayer for Wednesday, 30 September 2026, and a general assembly in Abuja on Thursday, 1 October. Blueprint, a Nigerian daily, carried the announcement on 23 September 2026.

Nigeria’s National Hajj Commission (NAHCON) confirmed a final 2026 quota of 50,000 pilgrims, down from an initial 95,000. By 21 May 2026 it had flown 38,888 pilgrims to Saudi Arabia on 98 flights.

Christianity in Nigeria, Catholic, Anglican and Pentecostal

Christians are about 43% of Nigerians in Pew’s 2020 estimate. In the 2023-24 DHS, Catholics were 8.2% of women and other Christians 33.7%.

The Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), the umbrella body of churches, puts mainline Protestants, including Anglicans, at 25% to 30% of Christians. It puts Pentecostals at about 30%, evangelicals at 10% and African-instituted churches at 5% to 10%, the State Department says.

Catholics, about a quarter of Christians in a 2011 Pew figure, speak through the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria. As of July 2026 the Church of Nigeria (Anglican) is led by Archbishop Henry Ndukuba, enthroned as Primate on 25 March 2020.

Pentecostal churches give Nigerian Christianity its most visible megachurches, and two networks stand out. As of March 2026, Pastor Enoch Adeboye is the worldwide general overseer of the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG).

As of October 2026, Living Faith Church Worldwide, or Winners’ Chapel, says its founder, Bishop David Oyedepo, oversees over 21,000 Nigerian churches. Its Canaanland headquarters in Ota houses Faith Tabernacle, which the church says is reputedly the world’s largest single congregation.

In Pew’s 2009 survey, 26% of Nigerian Christians belonged to Pentecostal denominations, the largest Protestant family. Anglicans were 9%, African-initiated churches 8% and Baptists 8%.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Traditional Religion and Mixed Beliefs

Traditional religions are a small share of declared affiliation, at 0.4% of women and 0.9% of men in the 2023-24 DHS. Many Nigerians still blend Indigenous practices with Islam or Christianity, the US State Department says.

Beliefs outside the two big faiths remain common. Pew said in November 2025 that about seven in ten Nigerian adults believe spells, curses or magic can influence lives.

Yoruba traditional religion, known as Isese, honours deities including Osun, the goddess of fertility. UNESCO inscribed the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove, 75 hectares of forest on the edge of Osogbo, as a World Heritage site in 2005.

Followers of traditional religion can face legal risk where insult laws apply. In August 2023 authorities detained an Isese priest and activist for insulting an emir and other Muslim leaders, the State Department says.

Religion and Political Power

The 1999 constitution bars the federal and state governments from adopting a state religion. It also guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to change one’s faith.

The constitution prohibits parties that limit membership by religion or carry religious names, the State Department says. Civil courts rank above sharia and customary courts, so clerics do not hold final legal authority.

Party tickets are often judged by their balance between Christians and Muslims and between north and south. Section 14 of the constitution adds a formal federal character rule for government appointments.

In July 2022 Bola Tinubu named Kashim Shettima, a fellow Muslim, as his running mate. The Peoples Gazette, a Nigerian news site, called it the first major-party ticket with two Muslims since 1993.

CAN had warned against it, arguing that Nigeria’s roughly equal Christian and Muslim populations should be reflected on a ticket. Tinubu, profiled in Who Is Bola Tinubu, won the 2023 election and took office on Monday, 29 May 2023.

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has set the presidential vote for Saturday, 16 January 2027. INEC’s final candidate list of 12 September 2026 names Tinubu and Shettima again as the ruling-party ticket, ThisDay and Sahara Reporters said.

Two councils speak for the faiths in national affairs, the NSCIA for Muslims and CAN for Christians. The Nigeria Inter-Religious Council (NIREC) also brings Muslim and Christian leaders together, the State Department says.

At a press conference for CAN’s 50th anniversary on Friday, 2 October 2026, Archbishop Okoh urged parties not to weaponise religion. Blueprint, a Nigerian daily, quoted him saying Nigerians had seen enough bloodshed and division in election periods.

Complaints about balance come from both sides. In September 2023 the Muslim advocacy group Muslim Rights Concern said appointments under Tinubu favoured Christians, the State Department records.

Sharia in the Northern States

Sharia, or Islamic law, operates beside the common law in 12 northern states and the Federal Capital Territory. Section 275 of the constitution lets any state that wants one set up a sharia court of appeal.

The 12 states with sharia penal codes generally apply them only to Muslims, and the codes were first approved in 1999. Civil courts rank above sharia courts, and sentences can be appealed to them.

Kano, Zamfara, Sokoto and Yobe have Hisbah boards that help enforce sharia rules among Muslims. Citizens of any faith can choose sharia courts for civil cases, and Zamfara makes sharia courts mandatory for Muslims in criminal cases.

Blasphemy is an offence in both the secular and sharia legal systems. In the 12 sharia states, insulting the Quran or a recognised prophet carries the death penalty.

The State Department says no such sentence has been carried out since 1999, though some people have been sentenced. Pew says sharia codes have been used against Muslims accused of same-sex activity, and blasphemy laws against Muslims, Christians and humanists.

Violence and Religious Tensions

Nigeria faces several overlapping kinds of violence, and its causes are contested. The US State Department’s 2023 report says religion, ethnicity, land and crime are closely linked, making many incidents hard to classify.

In the North East, militant groups Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province have attacked churches and mosques, Pew says. Pew adds that Muslims and Christians alike have been attacked, kidnapped and killed by armed gangs.

In the Middle Belt, Pew says, tension between mostly Christian farmers and Muslim herders has caused violent conflict over land. The State Department says multiple sources see banditry, not religion, as the main driver of violence in the North West.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) says non-state actors regularly kill, kidnap and attack Christians, Muslims and traditionalists. It also says the government tolerates, inadequately responds to or fails to hold violators accountable.

President Donald Trump designated Nigeria a Country of Particular Concern on 31 October 2025, a US label for severe religious-freedom violations. On 3 December 2025 the State Department announced a visa policy that applies to violators of religious freedom, including in Nigeria.

The Nigerian government has disputed claims that Christians are being persecuted for their faith, Pew noted in November 2025. In May 2023 the Sultan of Sokoto said recent killings were not related to religion, the State Department records.

For regional detail on crime and security, see the Rio Times guide to Nigeria security and crime. Visitors should check current US travel advice before planning trips to the north and the Middle Belt.

Festivals and Daily Life

Federal public holidays follow both major faiths. The government declared Thursday, 19 March and Friday, 20 March 2026 for Eid-ul-Fitr, which ends Ramadan.

It declared Friday, 3 April and Monday, 6 April 2026 for Easter. In December 2024 it declared Wednesday, 25 December 2024 and Thursday, 26 December 2024 for Christmas and Boxing Day.

Eid al-Adha follows the Hajj, whose climax fell on Tuesday, 26 May 2026. Nigerian pilgrims formed one of the largest national contingents outside the Arab world, the state broadcaster Voice of Nigeria said.

In Kano, the Eid durbar, called Hawan Idi, is a procession from the Eid praying ground to the Emir’s Palace. In March 2026 the Kano government changed or suspended several durbar events for security reasons, the Voice of Nigeria said.

The Osun-Osogbo festival is an annual procession lasting twelve days in July and August. UNESCO says it renews the mystic bonds between the goddess Osun and the people of the town.

Lagos stages the Eyo festival, or Adamu Orisa Play, a masquerade procession that honours notable people who have died. Voice of Nigeria said the 2025 edition was set for Saturday, 27 December 2025 at Tafawa Balewa Square after an eight-year gap.

Faith runs through daily routines. Pew’s 2009 survey found over nine in ten Muslims fasting in Ramadan and over eight in ten Christians fasting in Lent.

In the same survey 67% of Nigerians welcomed religious leaders speaking on political questions, in roughly equal shares of Christians and Muslims. Some 58% called religious conflict a very big problem, behind unemployment at 89% and corrupt leaders at 81%.

The constitution says no pupil may be forced to take part in religious instruction or ceremonies of another faith. Faith groups also run universities, such as Covenant University in Ota, which the Living Faith website credits to Bishop Oyedepo.

The constitution also tells the state to encourage interfaith marriages and associations that cut across religious lines. NIREC met Muslim and Christian leaders in Abuja in December 2023 to discuss peaceful coexistence, the State Department says.

The Rio Times guide to Nigeria culture profiles key figures behind the country’s festivals and arts. Its media coverage is in the Nigeria media landscape guide.

What It Means for US Readers

US visitors and business travellers should plan around public holidays for Eid, Easter and Christmas. In the 12 sharia states, penal codes generally apply only to Muslims, but local religious customs deserve respect.

Policy readers should note that religion now features in US-Nigeria relations through the Country of Particular Concern designation and the visa policy. The State Department’s 2023 report and USCIRF’s Nigeria page are the main US government sources to follow.

Investors in Nigerian assets should watch the 16 January 2027 election, where faith, region and security shape voting and turnout. Church and mosque networks also run schools and universities, which gives faith leaders influence beyond worship.

In Abuja, the National Mosque and the National Christian Centre stand near each other, as Pew’s photo caption notes. Practical advice is in the Rio Times Abuja and Lagos city guides and the Nigeria news hub.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bets give Bola Tinubu a 73.5% chance of winning the Nigerian presidential election and Peter Obi 20%. The prices stood at 10:50 a.m. ET on 16 October 2026, with about US$131,000 traded on the market.

The market asks who will win, not which faith the winner follows, and it does not measure religious voting. These are bets on an outcome, not opinion polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

No census count of religion has been published since 1963, so the true Muslim-Christian balance is not known. Estimates range from a near-even split to a Muslim majority of about 56%, depending on method and year.

Reliable numbers for Shia Muslims, Sufi orders and traditional believers are scarce, and the 12% Shia figure is a self-description from 2009. The 2023-24 DHS also skipped 20 of 1,400 clusters where security made fieldwork impossible, including 10 in Zamfara.

How many attacks are driven by religion, rather than land, crime or politics, is disputed and cannot be settled from public data. The Nigerian government disputes claims of persecution, while USCIRF calls religious freedom conditions particularly severe.

The faith balance of tickets other than the ruling party’s was not confirmed in the sources reviewed. How often NIREC has met since December 2023 was also not confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main religion in Nigeria?

Islam holds a narrow majority in recent estimates, at 56.1% in Pew’s 2020 estimate and 57.6% of women in the 2023-24 DHS. Christians are the second large group, at about 41% to 43%.

Does Nigeria have an official religion?

No, the constitution bars federal and state governments from adopting a state religion. Twelve northern states nonetheless apply sharia penal codes, generally only to Muslims.

Why is there no census figure for religion in Nigeria?

The 2006 census did not ask about religion. In March 2023 the National Population Commission said its planned census would also leave out religion and ethnicity because both are sensitive.

Which Nigerian states use sharia law?

Twelve northern states have sharia penal codes, and sharia courts also operate in the Federal Capital Territory. The codes generally apply only to Muslims, and sentences can be appealed to civil courts.

Which are the biggest churches in Nigeria?

Large churches include the Catholic Church, the Church of Nigeria (Anglican), the Redeemed Christian Church of God and Winners’ Chapel. The Christian Association of Nigeria is the umbrella body for churches.

What are the main religious festivals in Nigeria?

Eid-ul-Fitr, Easter and Christmas are federal public holidays, and Eid al-Adha follows the Hajj. Local festivals include Osun-Osogbo in Osogbo and the Eyo festival in Lagos.

Is religious violence a risk for visitors to Nigeria?

Violence varies by region, and the US State Department says religion, ethnicity, land and crime are closely linked. Visitors should check current US travel advice, especially for the north and the Middle Belt.

World.title: Ghana Media Landscape Explained
World.content:
GHANA · MEDIA

Key Facts — The basics Ghana media mixes state-owned and private outlets: as of the second quarter of 2026, 571 FM radio stations and 124 TV operators were on air, and 26.3 million Ghanaians were online in October 2025.

— Why it matters Ghana ranked 39th of 180 countries in the 2026 press freedom index, up 13 places from 2025, so US readers get a fairly open news market where journalists still face alleged assaults by soldiers.

— The numbers Ghana scored 72.20 points in the 2026 press freedom index against 67.13 in 2025, and the regulator had authorised 793 FM stations and 170 TV operators by the second quarter of 2026.

— Who is who The state owns Graphic Communications, the New Times Corporation and broadcaster GBC; Multimedia Group, founded by Kwasi Twum in 1995, runs Joy and Adom; the National Media Commission oversees state media and the National Communications Authority licenses broadcasters.

— What to watch Watch whether the promised misinformation bill reaches Parliament, whether the August 2026 fines of GH¢20,000 (about US$1,700) per institution improve Right to Information compliance, and where Ghana lands in the 2027 press freedom index.

— Prediction markets Kalshi gives President John Mahama’s NDC a 59.5% chance and the opposition NPP 40.5% in its market “Ghana parliamentary election winner?” labelled “In 2028” (16 October, 10:48 a.m. ET).

— What it means for you US travellers, investors and expats can read open, English-language Ghanaian news every day, but should weigh party-linked ownership and treat viral WhatsApp and Facebook claims with care.

Ghana media blends state-owned newspapers and broadcasters with a lively private radio, TV and online sector. This guide maps who owns what, how it is regulated and how free it is as of October 2026.

Ghana media spans state-owned newspapers, 571 operating FM radio stations and 124 broadcasting TV operators as of the second quarter of 2026. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a Paris press-freedom group, ranked Ghana 39th of 180 countries in 2026.

For US readers, this landscape decides which sources to trust on Ghana’s politics, economy and safety. Daily news from the country is collected on the Rio Times Ghana page, and related guides are linked below.

Ghana Media by the Numbers

The National Communications Authority (NCA), the state regulator, had authorised 793 FM radio stations by the second quarter of 2026. Of those, 571 were operating on air.

The NCA had also authorised 170 TV operators by the same quarter, and 124 of them were broadcasting. The largest group is 96 free-to-air single satellite channels.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Sudan's army chief sends Trump a message on peace” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Online, 26.3 million Ghanaians were using the internet in October 2025, or 74.6% of the population, DataReportal calculated. The same report counted 41.8 million mobile connections, equal to 119% of the population.

Newspapers, From the Daily Graphic to The Chronicle

Graphic Communications Group Ltd (GCGL) publishes the Daily Graphic and is a state-owned enterprise, says the State Interests and Governance Authority. Britain’s Daily Mirror Group founded it in 1950 as the West African Graphic Company.

The state acquired it in 1962, made it a statutory body in 1971 and made it a limited company in 1999. GCGL also publishes The Mirror, Graphic Sports and Graphic Showbiz.

The Ghanaian Times belongs to the New Times Corporation, a 100% state-owned company that also publishes the Weekend Spectator. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first president, founded it in 1957 as The Guinea Press.

Private titles include The Chronicle and the Daily Guide, which Western Publications publishes. RSF’s 2017 audit recorded Frederick Blay as Western Publications’ 66% owner and then acting chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP).

The NPP is a conservative party, and the audit named Nana Kofi Coomson as The Chronicle’s owner only from online sources. Print was concentrated in 2017: the top four publishers reached 95.9% of readers, and a state-run title was the choice of 72.1%.

Broadcasters From GBC to Joy News and TV3

The Ghana Broadcasting Corporation (GBC) is the public broadcaster, and the NCA counts every station GBC runs as a public station. On 19 August 2026 the National Media Commission named a new GBC board chaired by Francis Mills Robertson.

The Multimedia Group, founded in 1995 by Kwasi Twum, owns Joy 99.7 FM, the first private radio station licensed in Ghana. It calls itself the largest independent commercial media company in Ghana, with about 700 staff.
