World.title: Experts See New Opportunities for Central Asia-Azerbaijan Cooperation in C6 Format
World.content:
ASTANA – The emerging C6 cooperation format, bringing Azerbaijan and the five Central Asian countries together, could strengthen regional trade, transport connectivity and investment, but its success will depend on turning political commitments into concrete projects, experts said during an online webinar on Oct. 15.

The discussion examined the implications of Azerbaijan’s participation in the Central Asian Consultative Meetings, which expanded the traditional C5 format into C6, and the outcomes of the recent Avaza summit in Turkmenistan.

The participants discussed how the expanded format could strengthen economic integration, improve regional connectivity and help countries address shared challenges while preserving their national interests.

From political dialogue to practical cooperation

Zhandos Shaimardanov, director of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, described the Avaza summit as a key milestone in regional cooperation, arguing that closer integration does not require countries to sacrifice sovereignty or choose between international partners.

“Regional cooperation is not a zero-sum game,” he said, adding that stronger ties could benefit each country while strengthening the region as a whole.

He noted that Central Asian countries had initially focused on building national institutions and foreign policy priorities after gaining independence. Today, stronger economies and changing regional dynamics have created greater opportunities for cooperation.

“Azerbaijan’s inclusion in the format opens a new trans-Caspian dimension, connecting Central Asia more closely with the South Caucasus and broader markets,” Shaimardanov said.

The key test will be whether the countries can translate joint initiatives into investment, stronger regional value chains and tangible economic benefits.

“With Azerbaijan’s inclusion in the regional format, this is a timely opportunity to revisit previously proposed initiatives and align the priorities and visions of all six participating countries. The expanded format brings a broader economic geography and new opportunities, making it important to reassess our shared priorities,” Shaimardanov said.

Farid Shafiyev, chairman of Azerbaijan’s Center for Analysis of International Relations and Multiculturalism, also described the Avaza summit as a turning point, saying it reaffirmed the willingness of countries on both sides of the Caspian Sea to develop the C6 framework.

He noted that the summit produced concrete steps, including agreements on the framework’s consultative procedures. Over time, the format could develop into a more structured regional organization, although its evolution will depend on the countries’ priorities and the complex geopolitical environment.

Shafiyev cited growing economic ties as evidence of progress.

“Trade between Azerbaijan and Central Asian countries has increased by 50%. Around 400 companies with capital from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are operating in Azerbaijan, as well as joint investment funds established between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan and between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan,” Shafiyev said.

According to him, these developments demonstrate that cooperation is moving beyond diplomatic dialogue toward investment and business activity.

Joint production and regional connectivity

Javlon Vakhabov, managing director of Uzbekistan’s International Institute for Central Asia, highlighted a growing convergence among regional leaders on the need to develop joint production, coordinate infrastructure investments and focus on implementation.

He pointed to Uzbekistan’s proposal for a Six Countries, One Product initiative as an example of how the countries could pool their capabilities to produce goods and compete in international markets.

The summit also underscored the importance of removing transport, customs and tariff barriers, developing complementary production facilities and strengthening regional supply chains.

The Middle Corridor, which connects Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Europe across the Caspian Sea, remains central to these efforts. Greater coordination of transport infrastructure could reduce delivery times and costs while making regional exports more competitive.

“The countries could also explore cooperation in energy, industrial production and alternative transport routes,” Shafiyev said.

Azerbaijan’s participation broadens the region’s access to international markets and creates opportunities for closer cooperation with partners in Türkiye and Europe, while also opening avenues for trade with other regions.

Digitalization and trade facilitation

The experts emphasized that closer economic integration will require practical measures to make cross-border trade more efficient.

Shaimardanov proposed launching a pilot initiative to improve the digital exchange of trade and transport information between Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Such a system could allow shipment information to be submitted once and shared securely among customs authorities, railway operators and ports.

According to Zuhra Halimova, senior adviser at CAPS Unlock in Tajikistan, digitalization must be accompanied by compatible regulations, clear data-sharing rules and effective institutions. Countries should build on existing national systems and expertise rather than create additional platforms without a clear purpose.

She also highlighted the need to strengthen trade facilitation and address regulatory barriers that hinder cross-border economic activity.

Water and energy security among shared priorities

Beyond trade and transport, the discussion highlighted water and energy security as areas requiring closer regional coordination.

Halimova noted that climate change and melting glaciers are increasing pressure on water resources, with implications for agriculture, hydropower and energy supplies across the region.

“Climate change in Central Asia and the Caucasus, particularly around the Caspian Sea, requires a coordinated regional response rather than separate national approaches. Water and energy security could become key areas of cooperation within the C6 framework,” Halimova said.

She emphasized the importance of improving water management, strengthening regional dialogue and coordinating water and energy policies to address challenges that cross national borders.

The participants also discussed opportunities to expand energy cooperation, including renewable energy and cross-border infrastructure.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins World Bank Initiative to Attract $20 Billion in Minerals Investment
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has become the first country in Central Asia to join the World Bank Group’s Metals and Minerals Compact, a partnership aimed at attracting around $20 billion in investment by 2031 and expanding the country’s mineral resource base and processing capacity.

The official accession ceremony took place on Oct. 16 on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund in Thailand. Kazakhstan was represented by Yerlan Galiyev, chairman of the board of the National Geological Service under the Ministry of Industry and Construction, reported the Prime Minister’s press service.

Developed by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, and the World Bank Group, the country compact establishes a framework for cooperation in the metals and minerals sector for 2026-2030. It brings together the World Bank Group’s financial, analytical and technical support to advance the country’s industrial and investment priorities.

The compact builds on Kazakhstan’s existing development strategies, including the National Development Plan through 2029, the Concept for the Development of the Geological Industry for 2023-2027, and the Comprehensive Plan for the Development of the Rare and Rare Earth Metals Industry for 2024-2028.

The targeted investment of approximately $20 billion by 2031 is expected to support the expansion of mineral exploration, the development of mining and processing facilities, the adoption of modern technologies and the construction of supporting infrastructure.

The partnership focuses on three areas.

The first is improving public policy and regulatory frameworks for the mining and metallurgical complex to strengthen transparency, regulatory predictability and the investment climate, while promoting international environmental and social standards.

The second involves developing geological exploration, infrastructure and workforce capacity. Priorities include digitizing geological data, improving energy and transport infrastructure, introducing advanced metal-processing technologies and training qualified specialists.

The third focuses on attracting private investment into mineral extraction and downstream processing. The World Bank Group will support investment projects through financial and guarantee instruments, with an emphasis on higher-value-added production and international investor participation.

“Kazakhstan is committed to the principles of responsible and sustainable development of the mineral resource sector. Cooperation with the World Bank Group supports the implementation of national priorities in raw material processing and the expansion of higher-value-added production,” said Minister of Industry and Construction Yersaiyn Nagaspayev.

He added that Kazakhstan expects the partnership to strengthen the sector’s competitiveness and resilience, diversify the economy and improve the use of the country’s natural resource potential.

Implementation of the compact is expected to promote deeper processing of raw materials, create new jobs and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in global production chains.

World.title: Kazakhstan Calls for Restraint, Diplomacy to Prevent Further Escalation in Middle East
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan called on all parties in the Middle East to exercise maximum restraint and prioritize dialogue and diplomacy, reaffirming its support for a two-state solution and the need to prevent further escalation.

Kazakhstan’s position was presented by Permanent Representative to the United Nations Kairat Umarov during the UN Security Council’s quarterly open debate on the situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question, held at UN Headquarters under the Presidency of Greece, reported the Foreign Ministry’s press service on Oct. 16.

The meeting featured 70 speakers, with Ramiz Alakbarov, acting UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, delivering the main briefing.

In his statement, Umarov expressed concern over continued tensions in the Middle East and stressed the need for political and diplomatic settlement to conflicts and the prevention of further escalation.

Kazakhstan reaffirmed its principled support for the Two-State solution and the New York Declaration as a framework for concrete steps towards this objective. Particular emphasis was placed on unhindered humanitarian assistance, the protection of civilians and the recovery of Gaza, as well as the central role of the United Nations, including the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA).

Kazakhstan also expressed its readiness to make a practical contribution to the stabilization and recovery of Gaza, including through civilian reconstruction, food security and digitalization. In this context, partners were encouraged to utilize the potential of the Astana-based Islamic Organization for Food Security.

The statement also highlighted Kazakhstan’s intention to join the Abraham Accords, which are viewed as an additional platform to support the UN-led political process towards the Two-State solution.

Kazakhstan confirmed its readiness to continue constructive engagement in support of peace and stability in the Middle East.

World.title: Middle Corridor Could Add $58 Billion to Regional GDP by 2040, World Bank Says
World.content:
ASTANA – The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor could increase the combined gross domestic product of countries along the route by 3.3% and generate around two million jobs by 2040 if governments invest in infrastructure and improve cross-border coordination, according to a World Bank report presented in Astana on Oct. 15.

“The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, also known as the Middle Corridor, is more than a transit route. It can help Central Asian countries connect with global markets, attract investment, diversify their economies and create business opportunities,” said Andrei Mikhnev, World Bank country manager for Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

Speaking at the New Silk Way business forum, Mikhnev noted that Central Asia’s strategic location between Europe and Asia creates opportunities, but geography alone is not enough to deliver economic benefits.

“The European Union has even nailed the term ‘Global Gateway,’ of which this transport corridor is an important part. But geography alone does not create opportunities. The challenge is to turn connectivity into economic value, and transit flows into broader development,” he said.

Countries along the corridor have invested in railways, roads, ports, logistics facilities and border crossings, while pursuing reforms to facilitate trade and strengthen regional cooperation

According to Mikhnev, further progress will depend on more closely coordinated operations, streamlined border procedures, digitalization and greater private sector participation.

Trade volumes expected to grow

Luis Blancas, World Bank’s senior transport and logistics specialist, presented the report’s findings, describing the corridor as a platform for private investment, job creation and economic growth.

He noted that the route offers distinct benefits depending on countries’ geographic locations and trade needs.

“For the five Central Asian countries, the corridor provides access to global markets and helps diversify trade routes. For the South Caucasus and Türkiye, it offers a more direct connection to Europe, Central Asia and East Asia. For China and Western Europe, it provides an alternative for containerized freight,” Blancas said.

The corridor is also complementary to other Eurasian trade routes, rather than necessarily competing with them, because each route has different costs, operating conditions and advantages for particular types of cargo.

According to the Middle Corridor Association, total freight volumes on the route grew at an average annual rate of 34% between 2021 and 2025. Containerized freight volumes increased by an average of 32% annually over the same period.

The World Bank projects that total freight volumes could rise from about 9 million metric tons in 2023 to nearly 24 million metric tons by 2040, even without additional infrastructure investment beyond projects and facilities in place at the end of 2025.

With further infrastructure investment, volumes could reach 32 million metric tons by 2040. Non-oil freight volumes could increase to about 16 million metric tons, approximately 4.5 times the 2023 level.

Without additional investment, the corridor could miss out on 33% of potential total freight volumes and nearly 90% of potential non-oil freight volumes, according to the report.

The report estimates that infrastructure investment could boost the combined GDP of corridor countries by 3.3%, equivalent to $58 billion at current prices, through increased imports and exports by 2040. The estimate does not include the potential impact of transit trade.

Infrastructure is not the only challenge

Blancas noted that although infrastructure investment remains important, the corridor’s main challenge is likely to be operational performance rather than a lack of physical capacity.

The World Bank identified 16 critical bottlenecks along the corridor, with an estimated cost of around $25 billion to address them. According to the report, 75% of the identified bottlenecks, accounting for 85% of the estimated investment cost, were being addressed.

“The remaining 25% of the projects have not yet entered the implementation phase but are firmly included in government plans and are expected to proceed,” Blancas said.

Investments have already improved capacity on key sections of the network. In Kazakhstan, for example, the double-tracking of the Dostyk-Moiynty railway line reduced its estimated capacity utilization from 100% in 2023 to about 40%, according to the report.

However, infrastructure improvements alone will not necessarily make the corridor competitive with alternative routes for containerized freight between China and Europe.

For a shipment from Chongqing, China, to Budapest, Hungary, average delivery times on the Middle Corridor currently range from 47 to 50 days, compared with about 45 days by sea and 18 days via the Northern Corridor, according to the World Bank’s analysis.

Blancas highlighted that additional infrastructure investment could reduce delivery times on the fastest Middle Corridor route to around 26-27 days by 2040, while the Northern Corridor could offer delivery in around 19 days.

“According to our modeling projections, combining infrastructure investment with improvements in trade facilitation, service delivery and cross-border collaboration would allow the fastest route along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor to close the performance gap with the Northern Corridor by 2040,” he said.

Call for closer regional cooperation

The report proposes a framework called the TCTC Assessment and Response Structure, or TARS, to improve cross-border cooperation. It includes a shared system for measuring corridor performance, a public-private advisory committee and a platform for intergovernmental decision-making.

Blancas said inconsistent data and fragmented coordination make it difficult for governments and businesses to plan effectively. A common evidence base would help participating countries identify bottlenecks, assess progress and coordinate investment decisions.

The report also calls for simplifying transport documentation.

“Moving a container between China and Europe along the corridor currently requires around 15 documents, many of which contain overlapping information,” Blancas said.

The World Bank proposes introducing a single digital Transport, Transit and Trade document, known as T3, alongside a decentralized digital system that would allow national platforms to exchange information while preserving data sovereignty.

Another recommendation is to establish a joint railway and shipping undertaking involving the corridor’s main railway operators and shipping lines. The initiative could improve coordination across rail and maritime segments and support more reliable, time-specific freight services.

World.title: Satellite Solutions for Food Security
World.content:
Global food security faces a number of pressures, including conflict, climate change, pollution and overexploitation. North and Central Asia is a region at risk, with human activity contributing to significant levels of desertification in drylands and other fragile biomes. Agriculture is a major source of employment in the region, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the working population in Tajikistan, more than 30 per cent in Azerbaijan and Georgia and more than 20 per cent in Armenia, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Agriculture underpins the livelihoods of rural populations, which are often among the poorest sectors of society.

With greater efficiency and optimization, the agricultural sector can save water and resources, increase yields and adapt to new climatic realities. That kind of innovation is the theme of this year’s World Food Day (16 October) “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” Across North and Central Asia, geospatial technology is already helping both farmers and policymakers. Making the most of it, however, depends as much on skills and on institutions working together as on the technology itself.

Geospatial technology can support farmers in decision-making processes through online platforms and applications. In Kazakhstan, the application AgroData integrates data from 226 agrometeorological stations, giving farmers real-time information on weather, soil moisture and crop health. Farmer App in Azerbaijan and KosmosAgro in the Russian Federation offer similar tools, from monitoring vegetation growth to estimating yields and spotting pests.

Kyrgyzstan has partnered with the World Food Programme in a project that equipped around 5,000 rural community members and farmers to interpret and apply climate information from new portable equipment deployed across 13 sites. Kyrgyzstan is also building AgroMap, a free application for farmers which will provide real-time information on environmental and agronomic conditions

Satellite technology can also help guide policy at the local and national levels. In Turkmenistan, geographic information system technology has been employed around Lake Altyn Asyr to identify suitable areas for agriculture. In Kazakhstan, the AgroSpace platform provides geospatial data on agricultural land to justify subsidy applications by the mapping and verification of field borders, crop history and current crop conditions.

Putting these tools to work also depends on skills. In 2024, ESCAP – with funding from the Russian Federation – launched a project to strengthen the capacity of Central Asian countries to use Earth observation (EO) and geospatial technologies for monitoring agricultural conditions and the impacts of drought. By July 2026, its training activities had engaged over 140 technical staff and experts from space agencies, hydrometeorological services, research institutions and universities.

The project, which spans Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, draws on technical support from Regional Drought Mechanism service nodes in China, India and the Russian Federation. It has also supported countries in operationalizing national drought monitoring systems, including the demonstration of a prototype national portal, led by Uzbekspace, for accessing, visualizing and analysing EO-derived drought and crop information. Cloud-based EO platforms have also helped address digital infrastructure and connectivity constraints in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Institutions matter too. For satellite data to consistently guide food and agriculture policy, it needs to find its way into official statistics. That depends on two sets of institutions that have not always worked together. National statistical offices hold census and survey data and the mandate to produce and publish official figures; geospatial and cadastral agencies hold the maps, imagery and land records that tie those figures to a place. The Global Statistical Geospatial Framework (GSGF), developed jointly by the global statistical and geospatial communities, sets out how the two can be linked.

Uzbekistan is putting the GSGF into practice. Alongside its first population and agricultural census since independence, the National Statistics Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan is using satellite imagery for land-cover mapping, starting with the Tashkent region. The approach combines satellite imagery and machine learning with cadastral parcel boundaries, so that land cover and cropland can be measured field-by-field rather than pixel-by-pixel. This matters where farmland is divided into many small plots and fields are often cropped twice a year. Field validation will check the model’s accuracy. The aim is to apply the method nationally and lay the groundwork for estimating crop area and production.

Neighbouring Kyrgyzstan shows where such collaboration can lead. With support from ESCAP’s project on Big Data for Official Statistics, the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic and Kyrgyzgiprozem, the national land management institute, geocoded the 2022 population census and used geospatial data to produce SDG indicators on rural road access and land consumption, which informed the country’s 2025 Voluntary National Review. The Committee has since adopted a national roadmap to extend the approach to further indicators.

As extreme weather events become more frequent and as slow-onset environmental crises unfold, the need for adaptation and resource management is clear, and geospatial innovation, backed by the right skills and institutions, can help meet it. The challenges North and Central Asia face are representative of those faced by the world, and its successes can serve as inspiration to us all. Many of the examples above feature in ESCAP’s forthcoming Geospatial Practices for Sustainable Development in North and Central Asia 2026: A Compendium, which showcases 100 practices from across the subregion.

The authors are Kareff May Rafisura, Chief of the Disaster Risk Reduction Section, ESCAP; Richard Pearce Tonkin, Statistician, ESCAP and Ladislav Charouz, Former Contractor, ICT and Disaster Risk Reduction Division.

World.title: 10,000 lari instead of flat: What Georgia’s government is offering displaced people
World.content:
Georgia’s housing programme for displaced people

The government is offering displaced families the option of receiving cash instead of housing. The compensation amounts to 10,000 lari (around $3,860) for each eligible family member. These are the terms of a new programme announced by the government formed by the Georgian Dream party.

The authorities hope this mechanism will speed up the process of resettling displaced people. However, experts warn that the sum is unlikely to cover the cost of buying a home. Families who accept the payment will also lose access to further government support.

What is changing?

The new programme gives displaced people an additional option: instead of waiting for the state to buy them a flat or house, they can apply for cash compensation.

Participation is voluntary. The government says it will continue building apartment blocks and running its housing purchase programme in rural areas for those who do not opt for compensation.

The housing programme for displaced people was launched under the Saakashvili administration. According to Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, it will continue for at least another ten years.

On 12 October 2026, Kobakhidze announced a new programme for those unwilling to wait for apartment blocks to be built. It offers compensation of 10,000 lari for each family member.

As Irakli Kobakhidze announced, the government has allocated 58 million lari (around $22.4 million) to the programme this year. He estimates that existing resettlement schemes will need at least another ten years to meet the needs of all the families still waiting for housing.

Who is eligible for the payment?

Under the ministerial order, people qualify for compensation if they hold internally displaced person (IDP) status, qualify for long-term housing assistance and have not previously benefited from the relevant government programme.

The agency will verify each family’s composition and check who lives at the address listed in the application. It will pay the compensation no later than 45 calendar days after the application period closes.

A family of four whose members all qualify would therefore receive a total of 40,000 lari. However, simply belonging to the same family does not guarantee eligibility: the authorities must confirm each person’s entitlement separately.

Does eligibility extend to children and descendants?

Internally displaced person (IDP) status does not apply only to people who personally left an occupied territory. A child whose parent holds IDP status can also qualify.

However, obtaining IDP status and applying for state-provided housing are two different things. A child’s IDP status does not automatically mean that the state must provide them with housing.

When allocating housing, the state considers people born before 1 January 2023. Those who were minors on that date count as members of their family when the authorities allocate housing to their parents or other adult relatives. In other words, the state takes children into account when determining the size and other parameters of the family’s accommodation, but they cannot claim a separate flat once they reach adulthood.

As a rule, the state’s obligation to provide housing does not extend to children born on or after 1 January 2023. There is one exception: if an IDP parent or parents die before receiving housing, the child becomes entitled to the accommodation that the state would have provided to their parent or parents.

Why is the programme facing criticism?

One of the main criticisms concerns property prices. Critics question whether families forced to leave their homes can afford to buy another property with the proposed payment, particularly if they have no savings.

The Social Justice Center has issued a statement on the financial compensation scheme for displaced people. The organisation warns that the initiative could leave families without housing or savings facing homelessness and social exclusion.

The Social Justice Center points out that the government has not explained how it calculated the 10,000-lari payment. It also remains unclear whether the authorities based the figure on any property market research. The organisation further stresses that even several tens of thousands of lari — the amount a large family might receive — may not be enough.

The organisation is also seeking clarification on whether families must use the money specifically to buy a home, and what support, if any, they can expect if they cannot afford one.

This question is particularly important because the official order defines the compensation as a form of “long-term resettlement”, implying that the payment comes in exchange for housing. The organisation is urging the authorities to explain the programme’s legal consequences in advance and guarantee continued support for families.

How many families are still waiting for housing?

According to the Public Defender’s report, Georgia had 300,492 internally displaced people and 97,280 displaced families at the end of 2025. Of these, 45,160 families had yet to receive long-term housing. Georgia

In 2025, various programmes resettled 4,636 families. The report continues to highlight delays in construction, insufficient funding for temporary rental accommodation and safety concerns over some residential buildings.

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat”

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat,” Koka Markelia, 26, tells JAMnews. His parents were displaced from Abkhazia.

Koka works as a programmer. He finished school in Zugdidi but could not find a job there, so he stayed in Tbilisi. He has been renting a flat with his parents for more than ten years.

He wants to get married and move out on his own. He says he has a stable job, but under the current rules, the bank will not approve a mortgage.

Everyone in the family works, although his parents are self-employed: his mother works as a nanny, and his father is a mechanic. Only Koka has an official income, so the bank will not grant the family a loan. He says 10,000 lari would not even cover the deposit required for a mortgage. As a result, he will not receive the compensation.

“How much do we pay in rent? If they had offered us a flat with a mortgage, we would already have our own home. What am I supposed to do with these 10,000 lari? What can I buy with that money? I would take it and spend it on little things because I could not do anything meaningful with it. So it is better not to accept the money; otherwise, I would lose the prospect of getting a flat one day,” Koka says.

We checked two popular property websites but could not find a house for 10,000 lari, either in Tbilisi or in the regions.

In Koka Markelia’s home town of Zugdidi, for example, we found just one house listed for 10,000 lari — and it is due for demolition. Even if the Markelia family pooled all its money, it could not buy a house in Zugdidi for 30,000 lari.

“We cannot even buy a house in Zugdidi for that amount. And even if we could, how would we move there? Would we find work? If I worked as a nanny there, I would earn less than a third of what I make now,” says Koka’s mother, Irma.

The government’s initiative has sparked sarcastic jokes online.

“I’m sitting here wondering whether to buy two flats with these 10,000 lari or compete with Coca-Cola,” Gela Khasaia, an activist displaced from Abkhazia who also rents a flat in Tbilisi, wrote on Facebook.

Why is resettlement taking decades?

The government laid the foundations for its long-term housing policy in a national strategy approved in 2007. In 2009, it also adopted an action plan to implement the strategy.

The process got off to a painful start, marked by serious disputes and human rights violations. A 2011 study by Amnesty International documented cases of forced evictions from temporary accommodation in Tbilisi, a lack of proper consultation with residents and difficulties finding sources of income after relocation.

At the time, the authorities offered people displaced from Abkhazia who lived in Tbilisi housing in other regions, prompting widespread protests. The main challenge of relocating to the regions was the loss of income and familiar social networks. Although families received renovated flats, they often found themselves in areas with few job opportunities and limited access to basic services.

Under the Georgian Dream government, the resettlement process has continued through several schemes: providing flats in newly built or renovated buildings, purchasing private houses and formally transferring ownership of homes that displaced people already occupy. According to the Public Defender’s report, 4,636 families received long-term housing in 2025, compared with 2,022 in 2024. Nevertheless, 45,160 families were still waiting for housing at the end of 2025.

The process continues to face construction delays and inadequate housing conditions. The Public Defender’s 2025 report notes that the 300-lari allowance for temporary rent does not cover displaced people’s needs. Concerns also remain over the safety of some buildings that the authorities have already transferred to families.

Georgia’s housing programme for displaced people

World.title: Russia seeks to retain Armenian railway concession as Yerevan avoids confrontation
World.content:
Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

“Armenia is not fixated on taking the concession away from Russia. The issue is ensuring that the railway operates to an adequate standard,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in response to a question about whether the authorities might strip South Caucasus Railway of its rights to operate Armenia’s railway network.

Since 2008, South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railways under a concession agreement. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession runs for 30 years. Since the Russian company took over, freight traffic has halved, some routes have ceased operating, and the company has yet to deliver on its mandatory investment commitments.

Pashinyan said Western companies were ready to invest, but they saw the existing Russian concession as an obstacle. Russia, meanwhile, considers further investment “economically unviable”.

“We say: fine, if it is economically unviable, then sell or transfer the concession rights to those who consider it viable. Alternatively, we will find ways to solve our problems ourselves,” the prime minister told journalists.

Pashinyan also said he had agreed with Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov to set up a joint working group. The group will have three months to answer all the Armenian government’s questions, including whether the Russian side is willing to invest in developing Armenia’s railway network. Yerevan will decide on its next steps only after that.

The prime minister believes the scale of any potential Russian investment could put an end to all “political debate”. In particular, he was referring to concerns that Western countries might refuse to use a railway network under Russian control.

“If Russia, for example, says, ‘I will invest $3 billion’, that means it has no concerns that the countries we mentioned might choose alternative routes. It would mean Russia is confident that these countries will use these railway lines and that its investment will pay off,” he stressed.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan told JAMnews that Yerevan’s concerns had political rather than economic or investment-related roots from the outset.

For some time, people have been saying that international partners are unwilling to use a railway network under a Russian concession. This, in turn, prevents Armenia from becoming a transit country. Meliksetyan believes Armenia has “made concessions” compared with its original position.

“By deciding to set up a working group, Armenia is trying to postpone the serious and painful consequences that could follow if Russia decides to use its leverage,” he said.

The political analyst recalled that Moscow had hinted at a possible increase in gas prices and was already applying economic pressure by banning Armenian exports.

In the expert’s view, the creation of an Armenian-Russian working group effectively turns the concession dispute into a “negotiation process”.

“Three months from now, another issue could emerge and take a further three months to discuss. The problem would remain unresolved, but this approach would help avoid further deterioration in relations with Russia,” he said.

Pashinyan: “We have no problem with the Russian concession”

The prime minister recalled discussions with the Russian side in April 2026. At the time, Russian partners said investment in Armenia’s railways was economically unviable and that investment from other countries would be unacceptable.

“During the blockade, we might have said, ‘Fine, we’ll manage somehow.’ But now, as the region opens up, we cannot accept leaving our railway in its current condition. It needs investment, and we are talking about substantial sums,” he said.

Pashinyan stressed that investment was essential if Armenia’s railway network was to compete with the Kars–Dilucu line that Turkey is building. At the same time, he noted that competition might not even become an issue, given the expected growth in freight traffic across the region.

Speaking about his talks with Belozerov, Pashinyan said he had made it clear to his Russian counterpart that Armenia did not object to Russian management under the concession agreement. However, Yerevan expected the railway to become competitive.

“Our analysis of how to achieve this goal shows that a change in the concession management model would be a rational approach, particularly by involving third countries in the process,” the prime minister said.

He added that Russian partners could put forward their own proposals if they knew how to resolve the issue.

Moscow has yet to offer any concrete solutions. However, Russian partners assured Armenia that sanctions would not obstruct railway operations.

Nikol Pashinyan outlined the strategic priorities that the Armenian government expects to address now that the region anticipates the reopening of all borders:

Reopening the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway section;

Building a facility in Akhurik to change wheelsets, as Turkish railways use a different track gauge;

Connecting the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway line to the Vanadzor–Gyumri line.

“We understand that this is an extremely difficult task, both in terms of investment and from a technical and organisational perspective. But we cannot simply say, ‘You know, there are difficulties, so we will not pursue this.’ We will approach our friends in the most friendly manner possible, but these issues must be resolved,” he stressed.

What Armenia’s prime minister and the head of Russian Railways discussed

The previous day, Pashinyan received a delegation led by Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov.

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Pashinyan stressed that his government aims to integrate Armenia’s railway network with those of neighbouring countries. The meeting covered:

Opportunities arising from regional developments;

Measures to improve the competitiveness of Armenia’s railways and integrate them into international transport routes;

Railway reconstruction projects, particularly the Gyumri–Akhurik–Turkish border line and the Yeraskh–Nakhchivan line, as well as the opportunities these projects would create;

Infrastructure development carried out by South Caucasus Railway under the concession agreement;

Management efficiency, existing problems and possible solutions.

Comment

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Russia proposed setting up an Armenian-Russian working group on the railway issue to delay the process and buy time.

In his view, Russia intends to maintain its presence in Armenia’s railway network. He explains that Moscow wants to take advantage of the expected reopening of regional transport links and secure a political role in the process.

“This matters to Russia economically, in terms of its image and in terms of its geopolitical presence in Armenia. Moscow does not want to lose a very important lever of influence as the region’s transport links reopen.”

Meliksetyan believes the Armenian authorities are trying to act constructively and avoid escalating tensions with Russia. In this context, he recalled the “instruments of blackmail” that Russia openly uses.

At the same time, the political analyst does not rule out the possibility of Russian investment in Armenia’s railways.

“The scale of this investment would not pose a significant problem for Russia. We are talking about just tens of millions of dollars. Even amid Russia’s current crisis, that is a very small sum. Its daily military spending runs into billions of dollars.”

According to Meliksetyan, three months of work by the Armenian working group are unlikely to persuade Russia to relinquish the concession.

“Formal decisions or partial amendments to the concession agreement in Armenia’s favour are possible. However, this is a political issue. In the near future, I do not see a political solution that would not lead to a further deterioration in Armenian-Russian relations.”

Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

World.title: Fidan says ‘everything is fine’ in Baku, but relations remain strained
World.content:
Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Baku on the evening of 14 October. The official reason for his visit was the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), where Fidan represented Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. However, the visit came amid worsening relations between the two countries in recent weeks, putting every detail under close scrutiny.

Azerbaijan’s Youth and Sports Minister Farid Gayibov greeted Fidan at Heydar Aliyev International Airport. The decision to assign him to welcome the Turkish foreign minister prompted mixed reactions on social media in both Azerbaijan and Turkey. On 15 October, Fidan met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Later that day, during the summit, he left the hall along with representatives of several other delegations when Israeli President Isaac Herzog began his speech.

After his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said relations between the two countries remained strong and unbreakable. However, his remarks also acknowledged that disagreements existed between Baku and Ankara.

One of the main factors behind the deterioration in relations has been the de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. JAMnews examined the issue in detail in an earlier article. This time, however, the focus is on a different question:

What is happening in relations between Baku and Ankara, and how serious is the growing chill between them?

Fidan’s message: “There are disagreements, but…”

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan at a dinner hosted by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku to mark the seventh CICA summit. Photo: president.az

Speaking to journalists in Baku, Fidan said relations between the two countries had stood the test of wars and crises, while their leaders shared an “unbreakable friendship and brotherhood”. He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had given him special instructions before the trip.

At the same time, the minister openly acknowledged that the two countries might hold different positions on certain issues. Fidan stressed that neither side should allow these disagreements to damage their strategic relationship:

“We are a people with an ancient history. We must resolve our problems as befits a people with such a past: by sitting down at the negotiating table and discussing them in a civilised manner.”

The minister also said the two sides should not turn their differences into a propaganda tool on social media. He said his conversation with Aliyev had followed this approach, with the Turkish side hearing the Azerbaijani president’s position and his assessment of the situation.

Fidan did not explicitly mention the hijab issue, Israel or Aliyev’s speech on 2 October. However, his references to “our problems”, “differences in approach” and the “use of disagreements” suggest that Ankara acknowledges the existence of tensions but prefers to address them through diplomatic channels rather than in public.

Meanwhile, photographs from the visit attracted the most attention on social media. Some users analysed Fidan’s body language, noting that he appeared relaxed both at the airport and during his meeting with the president, as though relations between the two countries faced no problems. Although such assessments are subjective, they show how closely the public watches every gesture by representatives of Baku and Ankara.

However, the most notable moment of the visit came during Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech. At the summit in Baku, Fidan refused to listen to Herzog and left the hall. Just a month earlier, the decision by an Azerbaijani representative to remain in the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the UN General Assembly had drawn sharp criticism in Turkey.

What triggered the tensions?

A series of events over the past three weeks has heightened tensions between Baku and Ankara:

23 September — Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Millions spent on Patriarch’s funeral: scandal involving Georgia’s former culture minister Tinatin Rukhadze
World.content:
Scandal involving former officials in Georgia

On 14 October 2026, Davit Okitashvili, a supporter of the Georgian Dream party, publicly accused former Culture Minister Tinatin Rukhadze of misusing funds allocated for the funeral of the Patriarch of Georgia and called on the prosecutor’s office to launch an investigation. Okitashvili also criticised former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze, whom he described as Rukhadze’s political patron.

Other Georgian Dream supporters also responded to Okitashvili’s allegations. Opposition figures believe such attacks on former senior officials may be intended to pave the way for their arrests.

How much did the Patriarch’s funeral cost?

Patriarch Ilia II was buried on 22 March 2026. The government allocated a total of 5.59 million lari to organise the funeral, distributing the funds among six government agencies. The largest share — 3 million lari — went to the Ministry of Culture, which Tinatin Rukhadze headed at the time.

It later emerged that the authorities had not spent more than half of the allocated funds. On 8 May, the government revised the funding to reflect actual expenditure, reducing the total to 2.56 million lari.

Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations

From ‘crown prince’ to prisoner: Irakli Garibashvili’s break with Georgia’s ruling party

Patriarch’s funeral: farewell ceremony of unprecedented scale in Tbilisi. Photos/videos

The Ministry of Culture spent just 722,600 lari of the 3 million lari originally allocated to it. The remaining 2.28 million lari went unspent.

However, it remains unclear exactly how the ministry spent the 722,600 lari: who received the money, what services they provided and how transparently the ministry selected contractors.

September: first questions and the prime minister’s response

Questions about spending on the Patriarch’s funeral emerged in September, following an investigative report by the Pirveli television channel.

Acting Culture Minister Mikheil Kiknadze initially said that the audit documents reflected the shortcomings investigators had identified. However, he later added: “I did not say that there had been any violations.”

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on the issue on 14 September. He said the Ministry of Culture had spent only 722,000 lari of the 3 million lari allocated to it.

“If anyone had wanted to steal the money, they could easily have taken all three million,” Kobakhidze said.

He also made the following promise:

“This is preliminary information. I will examine the matter in greater detail and provide the public with a detailed account.”

The Patriarchate defends Rukhadze

On 16 September, Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Patriarchate’s public relations service, issued a statement.

He said the Patriarchate had known from the outset that a significant portion of the money allocated for the funeral would remain unspent.

“During that period, we were in frequent contact with Ms Tika Rukhadze, and we knew from her that most organisations and individuals who provided various services had declined any remuneration or payment,” Jaghmaidze wrote.

He expressed hope that people would stop using the Patriarch’s name as a pretext for unfounded accusations and slander.

What links Tika Rukhadze to Tikhart?

According to Transparency International Georgia, Tinatin Rukhadze earned 410,000 lari as a consultant for Tikhart, an event management company, in the two years before she became culture minister.

The organisation also reports that Tikhart secured government contracts worth a total of 3.8 million lari through direct procurement, bypassing competitive tenders.

These circumstances raise questions about whether the company also received payment for organising the Patriarch’s funeral. However, no publicly available information confirms that it did.

Transparency International Georgia has called on the Ministry of Culture to disclose who received the 722,600 lari spent on the funeral and specify which services they provided.

Another problem is that the government does not have to disclose procurement information for purchases financed through the government’s reserve fund. This makes it harder for the public to scrutinise how the authorities spend public money.

The minister’s resignation and a new political climate

Tinatin Rukhadze became culture minister in October 2024. On 28 July 2026, she left the post, citing health reasons. No evidence has established a link between her resignation and the allegations concerning funeral expenditure.

On 15 September, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Maia Bitadze, a Georgian Dream MP, as culture minister, specifically praising her integrity.

Around the same time, Mamuka Mdinaradze also left his political post as head of the State Security Service. Rukhadze and Mdinaradze subsequently became targets of coordinated public attacks.

October: accusations from a Georgian Dream supporter

On 14 October, Davit Okitashvili, president of the Georgian Chamber of Culture and an active Georgian Dream supporter, publicly accused Tinatin Rukhadze of obstructing his projects and damaging his reputation. He also described Mamuka Mdinaradze as the former minister’s patron.

Okitashvili raised questions about the cost of the Patriarch’s funeral and called on the prosecutor’s office and the State Audit Office to investigate the spending. In a post, he asked Rukhadze:

“Ms Tika, where did the millions go?!”

Other Georgian Dream representatives supported Okitashvili’s post, including party activist and MP Dimitri Samkharadze.

What does Mamuka Mdinaradze have to do with it?

Okitashvili did not limit his attacks to the former culture minister.

He claimed that Mamuka Mdinaradze had acted as Rukhadze’s political patron. According to Okitashvili, Mdinaradze helped secure her appointment as minister, and she subsequently acted under his influence.

In an interview with Palitranews on 15 October, Okitashvili repeated these allegations. He also claimed that both Rukhadze and Mdinaradze had betrayed Georgian Dream.

However, he noted that the prosecutor’s office had not contacted him.

Georgian Dream representatives also responded to Okitashvili’s accusations.

MP Tengiz Sharmanashvili said the prosecutor’s office should ask Okitashvili what evidence he had. If his claims proved credible, investigators should question those involved, including Rukhadze and Mdinaradze.

Opposition warns of possible arrests

The opposition also reacted to the October developments.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Okitashvili’s statements might be intended to prepare the public for the possible arrests of Tinatin Rukhadze and Mamuka Mdinaradze.

Gvaramia suggested that Bidzina Ivanishvili could be behind the process.

Ana Tsitlidze, a representative of the United National Movement, accused Rukhadze and Bakur Bakuradze, the former director general of Rustavi 2, of embezzling funds allocated for the Patriarch’s funeral. She also suggested that authorities might arrest Mamuka Mdinaradze.

Former MP Eka Beselia suspected that Okitashvili’s statement might form part of a pre-planned process. She said that if an investigation began immediately after his statement, it would confirm her suspicions.

Scandal involving former officials in Georgia

World.title: ‘Deadly consequences’: How lack of proper prison in Abkhazia leads to further crimes
World.content:
The recent murder of a Russian tourist has exposed problems with prison sentences in Abkhazia. Edgar Abukhba, who stands accused of murdering Amina Bikbova, received a nine-year sentence for a previous serious crime. In practice, however, he served only half that time. This proved fatal for his next victim.

Amina’s murder prompted Abkhazian society to take a closer look at how courts enforce their rulings. It emerged that in Abkhazia, a sentence tells you very little about how long someone will actually spend in prison. The republic has no proper prison, and a complicated system of “penitentiary arithmetic” determines how much time a person spends behind bars. Even those who apply the rules struggle to make sense of them.

One last coffee

Amina Bikbova’s family had a rule: call her mother every evening. The 26-year-old followed it without fail when she travelled to Abkhazia with her friend Adila for a holiday in September 2026. But one evening, she did not call and failed to answer her phone either. The next day, her phone remained silent. Her family then realised that something serious had happened.

Amina Bikbova

The circumstances surrounding Amina’s final day are known from accounts given by her family and witness testimony reported by Abkhazian and Russian media. Amina and Adila met Edgar Abukhba, a 25-year-old fruit seller. A couple of days later, he invited Amina for coffee. Adila says she tried to talk her friend out of going, but failed. Amina went to meet Edgar and never returned.

During his initial questioning, he denied any wrongdoing. He claimed that he and Amina had simply had coffee, after which she got into someone’s car and drove away. Investigators quickly disproved this account, and Edgar admitted that they had argued, that he had strangled Amina and left her body in bushes beside the road.

A familiar name

Edgar Abukhba

For Abkhazians who follow local crime reports, the surname Abukhba sounded familiar. In July 2019, a 24-year-old Russian tourist suffered a brutal attack in central Sukhum. Her assailants beat, raped and robbed her. Everyone familiar with the case said they had rarely encountered such brutality. Authorities arrested Edgar Abukhba on suspicion of the crime. The case took more than two years to reach court, and in 2021 a judge sentenced him to nine years in prison.

If the nine-year sentence is counted from 2019, when Abukhba entered pre-trial detention, he should not have been released before 2028. Yet by the summer of 2026, he was already selling fruit in Gagra.

Sentences without a prison

Court rulings specify the regime under which a convicted person must serve their sentence, and this affects the time they spend in prison. But Abkhazia has no prison colony with different security regimes, which creates confusion. Officials recalculate sentences differently depending on how much time a prisoner has spent under various conditions. The final figure depends on the coefficient they apply and can differ significantly from the court’s verdict.

Got that? No, of course not. For anyone unfamiliar with the system, it is almost impossible to understand. Even staff at the relevant institutions struggle to explain on the spot how they calculate a particular sentence, how long a specific prisoner will serve and when they will be released.

Perhaps this explains why a man who, on paper, received a nine-year prison sentence attacked another woman long before that term had expired.

Leniency vs prudence

There is another legal complication in Edgar Abukhba’s case. He was still a minor when he committed his first crime, and under Abkhazian law, courts must not take juvenile convictions into account in the future.

There are two opposing views on this rule.

The logic of juvenile justice holds that a teenager’s actions should not determine the rest of their life. But this approach conflicts with public safety concerns, which suggest that authorities cannot simply ignore a proven threat posed by an individual.

Many countries face this dilemma, but they also assess risks before releasing offenders and supervise them afterwards. They may also restrict where former prisoners can work or live and impose other measures. Abkhazia, however, has no such safeguards in place.

A tarnished reputation

Cynical as it may sound, Abkhazia’s tourism sector — and, consequently, its budget — can also be counted among the “victims” of this tragedy.

Abkhazia effectively lives off Russian tourists, who provide the republic’s main source of income. Its reputation as a safe holiday destination is vital to its survival. Now, Amina Bikbova’s murder has left a major black mark on that reputation. This is particularly troubling because it is not the first attack on tourists.

Tourists may forgive reckless taxi drivers or poor service. But they are unlikely to accept the idea that killers who have not served their full sentences can freely walk the streets in search of new victims.

Many Abkhazian lawyers believe the authorities should publish a breakdown of Edgar Abukhba’s first sentence, including the coefficients they applied and his release date. In other words, they should at least explain why he regained his freedom so quickly. Perhaps the authorities should also review the system for calculating prison sentences. Better still, they should finally build a proper prison colony so that no one has to perform these calculations in the first place.

The public, meanwhile, wants an open trial in this case. People are waiting for an explanation of how this mysterious coefficient can allow rapists and murderers to walk free earlier than petty thieves.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.
