World.title: ‘Whether we should ‘marry’ the EU is question for future’, Armenia’s foreign minister says about EU membership
World.content:
Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

The Armenian parliament approved a law launching the country’s EU accession process in spring 2025. However, only now has Armenian society begun to hold “serious, in-depth” discussions about membership. Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Ararat Mirzoyan made the remarks on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.

During a panel discussion entitled “Half-Readiness or a Gradual Approach: Rethinking EU Enlargement”, Mirzoyan was asked where the train taking Armenia towards Europe would ultimately stop. The minister replied that nobody knew — neither Armenia, nor the EU, nor its member states.

He said the good news was that both Armenia and the European Union were enjoying their current process of engagement.

“So let us enjoy these warm relations, discover new opportunities and explore new dimensions of cooperation. At some point in the future, we can sit down together and discuss whether we should ‘get married’,” Mirzoyan said.

During the panel discussion, the minister also addressed the reopening of the Armenian-Turkish border and the peace process with Azerbaijan.

He stressed that Armenia’s efforts to improve relations with its neighbours do not stem from its desire to integrate with European institutions.

Moreover, he assured the audience that this process would continue regardless of other factors.

“On the other hand, we should acknowledge that if our goal is to become a full member of the European Union, problems or conflicts with our neighbours are likely to become an obstacle along the way,” Ararat Mirzoyan noted.

Armenia and the EU are pursuing more than just political dialogue

“Our relations with the European Union have reached an unprecedented depth, covering a wide range of areas and forms of cooperation. We are holding a dialogue on visa liberalisation. The EU has established a monitoring mission in Armenia, which continues to operate and monitor the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. We recently welcomed a second mission. Although temporary, it operates on a permanent basis and helps us counter hybrid threats.

Although we are not an EU candidate country, the Union has granted us preferential trade access with its member states.

This is the latest development. The EU has approved autonomous trade measures to help Armenia diversify its export markets. We have also signed an agreement with the Union that will allow us to take part in various EU missions around the world.

Moreover, although we are not a candidate country, we have received a Resilience and Growth Plan and assistance from the EU, including support through the European Peace Facility.

Our cooperation therefore extends beyond support for political dialogue, the economy and trade. It also covers security, foreign policy and other areas.

Together with the European Union, we continue to explore new opportunities as we seek to strengthen our ties even further.”

On unblocking transport links, the interests of major powers align

“In my country, and probably across the entire South Caucasus region, the interests of the US and the EU do not conflict. On the contrary, they work together very well.

The United States is actively involved in the South Caucasus. In particular, it is taking part in efforts to open and unblock transport links between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

This will provide a vital transport connection, for example between Portugal and China, linking the West and the East.

I believe the EU and its member states will also benefit from this process.

Thus, many countries and major powers around the world share an interest in unblocking the South Caucasus.”

Opening the Armenian-Turkish border is entirely possible

“We are normalising relations with Turkey. The border remains closed, but I believe the process has already reached a significant level of maturity.

It is entirely possible that tomorrow morning we will wake up and see this headline in the news: ‘Armenia-Turkey border opens’.”

Peace with Azerbaijan and the situation in neighbouring countries

“In our case, Armenia’s neighbours are a critically important factor. Let us look at them.

Azerbaijan. We recently established peace and began bilateral trade. We are opening our territories to transport and transit, and unblocking regional communications. However, several sensitive issues still need to be resolved.

To the west lies Turkey, with which we are engaged in intensive dialogue. We are normalising relations, but the border remains closed.

To the south lies Iran, with its complex regional situation, specific conditions and challenges.

To the north lie Georgia and Russia […].

**As for Georgia, imagine how much easier the situation would be if it continued on its path towards EU integration. That would bring about significant changes.”

Moscow’s reaction must be managed carefully

“As for Russia, you can imagine how it might react to Armenia joining the EU, given the specific nature of our relationship with that country.

Historically, we have had very close ties, and we continue to maintain close relations to this day. However, we must manage any potential reaction carefully.

Nobody wants to make new enemies. Nor are we interested in harming any third party.”

Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

World.title: Azerbaijani government websites hit by cyberattack allegedly originating in Turkey
World.content:
Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

More than 100 government domains in Azerbaijan were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted access to several government agencies’ websites. According to the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security, the attacks began at around 22:00 Baku time on 13 October. The agency said a foreign hacking group was behind them.

The agency said technical measures had helped limit the impact of the cyberattack and keep the websites running reliably. However, it has not disclosed detailed information about how the attack was carried out, who organised it or what motivated it.

As Meydan TV reports, one theory under discussion is that the cyberattack may have links to Turkey.

The incident has prompted debate about the resilience of the country’s digital government infrastructure and the possible political motives behind the attack. Available information confirms that the websites experienced disruptions, but it is not yet possible to assess the full scale of the cyberattack or its consequences.

Clarify the agency’s responseTighten the final paragraphUse more cautious attribution

Which websites were targeted?

According to initial reports in local media, users experienced access problems with the websites of the Cabinet of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Health and the State Examination Centre. An official statement confirming a cyberattack followed simultaneous disruptions affecting several government websites.

According to official figures, the attack targeted more than 100 domains. However, this does not mean that the attackers managed to disrupt all these websites or gain unauthorised access to their systems. The number of resources targeted must be distinguished from the number of systems that actually suffered damage.

The official statement does not specify which websites became unavailable or how long the disruptions lasted. It is also unclear whether the outages affected only information pages or disrupted electronic services as well. The State Service for Special Communications and Information Security says it is continuing its cybersecurity measures.

The nature of the cyberattack remains unclear

Disrupting a website and gaining unauthorised access to its database are two different types of cybersecurity incident. In the first case, users lose access to the resource. In the second, the confidentiality and integrity of data may be at risk.

One common method of disrupting websites is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. This involves sending a large volume of requests to a server simultaneously from different sources. The resulting traffic overloads the servers or network infrastructure, leaving legitimate users’ requests unanswered. Such an attack can disrupt a website without anyone gaining unauthorised access to its database.

There is no official confirmation that the latest cyberattack in Azerbaijan used this particular method. Authorities have also published no findings from checks for possible data leaks. The available information therefore does not establish either that personal data belonging to citizens were stolen or that the authorities have fully resolved all the consequences of the attack.

The restoration of websites indicates that users have regained access to them. However, determining whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to the systems or whether any data leaked requires a separate technical investigation.

Possible motives and speculation about links to Turkey

Cyberattacks on government websites may aim not only to disrupt online services but also to express political views, attract public attention or undermine trust in state institutions. In its report on denial-of-service attacks, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) lists political and ideological objectives, as well as financial interests, among the possible motives behind such attacks.

The specific motives behind the latest cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites remain unknown. The fact that the incident occurred amid political tensions has prompted speculation about a possible link between the events. However, further evidence is needed to substantiate such claims.

According to Meydan TV, social media users are discussing a possible link between the cyberattack and Turkey. The outlet examines this speculation against the backdrop of protests by members of some religiously conservative groups in Turkey against restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools, as well as Baku’s relations with Israel. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani embassy in Ankara and the country’s consulate general in Istanbul.

However, no evidence has established a link between the cyberattack and these protests or any groups in Turkey. The Azerbaijani authorities have also refrained from naming specific countries or organisations in their official statement.

The phrase “foreign hacking group” used in the official statement does not, in itself, indicate that any foreign state was involved. Identifying those who organised and carried out the attack, establishing their motives and determining whether they have links to state institutions will require a separate investigation.

Warning about cyber threats issued five days before the attack

On 8 October, five days before the cyberattack, Azerbaijan’s Electronic Security Service published a warning about active cyber threats targeting several information systems. The statement noted that some attacks involved outdated database management software and default login credentials that administrators had failed to change.

The warning also said that attackers who gained access to inadequately protected systems could use them to launch attacks against other resources. The service advised administrators to update their software, change default passwords, restrict access to systems and monitor suspicious activity.

The service did not report any possible connection between this warning and the cyberattack that began on 13 October. There is currently no evidence to suggest that the two incidents formed part of the same operation. Nevertheless, the warning highlights that cybersecurity depends not only on responding to attacks but also on regularly updating software and controlling access to systems.

Questions left unanswered after services were restored

One of the key criteria for assessing the impact of a cyberattack is the extent to which it disrupts government electronic services. The temporary unavailability of an informational website can have very different consequences for users from disruptions to systems for submitting documents, registering applications and processing requests.

No specific data has yet been published on whether the latest cyberattack interrupted users’ transactions, caused people to miss deadlines for submitting documents or applications, or resulted in data loss. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the actual damage caused by the incident based solely on the number of domains targeted.

Future official statements will be particularly important in clarifying which services were affected, whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to internal systems, and what the security checks found regarding personal data.

The restoration of the websites demonstrates that the authorities have taken steps to respond to the cyberattack. However, a fuller assessment of how resilient the country’s digital government infrastructure proved to be against such threats will only be possible once more detailed information becomes available.

Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

World.title: Škoda plant to open in Baku: Project progress so far
World.content:
Škoda Group plans rail vehicle production plant in Baku

Czech company Škoda Group plans to establish a rail vehicle production and maintenance facility in Baku.

The project could boost local industry, create jobs and facilitate technology transfer. However, investment figures, production capacity and a timeline have yet to be announced.

Czech transport equipment manufacturer Škoda Group has announced plans to establish a production facility and maintenance centre in Azerbaijan. The company aims to eventually use the facility to serve customers not only in Azerbaijan but also across the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

The plans emerged on 12 October during a meeting between Czech Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik and representatives of Azerbaijan Transport and Communication Holding (AZCON). The meeting was attended by AZCON head Shahin Babayev, Baku Metro chairman Vusal Aslanov and Azerbaijan Railways chairman Rovshan Rustamov.

Škoda Group vice-chairman Tomáš Ignačák said the company intended to establish a joint venture with a local partner in Azerbaijan and gradually expand production.

The proposal covers not only the supply of finished rolling stock but also maintenance services, training for local specialists, the involvement of Azerbaijani companies in component supply chains and the transfer of European manufacturing technologies.

However, the project remains at the proposal stage, with no investment agreement signed so far.

What is Škoda Group planning in Azerbaijan?

Škoda Group is one of Europe’s rail transport manufacturers. The company produces metro trains, trams, suburban electric trains, trolleybuses, as well as vehicle control and drive systems.

Škoda Group should not be confused with carmaker Škoda Auto. The latter is owned by Volkswagen Group, while Škoda Group, which specialises in rail transport, is part of Czech investment group PPF.

According to the company, it has production facilities in the Czech Republic, Finland and Turkey. In 2025, the group’s revenue, including figures from Turkish manufacturer TEMSA, reached €1.45bn.

Škoda Group’s proposal to Azerbaijan focuses primarily on modernising the metro and suburban rail networks. The planned joint venture would gradually develop local production and maintenance capabilities, using local resources and facilities.

One potential benefit would be reduced dependence on foreign manufacturers for maintenance, spare parts and repairs throughout the service life of rail vehicles.

Training local engineers and technicians could also become an important part of long-term industrial cooperation. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on which production and maintenance operations are carried out at the new facility.

Baku Metro expansion creates new opportunities

Škoda Group’s interest in the Azerbaijani market coincides with the country’s plans to expand its public transport infrastructure. Under a state programme approved in January 2025, Baku plans to build 10 new metro stations, modernise existing lines and purchase 299 new carriages by 2030.

In addition to new stations, the programme includes expanding train depots, upgrading power supply systems and increasing the metro network’s capacity. According to AZCON, around $2.5bn is earmarked for the expansion.

In June 2026, Baku Metro and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signed loan agreements worth a total of $180m to finance the first phase of the expansion. The funds will primarily support ongoing work at the Darnagul and Khojasan train depots, as well as upgrades to existing metro stations.

Azerbaijan has therefore already approved a metro modernisation programme and secured funding for several projects. The Czech company’s proposal aims to meet potential demand for equipment, maintenance services and industrial cooperation arising from these plans.

How much production will take place locally?

One of the key factors determining the project’s economic significance will be the scale of production established in Azerbaijan.

Rail vehicle manufacturing involves various levels of localisation. Some facilities specialise in assembling components imported from abroad and testing finished vehicles. Others also manufacture metal structures and electrical equipment, and carry out engineering and design work. Each model requires different levels of investment, technical infrastructure and skilled personnel.

Azerbaijan already has experience assembling metro carriages at local facilities. In 2024, Baku Metro began assembling new-generation carriages using existing infrastructure. According to official figures, under a contract to supply 65 carriages between 2024 and 2026, specialists from the manufacturer also took part in assembling, commissioning and testing rolling stock in Azerbaijan.

This experience demonstrates that existing infrastructure can be used for final assembly and technical testing. However, it remains unclear how Škoda Group’s proposed model would differ from current practices.

The company has yet to disclose which stages of production would take place in Azerbaijan, what proportion of components would be locally manufactured, the terms of technology transfer or the facility’s annual production capacity. These indicators will help assess how much added value the project could generate for local industry.

Even if the facility initially focuses only on assembly and maintenance, the project could help train skilled workers and expand rolling stock repair capabilities. However, manufacturing more complex components in Azerbaijan would require additional investment and a steady flow of orders.

Škoda Group is not the only contender

Azerbaijan’s talks on purchasing new metro carriages and introducing modern technologies are not limited to the Czech company. In January 2026, Baku Metro officials met representatives of Swiss company Stadler Rail Group. They discussed the possible purchase of up to 300 new carriages, reducing operating costs and introducing modern signalling systems.

In February, a Škoda Group delegation led by CEO Petr Novotný also held talks with Baku Metro officials. Discussions focused on purchasing new carriages and prospects for long-term technological cooperation. Potential cooperation between AZCON and Škoda Group had also been discussed in May 2025.

These meetings indicate that Azerbaijan is exploring opportunities to involve international suppliers in modernising Baku Metro. However, Škoda Group’s proposal to establish a facility in Baku does not mean the company has secured orders for the carriages envisaged under the state programme.

Key criteria for selecting suppliers will include compliance with technical requirements, purchase price, energy consumption, maintenance costs and long-term operating conditions.

Localising production in Azerbaijan could bring additional economic benefits. However, its impact on procurement costs and competition will depend on the specific commercial proposals.

What does Uzbekistan’s experience show?

Škoda Group already has experience of a similar cooperation model in Central Asia. In April 2026, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the supply of 10 electric trains to Uzbekistan and their maintenance.

The project, worth more than €120m, also includes establishing a joint venture, localising maintenance services and training specialists. The company also plans to launch a Škoda Academy educational programme in Uzbekistan.

This example shows that Škoda Group’s cooperation model goes beyond supplying rolling stock to include developing local maintenance infrastructure and transferring technology. However, its projects in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are at different stages.

In Uzbekistan, the number of trains and project cost have already been agreed, and a strategic cooperation agreement has been signed. In Azerbaijan, the company has so far only announced plans to establish a production and maintenance facility.

The proposed Baku facility’s potential to serve regional markets will also depend on commercial prospects. This would require orders from neighbouring countries, compliance with technical standards and competitive production costs.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Armenia hold talks on cooperation in AI
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Armenian President Vahagn Khachaturyan discussed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation, including the possibility of establishing a joint venture in artificial intelligence, in Yerevan on October 16.

According to the press service of the Kyrgyz president, the talks took place as part of Sadyr Japarov’s official visit to Armenia.

The sides explored opportunities for cooperation in the economy, investment, transport, agriculture, information technology, education and tourism.

Particular attention was paid to expanding cooperation in information technology and exploring an initiative to establish a joint venture in artificial intelligence.

The Armenian president noted the high level of political relations between the two countries and emphasized the importance of regular contacts at various levels and mutual support within international organizations.

In turn, Sadyr Japarov stated that his visit marked the first official visit by a Kyrgyz president to Armenia. He expressed confidence that the visit would give fresh impetus to the development of bilateral relations.

The sides also discussed strengthening political dialogue, expanding interregional ties and enhancing cooperation in environmental protection, biodiversity conservation and the preservation of mountain ecosystems.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Bangladesh discuss expanding bilateral cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov discussed bilateral cooperation with Bangladesh, the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry’s press service reported.

On October 16, Bayramov met with Humayun Kabir, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs, on the sidelines of the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA).

The sides welcomed the successful outcomes of the 7th CICA Summit and discussed prospects for developing bilateral relations between Azerbaijan and Bangladesh, as well as cooperation within international and regional organizations.

They emphasized the importance of political dialogue and mutual visits between the two countries and explored opportunities to expand bilateral ties in various areas. The sides also highlighted the significance of an agreement exempting holders of diplomatic and service passports from visa requirements.

The meeting addressed opportunities to develop cooperation in energy, education, humanitarian affairs and other fields, make effective use of existing opportunities, and strengthen people-to-people ties.

The sides also emphasized the importance of cooperation and mutual support within the United Nations. They welcomed the meeting held with the President of the UN General Assembly, who is Bangladesh’s foreign minister, and noted the importance of continuing joint efforts on multilateral platforms.

Cooperation opportunities related to the summit of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, which Azerbaijan is scheduled to host next year, were also discussed.

Bayramov emphasized the importance of cooperation within the Non-Aligned Movement, including through its Parliamentary Network and Youth Organization. He highlighted the need to further develop interparliamentary ties and contacts among young people through these mechanisms.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other regional and international issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, UNESCO discuss cooperation on education, science and culture
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Director-General of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Khaled El-Enany discussed expanding cooperation in education, science, culture and the preservation of natural heritage during a meeting in Yerevan on October 16.

According to the press service of the Kyrgyz president, the meeting took place on the sidelines of the Leaders’ Summit held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17).

During the talks, Sadyr Japarov emphasized the importance of cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and UNESCO, including in light of the country’s election to the organization’s Executive Board for 2025–2029.

Particular attention was paid to preparations for the Second Global Mountain Summit, Bishkek+25, which will be held in Bishkek on October 21-23, 2027.

Sadyr Japarov invited the UNESCO Director-General to participate in the event, which aims to strengthen international cooperation on the sustainable development of mountain regions.

In addition, the president provided an update on Kyrgyzstan’s initiative to establish an international trust fund under the auspices of the UN to preserve the ecosystem of Lake Issyk-Kul.

Furthermore, he expressed hope that UNESCO would provide expert support and help attract international partners to implement the initiative.

In turn, El-Enany highlighted the significance of Sadyr Japarov’s address at COP17, which focused on biodiversity conservation and the protection of natural heritage.

He also emphasized Kyrgyzstan’s contribution to preserving and promoting nomadic culture and confirmed UNESCO’s readiness to support its promotion internationally.

The sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening their partnership, including in academic, educational and cultural fields, and to advancing initiatives of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans 2027 global conference on state-owned enterprises
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Baku is expected to host the Global Conference on State-Owned Enterprises in 2027, according to a press release from Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Finance.

On October 15, Azerbaijan’s First Deputy Finance Minister Anar Karimov took part in a meeting of the Constituency Group represented by Azerbaijan, held on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand.

The meeting was also attended by the Central Bank of Azerbaijan Governor and World Bank Governor for Azerbaijan, Taleh Kazimov.

Participants discussed the global economic and financial market situation, as well as measures taken by the IMF and World Bank Group to reduce poverty and support economic development in developing countries.

On October 16, Karimov attended the plenary session of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings. The event brought together senior representatives of government bodies, governments of member countries, central banks and international financial institutions.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga delivered reports on the global economic situation, prospects for global growth and key challenges. Their remarks also addressed rising global public debt and the need to ensure debt sustainability, particularly in developing countries.

On the same day, Karimov met with IMF Deputy Managing Director Bo Li. They discussed Azerbaijan’s economic situation and development prospects, trends in key macroeconomic indicators, and current and future areas of cooperation with the Fund.

Karimov outlined measures taken in Azerbaijan to maintain macroeconomic stability, diversify the economy and strengthen fiscal sustainability. He also discussed reforms to improve and digitize public financial management, develop the non-oil sector, diversify budget revenues, introduce performance-based budgeting and strengthen fiscal risk monitoring.

The first deputy minister emphasized the importance of cooperation with the IMF on public financial management, medium-term budget planning, fiscal rules and institutional capacity building. He also highlighted the need to expand the Fund’s technical assistance to support continued reforms in these areas.

Li, in turn, shared his views on how slowing global economic growth and risks in the international economic environment could affect countries’ development prospects. He positively assessed Azerbaijan’s progress in economic diversification, increasing non-oil revenues and strengthening fiscal sustainability, and expressed the IMF’s readiness to continue supporting the country in these areas.

The Azerbaijani delegation also met with Antonella Bassani, World Bank Vice President for Europe and Central Asia, to discuss ongoing cooperation with the Bank and its future prospects.

Both sides praised the World Bank’s continued support for Azerbaijan’s development priorities and reform agenda. They noted that the long-standing partnership makes a significant contribution to the country’s socioeconomic development and institutional capacity.

Karimov outlined reforms implemented in Azerbaijan to monitor state-owned enterprises and analyze their financial statements, and praised the World Bank’s technical assistance in this area.

The meeting also addressed a preliminary agreement with the World Bank to hold the next Global Conference on State-Owned Enterprises in Baku in 2027, with the participation of authorities responsible for monitoring such enterprises. Preparations for the event are underway.

During the visit, the delegation also met with representatives of Bank of America to discuss Azerbaijan’s access to international capital markets, diversification of sovereign financing instruments and prospects for cooperation in financing major infrastructure projects.

The sides exchanged views on making effective use of international financial markets and enhancing Azerbaijan’s investment appeal.

At a meeting with Patrick Loszewski, Executive Director of the IMF Constituency Group represented by Azerbaijan, participants discussed key areas of cooperation with the Fund, engagement within the framework of Article IV consultations and Azerbaijan’s macroeconomic priorities.

They emphasized the importance of strengthening Azerbaijan’s representation in the Constituency Group and continuing coordination within the structure.

The Azerbaijani delegation also met with representatives of international rating agency Moody’s to exchange views on Azerbaijan’s sovereign credit profile, its position in international financial markets and measures to strengthen investor confidence.

Karimov said Azerbaijan’s sovereign credit rating upgrade to investment grade was an important sign of international recognition of the country’s macroeconomic stability, strong fiscal position and external resilience.

He described Moody’s upgrade of Azerbaijan’s sovereign rating from Ba1 to Baa3, while maintaining a positive outlook, as an important step in the international recognition of the results of ongoing economic reforms.

The delegation also met with representatives of French banking group Société Générale to review current cooperation and its prospects.

The discussions covered potential cooperation in financing investment projects in Azerbaijan, expanding financing opportunities for the private sector, and developing digital financial solutions and sustainable finance, the Ministry of Finance’s press release said.

World.title: Violent clashes involving slingshots during West Bank olive harvest
World.content:
Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and journalists in the occupied West Bank, using slingshots to hurl rocks from hilltops around the village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.

The violent attacks happened during the yearly olive harvest, which is regularly a flashpoint between the settlers and Palestinians who rely on the crop as a source of income.

Some of the settlers set fire to the olive trees, sending smoke billowing across the area.

Olive trees were set alight during clashes in Abu Falah near Ramallah. (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

Veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was among those attacked, despite wearing a flak jacket emblazoned with the word "press".

She was beaten by settlers, who stole her camera and phone, before being taken to hospital in Ramallah after other journalists rushed to her aid once the settlers had pulled briefly back from the area.

"We saw in the distance in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men," Ms Levine told journalists in hospital, fighting back tears.

Loading...

"I had a 500 millimetre lens that you could see the mask with slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground.

" Luckily, I had my flak jacket and my helmet. Otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here because they just kept kicking me, and kicking me in, like, probably 50 times. "

Ms Levine questioned the parents of the violent settlers, many of whom are often teenage boys or young men.

"I don't know how a parent can raise such monsters," she said.

"They are giving everyone in the country a horrible reputation.

"And unfortunately, everyone is seeing them who they are. And you know what? Sadly, none of them will be prosecuted. I am sure of it."

IDF investigating incident in West Bank

Witnesses reported seeing soldiers from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), who were called to the area, fire tear gas at Palestinians in the area.

'Israeli terrorists' target villagers' homes in days-long siege Palestinians in a small West Bank village have spent almost a week under siege from Israeli settlers, with members of the community accusing the Israeli military of complicity in the saga.

The IDF said it would examine "all circumstances surrounding the incident".

"Upon arriving at the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said.

"At another location where the confrontation took place, IDF soldiers fired warning shots into the air and subsequently toward a suspect who ran toward them carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them.

"The IDF strongly condemns this incident and views any manifestation of violence with utmost severity. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area."

Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray issued a note to staff about the attack.

"While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

"The safety of our journalists is of paramount importance for The Post, as is the right of journalists everywhere to report freely and the responsibility of authorities to protect journalists doing their work.

"We will press for an investigation and support Heidi in the wake of this shocking attack."

It came a week after settlers attacked a photographer from AFP in the West Bank.

Concerned statements have left Israel's impunity intact Even the United States is now criticising Israel's ongoing settler violence in the West Bank as Benjamin Netanyahu, once the "Trump whisperer", becomes the Trump ignorer.

While attacks by settlers on foreigners, particularly journalists, often get attention due to the fact they happen with media witnesses, Palestinians argue they bear the brunt of the violence on a daily basis.

Humanitarian organisations, including the United Nations, have reported a surge in settler violence since October 2023, emboldened by the decisions and policies of the right-wing Netanyahu Government which includes settlers in its ministerial ranks.

Israeli organisation Yesh Din said there had been 170 attacks since late September when the olive harvest began.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned settler violence in the West Bank, but has also tried to diminish the significance of it by repeatedly claiming it is just a handful of individuals breaking the law.

The IDF and Israel Police are regularly criticised for failing to prosecute settlers for their offences, while insisting they are taking a firm stance against criminals.

At least half a million Israelis live in settlements scattered across the occupied West Bank.

Their presence is considered illegal under international law.

World.title: A rugby union player has died the day before championship competition begins
World.content:
A South African rugby union player has died in a hotel in France, the day before the team were set to make their debut in the European Champions Cup.

French media reports said the Lions player was found unconscious in a shower cubicle at a hotel on the Ile de Re in La Rochelle on Friday, where the team had been staying since Tuesday.

South Africa Rugby officials said the identity of the player has not been announced while the team contacts his family in South Africa.

Emergency services were called shortly after 10am to treat the player, who was in cardio-respiratory arrest.

The reports said their attempts to resuscitate him were unsuccessful.

Saturday's match is now in doubt, along with two United Rugby Championship fixtures the Lions are scheduled to play in Scotland over the next fortnight.

The Lions did not respond to requests for comment.

European Professional Club Rugby confirmed no decision had yet been made on the La Rochelle fixture and that it would consult the Lions.

The death comes 10 years to the day after Anthony Foley, a coach for the Irish team Munster, passed away at the age of 42 in his Paris hotel ahead of a Heineken Cup match against compatriot Ronan O'Gara's French club, Racing 92.

O'Gara is now the coach of La Rochelle, and according to Irish media, he visited the Lions at their hotel on Friday to offer his condolences.

Reuters

World.title: At least three killed by Russian drones in Ukraine which cut power to 370,000
World.content:
At least three people have been killed by Russian drones in Ukraine, with strikes also hitting two shopping centres and key energy grid infrastructure.

Two people died and 12 more were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.

In the north-western region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk.

The attacks on Ukranian energy grids cut power to around 370,000 in the north-west after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.

More than 370,000 people in Ukraine lost power after Russian strikes. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

Crews set out to repair damage to the grid in Volyn and had reconnected about 100,000 people by later in the morning, Mr Romaniuk added.

The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn's regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.

Other attacks hit at least two shopping centre, one in the northern city of Sumy, which sits close to the front line, and one in the neighbouring region of Rivne, officials said.

The strikes in Sumy were the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.

Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping centre and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.

Russia publicises refinery strike

Russia publicly acknowledged a Ukrainian drone strike on a major oil refinery this week and broadcast images on state media, breaking its usual practice in order to highlight the attack that US President Donald Trump branded a "disgrace".

President Donald Trump announced the energy ceasefire despite neither Moscow or Kyiv confirming their involvement. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Ukraine has frequently struck Russian oil refineries in attacks that officials typically describe as hits on "industrial enterprises".

The target of Thursday's attack in Ryazan was immediately identified by the regional governor as one of Russia's largest refineries.

For the first time since the start of the war, state TV showed the aftermath of the Ryazan refinery attack.

In a brief report, the Rossiya-24 channel showed the plant with a relatively small plume of black smoke rising from the sit, no fire was visible.

Russia is eager to publicise the incident, which took place four days after Mr Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, which neither side confirmed they had agreed to.

Ukraine said it paused such attacks for three days in deference to Mr Trump, but resumed because Russia had continued to pound its thermal power plants and other energy infrastructure.

European Union heads back Ukraine

European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Brussels on Friday.

The support is off the back of Mr Trumps remarks on Ukraine's strikes on Russia, a recent diesel deal signed between Russia and the US, and allegations the US is withholding critical intelligence from Ukraine.

Diesel deal unlikely to lower prices US President Donald Trump says his deal with Russia will drive down the cost of fuel but experts say its effect will be minimal.

"We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That's why we have to prepare for the winter," Mr Zelenskyy said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.

"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defence and funding."

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.

"Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell," he said.

"We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs. Because always, at the start [and] at the end of every conversation.

" People need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting … for us. "

Reuters/AP

World.title: Freshly unearthed abuse claim ahead of notorious paedophile's prison release
World.content:
A freshly unearthed allegation against one of WA's worst serial paedophiles who molested dozens of teenage boys is under scrutiny by authorities, just weeks out from a decision on his release from prison after 15 years.

Dennis McKenna abused students in the 1970s and '80s while he was the warden at St Andrew's Hostel, a boarding lodge in the town of Katanning, 290 kilometres south-east of Perth.

McKenna used a combination of favouritism, intimidation and threats to abuse teenage boys under a veil of secrecy at the hostel.

Justice Marcus Solomon is weighing up what life will look like for McKenna when his sentence of more than 15 years expires later this year.

But in an extraordinary development outside court on Friday, McKenna's victims claimed there may be at least one more abuse survivor who complained to police.

Tony Buti says High Risk Serious Offender applications are conducted independently by the State Solicitor's Office. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Attorney-General Tony Buti has confirmed to the ABC that information about the complaint had been provided to the State Solicitor's Office.

"They are considering it," he said.

Prosecutors have sought to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which could have him jailed indefinitely or see him face tough restrictions for the rest of his life upon release.

"Dennis McKenna's offending against children is abhorrent, and I condemn his behaviour in the strongest possible terms," Mr Buti.

"If anyone has allegations against Mr McKenna I would strongly encourage them to go to the police so the allegations can be properly investigated."

Freshly unearthed allegation

McKenna's brazen and repetitive offending of hostel students was revealed over the course of four separate court cases between 1991 and 2015.

Dennis McKenna has spent more than 15 years behind bars. (ABC News)

McKenna was jailed in 1991 but released after a year and 10 months on parole. Police laid further charges in the late 2000s and he was jailed in 2011 for a 15-and-a-half year term.

Expert evidence given to the court by a forensic psychologist and psychiatrist pointed to a lack of offending between 1993 and 2011 as a reason that McKenna would be a low risk of committing a serious offence in the future.

But Maggie Dawkins, a whistleblower who worked in Katanning during McKenna's period of offending, said today that she knew of a police report made in 2004 or 2005 by a man who claimed he was assaulted by the paedophile.

Maggie Dawkins (right) says another man claimed to have been assaulted by McKenna. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

McKenna was not charged in relation to that matter, meaning it was not disclosed or taken into account in the proceedings.

But Ms Dawkins questioned how a decision about McKenna's release could be made based on the belief he had not offended between 1993 and 2011, given the police report.

"We know that this man went to the police and made a police complaint. There is an incident number," she said.

"The expert witnesses haven't had a chance to even know that information."

Maggie Dawkins hugs a supporter outside court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

That complaint is the one now under consideration by the State Solicitor's Office.

The deciding factor

Justice Solomon is deciding whether to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which would see him face tough restrictions as to where he could go and who he could socialise with.

He could impose a continuing detention order, meaning McKenna would be locked up for life, but state prosecutor Brett Tooker and McKenna’s lawyer Joel Grinceri said a restriction order would be more appropriate.

Joel Grinceri is representing McKenna in court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

The court heard from various experts about McKenna's capacity to reoffend. Among them was forensic psychiatrist Peter Wynn Owen, who considered the risk low, primarily due to his advanced age and lack of offending between his 1991 and 2011 jail sentences.

Survivors watch as 'house of horrors' hostel demolished Demolition has begun at the site of one of state's worst cases of institutionalised child sexual abuse, where dozens of boys were harmed by paedophile Dennis John McKenna.

But Dr Wynn Owen said the serial paedophile continued to "categorically" deny any offending after 1981.

"[He] attributes blame to victims, suggests victims in fact instigated aspects of the offending," he told a hearing in July.

"If an individual is denying offending, it suggests they are not going to be able to engage with treatment."

Dr Wynn Owen said McKenna continued to hold distorted views that, in his mind, minimised or justified his offending.

"This distortion … enabled him to continue to offend over a long period of time," he said.

Justice Solomon's decision is due to be handed down in November, weeks before McKenna’s sentence is due to expire.

World.title: Lithium mine expansion could rival global leader
World.content:
A West Australian mining company will spend more than $1 billion on an expansion in the state's north-west despite falling prices for the commodity.

In a statement to the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX), PLS Group Limited announced it would push ahead with plans to increase spodumene concentrate production to about 2 million tonnes per annum at its Pilgangoora lithium mine, 140 kilometres south-east of Port Hedland.

The company is investing $1.9 billion in the project, which will include building a new processing facility named Jimmagunya by Nyamal elders, meaning spring country.

The PLS Pilgangoora site in WA will expand. (Supplied)

PLS managing director and CEO Dale Henderson said in the statement he was determined to ensure the company was competitive in the lithium market.

"Pilgangoora has grown significantly over the past decade and as we look ahead, we are continuing to invest in the infrastructure needed to support the long-term potential of this world-class asset," he said.

"These [changes] are expected to reduce operating costs, improve productivity, and strengthen the existing operation while also providing the infrastructure capacity required to support the increased scale of P2000."

The company has also announced a $600 million infrastructure investment over three years.

That includes upgrading access roads, co-funded by the state government, building a new 1,200-bed permanent workers' village and a mine services facility.

Funding for both will be underpinned by the company's existing cash balance and operation cashflows from existing production.

The statement said lithium had been a strong growth market over the past decade, with forecasts for it to grow by 8 per cent per annum until 2040.

Demand high, while price low

If the company's predictions are correct, the expansion would make the PLS mine rival Talison's Greenbushes mine in WA's South West as Australia's largest hard rock lithium mine.

Talison Lithium operates the Greenbushes mine in the state's South West. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

PLS predicts Pilgangoora will produce 2 million tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate when it is fully operational in 2029.

Mining analyst Peter Strachan said demand for lithium had been steadily growing, but costs were falling.

"Despite the fact that the demand for lithium is strong because of the strong electric vehicle demand globally, the price of spodumene concentrate has fallen," he said.

"The market for lithium miners in Australia has been quite weak on the back of this falling commodity price."

Lithium prices have now almost halved from their May highs of $US3,000 per tonne to $US1,505 per tonne for spodumene and about $US15,500 per tonne for lithium carbonate.

Peter Strachan says demand for lithium is high due to EVs. (Supplied: Peter Strachan)

"Mines which were closed two or three years ago when the price really fell are now coming back online," Mr Strachan said.

"It's a supply issue that's been pushing down the price of lithium."

Mr Strachan said Talison Lithium, which owns the Greenbushes mine, would likely rein in operations to reduce its own costs off the back of the announcement.

"They will scale back, they'll choose to do the lowest cost operation," he said.

State government backs expansion

The WA government has welcomed the news, saying the expansion would create 1,000 jobs during construction and a further 500 ongoing operational roles.

"This is exactly the kind of investment that keeps Western Australians in work today and creates the jobs of tomorrow," Premier Roger Cook said.

Pilbara Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the move was a vote of confidence in the region.

Amber-Jade Sanderson says there will be more opportunities for Pilbara workers. (ABC News: Benjamin Gubana)

"The creation of about 1,500 jobs will deliver real opportunities for Pilbara workers, local businesses, and communities while strengthening the region's position as a global critical minerals powerhouse," she said.

WA's lithium industry sold almost 4 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate in 2025, the highest volume on record.

World.title: State authorities threaten legal action over council's homeless camp in park
World.content:
A Queensland government agency has threatened legal action against the City of Moreton Bay for "illegally" allowing homeless people to camp at a public park.

Economic Development Queensland (EDQ) issued the council a show cause notice, which gives the council an opportunity to explain why legal action should not be taken.

It comes after the City of Moreton Bay council turned Wyllie Park in Petrie into a free, designated campsite for homeless people in August.

An EDQ spokesperson said the site's lawfully approved purpose was as green space, and not as a homeless camp.

Wyllie Park was supposed to be a place where homeless people did not need to fear eviction. (Supplied: Beau Haywood)

"EDQ has responsibilities under the Act to regulate and ensure land is used lawfully within the Moreton Bay Central PDA," they said.

"The Queensland Government has available a range of support services for those experiencing homelessness with over $1 billion being invested in support services and crisis accommodation over the next four years."

Wyllie Park is in the Moreton Bay Central Priority Development Area, which means it falls within EDQ's remit.

Government not consulted

In August, Housing Minister Sam O'Connor criticised the City of Moreton Bay's decision to turn Wyllie Park into a designated homeless camp.

He told 612 ABC's Breakfast program clustering vulnerable campers in one area would cause safety risks and strain emergency services.

"We had no idea and we weren't consulted on it either. We found out through the council's press release," Mr O'Connor said.

"We weren't asked about it, and if we were asked about it we would have expressed some serious concerns about this model.

"We've had other councils look at this and we've expressed that concern to them, and they haven't gone forward."

Human rights violations

In March, the City of Moreton Bay was found guilty of violating the human rights of homeless campers by evicting them and destroying their belongings.

Wyllie Park falls within EDQ's jurisdiction as a priority development area. (Supplied: Beau Haywood)

The Supreme Court ruled that the council should not have evicted the campers when they did not have anywhere else to go.

None of the homeless campers involved in the court case had been offered social housing when they were threatened with fines and forced to move.

Peter Flannery says the camp was an alternative place to go. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

In August, Mayor Peter Flannery told 612 ABC's Drive program the camp would provide a place for homeless people to sleep without fear of eviction.

"We did learn from the court case that we shouldn't have been asking them to move when there wasn't somewhere else to go," Cr Flannery said.

"This is providing that somewhere else to go."

Evictions on the horizon

The Wyllie Park campsite was supposed to be a 12-month trial, offering 30 sites for up to 60 campers at a time.

The site would offer toilets, bins, lighting, CCTV, 24/7 security, and access to a range of government services and local charities.

Beau Haywood is worried about the future of Wyllie Park's campers. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Beau Haywood runs the charity Nourish Street, which feeds homeless people in Wyllie Park and across Moreton Bay.

Mr Haywood said he feared this latest news could mean another wave of homeless evictions.

"I'm disappointed in the Queensland government," Mr Haywood said.

"Although the situation in Wyllie Park wasn't perfect, it was thinking outside the square.

"My concern now is for the residents of Wyllie Park, and I really hope the Queensland government is planning on providing these people with accommodation."

The ABC has contacted the City of Moreton Bay for comment.

World.title: Marilyn Wallman inquest suspended after emergence of new witness
World.content:
A coroner has suspended an inquest into the disappearance of missing Mackay schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman after the emergence of a new witness.

Coroner David O'Connell said he anticipated Marilyn's family would suggest two brothers, Noel and Tommy Morris, were involved in her disappearance.

Noel Morris, who was married to Marilyn's cousin, had previously been identified as a person of interest but Tommy Morris was not scheduled as a witness.

The 14-year-old girl was last seen on March 21, 1972, while she was riding her bike to school.

A piece of her skull was found in a cattle paddock two years later at McGregor Creek, 40 kilometres from Mackay.

Members of the Wallman family outside the Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The Wallman family is represented at the inquest by Marilyn's brother Rex, who can sit at the bar table and question witnesses.

Mr O'Connell said he expected suspicions about the two members of the Morris family would be raised in the court.

"I am anticipating, from the division within the wider Wallman-Morris family, that there may be a suggestion put to me at the end of the inquest," Mr O'Connell said.

"That perhaps Noel Morris and Tommy Morris had some involvement in Marilyn's disappearance."

Noel Morris and his solicitor Robert Beamish. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The court heard Tommy Morris was believed to have left Mackay for South Australia in the months after Marilyn's disappearance.

Mr O'Connell said the two brothers were yet to appear and would need a chance to respond to any allegations.

"Accordingly, when we recommence, Mr Noel Morris and Mr Tommy Morris will have to be available to give evidence," he said.

The inquest will resume on December 8.

New public information

Mr O'Connell said new information from the public also had to be investigated before the inquest could continue.

He told Rex Wallman he realised the difficulty this may cause.

"But this is possibly our last opportunity to make progress for the matter," the coroner said.

Marilyn Wallman's siblings Rex, David and Lenore. (ABC Tropical North Danielle Jesser )

The court had heard progress in the inquest was slow because some witnesses and investigating officers were dead and others had cognitive decline.

Mr O'Connell said Michael Anthony Frances and Arthur Stanley Brown, whose involvement in Marilyn's disappearance was being considered, had also died.

He said those matters would "have to rely on investigation material".

Relatives search sugarcane farm

Witness Lyle Wright said he and his cousin Noel Morris were employed at the Goonyella coalmine, 145 kilometres west of Mackay, around the time Marilyn went missing.

Mr Wright told the court he decided to leave work early on the morning Marilyn disappeared and he drove to Mackay with her uncle, Tom Watson, to help search the Wallman farm.

Witness Lyle Wright leaving Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Solicitor Robert Beamish, representing Noel Morris, queried changes in Mr Wright's statements to police.

He said that, in 2015, Mr Wright told police he could not recall who travelled with him and that it "could have been 'Noelly' and Tom [Watson]".

In June this year, Mr Wright told police he recalled Noel Morris was in Mackay for the birth of his daughter on the day Marilyn disappeared.

Mr Beamish questioned the reliability of the recent statement, saying it was likely Mr Wright's evidence was more accurate in 2015.

" What we're getting at, is that his evidence becomes more certain over time as opposed to what ordinarily happens over the years. "

Car colour debated

The court heard Mr Wright told investigators in 2016 that Noel Morris drove the same type of Holden sedan police were looking for.

Mr Beamish said that, at the time, the witness described Mr Morris's car as a light-blue pastel colour Holden HD with a lighter coloured roof.

However, in a statement from 2015 shown to the court, Mr Wright described Noel Morris's car as a "bluey-greeny" 1965-model Holden.

Mr Wright told the court police had "sprung" the interviews on him, and that he had spent more time thinking about the events leading up to Marilyn's disappearance since then.

"I've probably contradicted myself over the years; I've been thinking about it."

World.title: Bush pub that inspired Slim Dusty's 'Humpty Doo Waltz' hits the market
World.content:
Once just a convenient place to pull in for a pint, the Humpty Doo Hotel has become a Northern Territory landmark.

For more than 50 years thirsty travellers have stopped at the pub, about 40 kilometres south-east of Darwin, on their way to Kakadu National Park.

Despite having what are claimed to be the largest buffalo horns in the Southern Hemisphere hanging behind the bar, it is not stereotypical Aussie pub charm that put the Humpty Doo Hotel on the map.

Rod Parry has been behind the bar at the Humpty Doo Hotel for almost 40 years. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

"It's the name," licensee Rod Parry says.

"Where do you find another Humpty Doo Hotel? You'll find a Railway, a Commercial, a Royal, but you'll never find [another] Humpty Doo Hotel."

Mr Parry has decided it's time to call last drinks and is putting the hotel up for sale after four decades of ownership.

"I think it's time I had a rest, let someone else take over the reins," he says.

"Thirty-nine years is half my lifetime."

Horses, crocs and a beer-sculling bull

Established in 1971, the pub survived Cyclone Tracy and is believed to be one of the Northern Territory's longest-licensed premises.

The pub has been a Territory landmark for many years. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Since Mr Parry purchased it in 1987 the venue has inspired bush ballads such as Slim Dusty's Humpty Doo Waltz and former NT administrator Ted Egan's The Man from Humpty Doo.

Mr Parry has seen plenty of patrons come through the doors in his time, including those with four legs.

"Horses stand at the bar with their riders, their riders have a couple of beers, and the horses stand there very quietly, maybe they watch the TV," he laughs.

"We've had a pig in here. The other day the girls called me and said, 'There's a wallaby in the men's toilet' — and the crocodile, last wet season, out the front of the bottle shop.

"It never stops."

Perhaps most notably, the hotel's Darwin Stubby drinking competition in 1988 was won by Norman the Brahman bull, who sculled a 2.25-litre stubby in 47 seconds, according to an ABC report.

Norman the imbibing Brahman at the 1988 Humpty Doo Hotel Darwin Stubby drinking contest. (ABC News)

Norman reportedly proceeded to wash that down with "half a dozen tinnies and a meat pie".

In 2016, a tiny donkey, a pony and a cow walked into the premises and police had to ask them to leave.

But Mr Parry says the customers he will miss the most are those with two legs — the generations of Top End locals who have grown up in the venue.

"A lot of those guys have passed away, but their children still drink here and their children's children come in," he says.

"I will miss the locals and I'll miss my staff, because some of them have been here for so many years."

Rod Parry says his staff have come to be like family. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

General manager Alex Taylor says the feeling is mutual.

"Working with him for 10 years, he has definitely become more of a family than anything else," she says.

"I don't really see Rod as my boss.

"He's helped me a lot through my career and my development and he's always been there just in general as well."

'World famous' pub

Although the business was "devastated" by the COVID-19 pandemic, in the past year the Humpty Doo Hotel has recorded more than 50,000 visitors.

It says staff turn around an average of 400 lunch meals every day during the dry season.

The bar area has remained untouched under Rod Parry's ownership. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

But the hotel's success can no longer just be purely attributed to its food and beverage sales, with its name recognisable worldwide.

"We send [shirts] to America, England, New Zealand, just in the mail. They buy them online," Mr Parry says.

"My daughter, years ago, was at Mount Everest Base Camp and she had a Humpty Doo Hotel shirt on there and she passed a guy on the track and he said, 'I've been there, that's great pub.'"

The apparel, emblazoned with buffalo horns, has also become a drawcard for Australian holiday-makers such as Perth road-tripper Mel Catchpole, who stopped in for a "nostalgic visit".

Mel Catchpole and her husband Nathan grabbed some merch during their visit. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

"As a child, my uncle lived in Humpty Doo and I was fortunate to travel up when I was very young — 11 — and then again at 18 years of age," she says.

Her husband, Nathan Catchpole, is visiting for the first time and says it's "a bit sad" to hear the hotel is up for sale.

"It's an iconic pub and [it's] sad to see it go to new owners," he says.

"It's an outback pub and we want to keep it that way."

Rowdy reckons the new owners shouldn't change a thing. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The news has also saddened Humpty Doo local Rowdy, who has been a regular patron for more than 45 years.

"It's handy and a good place to come to," he says.

"You can't change it much. Just keep it going how it is."

Looking for the right fit

Since purchasing the hotel all those years ago, Mr Parry has added a bottle shop, RV park, gaming machines and a bistro.

One thing he hasn't touched is the bar, which he hopes the new owners will also respect.

"It's an iconic pub. You can't change it," Mr Parry says.

"What are you going to do? Put carpet in here? It's not going to be the same.

"It'd just be like every other hotel in town if it's, like, air-conditioned, carpet, tiles — just doesn't work for Humpty Doo.

"We just walk in here with a firehose, hose it out in the morning, squeegee it, turn the fans off to dry the concrete — simple."

Brisbane-based hotel broker JLL put the 2.3-hectare property up for sale on Wednesday.

So far Mr Parry has been fielding interest from people all over Australia, but says he isn't willing to let it go to the wrong person.

The cast and crew from Top End Bub filmed part of the show at the Humpty Doo Hotel. (Supplied: Screen Territory)

"I had a call from a guy who owns a car yard. Mate, I don't think it's your bag to run a hotel," he says.

"You need to have some hospitality experience, because these days you need to have so many licences."

Expressions of interest for the new licensee will be open for a month.

World.title: Wentworth Park’s race has been run as crowd flocks for one last lap
World.content:
NationalNSWGreyhound racing Wentworth Park’s race has been run as crowd flocks for one last lap Jack Gramenz October 17, 2026 — 12:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The last race has been run at Wentworth Park as the end of greyhound racing at the Sydney venue is widely celebrated, for wildly different reasons. Friday night’s final of the Million Dollar Chase ended an era that began in 1932, and doggedly continued for years longer than some believe it should have. The crowd was larger than usual for the final night of races at Wentworth Park. George Chan Greyhounds vie for position on the final night of races at Wentworth Park. George Chan Putting it mildly, opinions are split on making dogs race one another. Those in favour consider it a sport, a hobby and a community of people who love dogs. For them, much was lost on Friday night.



Nathan Horrigan’s first trip to Wentworth Park was in the 1990s, as a child. It started a love for greyhounds that’s lasted this long. He’s trained 10 to 15 dogs over the years and had others as pets. “I’ve had a couple of good ones, and a couple of not so good ones,” Horrigan said. “I haven’t got any at the moment, but obviously, it’s still in my blood and that’s why I’m here.” Nathan Horrigan has fond memories of greyhound racing at Wentworth Park. There won’t be more to come. George Chan A man studies the odds at Wentworth Park on its final night of racing. George Chan



“Most people have pets and have dogs as pets, and these are just, sort of, that special pet for people,” Horrigan said. “They’re well looked after, better than most average pets,” he said. Spectators watch on as the greyhounds race. George Chan It’s a familiar line from those used to defending the industry, while others deride greyhound racing as cruel, out of date and out of chances. “People don’t realise how well greyhounds get looked after,” Stephen Arnold said.



“You have a look at the domestic dogs, mate, that are getting put down seven days a week at the RSPCA … they don’t want to talk about that, all they do is want to bring greyhound racing to its knees.” Arnold was found speaking into the phone with one hand and repeatedly raising the other as he engaged in a competitive bidding war with another man for Wentworth Park’s winning post on Friday, the auction raising funds for the Mark Hughes Foundation. The post is bound for greyhound trainer Andy Lord’s property, Arnold said. Stephen Arnold placing a bid as the winning post at Wentworth Park was auctioned off on Friday night. Jack Gramenz “We were just going to keep going,” he said of the bidding battle that eventually ended at $16,500. Arnold, who is “going on 72”, has been coming to Wentworth Park for 50 years.



Related Article Analysis

Greyhound racing Urine samples, soft-serves and an empty grandstand: A night out at the greyhound track “There’s a lot of great memories. It’s going to be a sad night at the end,” he said. “But, with time, we move on.” Tommy Cahill first came to Wentworth Park as a boy, aged 12. It’s where he celebrated becoming a man on his 18th birthday. Friday night brought with it emotion and nostalgia. “I was sitting on the tram here thinking, ‘f---, this is the last time,’” Cahill said.



Tommy Cahill (left) and Charlie Farr-Jones in the stands on the final night of greyhound racing at Sydney’s Wentworth Park. Jack Gramenz It’s been just over a decade since former premier Mike Baird backed down on plans to ban greyhound racing across the state. Despite Wentworth Park’s demise, Gaming and Racing Minister David Harris this week said greyhound racing still has “a strong future across metropolitan and regional NSW”. Greyhound Racing NSW has announced plans to redevelop a site at Richmond on Sydney’s north-west fringe to replace Wentworth Park. Arnold is in favour. “It could go to no other place but Richmond,” he said. The crowd at Wentworth Park for the final night of greyhound racing on Friday. George Chan



Horrigan is less sure. “It’s probably a good idea because a lot of trainers are from there, but the people in the city probably won’t venture to Richmond on a Saturday night to go and enjoy a night at the dogs,” he said. Related Article Development Last dash at Wentworth Park triggers fight over Sydney’s future home of greyhound racing “This is the home of greyhound racing, it’s been here a long time. [Richmond] wouldn’t feel the same,” Horrigan said. Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore, among those who instead call Friday’s main event the “Million Dollar Disgrace”, won’t miss the place.



She said Wentworth Park’s closure should be the beginning of the end for greyhound racing “not the start of its next chapter elsewhere”. “Tens of thousands of people living in high density on the doorstep of the stadium will soon benefit, as it is returned to public parkland,” Moore said on Friday. Among those living on the stadium’s doorstep are the people who sleep under the nearby railway viaduct, where the queue to get in at one entrance almost reached on Friday night. Lexi, a former racing greyhound, at a rally outside Wentworth Park on Friday night, the last night of greyhound racing at the venue in inner Sydney. George Chan In the midst of a housing crisis, there is hope up to 2500 homes will one day join 4800 others planned or approved in the area. The best hope to purchase one might have been winning Friday night’s final race, given the typical prices for a newly built unit in inner Sydney.



Animal Justice Party MP Emma Hurst said Wentworth Park was “one of Australia’s deadliest greyhound racing tracks” and its closure was cause for celebration. “Wentworth Park belongs to the community. It doesn’t belong to an industry that is killing dogs simply for a hobby,” Hurst said on Friday. She blamed “spineless” governments for allowing greyhound racing to continue. A greyhound steps on a banner during a rally near Wentworth Park on the final night of greyhound racing at the venue. George Chan For those who are interested in greyhound racing, Magical Ang led from the front and hit her top speed of 68.9km/h on her way to winning the Million Dollar Chase in 29.46 seconds.



Racegoer Paul Margerum celebrated in the stands when the dogs passed the post for the final time, as he won a much less life-changing sum of about $400. He bet on Magical Ang because of the dog’s similar name to his wife Anji. Fireworks as ‘Wenty’ marks an end. Getty Images Fireworks exploded over the dog track before Newcastle band The Screaming Jets took to the stage. Some in attendance took the opportunity to grab a souvenir, snapping off chairs in the grandstand, tearing down banners around the track or scooping some of its loam in a jar to take home. Despite initial requests to stay off the track, a few dozen set off running a lap anyway, setting some of the slowest laps Wentworth Park has ever seen, or ever will. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: $70 million makeover returns landmark Bangkok hotel to pinnacle of luxury
World.content:
Travel newsSouth-East Asia $70 million makeover returns landmark Bangkok hotel to pinnacle of luxury Julietta Jameson October 17, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
