When a Peninsula hotel opened across the road from the green expanse of the elite Royal Bangkok Sports Club in 1983, it ushered in a new era of luxury for the Thai capital. The city was not short on grand hotels. The Oriental was already a legend on the Chao Phraya River, the Siam InterContinental had brought international-chain glamour to Bangkok in the 1960s, and the Dusit Thani, opened in 1970, had become a striking symbol of modern Thai hospitality. But the Hong Kong-owned Peninsula occupied rarefied territory in the hospitality world. Bangkok was only the third city in the world to get one, after Hong Kong and Manila, with the brand choosing its locations carefully and creating hotels intended to become landmarks. A garden pool villa at Anantara Siam. Designed by acclaimed hotel architect George Wimberley, the Bangkok Peninsula was indeed in an excellent position, and it had the grand proportions that were Peninsula’s trademark, including an imposing lobby that took its cues from its famous Hong Kong sister, with soaring ceilings and a sweeping staircase. Rooms were unusually generous, while teak, silk, Thai art, garden courtyards and lotus ponds created a distinctly local sense of place. Its tenure was brief, however. A change in ownership saw it become The Regent Bangkok in 1985. Four Seasons took over management in 1994 and renamed it Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok in 2003; in 2015 it became Anantara Siam Bangkok, joining the Thai-born luxury brand’s existing riverside resort.



(The Peninsula name, meanwhile, returned to the city in 1998, this time on the Chao Phraya, where it remains today.) Now, 43 years after that original Peninsula opened its doors, its successor is beginning another life. 



Meanwhile, Bangkok is in the midst of another burst of hotel ambition, with thousands of new rooms scheduled to open over the next few years and much of the development concentrated at the upscale and luxury end of the market. The hotel is wrapped around gardens and courtyards in the heart of one of Asia’s most densely developed cities. Some of the world’s biggest hotel names have arrived, or are arriving in Thailand for the first time. Others are raising their bets on Bangkok. Aman Nai Lert Bangkok opened in 2025 in another of the city’s green enclaves. With just 52 suites, starting at an enormous 94 square metres, and a three-storey, 1500-square-metre wellness centre, it pushed Bangkok further into the international ultra-luxury market. Poolside at Anantara Siam. The Ritz-Carlton Bangkok debuted in 2025 at the vast One Bangkok development overlooking Lumpini Park, followed by Andaz One Bangkok in late 2025. Fairmont made its Thai debut with Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit in 2026.



Bangkok’s Chao Phraya River. iStock On the river, Capella Bangkok and the Four Seasons Bangkok at Chao Phraya River have already helped establish a new generation of resort-like urban hotels. Next comes The Langham, Custom House, Bangkok, transforming the city’s handsome 1888 former Custom House on the banks of the Chao Phraya. For travellers, though, it’s not just the size of Bangkok’s hotel pipeline that matters. It’s what all this competition means when it comes time to book a room. Related Article Luxury holidays Resort chain Aussies love opens new location in Thailand Bangkok has long been one of the world’s great cities for affordable luxury. Five-star hotels that would require a serious splurge in London, New York, Singapore or Sydney have traditionally been available here at considerably more approachable prices. That’s still true, but the market is changing. At the very top, Bangkok now has hotels playing unapologetically in the global ultra-luxury league, with rates to match. Look below that stratospheric level, however, and Bangkok’s extraordinary depth of good hotels remains. Established five-stars now find themselves competing not only with one another but with a procession of glamorous newcomers, giving travellers a breadth of choice that’s difficult to match in many other major cities.



But for Anantara, in 2026, even though it is surrounded by spectacular new hotels reaching ever higher into the skyline, all that space, greenery and history it affords makes it feel like the pinnacle of Bangkok luxury all over again. See anantara.com

World.title: Why the world’s biggest cruise ships are getting even bigger
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Last year I reported on the rise of very small cruise ships, if you can call them that, since some are so compact they only carry a dozen guests. But at the opposite end of the scale, cruise ships are getting ever larger. In 2000, the world’s biggest ship was Royal Caribbean’s Voyager of the Seas at 137,276 gross tonnage (GT), a measure of a ship’s internal volume rather than weight.

The 10 largest ships have doubled on average in volume since that time. Royal Caribbean’s Icon of the Seas, launched in early 2024, is 248,663 GT. The megaship is 364.75 metres long with 20 decks and a maximum capacity of 5610 passengers and 2350 crew.

No, it’s not an island – it’s Icon of the Seas, which launched in 2024 with capacity for 5610 passengers and 2350 crew.

Icon was the world’s largest ship in 2024 but two more Icon-class ships, Star of the Seas and Legend of the Seas, have since sailed out, and two more Icon-class ships are on order.

They make Norwegian Cruise Line’s latest ship Norwegian Aqua seem small with a 3571-passenger capacity, but in the 2030s the line will be launching four new ships that carry 5000 passengers and are just shy of Icon at 225,000 GT.

World.title: Copying One Nation will leave Australians poorer, Morrison minister warns
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Copying One Nation will leave Australians poorer, Morrison minister warns Shane Wright October 16, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Populist political movements will pull apart the nation’s mainstream parties if they fail to turn around the Australian economy by adopting major tax, housing and migration reforms, the country’s longest-serving finance minister has warned. Mathias Cormann, who served as finance minister in the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison governments and is now the head of the OECD, will use a speech in Brisbane on Saturday to urge both sides of politics to embrace a reform agenda stretching from the GST to planning regulations to lift living standards and quell left and right populists like One Nation. Mathias Corman is warning that major parties will be wiped out if they simply ape the policies of populists. Dominic Lorrimer Cormann will concede many of the problems facing the country developed while he was in office as the appetite for reform was suppressed by a mining boom that filled budget coffers and boosted incomes. His intervention, in an address to the right-leaning Centre for Independent Studies think tank, follows the release of a biography by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg, who has in the past week warned the Liberal Party must reconnect with the political centre if it is to remain relevant to voters.



Frydenberg also called for an increase in the GST, and the scrapping of some exemptions, with the revenue used to fund substantial income tax cuts. But Cormann will use the speech to outline a broader policy agenda, arguing that the increased support for populist political movements was being driven in part by the failure of major parties to improve living standards through difficult but necessary economic reforms. Loading In a clear warning to the Coalition, Cormann will say that simply aping populist policies will drive voters further into the hands of extreme parties. “Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will argue.



“The evidence for that is now extensive, from Britain to France to Germany, where mainstream parties that borrowed the insurgents’ agenda shrank while the insurgents grew. Related Article Political leadership ‘Things have to change’: Frydenberg criticises Liberal Party under Taylor’s leadership “The parties that have held their ground did so by out-performing the populists, not by imitating them.” Cormann will date the decline in appetite in this country for reform from 2005, when John Howard was prime minister, arguing the revenue unleashed by the then-mining boom made it easier for all political parties to shun difficult policy decisions. “This was not one side’s failure. The appetite for reform faded across the political divide, in business and in the union movement as much as in parliament,” he will say.



“When times feel good, because a boom is hiding a slow drift, the public sees no reason to accept that bargain. Politicians who propose it are punished for solving a problem nobody can yet see or feel.” Cormann will use the speech to outline areas for reform. These include the tax system, with the former minister arguing the GST needs to be increased and broadened, income tax rates sliced and indexed to inflation, while state stamp duties should be replaced with “more efficient” land and property taxes. He will also say the company tax rate is no long internationally competitive and should be reduced. In what would be a challenge to his own party, particularly at the state level, Cormann will argue the only way to bring down rents on homes is to sharply boost supply. This should include the right to build medium-density housing near every rail and major bus line in capital cities with approval against a code completed within 30 days.



The Coalition has promised to reduce net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years before gradually increasing it to 160,000. One Nation has gone further, advocating negative net migration for three years. Related Article One Nation ‘Smarmy management consultant’: Hanson attacks Taylor, Liberals in fiery CPAC speech Under both policies, Australia would have hundreds of thousands fewer workers, consumers and taxpayers over the coming years compared to current policy settings. The Belgian-born Cormann, who moved to Australia in 1995, said the public concern about migration had been driven by the long-term failure to build more homes and infrastructure to keep up with population growth. But he cautioned that deep cuts to migration would ultimately hurt the economy and Australians’ living standards.



“Australia is one of the very few advanced economies whose workforce is still projected to grow over the next 40 years,” Cormann will say. “Take that away, and the arithmetic turns on us. The number of Australians over 85 triples regardless, and health spending climbs from 4 to more than 6 per cent of national income regardless. “We cannot have fewer workers and more hospitals, more aged care, a bigger pension bill and more defence all at the same time.” Australia is in the midst of an AI building boom that has prompted push back in some communities. There are also concerns about AI, its impact on the jobs market and how it may upend workplaces. But Cormann will argue Australia needs to become the easiest country in the region to deploy AI rather than put up barriers to data centre construction and to the use of the technology.



“If history teaches anything, it is that protecting yourself from an innovation you are worried about does not stop the innovation. It happens anyway, somewhere else,” he will say. “The productivity dividend from AI will go to the countries that adopt fastest, not to those that regulate first. So apply the laws Australia already has, through the regulators it already has, rather than building a stand-alone AI regulator.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Carlton off-field crisis deepens after defender blows 0.174, charged with drink-driving
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Carlton off-field crisis deepens after defender blows 0.174, charged with drink-driving Andrew Wu, Greg Dundas and Roy Ward Updated October 16, 2026 — 10:12pm ,first published October 16, 2026 — 10:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of football news: Two Carlton players suspended for off-field indiscretions.

Viney appears in Eagles colours, vows to make impact on field. Carlton’s senior leaders are fuming after defender Wade Derksen was busted for “high-range” drink-driving, blowing well over three times the legal limit and becoming the third Blue embroiled in an off-field issue since the end of the season. The Blues have suspended Derksen for all their pre-season games and the first three matches of the 2027 home-and-away campaign after he returned a reading of 0.174 in a roadside breath test in Jabiru, about 250 kilometres from Darwin, in the Northern Territory the night before the AFL grand final. Wade Derksen has been suspended for all the Blues’ pre-season games, as well as the first three matches of the 2027 home-and-away campaign. Getty Images In a statement provided to this masthead on Friday night, Northern Territory police said: “Gunbalanya Police conducted an RBT on the Arnhem Highway in Kakadu, near the Oenpelli Road intersection.



“A 25-year-old male was subjected to a roadside breath test and returned a positive indication for alcohol. The male was arrested for the purpose of a secondary analysis and conveyed to Jabiru Police Station where he returned a high-range result of 0.174. “The male was issued an immediate licence suspension and issued with a Notice to Appear at Darwin Local Court on 10 November 2026 for Drive High Range Blood Alcohol Content.” In the Northern Territory, a high-range blood alcohol reading is equal to or more than 0.15, triple the legal limit. First-time drink-driving offences involving a BAC reading of more than 0.15 can result in a minimum of 12 months licence disqualification, a fine of up to $1940, or maximum imprisonment of 12 months. The Derksen revelation came just hours after defender Lachie Cowan was hit with a two-game ban by the AFL for conduct unbecoming following investigations of “his use of an illicit substance last weekend” by the Blues and the league. Forward Will Hayward admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. He was not sanctioned.



Angry Blues bosses have expressed their disappointment to Derksen and Cowan, and told the pair their poor decision-making had let down the club. Carlton coach Josh Fraser and football boss Chris Davies. Getty Images The Blues became aware of Derksen’s troubles when he self-reported last month and were working out his penalty when Cowan and Hayward had their misadventures, delaying an announcement on the backman’s penalties. After slow starts to their past two seasons, the Blues will kick off their 2027 campaign without two defenders from the team that bowed out in the elimination final against Geelong last month. Loading



“While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade’s conduct falls well below the standards we expect,” Carlton football boss Chris Davies said. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes “Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions.” Derksen had won the hearts of Blues fans by driving four days from Darwin to Melbourne for pre-season training to earn a spot on the list. He was given a two-year contract extension after strong form filling in for the injured Jacob Weitering. That feelgood story now has a sour postscript. Derksen, who must complete relevant counselling as part of his sanctions, has apologised for his behaviour.



“I want to express how sorry I am for what I did,” Derksen said. “The choice I made to get behind the wheel that day was unacceptable and is a moment I deeply regret. I have let a lot of people down, and for that I apologise.” Carlton defender Lachie Cowan. Getty Cowan apologised and thanked the medical professional who helped him after he collapsed at a party last weekend. “I should never have put myself in such a vulnerable situation, I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club,” Cowan said in a statement released by Carlton.



Related Article AFL 2026 Cowan to be hit with two-match ban, Hayward to avoid suspension after house party “I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was OK. “This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this.” Cowan was also issued with a $5000 suspended fine and now has an adverse finding listed against his name under the AFL’s illicit drugs policy. “AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations. They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances. Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions,” the league’s chief operating officer Tom Harley said in confirming the penalty on Friday.



In finding Cowan guilty of conduct unbecoming, the AFL said it considered the “circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public”. The league said it would require Cowan to undertake education on illicit substances and their effects additional to the mandatory training all players do. The players will all be undertaking fresh training through in November and December as the league prepares to introduce its new illicit drugs policy. When they return for training in January, every single AFL player will be hair-tested, the readings of which will trace back the previous three to six months. The incident involving Cowan at the weekend was first investigated by his club. Carlton passed its information to the AFL, and further enquiries were conducted. Carlton said it investigated the weekend’s matter involving Cowan while also providing him with wellbeing support. “Most importantly, we are thankful that Lachie is OK and received the medical attention he needed,” Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said in the Blues’ statement.



“We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake. Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward.” On Friday, newly unveiled West Coast recruit, and 2021 Melbourne premiership player, Jack Viney made clear his view on illicit drugs within the sport. “There is no place for drugs or illicit drugs in the AFL,” Viney said. “So whatever the policy that the AFL and AFLPA think is reasonable, I’m fully supportive of it.” The AFL Players’ Association said it was “unacceptable” that players were penalised after seeking medical treatment for an issue that would otherwise have remained private.



“As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it,” AFLPA chief James Gallagher said. Viney vows to make impact on the field out west Roy Ward Jack Viney isn’t moving his family to Western Australia to begin his coaching career – he’s doing it because he still believes he can play at the top level. New West Coast Eagles midfielder Jack Viney speaks to the media on Friday. Roy Ward



The new West Coast Eagles recruit spoke to media on Friday wearing his new club colours after 14 years and a breakthrough 2021 premiership with Melbourne. Much was said during the trade period about Viney’s move to the Eagles being based on his desire to move into coaching, but the 238-game midfielder made it clear he is heading west as a player first and a coach later despite Achilles surgery and a back injury keeping him to one game last season. Related Article AFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period “I’m really confident in my body and my ability, and that’s a big reason why I made this decision,” Viney said. “No doubt, I’ve had a really difficult year, the most disrupted and frustrating of my career in 14 years in the system.



“I understand you are only as good as your last game, but I’m keen and eager to get over to the Eagles, prove what I’m about and get a lot of hard work in over the pre-season.” Viney and wife Charlotte will move their three daughters to WA, and the player admitted it would hurt to leave his close family, including his dad Todd, also a former Melbourne captain and nowadays football boss at North Melbourne. “It’s going to be tough leaving. We are an extremely close family,” Viney said. Harley Reid of the Eagles is tackled by Jack Viney of the Demons in 2024. Getty Images “Our girls are six, four and one. When we spoke to the older two about the move, they loved it – when we broke the news to them that the deal was finally done, the kids jumped with excitement and joy. They are definitely on board.”



Leaving the Demons was a difficult process for Viney, but he said an honest post-season meeting with coach Steven King who made it clear the club was moving on. “The new coach wanted to go in a different direction and I can respect the decision,” Viney said. “While I still have plenty to give and great football to play, I’m coming off my most disrupted season and I wasn’t able to make a great first impression. Jack Viney, celebrating the Dees’ 2021 flag, is a key cog in the club’s engine room. AFL Photos “It definitely took some time to sink in, I had envisioned being a one-club player, so it definitely took me by surprise.



“But once you start looking at the opportunities, I reminded myself of some of Neale Daniher’s wisdom about life not promising to be fair, and I quickly became excited about the opportunity to play football for the Eagles.” Viney will be joined at the Eagles by Dees teammate and WA native Trent Rivers, and revealed he had already had some funny interactions with the club’s young midfield duo of Harley Reid and Willem Duursma. Related Article AFL 2026 Seven flag stars have left the Demons in the past year. But their list guru says they’re ‘ahead of the curve’ “Willem was the first one to message me, although he got my name wrong as he called me Trent,” Viney said with a laugh. “When I get over there, I’ll have to sort him out. No, I think they have a terrific young midfield who I haven’t met before, so I’m looking forward to building new relationships.”



Viney recalled tagging Reid in a game during the Eagles’ star’s first season. He also revealed young defender Reuben Ginbey “scares me”, saying he won’t be trying to take the number seven jumper from him. Eventually, Viney wants to move into coaching, and his Eagles deal will allow for that to happen, but he isn’t moving upstairs yet. “I’m planning to play footy for as long as I can, and I’ll squeeze everything out of it,” Viney said. “When I have to hang up the boots, we will have those conversations, as coaching is something I want to continue to explore.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBushfires Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study Courtney Kruk October 16, 2026 — 9:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Bushfires are impacting Queensland’s urban air quality more frequently and more severely than previously understood, new research has found, with pollution travelling further across the state, and for longer, increasing public health risks. The study led by researchers from the Queensland University of Technology analysed air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites across Queensland between 2008 and 2023. It found bushfire smoke can increase fine particle pollution (PM2.5) by up to 160.5 per cent during a fire event, and ozone levels by up to 33.2 per cent during fire-active seasons (July to December). A QUT-led study found bushfire smoke is affecting Queensland urban air quality more often and more severely than previously understood. Nick Moir Between 2018 and 2023, bushfire-impacted hours during the fire-active season were approximately three times more frequent, compared with 2008–2017.



Lead researcher Dr Zijun Li said climate change has increased the frequency and ferocity of bushfires, with longer burn times increasing pollution levels. Related Article Exclusive

Pollution Air pollution kills 1 million a year – hundreds of whom are Australians “Climate change and heatwave conditions are favouring the conditions of the bushfires,” Li said. “Bushfire smoke is not only a problem for communities located near fires. “Our research shows emissions can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres and significantly affect air quality in urban areas far from the source.



“As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of bushfires in many regions, understanding how smoke affects urban air quality is becoming increasingly important.” PM2.5 – the fine particle matter emitted during wildfires – is small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, and is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts. Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao moved from China to Australia as a child because of his asthma. Gold Coast University Hospital Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao has suffered asthma since early childhood, and moved from China to Australia when he was 11 because of the difference in air quality. “Industrial smoke and allergies are the main [asthma] triggers for me,” Zhao, who grew up in Adelaide, said.



“[In China] we lived in a heavily industrialised area as well. The dust, smoke, air quality … some days you could barely see five metres in front of you because of how bad it was. “So my parents made the decision to move over to Australia.” Since moving from South Australia to Queensland, Zhao said his exposure to bushfire events has been minimal. But he can feel changes to air quality, and worries about the impact of longer and more severe bushfire seasons. “I look at it from both sides, as a doctor and a patient myself,” he said. “For me, it gets a little bit harder to breathe whenever there’s smoke in the air, to the point where I’ll probably preemptively take some more of my puffers.



(Left to right) Huon Morton, Dr Zijun Li, Adjunct Professor Zoran Ristovski and Mr Hongzhi Zhang worked on the study analysing air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites in Queensland. Queensland University of Technology “[In the public health system] the number of resources that we do have is finite … so an increase in bushfires would definitely put a stress on both things.” Li said the research also revealed insights into how bushfire smoke behaves and affects communities, with stronger fires affecting urban pollutants. “Ozone formation is complex. We found bushfire emissions can interact with local urban emissions, particularly nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry, to increase ozone concentrations,” Li said. “This means bushfire smoke can worsen air quality even when the fires are a long way from the city.”

World.content:
NationalQueenslandHotels Victory for developers planning new tower over popular CBD pub Cameron Atfield October 16, 2026 — 9:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A planned 51-storey hotel tower above Brisbane’s landmark Victory Hotel CBD pub has received council approval, paving the way for a major accommodation development ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Brisbane City Council approved Precision Group’s proposed Victory Tower, a 206.6-metre development behind and above the heritage-listed hotel, on Monday. As part of the approval, Precision Group would be required to pay almost $2 million in infrastructure charges to the council. Precision Group is planning a new tower behind the Victory Hotel in Brisbane Bureau Proberts The new tower would be built on the site of the pub’s popular beer garden.



The approval marks a significant milestone for the project, which would transform the site into a 284-room hotel with restaurants, function spaces, wellness facilities, a rooftop bar and a swimming pool on the 40th floor. The 16,000-square-metre tower will be built on a 924-square-metre site and occupies the area currently used as the Victory’s Charlotte Street-facing beer garden. Precision Group founder and chief executive Shaun Bonett said the development would help address Brisbane’s hotel room shortage as the city prepares for the 2032 Games. “The critical shortfall of hotel rooms in Brisbane is well documented and the demand for accommodation is accelerating,” he said. “The Victory Hotel is one of Brisbane’s most recognised hospitality landmarks.



“Our vision is to honour that history while giving the site a new future, bringing together heritage, hotel accommodation, hospitality, wellness and rooftop experiences in a way that contributes to the city well beyond 2032.” A year ago, Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said a lack of sufficient accommodation was something that kept him up at night and, just last month, industry leaders discussed innovative ways, such as cruise ships and camping, to address the expected shortfall. The new Victory Tower would include a rooptop bar. Bureau Proberts Designed by Bureau Proberts, the slender tower has been positioned in the north-eastern corner of the site at the corner of Edward and Charlotte streets. Planning documents argued the design’s narrow footprint and setbacks would preserve views of the historic pub, which has operated on the site since 1855 and was recognised by the council as the oldest remaining pub in Brisbane’s CBD.



The project was supported by heritage architect Ruth Woods, who previously advised that the development would not compromise the prominence of the Victory Hotel or neighbouring heritage-listed buildings, including the former Metro Arts building. Related Article Pubs ‘Remarkable hotel’: Plans for a rooftop bar, balcony at the Victory If built, the tower would include a publicly accessible rooftop bar with panoramic city and river views, along with hospitality spaces intended to connect with the refurbished hotel below. Precision said restoration work at the Victory Hotel was already under way. The heritage pub was being reconfigured into four venues – a sports bar and beer garden, a rooftop garden bar, a steakhouse restaurant and a basement speakeasy with a gaming room.



The company took direct control of the hotel’s operations earlier this year and said discussions were continuing with prospective hotel operators. “We are already seeing strong interest from respected hotel operators who recognise the strength of the location, the heritage of the Victory Hotel and the opportunity to help shape a new hospitality destination for Brisbane,” Bonett said. “Getting that partnership right matters. It will help ensure Victory Tower is not only successful as a hotel but also contributes meaningfully to the wider CBD precinct.” The construction timetable would not be confirmed until an agreement was reached, but Precision expected the tower to be completed before 2032. World.title: Wentworth Park’s race has been run as crowd flocks for one last lap
World.content:
NationalNSWGreyhound racing Wentworth Park’s race has been run as crowd flocks for one last lap Jack Gramenz October 17, 2026 — 12:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The last race has been run at Wentworth Park as the end of greyhound racing at the Sydney venue is widely celebrated, for wildly different reasons. Friday night’s final of the Million Dollar Chase ended an era that began in 1932, and doggedly continued for years longer than some believe it should have. The crowd was larger than usual for the final night of races at Wentworth Park. George Chan Greyhounds vie for position on the final night of races at Wentworth Park. George Chan Putting it mildly, opinions are split on making dogs race one another. Those in favour consider it a sport, a hobby and a community of people who love dogs. For them, much was lost on Friday night.



Nathan Horrigan’s first trip to Wentworth Park was in the 1990s, as a child. It started a love for greyhounds that’s lasted this long. He’s trained 10 to 15 dogs over the years and had others as pets. “I’ve had a couple of good ones, and a couple of not so good ones,” Horrigan said. “I haven’t got any at the moment, but obviously, it’s still in my blood and that’s why I’m here.” Nathan Horrigan has fond memories of greyhound racing at Wentworth Park. There won’t be more to come. George Chan A man studies the odds at Wentworth Park on its final night of racing. George Chan



“Most people have pets and have dogs as pets, and these are just, sort of, that special pet for people,” Horrigan said. “They’re well looked after, better than most average pets,” he said. Spectators watch on as the greyhounds race. George Chan It’s a familiar line from those used to defending the industry, while others deride greyhound racing as cruel, out of date and out of chances. “People don’t realise how well greyhounds get looked after,” Stephen Arnold said.



“You have a look at the domestic dogs, mate, that are getting put down seven days a week at the RSPCA … they don’t want to talk about that, all they do is want to bring greyhound racing to its knees.” Arnold was found speaking into the phone with one hand and repeatedly raising the other as he engaged in a competitive bidding war with another man for Wentworth Park’s winning post on Friday, the auction raising funds for the Mark Hughes Foundation. The post is bound for greyhound trainer Andy Lord’s property, Arnold said. Stephen Arnold placing a bid as the winning post at Wentworth Park was auctioned off on Friday night. Jack Gramenz “We were just going to keep going,” he said of the bidding battle that eventually ended at $16,500. Arnold, who is “going on 72”, has been coming to Wentworth Park for 50 years.



Related Article Analysis

Greyhound racing Urine samples, soft-serves and an empty grandstand: A night out at the greyhound track “There’s a lot of great memories. It’s going to be a sad night at the end,” he said. “But, with time, we move on.” Tommy Cahill first came to Wentworth Park as a boy, aged 12. It’s where he celebrated becoming a man on his 18th birthday. Friday night brought with it emotion and nostalgia. “I was sitting on the tram here thinking, ‘f---, this is the last time,’” Cahill said.



Tommy Cahill (left) and Charlie Farr-Jones in the stands on the final night of greyhound racing at Sydney’s Wentworth Park. Jack Gramenz It’s been just over a decade since former premier Mike Baird backed down on plans to ban greyhound racing across the state. Despite Wentworth Park’s demise, Gaming and Racing Minister David Harris this week said greyhound racing still has “a strong future across metropolitan and regional NSW”. Greyhound Racing NSW has announced plans to redevelop a site at Richmond on Sydney’s north-west fringe to replace Wentworth Park. Arnold is in favour. “It could go to no other place but Richmond,” he said. The crowd at Wentworth Park for the final night of greyhound racing on Friday. George Chan



Horrigan is less sure. “It’s probably a good idea because a lot of trainers are from there, but the people in the city probably won’t venture to Richmond on a Saturday night to go and enjoy a night at the dogs,” he said. Related Article Development Last dash at Wentworth Park triggers fight over Sydney’s future home of greyhound racing “This is the home of greyhound racing, it’s been here a long time. [Richmond] wouldn’t feel the same,” Horrigan said. Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore, among those who instead call Friday’s main event the “Million Dollar Disgrace”, won’t miss the place.



She said Wentworth Park’s closure should be the beginning of the end for greyhound racing “not the start of its next chapter elsewhere”. “Tens of thousands of people living in high density on the doorstep of the stadium will soon benefit, as it is returned to public parkland,” Moore said on Friday. Among those living on the stadium’s doorstep are the people who sleep under the nearby railway viaduct, where the queue to get in at one entrance almost reached on Friday night. Lexi, a former racing greyhound, at a rally outside Wentworth Park on Friday night, the last night of greyhound racing at the venue in inner Sydney. George Chan In the midst of a housing crisis, there is hope up to 2500 homes will one day join 4800 others planned or approved in the area. The best hope to purchase one might have been winning Friday night’s final race, given the typical prices for a newly built unit in inner Sydney.



Animal Justice Party MP Emma Hurst said Wentworth Park was “one of Australia’s deadliest greyhound racing tracks” and its closure was cause for celebration. “Wentworth Park belongs to the community. It doesn’t belong to an industry that is killing dogs simply for a hobby,” Hurst said on Friday. She blamed “spineless” governments for allowing greyhound racing to continue. A greyhound steps on a banner during a rally near Wentworth Park on the final night of greyhound racing at the venue. George Chan For those who are interested in greyhound racing, Magical Ang led from the front and hit her top speed of 68.9km/h on her way to winning the Million Dollar Chase in 29.46 seconds.



Racegoer Paul Margerum celebrated in the stands when the dogs passed the post for the final time, as he won a much less life-changing sum of about $400. He bet on Magical Ang because of the dog’s similar name to his wife Anji. Fireworks as ‘Wenty’ marks an end. Getty Images Fireworks exploded over the dog track before Newcastle band The Screaming Jets took to the stage. Some in attendance took the opportunity to grab a souvenir, snapping off chairs in the grandstand, tearing down banners around the track or scooping some of its loam in a jar to take home. Despite initial requests to stay off the track, a few dozen set off running a lap anyway, setting some of the slowest laps Wentworth Park has ever seen, or ever will. World.title: $70 million makeover returns landmark Bangkok hotel to pinnacle of luxury
World.content:
Travel newsSouth-East Asia $70 million makeover returns landmark Bangkok hotel to pinnacle of luxury Julietta Jameson October 17, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. When a Peninsula hotel opened across the road from the green expanse of the elite Royal Bangkok Sports Club in 1983, it ushered in a new era of luxury for the Thai capital. The city was not short on grand hotels. The Oriental was already a legend on the Chao Phraya River, the Siam InterContinental had brought international-chain glamour to Bangkok in the 1960s, and the Dusit Thani, opened in 1970, had become a striking symbol of modern Thai hospitality. But the Hong Kong-owned Peninsula occupied rarefied territory in the hospitality world. Bangkok was only the third city in the world to get one, after Hong Kong and Manila, with the brand choosing its locations carefully and creating hotels intended to become landmarks. A garden pool villa at Anantara Siam. Designed by acclaimed hotel architect George Wimberley, the Bangkok Peninsula was indeed in an excellent position, and it had the grand proportions that were Peninsula’s trademark, including an imposing lobby that took its cues from its famous Hong Kong sister, with soaring ceilings and a sweeping staircase. Rooms were unusually generous, while teak, silk, Thai art, garden courtyards and lotus ponds created a distinctly local sense of place. Its tenure was brief, however. A change in ownership saw it become The Regent Bangkok in 1985. Four Seasons took over management in 1994 and renamed it Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok in 2003; in 2015 it became Anantara Siam Bangkok, joining the Thai-born luxury brand’s existing riverside resort.



(The Peninsula name, meanwhile, returned to the city in 1998, this time on the Chao Phraya, where it remains today.) Now, 43 years after that original Peninsula opened its doors, its successor is beginning another life. 



Meanwhile, Bangkok is in the midst of another burst of hotel ambition, with thousands of new rooms scheduled to open over the next few years and much of the development concentrated at the upscale and luxury end of the market. The hotel is wrapped around gardens and courtyards in the heart of one of Asia’s most densely developed cities. Some of the world’s biggest hotel names have arrived, or are arriving in Thailand for the first time. Others are raising their bets on Bangkok. Aman Nai Lert Bangkok opened in 2025 in another of the city’s green enclaves. With just 52 suites, starting at an enormous 94 square metres, and a three-storey, 1500-square-metre wellness centre, it pushed Bangkok further into the international ultra-luxury market. Poolside at Anantara Siam. The Ritz-Carlton Bangkok debuted in 2025 at the vast One Bangkok development overlooking Lumpini Park, followed by Andaz One Bangkok in late 2025. Fairmont made its Thai debut with Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit in 2026.



Bangkok’s Chao Phraya River. iStock On the river, Capella Bangkok and the Four Seasons Bangkok at Chao Phraya River have already helped establish a new generation of resort-like urban hotels. Next comes The Langham, Custom House, Bangkok, transforming the city’s handsome 1888 former Custom House on the banks of the Chao Phraya. For travellers, though, it’s not just the size of Bangkok’s hotel pipeline that matters. It’s what all this competition means when it comes time to book a room. Related Article Luxury holidays Resort chain Aussies love opens new location in Thailand Bangkok has long been one of the world’s great cities for affordable luxury. Five-star hotels that would require a serious splurge in London, New York, Singapore or Sydney have traditionally been available here at considerably more approachable prices. That’s still true, but the market is changing. At the very top, Bangkok now has hotels playing unapologetically in the global ultra-luxury league, with rates to match. Look below that stratospheric level, however, and Bangkok’s extraordinary depth of good hotels remains. Established five-stars now find themselves competing not only with one another but with a procession of glamorous newcomers, giving travellers a breadth of choice that’s difficult to match in many other major cities.



But for Anantara, in 2026, even though it is surrounded by spectacular new hotels reaching ever higher into the skyline, all that space, greenery and history it affords makes it feel like the pinnacle of Bangkok luxury all over again. See anantara.com

World.title: Why the world’s biggest cruise ships are getting even bigger
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Last year I reported on the rise of very small cruise ships, if you can call them that, since some are so compact they only carry a dozen guests. But at the opposite end of the scale, cruise ships are getting ever larger. In 2000, the world’s biggest ship was Royal Caribbean’s Voyager of the Seas at 137,276 gross tonnage (GT), a measure of a ship’s internal volume rather than weight.

The 10 largest ships have doubled on average in volume since that time. Royal Caribbean’s Icon of the Seas, launched in early 2024, is 248,663 GT. The megaship is 364.75 metres long with 20 decks and a maximum capacity of 5610 passengers and 2350 crew.

No, it’s not an island – it’s Icon of the Seas, which launched in 2024 with capacity for 5610 passengers and 2350 crew.

Icon was the world’s largest ship in 2024 but two more Icon-class ships, Star of the Seas and Legend of the Seas, have since sailed out, and two more Icon-class ships are on order.

They make Norwegian Cruise Line’s latest ship Norwegian Aqua seem small with a 3571-passenger capacity, but in the 2030s the line will be launching four new ships that carry 5000 passengers and are just shy of Icon at 225,000 GT.

World.title: Copying One Nation will leave Australians poorer, Morrison minister warns
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Copying One Nation will leave Australians poorer, Morrison minister warns Shane Wright October 16, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Populist political movements will pull apart the nation’s mainstream parties if they fail to turn around the Australian economy by adopting major tax, housing and migration reforms, the country’s longest-serving finance minister has warned. Mathias Cormann, who served as finance minister in the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison governments and is now the head of the OECD, will use a speech in Brisbane on Saturday to urge both sides of politics to embrace a reform agenda stretching from the GST to planning regulations to lift living standards and quell left and right populists like One Nation. Mathias Corman is warning that major parties will be wiped out if they simply ape the policies of populists. Dominic Lorrimer Cormann will concede many of the problems facing the country developed while he was in office as the appetite for reform was suppressed by a mining boom that filled budget coffers and boosted incomes. His intervention, in an address to the right-leaning Centre for Independent Studies think tank, follows the release of a biography by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg, who has in the past week warned the Liberal Party must reconnect with the political centre if it is to remain relevant to voters.



Frydenberg also called for an increase in the GST, and the scrapping of some exemptions, with the revenue used to fund substantial income tax cuts. But Cormann will use the speech to outline a broader policy agenda, arguing that the increased support for populist political movements was being driven in part by the failure of major parties to improve living standards through difficult but necessary economic reforms. Loading In a clear warning to the Coalition, Cormann will say that simply aping populist policies will drive voters further into the hands of extreme parties. “Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will argue.



“The evidence for that is now extensive, from Britain to France to Germany, where mainstream parties that borrowed the insurgents’ agenda shrank while the insurgents grew. Related Article Political leadership ‘Things have to change’: Frydenberg criticises Liberal Party under Taylor’s leadership “The parties that have held their ground did so by out-performing the populists, not by imitating them.” Cormann will date the decline in appetite in this country for reform from 2005, when John Howard was prime minister, arguing the revenue unleashed by the then-mining boom made it easier for all political parties to shun difficult policy decisions. “This was not one side’s failure. The appetite for reform faded across the political divide, in business and in the union movement as much as in parliament,” he will say.



“When times feel good, because a boom is hiding a slow drift, the public sees no reason to accept that bargain. Politicians who propose it are punished for solving a problem nobody can yet see or feel.” Cormann will use the speech to outline areas for reform. These include the tax system, with the former minister arguing the GST needs to be increased and broadened, income tax rates sliced and indexed to inflation, while state stamp duties should be replaced with “more efficient” land and property taxes. He will also say the company tax rate is no long internationally competitive and should be reduced. In what would be a challenge to his own party, particularly at the state level, Cormann will argue the only way to bring down rents on homes is to sharply boost supply. This should include the right to build medium-density housing near every rail and major bus line in capital cities with approval against a code completed within 30 days.



The Coalition has promised to reduce net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years before gradually increasing it to 160,000. One Nation has gone further, advocating negative net migration for three years. Related Article One Nation ‘Smarmy management consultant’: Hanson attacks Taylor, Liberals in fiery CPAC speech Under both policies, Australia would have hundreds of thousands fewer workers, consumers and taxpayers over the coming years compared to current policy settings. The Belgian-born Cormann, who moved to Australia in 1995, said the public concern about migration had been driven by the long-term failure to build more homes and infrastructure to keep up with population growth. But he cautioned that deep cuts to migration would ultimately hurt the economy and Australians’ living standards.



“Australia is one of the very few advanced economies whose workforce is still projected to grow over the next 40 years,” Cormann will say. “Take that away, and the arithmetic turns on us. The number of Australians over 85 triples regardless, and health spending climbs from 4 to more than 6 per cent of national income regardless. “We cannot have fewer workers and more hospitals, more aged care, a bigger pension bill and more defence all at the same time.” Australia is in the midst of an AI building boom that has prompted push back in some communities. There are also concerns about AI, its impact on the jobs market and how it may upend workplaces. But Cormann will argue Australia needs to become the easiest country in the region to deploy AI rather than put up barriers to data centre construction and to the use of the technology.



“If history teaches anything, it is that protecting yourself from an innovation you are worried about does not stop the innovation. It happens anyway, somewhere else,” he will say. “The productivity dividend from AI will go to the countries that adopt fastest, not to those that regulate first. So apply the laws Australia already has, through the regulators it already has, rather than building a stand-alone AI regulator.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Carlton off-field crisis deepens after defender blows 0.174, charged with drink-driving
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Carlton off-field crisis deepens after defender blows 0.174, charged with drink-driving Andrew Wu, Greg Dundas and Roy Ward Updated October 16, 2026 — 10:12pm ,first published October 16, 2026 — 10:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of football news: Two Carlton players suspended for off-field indiscretions.

Viney appears in Eagles colours, vows to make impact on field. Carlton’s senior leaders are fuming after defender Wade Derksen was busted for “high-range” drink-driving, blowing well over three times the legal limit and becoming the third Blue embroiled in an off-field issue since the end of the season. The Blues have suspended Derksen for all their pre-season games and the first three matches of the 2027 home-and-away campaign after he returned a reading of 0.174 in a roadside breath test in Jabiru, about 250 kilometres from Darwin, in the Northern Territory the night before the AFL grand final. Wade Derksen has been suspended for all the Blues’ pre-season games, as well as the first three matches of the 2027 home-and-away campaign. Getty Images In a statement provided to this masthead on Friday night, Northern Territory police said: “Gunbalanya Police conducted an RBT on the Arnhem Highway in Kakadu, near the Oenpelli Road intersection.



“A 25-year-old male was subjected to a roadside breath test and returned a positive indication for alcohol. The male was arrested for the purpose of a secondary analysis and conveyed to Jabiru Police Station where he returned a high-range result of 0.174. “The male was issued an immediate licence suspension and issued with a Notice to Appear at Darwin Local Court on 10 November 2026 for Drive High Range Blood Alcohol Content.” In the Northern Territory, a high-range blood alcohol reading is equal to or more than 0.15, triple the legal limit. First-time drink-driving offences involving a BAC reading of more than 0.15 can result in a minimum of 12 months licence disqualification, a fine of up to $1940, or maximum imprisonment of 12 months. The Derksen revelation came just hours after defender Lachie Cowan was hit with a two-game ban by the AFL for conduct unbecoming following investigations of “his use of an illicit substance last weekend” by the Blues and the league. Forward Will Hayward admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. He was not sanctioned.



Angry Blues bosses have expressed their disappointment to Derksen and Cowan, and told the pair their poor decision-making had let down the club. Carlton coach Josh Fraser and football boss Chris Davies. Getty Images The Blues became aware of Derksen’s troubles when he self-reported last month and were working out his penalty when Cowan and Hayward had their misadventures, delaying an announcement on the backman’s penalties. After slow starts to their past two seasons, the Blues will kick off their 2027 campaign without two defenders from the team that bowed out in the elimination final against Geelong last month. Loading



“While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade’s conduct falls well below the standards we expect,” Carlton football boss Chris Davies said. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes “Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions.” Derksen had won the hearts of Blues fans by driving four days from Darwin to Melbourne for pre-season training to earn a spot on the list. He was given a two-year contract extension after strong form filling in for the injured Jacob Weitering. That feelgood story now has a sour postscript. Derksen, who must complete relevant counselling as part of his sanctions, has apologised for his behaviour.



“I want to express how sorry I am for what I did,” Derksen said. “The choice I made to get behind the wheel that day was unacceptable and is a moment I deeply regret. I have let a lot of people down, and for that I apologise.” Carlton defender Lachie Cowan. Getty Cowan apologised and thanked the medical professional who helped him after he collapsed at a party last weekend. “I should never have put myself in such a vulnerable situation, I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club,” Cowan said in a statement released by Carlton.



Related Article AFL 2026 Cowan to be hit with two-match ban, Hayward to avoid suspension after house party “I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was OK. “This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this.” Cowan was also issued with a $5000 suspended fine and now has an adverse finding listed against his name under the AFL’s illicit drugs policy. “AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations. They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances. Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions,” the league’s chief operating officer Tom Harley said in confirming the penalty on Friday.



In finding Cowan guilty of conduct unbecoming, the AFL said it considered the “circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public”. The league said it would require Cowan to undertake education on illicit substances and their effects additional to the mandatory training all players do. The players will all be undertaking fresh training through in November and December as the league prepares to introduce its new illicit drugs policy. When they return for training in January, every single AFL player will be hair-tested, the readings of which will trace back the previous three to six months. The incident involving Cowan at the weekend was first investigated by his club. Carlton passed its information to the AFL, and further enquiries were conducted. Carlton said it investigated the weekend’s matter involving Cowan while also providing him with wellbeing support. “Most importantly, we are thankful that Lachie is OK and received the medical attention he needed,” Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said in the Blues’ statement.



“We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake. Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward.” On Friday, newly unveiled West Coast recruit, and 2021 Melbourne premiership player, Jack Viney made clear his view on illicit drugs within the sport. “There is no place for drugs or illicit drugs in the AFL,” Viney said. “So whatever the policy that the AFL and AFLPA think is reasonable, I’m fully supportive of it.” The AFL Players’ Association said it was “unacceptable” that players were penalised after seeking medical treatment for an issue that would otherwise have remained private.



“As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it,” AFLPA chief James Gallagher said. Viney vows to make impact on the field out west Roy Ward Jack Viney isn’t moving his family to Western Australia to begin his coaching career – he’s doing it because he still believes he can play at the top level. New West Coast Eagles midfielder Jack Viney speaks to the media on Friday. Roy Ward



The new West Coast Eagles recruit spoke to media on Friday wearing his new club colours after 14 years and a breakthrough 2021 premiership with Melbourne. Much was said during the trade period about Viney’s move to the Eagles being based on his desire to move into coaching, but the 238-game midfielder made it clear he is heading west as a player first and a coach later despite Achilles surgery and a back injury keeping him to one game last season. Related Article AFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period “I’m really confident in my body and my ability, and that’s a big reason why I made this decision,” Viney said. “No doubt, I’ve had a really difficult year, the most disrupted and frustrating of my career in 14 years in the system.



“I understand you are only as good as your last game, but I’m keen and eager to get over to the Eagles, prove what I’m about and get a lot of hard work in over the pre-season.” Viney and wife Charlotte will move their three daughters to WA, and the player admitted it would hurt to leave his close family, including his dad Todd, also a former Melbourne captain and nowadays football boss at North Melbourne. “It’s going to be tough leaving. We are an extremely close family,” Viney said. Harley Reid of the Eagles is tackled by Jack Viney of the Demons in 2024. Getty Images “Our girls are six, four and one. When we spoke to the older two about the move, they loved it – when we broke the news to them that the deal was finally done, the kids jumped with excitement and joy. They are definitely on board.”



Leaving the Demons was a difficult process for Viney, but he said an honest post-season meeting with coach Steven King who made it clear the club was moving on. “The new coach wanted to go in a different direction and I can respect the decision,” Viney said. “While I still have plenty to give and great football to play, I’m coming off my most disrupted season and I wasn’t able to make a great first impression. Jack Viney, celebrating the Dees’ 2021 flag, is a key cog in the club’s engine room. AFL Photos “It definitely took some time to sink in, I had envisioned being a one-club player, so it definitely took me by surprise.



“But once you start looking at the opportunities, I reminded myself of some of Neale Daniher’s wisdom about life not promising to be fair, and I quickly became excited about the opportunity to play football for the Eagles.” Viney will be joined at the Eagles by Dees teammate and WA native Trent Rivers, and revealed he had already had some funny interactions with the club’s young midfield duo of Harley Reid and Willem Duursma. Related Article AFL 2026 Seven flag stars have left the Demons in the past year. But their list guru says they’re ‘ahead of the curve’ “Willem was the first one to message me, although he got my name wrong as he called me Trent,” Viney said with a laugh. “When I get over there, I’ll have to sort him out. No, I think they have a terrific young midfield who I haven’t met before, so I’m looking forward to building new relationships.”



Viney recalled tagging Reid in a game during the Eagles’ star’s first season. He also revealed young defender Reuben Ginbey “scares me”, saying he won’t be trying to take the number seven jumper from him. Eventually, Viney wants to move into coaching, and his Eagles deal will allow for that to happen, but he isn’t moving upstairs yet. “I’m planning to play footy for as long as I can, and I’ll squeeze everything out of it,” Viney said. “When I have to hang up the boots, we will have those conversations, as coaching is something I want to continue to explore.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBushfires Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study Courtney Kruk October 16, 2026 — 9:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Bushfires are impacting Queensland’s urban air quality more frequently and more severely than previously understood, new research has found, with pollution travelling further across the state, and for longer, increasing public health risks. The study led by researchers from the Queensland University of Technology analysed air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites across Queensland between 2008 and 2023. It found bushfire smoke can increase fine particle pollution (PM2.5) by up to 160.5 per cent during a fire event, and ozone levels by up to 33.2 per cent during fire-active seasons (July to December). A QUT-led study found bushfire smoke is affecting Queensland urban air quality more often and more severely than previously understood. Nick Moir Between 2018 and 2023, bushfire-impacted hours during the fire-active season were approximately three times more frequent, compared with 2008–2017.



Lead researcher Dr Zijun Li said climate change has increased the frequency and ferocity of bushfires, with longer burn times increasing pollution levels. Related Article Exclusive

Pollution Air pollution kills 1 million a year – hundreds of whom are Australians “Climate change and heatwave conditions are favouring the conditions of the bushfires,” Li said. “Bushfire smoke is not only a problem for communities located near fires. “Our research shows emissions can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres and significantly affect air quality in urban areas far from the source.



“As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of bushfires in many regions, understanding how smoke affects urban air quality is becoming increasingly important.” PM2.5 – the fine particle matter emitted during wildfires – is small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, and is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts. Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao moved from China to Australia as a child because of his asthma. Gold Coast University Hospital Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao has suffered asthma since early childhood, and moved from China to Australia when he was 11 because of the difference in air quality. “Industrial smoke and allergies are the main [asthma] triggers for me,” Zhao, who grew up in Adelaide, said.



“[In China] we lived in a heavily industrialised area as well. The dust, smoke, air quality … some days you could barely see five metres in front of you because of how bad it was. “So my parents made the decision to move over to Australia.” Since moving from South Australia to Queensland, Zhao said his exposure to bushfire events has been minimal. But he can feel changes to air quality, and worries about the impact of longer and more severe bushfire seasons. “I look at it from both sides, as a doctor and a patient myself,” he said. “For me, it gets a little bit harder to breathe whenever there’s smoke in the air, to the point where I’ll probably preemptively take some more of my puffers.



(Left to right) Huon Morton, Dr Zijun Li, Adjunct Professor Zoran Ristovski and Mr Hongzhi Zhang worked on the study analysing air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites in Queensland. Queensland University of Technology “[In the public health system] the number of resources that we do have is finite … so an increase in bushfires would definitely put a stress on both things.” Li said the research also revealed insights into how bushfire smoke behaves and affects communities, with stronger fires affecting urban pollutants. “Ozone formation is complex. We found bushfire emissions can interact with local urban emissions, particularly nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry, to increase ozone concentrations,” Li said. “This means bushfire smoke can worsen air quality even when the fires are a long way from the city.”

World.title: Victory for developers planning new tower over popular CBD pub
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHotels Victory for developers planning new tower over popular CBD pub Cameron Atfield October 16, 2026 — 9:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A planned 51-storey hotel tower above Brisbane’s landmark Victory Hotel CBD pub has received council approval, paving the way for a major accommodation development ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Brisbane City Council approved Precision Group’s proposed Victory Tower, a 206.6-metre development behind and above the heritage-listed hotel, on Monday. As part of the approval, Precision Group would be required to pay almost $2 million in infrastructure charges to the council. Precision Group is planning a new tower behind the Victory Hotel in Brisbane Bureau Proberts The new tower would be built on the site of the pub’s popular beer garden.



The approval marks a significant milestone for the project, which would transform the site into a 284-room hotel with restaurants, function spaces, wellness facilities, a rooftop bar and a swimming pool on the 40th floor. The 16,000-square-metre tower will be built on a 924-square-metre site and occupies the area currently used as the Victory’s Charlotte Street-facing beer garden. Precision Group founder and chief executive Shaun Bonett said the development would help address Brisbane’s hotel room shortage as the city prepares for the 2032 Games. “The critical shortfall of hotel rooms in Brisbane is well documented and the demand for accommodation is accelerating,” he said. “The Victory Hotel is one of Brisbane’s most recognised hospitality landmarks.



“Our vision is to honour that history while giving the site a new future, bringing together heritage, hotel accommodation, hospitality, wellness and rooftop experiences in a way that contributes to the city well beyond 2032.” A year ago, Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said a lack of sufficient accommodation was something that kept him up at night and, just last month, industry leaders discussed innovative ways, such as cruise ships and camping, to address the expected shortfall. The new Victory Tower would include a rooptop bar. Bureau Proberts Designed by Bureau Proberts, the slender tower has been positioned in the north-eastern corner of the site at the corner of Edward and Charlotte streets. Planning documents argued the design’s narrow footprint and setbacks would preserve views of the historic pub, which has operated on the site since 1855 and was recognised by the council as the oldest remaining pub in Brisbane’s CBD.



The project was supported by heritage architect Ruth Woods, who previously advised that the development would not compromise the prominence of the Victory Hotel or neighbouring heritage-listed buildings, including the former Metro Arts building. Related Article Pubs ‘Remarkable hotel’: Plans for a rooftop bar, balcony at the Victory If built, the tower would include a publicly accessible rooftop bar with panoramic city and river views, along with hospitality spaces intended to connect with the refurbished hotel below. Precision said restoration work at the Victory Hotel was already under way. The heritage pub was being reconfigured into four venues – a sports bar and beer garden, a rooftop garden bar, a steakhouse restaurant and a basement speakeasy with a gaming room.



The company took direct control of the hotel’s operations earlier this year and said discussions were continuing with prospective hotel operators. “We are already seeing strong interest from respected hotel operators who recognise the strength of the location, the heritage of the Victory Hotel and the opportunity to help shape a new hospitality destination for Brisbane,” Bonett said. “Getting that partnership right matters. It will help ensure Victory Tower is not only successful as a hotel but also contributes meaningfully to the wider CBD precinct.” The construction timetable would not be confirmed until an agreement was reached, but Precision expected the tower to be completed before 2032.
