World.title: Recap: Rugby League World Cup: Fetū Samoa v Jillaroos
World.content:
Australia's Jillaroos have proved too strong for Fetū Samoa in the women's Rugby League World Cup.

Australia ran in seven tries for a 40-0 victory in Sydney on Friday night.

But it was not entirely one-way traffic as Fetū Samoa put up a noteworthy defensive effort.

Earlier in the night, Toa Samoa had started their campaign with a hiss and a roar, beating France 78 - 4.

World.title: Toa Samoa give France a thrashing in World Cup opener
World.content:
Samoa kicked off their 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign with a strong 78-4 win over France at the CommBank Stadium in Sydney on Friday night.

Toa Samoa scored 14 tries in the process, four through replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo, and 22 points through the boots of Stephen Crichton, who kicked 11 goals.

Toa Samoa players showed a lot of emotions as their national anthem was sung and the Siva Tau battle challenge was laid down before kick-off.

And it took them just three minutes to get on the board with Deine Mariner running untouched out wide as the French defensive pattern was left wanting.

In the end the Blues of Samoa showed their fans and the world they are serious contenders, even though France was not as strong as many would have hoped for.

Co-captain and hard running forward Junior Paulo thanked the fans after the game, adding they are the reason the players do what they do.

"It's awesome to see the way they turn up," Paulo told Seven post match.

"It means everything to us.

"This is the reason why we play for our nation. To turn up here and see the crowd it means the world to us.

"We gotta dig deep out there; they are the reason."

Head coach Ben Gardiner told the players at halftime they needed to hang on to the ball longer, after their play had dropped heading into the last 10 minutes of the first 40.

Toa Samoa led 18-0 by the 10th minute mark, with two more touchdowns through Benaiah Ioelu in the sixth minute and Jermaine McEwen, in the eighth, as the team dominated play early.

Crichton kicked all three conversions for the 18-0 lead.

In the end they ran up 13 tries, with replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo claiming four on the night.

Fa'alogo replaced Mariner early in the first half after the first try-scorer of the night had to leave the field after he pulled his hamstring.

Luai, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Tabuai-Fidow, Brian To'o and Crichton combined to run hard against the French.

Up front, co-captain Paulo, Connelly Lemuelu, Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua were on fire, gaining valuable yards and territory every time they had the ball in hand.

Luai was the mastermind, with Harris-Tavita being the other option to command play.

Fa'alogo claimed his first try in Toa Samoa colours after the 10th minute before Tabuai-Fidow got his name on the score sheet.

France had their first visit into the Samoan territory in the 23rd minute but dummy-half Benjamin Garcia passed the ball forward 10 metres from the Samoan line and gave away the team's first real momentum.

But they got their first points on the board when Garcia sent the ball right close to the Samoan line, which saw Louis Grossemy finishing with a try in the corner in the 24th minute.

That was after a good defensive set inside their own 20-metre line won them a penalty and the ensuing sets saw them get a second penalty 10 metres out from the Samoan tryline.

The try seemed to have lifted the French, as they forced the Samoans into errors and put them under pressure a few times.

That also saw a drop in the Samoans' game as they dropped passes and knocked the ball on a few times.

Fa'alogo grabbed his second try in the 37th minute after some straight-up-the-middle runs by the forwards and Crichton slammed his conversion from out wide through the uprights, sending Samoa into a 34-4 lead at halftime.

The second 40

Gardiner's pep talk at halftime fired the Samoans back into action in the second spell.

He told Seven before resumption of play that the side needed to keep the ball and work on their game.

The team responded.

Crichton got Samoa's seventh try, two and half minutes after the restart, before Francis Manuleleua got his name on the board too.

Fa'alogo got Samoa's ninth try and his third for the night, running on to another Luai long pass, with 15 minutes to go, before adding his fourth some minutes later.

Warriors playmaker Tavita was on hand to touch down between the posts after another Luai show of his deft footwork, before centre Izack Tago managed to get a try to his name with eight minutes to go, with Crichton adding his ninth conversion, as Samoa went further up to 66-4.

Big forward Francis Molo, who previously played for the Cook Islands, powered his way over the French line for Samoa's 70th point in the game.

Crichton kicked his 10th conversion, and Samoa went up 72-4.

It was Ioelu who scored Samoa's 14th try in the dying seconds of the game after he jumped high to collect the ball that had bounced off the upright, from Crichton's attempted penalty kick.

World.title: Employment Court ruling over Calendar Girls sets 'important precedent' for country, dancers say
World.content:
An Employment Court decision regarding a Wellington strip club has set an important precedent for the entire country's adult entertainment industry, the dancers who pursued the case say.

This week, the Employment Court ruled that five dancers were employees of Calendar Girls when they worked at its Wellington club, not contractors.

The dancers took an employment case against the chain of adult venues after being effectively fired for challenging changes to their work conditions.

Cherida Fraser, from the Aotearoa Sex Workers Collective, told RNZ's Checkpoint the dancers had been handed a contract on a work night that reduced their proportion of fees, while also increasing the overall fees.

"They grouped together to address it and engage in good faith with the club and wrote their letter and tried to get a meeting with them," Fraser said.

"But this was denied and they were just terminated immediately, which was grossly unjust.

"They lost their livelihoods overnight when they were actually just trying to engage in good faith."

During a hearing earlier this year, the dancers argued they were effectively being treated as employees, not contractors.

In its ruling, the court highlighted the level of control Calendar Girls had over the dancers, with numerous restrictions in place.

"The way they performed and the services that were on offer, they weren't able to choose how much they charged for the services they offered on top of the baseline club fees," Fraser explained.

"Their attendance, their sick leave, they were expected to do regular shifts, they weren't able to take breaks when they wanted to."

Even the dancers' appearances were subject to scrutiny, Fraser said.

"Someone wanted to change their hair colour and that wasn't allowed.

"As well as that, they were restricted from working anywhere else. So there were significant trade restraints."

Audio player for " Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1958957%2Femployment-court-ruling-over-calendar-girls-sets-important-precedent-for-country-dancers-say

Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Financial penalties were in place for breaches of those restrictions. Dancers would be fined $200 if they stayed in changing rooms for too long, $100 for misuse of a cell phone, and $100 for wearing a g-string.

The "coercive threat of financial penalty" was outrageous, Fraser said.

She said the women felt energised by the Employment Court's ruling that they were employees, not contractors.

"And deservedly, this doesn't happen without personal cost to them," Fraser told RNZ's Checkpoint.

The women had shown "absolute fortitude" by putting their lives on hold to pursue the case, Fraser said.

She shared a statement from the dancers, where they said they were proud to have stuck it out and received some hard-earned closure.

"We're even more proud to have played a part in something much bigger than ourselves.

"We believe this judgment sets an important precedent for the adult entertainment industry on the whole."

Fraser said the ruling meant the dancers could now be compensated for unfair dismissal.

She said the decision would put other clubs on notice to treat their workers better.

"I think this is a very strong signal to the clubs to ensure that the contracts and the practices that go with those contracts are truly independent.

World.title: Worst staffing shortage Starship Hospital nurses have seen, as cancer treatments delayed
World.content:
Nurses at Auckland's Starship Children's Hospital say this is the worst nursing shortage they've seen, as cancer treatments are delayed.

On Thursday, Health Minister Simeon Brown confirmed some treatments were delayed up to seven days.

Do you know more? Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier on Thursday morning, Health New Zealand's Starship Hospital director Dr Greg Williams said the paediatric haematology/oncology service has had to reschedule some treatments due to a shortage of nurses.

"These decisions are not made lightly and are based on clinical need," he said, adding: "Starship is recruiting experienced and new graduate nurses as quickly as possible".

But two nurses who spoke to RNZ on the condition of anonymity, said staffing had been a critical issue for over a year.

They said there was a lack of experienced staff as nurses needed to complete a certain amount of qualifications, hours and training to be competent in chemotherapies, high-risk therapies and monitoring.

"We're getting a lot of new graduates - which is brilliant - but we need the staff to support them.

"We want to keep our new nurses not scare them away.

"It doesn't really help with our workload, at the moment they can't give chemotherapy or those high-risk therapies, so we still have to do them, as well as train the new nurses.

"It's not just the amount of nurses that we're employing, its the experience we need them to have..."

The nurses said new graduates only got two or three weeks working with another more experienced nurse and observing, before they were "on their own on the floor" in a children's oncology ward.

"It's intense, it's emotional and it's a really high-risk area. I just don't think two to three weeks is enough and we're not giving them enough support that they need to keep our staff and staff retention is really important for our kids."

A spokesperson for Brown earlier told RNZ vacancies at Health NZ were the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement, but the nurses disagreed.

"That is absolutely not the case."

They said some nurses left because they felt unsupported.

One thing the nurses did want to make clear to parents and the general public was patients would still receive support and care they needed.

"We will do everything we can to make sure we get those children seen and safely cared for," they said.

"The tricky thing is we're doing that at the detriment of our nurses.

"We want to reassure parents out there that their children will get the care and the treatment they need, the children are safe."

Following media reports in recent days, the nurses said many parents on the ward were stressed, worrying their children wouldn't get the care they needed.

"We want to reassure them all - and that is what we've spent most of the day doing... their kids will get the treatment that they need."

They said they wanted to thank the parents for messages of support they had received.

The nurses said however, they weren't currently able to spend the time really getting to know families like they used to, or spend time with the children and play with them.

"We purely come in now to do the treatment... and just get through the shift safely."

The bottom line they said, was they needed more experienced nurses.

"This is not a cry for money, we are not asking for another pay rise, we're crying out for more staff - and more staff who can train up our new starters."

They encouraged Brown to come to the hospital and meet with staff, to see what it was like in person.

"We'd be interested to speak to him if he's keen to, come and have a meeting with us, we'd be happy to have conversation."

They said Brown had not been to visit them in person before.

Brown said he had compassion and respect for all families supporting children at Starship Hospital and he was grateful to the staff who went "above and beyond every day".

"I am advised that all vacancies in ward 27B have been recruited with nurses either having already started in these roles or about to start. I expect Health NZ to ensure vacancies are recruited to as quickly as possible when they arise."

A spokesperson for Brown said he'd been in touch with people who had been at Starship in recent days and would soon be meeting with some parents of children receiving care there.

They said he had spoken with Health NZ's chief executive to seek an opportunity to meet with frontline staff and hear first-hand about "their important work and the care they provide to children and their families."

Health NZ have been approached by RNZ for comment.

On Thursday, a spokesperson for the minister said all children at Starship Hospital were still being treated, though a handful of chemotherapy sessions have been delayed for a few days - but no more than seven.

Two bone marrow transplants were moved "slightly", but both were still going ahead.

Williams said the oncology departments are being supported by staff in other parts of Starship and Auckland City Hospital.

World.title: Guam declares 'Condition of Readiness 3' as tropical depression approaches
World.content:
Guam has been placed in 'Condition of Readiness 3' as Tropical Storm Champi moves towards the Mariana Islands, with residents warned to prepare for potentially damaging winds, heavy rain and flooding.

A Condition of Readiness 3 means that destructive or damaging winds are possible or forecasted within 48 hours.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero ordered the alert.

The National Weather Service in Guam said the system, previously designated Invest 96W, is continuing to organise and strengthen.

Forecasters say the storm's track and intensity remain uncertain, but Guam could experience strong winds, heavy rainfall, flooding and hazardous marine conditions in the coming days.

Governor Leon Guerrero said the early declaration gives families, businesses and government agencies time to prepare before conditions deteriorate.

She has urged residents to secure their homes and ensure their families have essential supplies.

Residents are being advised to stock enough food, drinking water, medication and other emergency supplies for at least seven to 10 days.

They should also secure loose outdoor items, charge mobile devices, prepare flashlights and emergency radios, and review family emergency plans.

The governor has also urged the public to stay out of the water during storm conditions, warning that people who enter hazardous waters put both themselves and emergency responders at risk.

The Leon Guerrero-Tenorio administration, together with Guam Homeland Security and the Office of Civil Defense, is coordinating preparedness efforts with government agencies and emergency response partners.

Residents are urged to follow official updates from Guam Homeland Security and the National Weather Service.

Further announcements are expected as the system develops.

World.title: Cook Islanders urged to be prepared for potential cyclone
World.content:
Cook Islanders are being urged to get ready as a tropical depression brews in the country's waters, according to the Cook Islands Meteorological Service.

A tropical cyclone alert is now in force for the Cook Islands as TD01F moves towards the Southern Cook Islands.

The system is expected to strengthen and may develop into a category 1 tropical cyclone within the next 12-18 hours.

The Service's Director Maara Vaiimene said people should check around their houses for any loose objects that could become a problem when the wind comes.

"Make sure your house roof is steady, check on nearby trees that won't become a problem during strong winds," he said.

"Look at your communications, in terms of radio or tv, in the event the power goes out. People should also make sure they can communicate with neighbours or family to ensure they are safe, and that you are safe."

Vaiimene said the Emergency Cook Islands team has a response guideline for what people need to do in the event that the tropical depression becomes a tropical cyclone.

The Meteorological Service, which is working closely with the Fiji Meteorological Service, said the wind conditions associated with the tropical depression were similar to a tropical cyclone status.

"In the latest bulletin, they have indicated that the chances of the tropical depression forming in a tropical cyclone in the next day or two is high," Vaiimene said.

The Cook Islands is currently in an el nino climate situation.

Vaiimene said the El Niño weather phase over the region is contributing to the unusually early development of a possible tropical cyclone.

The official tropical cyclone season starts on November 1.

World.title: Thousands of people fled Europe for NZ during WWII. Survivors and descendants are reuniting for the first time
World.content:
Audio player for " Displaced European survivors of WWII gather in Palmerston North " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/community/1958055%2Fthousands-of-people-fled-europe-for-nz-during-wwii-survivors-and-descendants-are-reuniting-for-the-first-time

Displaced European survivors of WWII gather in Palmerston North Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

While Europe was in turmoil, New Zealand was embarking on an unprecedented period of growth.

As the babies boomed, almost 5000 displaced people from states such as Lithuania, Hungary and Poland arrived on our shores from 1949-1952, ready to get to work and blend in.

This weekend some survivors, and their descendants, are gathering in Palmerston North to mark an often overlooked chapter in Aotearoa's history.

Escape from Lithuania

Captured in a jaunty National Film Unit Weekly Review newsreel, a ship load of war-displaced people arrive in Wellington Harbour in 1949, after a long journey that began in Italy.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W_lDL7FrCws)

The New Zealand government had agreed to welcome them on humanitarian grounds and because the country needed labour.

Among those who arrived in 1949 was Jurgis Cibulskis, sister Audrone, and parents Mecisolvas and Stefanija, from Lithuania.

Jurgis Cibulskis soon adopted the first name George as his family began a new life, speaking a different language in an unknown country on the other side of the world.

"We left Lithuania in 1944 as the Russians were advancing," Jurgis, now 86, told RNZ this week.

Lithuania had already endured a brutal Nazi invasion before the tide of war turned.

"My father at that stage decided he wasn't going to face Russian occupation once more and he decided to get out.

"The whole family, without ever returning to the apartment we were living in, because that was going the wrong way, were given a horse and cart by relations who we were holidaying with and away we went."

Jurgis Cibulskis, with the book about his life that was published last year. RNZ/JIMMY ELLINGHAM

Perhaps too young to appreciate what was happening, Jurgis remembers the novelty of the horse and cart as his family joined a convoy of people leaving. He also remembers his parents looking after their children well, probably going hungry so the younger ones could eat.

They went to Germany, where Jurgis lost all the fingers on his right hand in an accident. He also learnt to speak fluent German.

His accident led the family to New Zealand, because Canada wouldn't take a child who might not be able to work as a physical labourer.

On arrival they were sent to the lower North Island town of Pahīatua, where they spent a few weeks learning English and how to be good New Zealanders at a camp best known for taking in Polish refugee children during WWII.

"We got good treatment. We couldn't complain," Jurgis remembered.

"Our first dinner in New Zealand - you wouldn't believe it, you know what they gave us? Good old New Zealand curry.

"We'd never smelt the curry flavour. We'd seen meat swimming in a light gravy, with raisins. Meat and raisins didn't feature in our diet."

They were hungry, so gratefully accepted the fare.

Daily life at the Pahīatua camp, from where the displaced people were sent to all parts of New Zealand SUPPLIED/HOLLAND FAMILY COLLECTION

The Cibulskis family were then sent to Auckland, where they settled. Jurgis' father initially worked as a dairy farmer in Northcote, before moving to other jobs, including carpentry.

The family ended up buying a home in Remuera, a suburb Jurgis still lives in, his apartment overlooking St Michael's church, where he married his wife of 58 years, Beverly. She died in 2022.

The pair had three children and six grandchildren.

Jurgis had a successful career in industry, including many years at Fibremakers New Zealand, and played plenty of sport. He captained Auckland's third grade rep softballers.

"I assimilated in New Zealand very quicky. I picked up the language, no problems. I had no accent almost immediately.

"The vocabulary took a while to develop, but I was able to make my way quite readily."

He did notice some resentment about New Zealand importing workers a couple of decades after the tough Depression years, though.

Jurgis is one of four original displaced people at this weekend's gathering, which includes a trip back to Pahīatua - although the camp there is long gone.

He'll travel to Palmerston North by overnight bus from Auckland and was looking forward to catching up with people from the Pahīatua camp, or their families.

Most displaced people had only about six weeks to learn English in classrooms at the Pahīatua camp. SUPPLIED/HOLLAND FAMILY COLLECTION

Workers wanted as New Zealand grew

Organiser Tania Kopytko, whose father Michael was a displaced person from Belarus, said there needed to be more recognition of this part of New Zealand history.

"This is the same period as the £10 Poms came. New Zealand needed manpower and it wanted to develop economically, and these people were part of that process.

"We're talking about 4000 who went through the Pahīatua camp, and a rapid turnover in some instances."

Many New Zealanders were kind to the new arrivals and helped them settle - others were not.

"It's sad to say, but in some instances where these people might not have spoken English very well and spoken to somebody up town, like their daughter in their own language, people felt quite happy about marching up to them and saying: 'You speak English in our country.'

Tania Kopytko and her father Michael in 1993. SUPPLIED/TANIA KOPYTKO

"I actually witnessed that myself," said Tania, who is in her early 70s and lives in Palmerston North.

"On the other hand, there was also extremely kind New Zealanders. My Aunty Lucy spent six weeks in the [Pahīatua] camp and still couldn't speak English, and was sent to work in a factory in Palmerston North. It was her neighbour who taught her to speak English."

Tania's father didn't go through the Pahīatua camp, instead meeting her mother, Olive, in London and returning to New Zealand with her.

The Palmerston North gathering, the first of its kind, is called Celebrating Our Stories, and Tania said the organisers were keen to know what further work was needed to record people's memories from this period, part of the wider Untold Stories project.

World.title: Jillaroos flex muscle in 40-point World Cup win over Samoa
World.content:
Australia's quest for a fourth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup has started with a bang courtesy of a 40-0 victory over Fetu Samoa.

Unbackable favourites leading into the tournament opener, the Jillaroos overcame an ill-disciplined opening 10 minutes to shut out Samoa in the seven-try rout.

Things were far from easy for Australia in the second half, but the damage was already done by half-time, with five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and reigning Dally M medallist Tamika Upton leading the way with two try assists apiece.

Kelleher, making her Jillaroos debut, was named player of the match, where she was dangerous in attack and her kicking game troubled Samoa.

Speaking to ABC Sport, Kelleher said she had been waiting a long time for her chance to play for the Jillaroos.

"It's a dream come true," she said.

"Was in the squad last year, but got my debut jersey this year. So excited and so happy to be here."

Despite the 40-point win, it was far from a perfect performance from the reigning world champions.

"We still have a lot of things to fix from today. It wasn't perfect out there," Kelleher said.

Samoa, in their first World Cup since 2008, had several chances early but lacked the class to capitalise against their much-fancied opponents.

Gold Coast Titans star Jaime Chapman ended her three-year Jillaroos exodus by scoring Australia's first try in the 11th minute, beating opposite winger Freedom Crichton Ropati out wide.

Australia's greatest ever try-scorer, Julia Robinson, lived up to her reputation seven minutes later when she beat three would-be defenders for her 23rd Jillaroos try in 14 appearances.

Tries to back-rower Shaylee Bent and hooker Keeley Nizza followed in quick succession before lock Olivia Kernick crossed moments before halftime to seal a 28-0 lead at the break.

Kernick turned playmaker in the opening five minutes of the second period when she handed the ball off for Keilee Joseph to extend the Jillaroos' lead.

Brave defence might have turned the tide for Samoa, who ground their way to more opportunities at the Jillaroos end over the final 25 minutes.

Prop Laikha Clarke went the closest to securing some consolation points for Samoa, but was ruled to have dropped the ball over the line.

Of further concern for Samoa was a suspected knee injury in the dying stages to centre Sarina Masaga.

A try in the final two minutes from Australian centre Jessica Sergis capped the Jillaroos' victory and extended their almost three-year unbeaten run.

Samoa's men thrashed France in the opening match of the day, putting on a record score to win 78-4.

World.title: PNG Chiefs to go ahead with NRL logo launch after court decision
World.content:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court before the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, which is also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand.

But a judge at today's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

"The PNG Chiefs welcome today's decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday,," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

NZ Rugby to protect 'Chiefs' name New Zealand Rugby has sought interim and final injunctions before the NRL's Papua New Guinea team is officially launched later this month.

"As the matter remains before the court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time."

The dispute continues, with an application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia under consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after NSW "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued today that the PNG Chiefs' use of "PNG Chiefs" and "Chiefs" interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs of brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC lawyer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opened next month.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Surgery giving Kiwis hope of Ponga playing again in World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga will undergo surgery on his broken arm but will remain in camp, with New Zealand not giving up on the superstar fullback playing again in the Rugby League World Cup.

Ponga failed to finish his long-awaited Test debut for the Kiwis, departing in the 70th minute of the 24-22 loss after suffering the injury earlier in the second half.

Receiving clearance earlier this year to switch his allegiance to New Zealand, Ponga delivered a stand-out performance at Western Sydney Stadium as his side fell to Australia in the Thursday night thriller.

The Newcastle skipper scored two tries while running 253 metres from 16 runs, making three line breaks and five tackle breaks.

He has been booked in for surgery after breaking the radius in his left arm but Kiwis team doctor Greg Macleod sounded hopeful about the prospect of Ponga playing again through the tournament.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

"We wish Kalyn all the best with his surgery today," Macleod said in a statement.

"We'll see how that goes but for now he will remain in camp."

The 28-year-old is viewed as critical to the New Zealand's hopes of claiming their first World Cup since 2008.

Coach Stacey Jones, whose side will face the Cook Islands in Christchurch next week before wrapping up their group stages matches against Fiji, said Ponga had played through pain.

"He couldn't catch a ball or anything like that. He was in a bit of discomfort," Jones said.

Ponga was replaced by Keano Kini as he trudged off late in the match and was seen on the sidelines with his arm in a sling.

"He's obviously disappointed, but there's a bit of upbeat about him too. He really wants to still be involved," Jones said.

If New Zealand decide Ponga's tournament is over, the Kiwis have the option to ask for clearance to add an additional player to their squad.

"He's a tough guy and obviously has a lot of pride in the black and white jersey, and he doesn't want to let his teammates down," Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"I thought he did an outstanding job. He's a freakish player, but he's also one of those tough players. We're feeling for him right now, but fingers crossed it's not too bad."

Jones said Kini would likely replace Ponga in next week's pool match.

The Kiwis' narrow loss to Australia was one that will burn Jones for a while.

Two of the Kangaroos' five tries were the result of interceptions and another two were from kicks.

The Kiwis dominated territory but lacked the polish to make Australia pay for their mistakes.

"Unfortunately, we were on the losing side, but we will learn from it, and we will get better and we will make some adjustments," Jones said.

"You go in that changing room and everyone's down, they're hurting.

"But you just bounce back and you get back into it. We know these boys, they work hard, they're professional. We'll be OK"
