World.title: Carlton suspends defender over high-range drink-driving charge
World.content:
Carlton has suspended defender Wade Derksen for drink driving on an off-season trip, allegedly blowing more than three times the legal limit.

The Blues suspended Derksen for all preseason games and up to round three of the AFL season next year.

The 25-year-old was charged with high-range drink-driving in Jabiru in the Northern Territory.

Derksen failed a roadside breath test late last month, allegedly returning a reading of 0.174.

Police said his licence was suspended and his case will be heard in court in the Northern Territory next month.

Cowan suspended by AFL The AFL hands down its sanction to Lachie Cowan following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

"While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade's conduct falls well below the standards we expect," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions."

Derksen joined Carlton at the start of the season after GWS de-listed him at the end of last year.

He played 15 games for the Blues this season.

The AFL announced earlier today that Carlton's Lachie Cowan had been suspended for two games after an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

World.title: Tahiti police gather evidence after pro surfer suspended over alleged incident
World.content:
Police in French Polynesia are gathering evidence following an alleged incident in Tahiti that has led world surf bodies to suspend a professional surfer from competitions.

Both the International Surfing Association (ISA) and World Surf League (WSL) announced this week they had suspended a male competitor after learning of the "serious" allegations.

Neither organisation has identified the suspended surfer, and the ABC has not independently verified their identity.

The Outerknown Tahiti Pro attracts international professional surfers. (AFP: Jerome Brouillet)

The WSL said the alleged incident happened at a private gathering in Tahiti in August, which was not affiliated with the organisation.

Surfing World magazine, which reported the suspension this week, said it understood the alleged incident occurred at a party after the final day of the Outerknown Tahiti Pro surfing event.

The alleged incident involved a teenage Australian female surfer and at least three men, it reported.

"[Surfing World] understands that NSW police have been advised of the allegations and have been in contact with surfing authorities," it reported.

However, Australian and French Polynesian police appear at odds regarding who has jurisdiction over the matter.

The ABC understands law enforcement officials in Tahiti believe they do not have jurisdiction, because the alleged victim reported their complaint to police in Australia.

It is also understood that local police in French Polynesia are now gathering evidence relating to the alleged incident to have ready for Australian law enforcement, but are yet to receive a formal request for information.

The World Surf League said its discipline committee suspended the professional competitor. (AFP: Martin Bureau)

NSW Police has declined to comment on the matter, saying that French Polynesian police have jurisdiction and carriage of the investigation.

The Australian Federal Police also said enquiries should be directed to local authorities.

'Serious allegations of abuse'

The ISA on Thursday said it had decided to provisionally suspend the professional surfer from "ISA-sanctioned" events "pending further investigation and review".

"The International Surfing Association is deeply concerned by recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community," it said in a written statement on Thursday.

"This precautionary decision has been taken in the interest of athlete safety and welfare, and does not constitute a determination of wrongdoing.

"The ISA remains committed to respecting due process, confidentiality, and the rights of all individuals concerned.

" The ISA firmly believes that all athletes have the right to participate in sport in a safe and respectful environment, free from harassment, violence and abuse of any kind. "

The WSL, which was first to suspend the surfer, on Sunday said it had suspended a surfer on the 2026 Men's Championship Tour after it was made aware of "allegations of a deeply serious nature involving the competitor".

It said it had offered to assist relevant authorities.

World.title: Teen killed in cricketing tragedy 'died by misadventure', coroner finds
World.content:
The grieving family of a 17-year-old boy who died in a cricketing tragedy say they are relieved a coroner will not recommend changes to the rules of the game their son loved.

Ben Austin was hit in the neck by a ball thrown with a side arm device while practising in the nets at Wally Tew Reserve in Ferntree Gully, in Melbourne's outer east, in October last year.

Cricket authorities confirmed at the time he was wearing a helmet but not a stem guard, which protects the neck.

Ben later died at the Monash Children's Hospital.

Coroner Simon McGregor on Friday confirmed the 17-year-old died as a result of misadventure by well-meaning young people using proper equipment at a "caring, well-run club".

Ben's parents Tracey and Jace wiped away tears as the facts were read at a directions hearing in the Coroners Court of Victoria, with legal teams for Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria also present.

Jace and Tracey Austin speak to media outside the Coroners Court of Victoria. (ABC News)

The coroner confirmed no adverse comments would be made about anyone's behaviour and "no individuals or organisations contributed to the cause of Ben's death".

He added that no recommendations or comments about rule changes would be made, paving the way for the summer cricket season to continue "in the normal way".

The coroner proposed commending the fact that some clubs and leagues had made safety changes without waiting to be told, with one bringing in neck guards and another banning the use of side arms.

But he said there was still some misunderstanding about individual clubs' ability to make safety changes, with some under the mistaken impression authorities would tell them what to do in response to safety issues.

The coroner is considering making a comment about the governance structure and how safety and best practice messages are conveyed.

The teenager's death shocked Ferntree Gully and the wider Melbourne cricket community. (ABC News)

Speaking after the hearing, Jace Austin said the lack of adverse findings and rule changes were exactly what Ben would have wanted.

"There's no way we want to change this great game," he said.

"But on the other hand, we don't want another Benny or Phil [Hughes, who died in similar circumstances in 2014].

"From what we've heard, it's exactly what we wanted."

With the anniversary of Ben's death nearing, he said the family would be coming together to reflect.

"Every day's tough, but when this comes to an end, this will be Benny's full stop, so you sort of want it to drag out."

"Every day's brutal to be honest."

Tracey Austin wore a necklace bearing her son's name.

"I've got him close to my heart," she said.

Jace and Tracey Austin say their family will be coming together to reflect on Ben's death. (ABC News: Wayne Hammond)

Cricket Victoria's Nick Cummins said the organisation would work through the coroner's initial comments and later findings.

"What we didn't want to do is go out and start finding solutions before we understood the coroner's findings," he said.

"Cricket is a safe sport. It's always been a safe sport. We have measures in place to make sure that's the case.

"But it's always important to have an open inquiry around incidents like this."

Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins attended the hearing on Friday. (ABC News)

He said the cricketing community had come together after Ben's death, with the Austin family raising $180,000 at a fundraiser last week.

"It's been incredibly heartening to see how cricket brings people together," he said.

The coroner's formal findings will be handed down before Christmas.

World.title: Cowan handed AFL suspension following illicit substance investigation
World.content:
The AFL has suspended Carlton's Lachie Cowan for two matches following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

The league said "the circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public" were also the subject of the investigation.

Cowan was found guilty of conduct unbecoming.

He will be suspended for the first two home-and-away matches of the 2027 season and issued with a $5,000 fine.

Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne The club has confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward have been admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

No action was taken against Cowan's Blues teammate Will Hayward, who was also admitted to hospital on Sunday due to a separate incident.

Cowan's sanction was handed down as the AFL confirmed its new illicit drugs policy would come into effect in January.

The league said all players would be hair tested upon their return to training in January, "with readings going as far back as three to six months prior".

Cown said he should not have put himself "in such a vulnerable situation".

"I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club," Cowan said in a Carlton statement.

"I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was okay.

"This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this."

The AFL Players' Association (AFLPA) released a statement in the wake of the AFL handing down its suspension.

"This has become a public matter because private information regarding players seeking medical treatment has been shared," AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher said in the statement.

"That is unacceptable."

Gallagher said Cowan's suspension could discourage players from seeking emergency medical assistance.

"We don't want players using illicit substances and that is why the [AFL's] illicit drugs policy is so important, with its overarching purpose to change behaviour and minimise harm," he said.

"However, it is contrary to this health and wellbeing model to sanction players after they have sought medical treatment, particularly in an emergency.

"As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it."

The Blues said Cowan's wellbeing remained the club's priority.

"Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is okay and received the medical attention he needed," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake.

"Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward."

Lachie Cowan issued an apology via the Carlton Football Club. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Cowan will be required to undertake further education above the current mandated training on illicit substances and their effects.

The league said the matter would "constitute a notifiable adverse finding under the AFL's illicit drugs policy".

"AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations," AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said in a league statement.

"They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances.

"Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions."

World.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
World.content:
Supercars will return to Phillip Island next year, helping plug an economic gap left by MotoGP's move to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

"We know Supercars fans are wrapped with this news. We know our drivers are wrapped because they love Phillip Island, they love the circuit and they can't wait," Mr Carbines said.

"It was critical that we got back out there and made sure we locked in something that was going to make a big difference to the community of Phillip Island and the vast coast, but also to bring Supercars back to the Island."

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on event-driven tourism.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

Victorian opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick and Bass Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead say the Coalition will back a motoring festival on Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"We know the government has announced supercars today from Federation Square," Mr Southwick said on Phillip Island.

"They don't care about Bass Coast, they don't care about the island.

"We're here today because we care and we know it all starts with homegrown events."

Motorsport central to Phillip Island

President of the Association of Motoring Clubs Keith Mortimer said motoring culture connected many people to Phillip Island.

He said the goal for the next 12 months was to ensure the first motoring festival's success and make sure the event "is here to stay".

He said motorsport, whether it's bikes, classic cars, or Supercars, connected many visitors to the island.

Keith Mortimer says motorsport connects many visitors to Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"There are some wonderful things to see here, around Churchill Island, around the chocolate factories, around the local produce," Mr Mortimer said.

"It really does have something for everyone."

Destination Phillip Island chief executive Kim Storey said one in four jobs on the island were connected to the visitor economy.

She said the five-year commitment will boost confidence in local accommodation, hospitality, retail and tourism.

"Supercars represents meaningful progress towards rebuilding major event visitation," she said.

"There is still important work ahead to replace lost demand across the year and support the broader economic transition facing Phillip Island and San Remo."

Tech.title: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multi-story ramp, launching off the edge, executing a mid-air “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters.

That’s what the people want, right? “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway.

Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. And the gushing praise and wide-eyed reactions on X, a platform already predisposed to absolving Musk of all his sins, were hard to avoid.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: Tesla

Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping. Equipping an electric supercar with 600 liters of compressed air, 10 directional cold-gas thruster nozzles, and a 2G suction-fan system directly inspired by SpaceX is undeniably rad. Seeing a 0-to-60 mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two.

Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third-party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.”

Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping.

Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits.

Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future.

Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s re-release is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies.

In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down, cars that can jump in the air, and cars that can accelerate very, very fast.

BYD’s Yangwang U9 Extreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating Rimac’s Nevera 268mph record. And the McMurtry Spéirling single-seater holds the record for quickest acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in 1.35 seconds. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm.

But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, than I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype.

It’s completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold.

Tech.title: Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to a report from Nieman Lab. The new terms, which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.

While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file. That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers.

The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Roberts pushes back on Nieman Lab’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN, Fox News, USA Today, and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell tells Nieman Lab.

Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,” Nieman Lab says.

Update, October 16th: Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.

Tech.title: This stretchy MagSafe storage pouch gives your phone a sizable trunk
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There’s a new storage upgrade option for smartphones compatible with wireless chargers and other magnetic accessories, but it won’t help if you’ve run out of room for apps, pics, and videos. The MagSafe Flex Pouch looks like a magnetic wallet for pairing a small stack of credit cards to your phone, but its storage capacity goes well beyond a few thin plastic cards thanks to an extremely stretchy silicone pouch.

The MagSafe Flex Pouch’s creators, a company called Ninja Labs, has a bunch of suggestions for how to use the $58 accessory on its website. You can use it as yet another MagSafe wallet but one that has enough capacity for all the credit, debit, membership, loyalty, and ID cards from your entire extended family. You can also squeeze your car’s fob in there, as well as wireless earbuds, lip balms, gum, snacks, makeup, a handful of loose change, or an obnoxious roll of cash.

The Flex Pouch is available with a clear silicone pocket or four solid colors including pink, blue, lavender, and black. Image: Ninja Labs

The stretchy pouch conforms to whatever’s stuffed inside it and because silicone naturally has a grippy texture the Flex Pouch should do a good job at ensuring nothing falls out if you don’t over fill it. And if the look of the translucent silicone isn’t doing it for you, the pouch is also available in opaque colors including black, pink, blue, and lavender, plus an additional option with a rainbow sparkly finish.

Tech.title: iPhone Duo orders are already delayed into 2027
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Delivery estimates for the iPhone Duo slipped into next year in less than an hour after Apple opened preorders for it at 8AM ET on Friday.

At the time of writing we are seeing late January delivery dates for every configuration on Apple’s website. The foldable is slated to launch in stores on October 23rd, and Apple typically reserves some units for in-store availability. So while online orders are delayed, you might be able to get one sooner in-person at an Apple Store.

The long delay could be due to high demand for Apple’s first foldable iPhone, low supply on Apple’s side, or a mix of both. Apple announced the iPhone Duo in September, featuring the shorter passport-style design Samsung introduced earlier this year. The Duo starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model and comes in “star white” and “night sky.” You can still preorder it on Apple’s website, but you might be in for a long wait before you get to unfold it.

Tech.title: The Sony Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting a promised update to Android 17
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When the midrange Sony Xperia 10 VI was announced over two years ago with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset and Android 14, Sony promised three major OS updates which would have included this year’s Android 17 release. However, according to a notice posted to the company’s UK support site, the Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting Android 17 after all.

In the notice Sony explains that a “detailed technical assessment” revealed that “limitations related to the device’s storage configuration” mean the Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate.” As a result, the company has “decided not to make this upgrade available” and apologized that the decision “falls short of our original announcement.”

Sony clarifies that while OS updates for the Xperia 10 VI are ending, the company will continue to provide four years of security updates which should extend until June 2028. Sony also points out that this specific issue only applies to the “Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications” and does not impact promised OS updates for other Xperia models. But since the technical requirements of future versions of Android aren’t yet known, it’s hard to take Sony at its word given today’s announcement.

Tech.title: The first vibe-coded gun is here
Tech.content:
Since gun-rights activist and alt-right-friendly agitator Cody Wilson made the first 3D-printed firearm 13 years ago, he’s helped usher in a chaotic era of untraceable ghost guns. Now he’s claiming another first: “the first AI-made gun.” It’s called the WASP.

I stood about 20 feet away as Wilson and his sidekick clamped the WASP to a DIY test mount outside Defense Distributed headquarters in Austin, Texas. The 3D-printed .22 caliber handgun is, in reality, little more than a pistol barrel attached to a spring-loaded plastic box. Its rudimentary design bears a resemblance to Wilson’s single-shot 3D-printed “Liberator,” albeit with some quintessentially AI-generated oddities, like a wacky, bubbly grip that doesn’t quite fit a human hand. It was aimed toward a shallow green slope in the backyard of a semi-residential neighborhood. A long black string ran from its trigger to Wilson, who sat crouched about 10 feet back behind a police riot shield.

“Three. Two. One.” I braced for a thunderous crack, but instead heard only a loud click. The world’s first AI-generated gun had misfired.

“This didn’t happen last time,” Wilson, annoyed, reassured me as he carried out some quick troubleshooting. The gun’s striker had hit the cartridge, he said, but failed to set off the primer. I quietly took another step back. After some more fiddling, Wilson declared the WASP ready for a second chance. This time, pulling the string produced a sharp bang, about as loud as a firecracker. Downrange, a cardboard target had a hole ripped through its top left corner. His colleague had suggested using a life-size cutout of Joe Biden, but Wilson shot that down as “too on the nose.”

The safety test completed, Wilson then unclamped the WASP, slipped on a protective glove, took aim at the cardboard target, and squeezed the trigger himself. Another bang. This time, a miss, slightly high. The AI gun, today at least, was two for three in terms of shots successfully fired.

A hand-drawn target in the backyard of the Defense Distributed headquarters in Austin, Texas. Image: The Verge

With the smell of gunpowder still lingering, I asked Wilson the obvious question: Why make this functionally suspect firearm in the first place? We’re in Texas, where buying a conventional gun is often easier than getting a driver’s license. He paused, taking issue with the premise.

“I would argue that what we’ve made is not an AI-generated gun, but an AI that can generate guns.”

His supposed AI gunsmith is a custom model he calls GatGPT. But instead of generating pasta recipes or travel plans, this unfiltered model answers questions about firearms. It’s trained on DEFCAD’s expansive library of gun files and can help enthusiasts pick out the exact parts they need for a build. Launched in 2012, DEFCAD (another Wilson-led project) is the world’s largest online repository of digital gun and component files. Gun safety advocates and lawmakers have argued sites like DEFCAD aid the proliferation of “ghost guns,” firearms made partly or entirely of components without a serial number. Wilson, meanwhile, has called access to firearms “a fundamental human right.”

“I would argue that what we’ve made is not an AI-generated gun, but an AI that can generate guns.”

Under US federal law, licensed gun makers are required to include serial numbers on the frames or receivers of guns they sell. Wilson and others in what’s referred to as the 3D2A movement say gun files aren’t actually guns, they are computer code, a form of protected speech. That core argument, whether or not gun codes are protected speech, has been argued in court cases for over a decade, with many often citing or involving Wilson. It’s possible the issue will wind up before the Supreme Court.

Now, Wilson claims, AI can also come up with its own unique designs. The results have a bizarre, surrealist quality emblematic of early generative art to the tune of Will Smith slurping spaghetti.

The WASP’s entire development, Wilson claims, from its name to safety tweaks (an early grip design could have cost someone a finger), resulted from a natural-language dialogue between the model and its human user. In other words, it’s essentially a vibe-coded gun. Though mostly a proof of concept, the WASP nonetheless fires real, lethal rounds and doesn’t have a serial number. Wilson believes AI-generated guns like this will only improve as GatGPT ingests more data, and as users engage with it.

But the WASP also poses another pressing public safety issue. Producing 3D-printed guns has gotten easier over the years, but it still fundamentally requires some technical know-how. Now, however, a novice armed with GatGPT could plausibly make a gun with only a handful of prompts. That’s exactly the kind of barrier-lowering that critics of 3D-printed guns, like Everytown, have spent years warning about.

“[Wilson] admits the goal here,” Everytown senior vice president for law and policy Justin Wagner told The Verge. “He wants to lower the barrier to entry so anyone, regardless of their background check status or legal eligibility [can] own a gun. He wants anyone to be able to design and manufacture weapons, and that’s dangerous.”

Everytown has played a prominent role in advocating for a pair of recently passed laws in New York and California that will require 3D printer manufacturers to install firearm-blocking software that can detect guns or gun parts and stop them before they are ever printed. (Experts have questioned how and if these methods would actually work.)

Wilson didn’t specifically cite evading detection as a reason for building an AI gun maker, but the development comes on the heels of his recent efforts to complicate firearm-blocking technology that New York and California will require in future 3D printers. In August, Wilson began rolling out a tool called Hochulization (a jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul) that he says subtly alters a file’s underlying hash, which functions as a kind of digital fingerprint. By late September, Wilson claimed to The Verge that users had already “Hochulized” files more than 26,000 times, with some users applying the treatment more than once. It’s one of the many ways Wilson has planted a flag in the evolving battle over how to regulate 3D-printed guns.

“He wants anyone to be able to design and manufacture weapons, and that’s dangerous.”

The core idea behind that “self-defense measure,” as Wilson calls it, is to stymie a purely hash-based gun detection system by rendering it unable to keep up with constantly changing hashes. A new AI-generated gun design also wouldn’t immediately be recognized in a gun detection database, since it didn’t exist yet. More sophisticated gun detection software goes beyond simple hashes and uses AI to try to predict whether a file is likely a gun or gun component before it prints. It’s unclear whether this type of software, which is still being developed, would reliably detect a sufficiently strange-looking AI-generated gun design.

“Individuals who intentionally aim to thwart safety regulations put themselves and New York communities at risk, which is why Gov. Hochul remains committed to combating emerging threats and the production of ghost guns and illegally manufactured guns, and strengthening regulations that keep New Yorkers safe,” Hochul spokesperson Jess D’Amelia told The Verge.

Defense Distributed’s AI didn’t just log on one day and suddenly decide to build a gun. It started with a specific request from a human to riff off an existing design. An employee asked the model to build a new gun based on a design called “Ergo Harlot,” itself a variation of the more popular “Harlot” model. Like the WASP, the Harlot is a compact single-shot handgun that fires a .22 caliber round. The AI prompter, according to chat logs viewed by The Verge, framed the assignment as a “challenge” and told the AI model its entry “must be completely and fully functional and have a unique design.”

Chat logs show the AI model responding with a plan for a new design called the WASP and submitting it for approval. The AI didn’t explain its name choice, though Wilson suggested it bears some physical resemblance to the insect. When I asked whether it’s possibly an abbreviation for “white Anglo-Saxon protestant,” he said it isn’t.

The AI model listed six key changes it made to the inspiration design, including a slightly longer barrel than the Harlot’s and a grip made of three grooved, circular lobes. Once a Defense Distributed employee approved the model’s plan, the logs show it checking and testing each component, much like how an AI coding agent such as Anthropic’s Claude Code works through a checklist when vibe-coding an app. The team then printed the WASP in its office on a Bambu Lab printer using standard plastic filaments, along with a handful of common metal parts for the firing pin and barrel. Wilson said the print took about six hours.

So is the WASP actually a good gun? Ashley Hlebinsky, a firearms historian and founder of consulting firm The Gun Code, told The Verge that it’s hard to judge without handling it, but several design choices stand out as odd. Most notably, the AI appears to have started making a trigger guard (the loop that normally protects a shooter’s finger) but doesn’t finish it, leaving the trigger exposed, for no apparent reason. The gun also seems to borrow from what are called modern “beavertail” grip designs. But bizarrely, the AI appears to have inverted its grip.

“It reminds me of times when I’ve prompted AI to draw a picture of a gun and it gets most of the way there but then has some weird parts missing,” Hlebinsky said. “It has an obvious futuristic, sci-fi appearance that reminds me of Marvin the Martian’s ray gun.”

Jonathan Ferguson, keeper of firearms and artillery at the Royal Armories Museum in Leeds, England, was more critical when asked if the WASP seemed functional.

“Functional? From a legal perspective, if it successfully fires a shot without a breech explosion, it’s a viable firearm, but so are two lengths of steel pipe with a firing pin and cap attached to the rear of one,” Ferguson told The Verge. “From a technical perspective, I would not call this a ‘sound’ or ‘good’ firearm. It does not appear to be comfortable to hold or easy to aim and, based on the test firing, seems to be only marginally functional.” If anything, Ferguson noted, he expected generative AI in 2026 to do a better job at designing a reliable firearm. “There are vestigial sights that can’t work, an open trigger guard, [and a] weirdly shaped grip.”

“This certainly is a development, [but] I don’t think it’s necessarily that novel. It’s another way to 3D print a gun,” Wagner said. “A victim of a mass shooting who was shot by a ghost gun told me when you get shot, it doesn’t matter if it’s a ghost gun, a 3D-printed gun, or a gun that got bought over the counter. They’re all just as lethal,” he added.

“From a technical perspective, I would not call this a ‘sound’ or ‘good’ firearm.”

Wilson is confident his AI’s design will improve, both in terms of functionality and aesthetic uniqueness, as the DEFCAD database grows. More gun files will help, but he expects the biggest gains will come from users chatting with the model and pushing it to refine its choices. (GatGPT is currently in limited early access.) Eventually, he predicts, constant back-and-forth between users and AI could dramatically speed up the pace at which new 3D-printed gun designs appear.

“This is all just spontaneous parallel thinking,” Wilson said. “I think you’ll see those cycles faster now because of AI.”

“It’s like you’re speedrunning the available possibilities, the materials, the platforms, the concepts,” he added.

A skeptic would say the WASP’s origins as essentially a remix of a previous designs makes its claims to true originality shaky. Like many half-baked AI movie scripts or janky generative art, the WASP conjures up the familiar feeling of AI slop, made manifest in the real world. Even Wilson admits it looks a bit like a “Fortnite gun.”

Still, Wilson maintains the WASP is fundamentally an AI creation and one that he’s ultimately not responsible for, even though his team’s prompts led to its creation. That position aligns with a broader argument Wilson’s made for the better part of a decade in legal skirmishes with the State Department and local lawmakers: that gun files are protected speech. In fact, Wilson said he doesn’t necessarily consider the WASP a gun at all until it’s printed and fired.

“This thing lives first as a digital organism,” he said.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo is now available to preorder at $1,999
Tech.content:
writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Few phones have been more anticipated than a foldable iPhone, but it’s finally here. The iPhone Duo was unveiled during Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.

Apple’s first foldable has a 5.4-inch outer screen, and it unfolds to show off its 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR screen. Apple Pencil support is coming later this year. While it lacks Face ID for facial unlocking, there’s a Touch ID sensor along its edge to identify your fingerprint. The device has an IP68 rating, with Ceramic Shield 2 on its back, with Ceramic Shield covering the front display. It has the same A20 Pro chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro. Notably, the Duo has the same 48-megapixel fusion camera as the 18 Pro, though it doesn’t have variable aperture.

The foldable will come in two colors, Star White and Night Sky, and starts at $1,999 for the 256GB version. You can preorder an unlocked version now ahead of its Friday, October 23rd release date from Apple and Best Buy.

Offers from carriers

If you’re looking to buy from a carrier, a few are offering promomtions.

AT&T is offering new and existing customers up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo with a qualifying trade-in, applied through 36 monthly bill credits. Customers switching to AT&T can also receive up to $800 via a reward card to help pay off their existing phone balance. Additionally, customers who activate a new eligible line online can save up to $200 per line through 36 monthly bill credits.

T-Mobile will offer up to $1,000 off the iPhone Duo with eligible trade-ins on an Experience Beyond or Go5G Next plan. Alternatively, you can get the same discount without a trade-in when adding a new line and switching from another carrier.

Verizon is waiving its $40 activation fee for new customers who preorder the iPhone Duo. You can pay $55.55 per month over 36 months at 0 percent APR. Alternatively, Verizon offers a Simplicity Pro package for $72.22 per month, which bundles the phone with additional perks like two extra TravelPass days per month, and lets you upgrade your phone up to two times within a rolling 12-month period.

Tech.title: Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro
Tech.content:
After setting up Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, I spent five minutes just staring at it. I wasn’t surprised by its MacBook Pro-like design or blown away by its bright display. I was trying to work out what I’d actually do with a $5,900 laptop.

This isn’t just any regular Windows laptop. Microsoft has teamed up with Nvidia to build a high-end laptop to showcase Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark chips. It’s a big moment for Windows on Arm, as these chips can run demanding AI models locally, alongside the latest AAA games and creative apps. The promise is compelling, but the reality of local AI is much messier.

Getting the most out of the Surface Laptop Ultra, especially my top-of-the-line model, requires coding experience or the patience to experiment with models and AI agents until you find something that works. If that sounds like you, Microsoft might have built the Windows laptop you’ve been waiting for. If not, this might not be the MacBook Pro competitor Microsoft was hoping for.

It feels like Microsoft has finally built the hardware to rival Apple’s pro laptops, thanks to an all-aluminum design, large haptic trackpad, and high-end finish. Even the “nightfall” color is just like Apple’s space black.

There are plenty of meaningful differences, though. The 15-inch MicroLED display can run at up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, at 262 pixels per inch (3270 x 2180); the MacBook Pro peaks at 1,600 nits. That makes it the brightest display Microsoft has ever shipped on a Surface Laptop. Unlike the MacBook Pro, it’s also a 3:2 touchscreen, perfect for writing code, reading text, or editing photos.

The port selection is similar to the MacBook Pro, with one very big change. You get three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, a single HDMI 2.1b port, SD card reader, and headphone jack. Where it really differs is Microsoft’s new Magnetic Connect. It works just like the old Surface Connect, but through the USB-C port on the right-hand side. Just bring the connector close to the port, and it snaps into place. When you’re not charging, that port works just like the rest of the USB-C ports on the laptop.

Magnetic Connect is one of my favorite additions on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I love how you can reverse the magnetic USB-C charging end, attach it to the power brick, and use the regular USB-C connector at the opposite end of the cable to charge the rest of your devices.

Left-side ports: HDMI, 2x USB-C, and a headphone jack. Right-side ports: SD card reader, USB-A, USB-C.

The haptic feedback on the large trackpad is also a welcome addition. It works with things like clicks, drags, and window alignment throughout Windows 11, and the tactile feedback triggers in apps like PowerPoint as you drag and align objects or images in a deck, too. It’s subtle enough to make it feel like you’re really moving windows or interfaces around, but I do wish more apps supported it.

Microsoft has included a 1080p front-facing camera above the screen. The quality is fine for video calls, and it supports Windows Hello face authentication and Windows Studio Effects like automatic framing, eye contact, and background blur.

Not all of the Surface Laptop Ultra hardware is impressive, though. I’ve had issues where I’ve unplugged the charger at 100 percent only for Windows to then immediately report 97 percent battery life. Plugging in would put it back to 100 percent and then it would immediately drop back to 97 percent again each time I unplugged.

The magnetic USB-C charger is an impressive addition.

It seemed weird so I asked Microsoft about the behavior, and it’s designed this way to make a battery last longer. “When it’s plugged in and the battery is full, the device pauses charging rather than constantly topping off, and resumes only once the level drops to 95 percent,” says Microsoft spokesperson Moses Nsereko. “This reduces wear over time. While plugged in, the indicator shows 100 percent to indicate a full charge. When you unplug, it shows the battery’s exact level right away, which may be a few percent lower.”

I’ve run into some issues with the display, too, where either things felt slightly laggy or there was noticeable ghosting. Moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail. Changing power settings from the default “best power efficiency” mode to “best performance” seemed to fix most of the laggy feeling, and the backlight ghosting seems to be less noticeable the longer you run the laptop.

I also heard some loud pops and bangs from the built-in speakers on the Surface Laptop Ultra. They were loud enough to sound like firecrackers, and I thought the battery was about to die before I realized it was just speaker interference. Rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra solved this one, but it’s happened a couple of times now.

Speaking of rebooting, I’ve noticed that rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra is surprisingly slow. This seems like something Microsoft could easily fix with an update, though.

The Surface Laptop Ultra can run complex local AI models.

Local AI models and agents

The RTX Spark that powers the Surface Laptop Ultra is designed with local AI models and agents in mind. The variant I’ve been testing has a 20-core CPU that was codesigned by Nvidia and MediaTek paired with a 6,144-CUDA-core GPU — roughly comparable to a mobile RTX 5060 — plus 128GB of unified memory and a 1TB Gen 5 SSD. It’s the top-of-the-line model at $5,899, and I think if you’re considering this particular laptop spec then you have a very specific use case in mind. The base version is $2,599, and it comes with an 18-core CPU, 5,120-CUDA -core GPU, and 24GB of unified memory.

Out of the box, Microsoft prompts Laptop Ultra owners to pick an AI agent. You can choose between Hermes, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. I tried out Hermes and OpenClaw over the past week, but I ran into issues getting OpenClaw to work initially. A reinstall fixed a gateway issue, and then I could name my agent and start using it for local AI tasks.

I configured both Hermes and OpenClaw to use the Qwen3.8-27B model, one of the more powerful local AI models. Because it uses the full power of the Surface Laptop Ultra, it will spin up its fans at full throttle and 100 percent GPU for even the most basic of queries. I asked Hermes to resize and convert some photos from PNG to JPG, a task that would take seconds using a PowerToy utility. It took minutes to complete, all while the fans were buzzing away and the laptop was getting hot.

It’s probably my fault for using such a large model for a basic task, but without testing every single local AI model it’s hard to know which one to pick for each task you need. I asked OpenClaw to build me a smart home dashboard, but it spent 30 minutes spinning up the laptop’s fans and calling various tools to eventually produce nothing but an error.

I don’t have a base Surface Laptop Ultra to test, but it’s easy to see that 24GB of unified memory will mean fewer local AI models to choose from.

Local AI models are best for coding tasks right now.

I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, or run a task across large datasets that would normally cost a lot of money in cloud tokens.

I did like that I could do things locally, though, without worrying about the privacy aspects of cloud models. I fed Hermes some audio and video files and it went ahead and created a local llama.cpp server to enable audio transcription. It took some fiddling to get it working, but it could certainly save me having to install transcription apps or pay for a cloud service like Otter.

The thing I didn’t like is that these agents are far from user-friendly, and I’m surprised that Microsoft or Nvidia hasn’t developed its own local AI interface that simplifies a lot of this work. I need to spend more time with both Hermes and OpenClaw, but as someone who doesn’t code it’s clear this is all really targeted toward developers and power users.

Gaming and creative tasks

The Surface Laptop Ultra might not be an official gaming laptop, but it’s certainly capable of running far more of the latest games than Apple’s MacBook Pro. Normally I’d be nervous about Windows on Arm and gaming, given the weak GPU on the Qualcomm Snapdragon X series chips. But this is the first time we’ve seen an Arm CPU paired with a stronger Nvidia GPU, and most games run well for a laptop that’s not the size of a gaming one.

Instead of running a bunch of benchmarks at different settings, I decided to try and find the optimal settings that would allow me to play at around 60fps or more in each game. Because this is an RTX GPU, you also get full support for DLSS, Frame Generation, and ray tracing. So you can enable Frame Generation if you want to get to 120fps to match the 120Hz display.

I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.

Most games will need to run at medium settings and DLSS performance or balanced to get around 60fps, but there are some exceptions where you’ll need to lower settings or resolution. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 40fps on medium settings and DLSS performance, and I only managed to bump this to 48fps on low settings. I also had to move Doom: The Dark Ages to low settings and DLSS performance to hit an average of 60fps.

Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra.

I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. It felt more like dropping down to console settings, and in some games it’s hard to distinguish the texture differences on a smaller display. I’m one of those gamers who prefers to run at 60fps with lower settings rather than max out the settings and have to play at 30fps, though.

While game compatibility is good for most titles, there are some where you’re going to run into emulation issues. Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered was limited to 30fps at 1440p regardless of whether I used low or medium settings. I believe this is because the game is CPU-heavy, so a native Arm port would probably help for this type of game.

There aren’t many native Arm games, though. I tried out the new Arm version of Marvel Rivals, and it averaged 64fps with medium settings and DLSS performance and 75fps with low settings. I think we’ll only see Arm ports where there’s a lot of CPU activity involved that the Prism emulator — which translates CPU instructions from x86 to Arm — can’t handle well enough, because otherwise it’s very capable.

We may see more Arm ports for games that have anti-cheat engines. Anti-cheat engines are a lot more complicated to emulate, so developers have to create Arm-compatible versions. While games like Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Fortnite all work out of the box, Nvidia and Microsoft are working with EA, Activision, and Riot Games to get titles like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Valorant, and League of Legends fully supported.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is also a very capable machine for creative and everyday tasks. I managed to export our 4K video test in two minutes and 18 seconds on the Surface Laptop Ultra using Premiere Pro. That’s around a minute behind the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro, but beats the base M5 chip and is around 30 seconds behind the M5 Pro. I did have to create this using Premiere Pro’s own export tool, rather than sending it to Media Encoder like how we usually run this test. There seems to be a bug in the beta Arm version of Media Encoder that prevented it from running the export correctly.

Where the Surface Laptop Ultra really falls behind Apple’s M5 chips is in CPU performance. Single-core and multi-threaded CPU tests like Geekbench or Cinebench show how much weaker the MediaTek CPU is against a $6,999-plus MacBook Pro 16 with an M5 Max or even an M6 Mac Mini. Even some of the GPU tests for Geekbench show the RTX Spark falling behind Apple’s MacBook Pro, and the Puget Bench Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and DaVinci Resolve are all noticeably behind the M5 Max.

I’ve also been testing the battery life of the Surface Laptop Ultra, which seems to be around seven hours if you’re using local AI models and a mix of apps and gaming. If you’re doing less intensive work, it’s averaging out at 10 hours or more. I’ll know more the longer I use the Laptop Ultra, so check back for updated battery impressions.

Surface Laptop Ultra is designed for Blender and other creative apps.

The Surface Laptop Ultra doesn’t really offer a clear performance advantage over the MacBook Pro outside of some AI workloads like image generation and the ability to run CUDA compute natively. It’s not transformative for the Windows world like the M1 chips were for macOS, largely because Qualcomm already supercharged Windows on Arm with its Snapdragon X series two years ago. That makes it difficult to recommend unless you’re specifically interested in running local AI models, coding, or experimenting with AI agents.

The Surface Laptop Ultra, and Nvidia’s RTX Spark in general, targets developers and power users who want a laptop that can handle those workloads alongside creative apps and the latest games. For that audience, there’s a lot to like. For everyone else, more affordable laptops can handle everyday productivity, creative work, and some light gaming without the hefty price premium.

Microsoft has come closer than ever to building a Windows alternative to the MacBook Pro. The hardware looks and feels great, and Nvidia’s GPU brings CUDA support and decent gaming capabilities to a high-end laptop design. But the Surface Laptop Ultra’s biggest selling point is also its biggest question mark: local AI. It all feels like a work in progress. If you’re ready to experiment with it, this could be a compelling glimpse of where Windows laptops could go next. If you’re not, it’s a lot of money to spend on an experiment.
