Tech.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
Tech.content:
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.

The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”

That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault, a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”

He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

Tech.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
Tech.content:
Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “superfakes,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.

Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.

“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.

The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.

“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”

This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.

Image Credits:Veritas x ATHLOS

The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.

The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.

Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.

Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon.

Tech.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
Tech.content:
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.

He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste.

“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.

He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.

“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”

Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.

And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.

“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.

The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.

“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”

He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.)

“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

Tech.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
Tech.content:
For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.

It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”

He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.

Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

Tech.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
Tech.content:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph acceleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.

All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.

Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”

Tesla Roadster-starman Image Credits:Tesla

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.

Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Tesla roadster event Image Credits:Tesla

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in “The Spy Who Loved Me” — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.

In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved on to other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.

“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

Tech.title: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
Tech.content:
Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.

Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.

Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.

“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.

Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

Tech.title: And the winner of Startup Battlefield at Disrupt 2026 is: Intero Biosystems
Tech.content:
For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200, and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner.

These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges.

After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.

We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:

Winner: Intero Biosystems

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.

Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.

Runner-up: Apate

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.

Read more about Apate in our separate post here.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. With more than 1,700 alumni having participated in the program, Startup Battlefield Alumni have collectively raised over $30 billion in funding with more than 200 successful exits.

Tech.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it
Tech.content:
Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.

“You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.”

Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down.

“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.”

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure.

“Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.”

Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles.

“It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.”

Tech.title: Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra Review: The First Real AI PC
Tech.content:
A new fleet of Windows laptops has arrived, and the Surface Laptop Ultra is its flagship vessel. Ever since it was announced, it's been one of my anticipated laptops of the year. It not only promises to be a beefed-up evolution of the Surface Laptop (a laptop I already really liked), but also debuts a brand-new piece of silicon: the Nvidia RTX Spark N1X "superchip."

The goal is a single laptop that can handle on-device AI, gaming, content creation, and nearly anything else you might throw at it. If that sounds a bit like a MacBook Pro, you're on the right track. But unlike previous attempts to dethrone Apple, the Surface Laptop Ultra is trading blows with the very best. I just wish it had the battery life to truly keep up with the MacBook Pro.

Killer Looks and Sounds

This isn't Microsoft's first foray into a more powerful laptop. The company first tried that in 2021 with the Surface Laptop Studio. At the time, it was the company's answer to the MacBook Pro: a laptop-tablet hybrid oriented toward the growing class of content creators and media professionals. It even came with a discrete graphics card (though not a particularly good one).

The Surface Laptop Ultra rejects the Studio's form-factor experimentation and opts for a more straightforward but polished approach. It's a powerful clamshell laptop that's designed for people who need the extra performance—whether for gaming, content creation, or on-device AI workflows. The ideal demographic, I suppose, is someone who does some of all of that.

At 4.4 pounds, the Surface Laptop Ultra is lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro but slightly thicker. It's actually the thickest of all the new N1X laptops, with HP's OmniBook Ultra being the thinnest. The Surface Laptop Ultra appears thinner than it actually is, though, thanks to the inventive way it hides its side vents—so discreet that it's hard to photograph them. The design has just enough small touches like that to make it stand out. There's also a soft dip into the keyboard well, with a unique look that matches the curved lip of the underside vents. I appreciate the modern vibe of the rounded screen corners, though some apps don't account for them well and nearly cut off elements of the Title Bar. One other minor annoyance is that there's no lip for your finger when the device is closed. You can slide your fingernail in between, but in most cases, you'll need two hands to open it.

Tech.title: AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector Review: A Top Buy
Tech.content:
It takes a special home theater projector to get me to stick through a movie like Supergirl. Critics panned it for dark themes, and its visually dark tones make it literally tough to see. But when I used the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max to project it onto a 120-inch screen with Dolby Atmos sound blasting from every corner of my basement, the film looked stunning.

The Aetherion Max, with its precise picture-quality settings and sharp 4K clarity, provides an experience rivaling that of a movie theater. Supergirl might suffer from bad CGI and even worse dialog, but the projector's features, like Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, brought the film to life, making reds and blues pop with amazing vividness.

Priced at $4,499, this ultrashort throw model sits right next to the wall or projector screen. In some ways, it reminds me of the LG Micro RGB Evo television with highly adjustable picture-quality settings. Ultimately, though, I'm a fan of the Aetherion Max because it projects a breathtakingly colorful image.

An Engineering Marvel, Except for the Remote

Photograph: John Brandon Photograph: John Brandon

Before taking stock of its powerhouse specs, I noticed the Aetherion Max's design. Shaped a bit like a Tesla Cybertruck, the silver projector has sharp edges that lend a modern look. The front of the machine (the side that faces you) has no buttons except a single white line that animates when you power it on—a detail I found to be distracting and then powered off. The other side (which faces the screen) is where you'll find three HDMI 2.1 ports (including one for eARC passthrough audio), a USB-A port for a local storage device, optical and 3.5mm audio-out ports, and a 1 GBps Ethernet port for wired streaming.

Tech.title: AI-Generated Hot Girls Are Ripping Off Comedians to Boost Their Horny Content
Tech.content:
Last week, the stand-up comedian Julia Jasunas was on Instagram when she got a DM from a fellow comic. Did she know, her friend wrote, that a random Instagram influencer had ripped off a joke from her stand-up act?

Initially, Jasunas was mad but not overly shocked. Plagiarism is not uncommon in the stand-up comedy world, and comics are “really sensitive about it, because there's not a ton of protection against it,” she tells WIRED. “So we all look out for each other.” Then she clicked on the link.

The video was of a purported stand-up comic named Aylen Skye, a buxom blond with leonine cheekbones and 250,000 Instagram followers. In the clip, Skye, wearing a crop top and Daisy Dukes, tells a joke about renting out a room in her two-bedroom apartment to a cute guy. To Jasunas’ shock, it was, verbatim, her joke, down to the “ums” and “ahs.”

Whoever Skye was, she didn’t appear to be a comic; the website she advertised in her video, AylenTV.com, redirected to NSFW content on Fanvue, a subscription-based OnlyFans competitor that markets itself as the “No1 AI monetisation platform for creators.” And not only did she appear to not be a comic, she also didn’t seem to be real. After looking at Skye’s comments section, Jasunas was fairly convinced she was AI.

“You look at any female comic’s comments section and you’ll see all these men berating her, objectifying her body, saying she’s not funny or the joke is bad,” she says. But with Skye, all of the comments were positive. “That’s how I knew she was fake,” she deadpans.

Tech.title: The Best Digital Wall Calendar (2026): Skylight, Everblog, Greenlight
Tech.content:
I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was bulky and expensive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using one at all, but to my surprise, digital wall calendars have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here’s everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they’re right for you.

Tech.title: Jabra Enhance Select M3 Review (2026): A Big Price for Small Wins
Tech.content:
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.

Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.

Tech.title: The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder
Tech.content:
There has been no shortage of coverage on Elizabeth Holmes, the Silicon Valley fraudster whose biotech startup Theranos reached a peak valuation of $9 billion in 2014 before its supposedly groundbreaking blood test machine was revealed to be vaporware. Books, magazine articles, documentaries, TV dramatizations—the exposés have piled up high.

So, you might ask yourself, why the hype for the forthcoming You Can See Everything, yet another documentary about Holmes, and one that spans three hours?

The excitement is thanks to Nathan Fielder, one of the film’s directors. (Fielder codirected the documentary with Lance Oppenheim). Fielder is a cult-favorite television auteur whose devotees have awaited his showdown with Holmes ever since rumors about him visiting her in prison surfaced last year.

Now that Fielder appears poised to break the containment of an obsessed fan base and conquer the cineplex, it behooves you to get caught up. This will not be a typical documentary: Fielder has made a career of heightened unreality, sowing confusion wherever he goes. To give you some notion of what to expect from his analysis of Holmes, here’s a rundown of his unusual and captivating style.

Business Bona Fides

One reason Fielder makes sense as an interlocutor for big tech’s most notorious con woman is his own history of corporate chicanery. In his breakout TV series Nathan for You (2013–2017), he contrived and implemented bizarre publicity stunts for struggling small businesses. (While he jokes that he “graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades,” the fact remains he did graduate, unlike Holmes, a Stanford University dropout.)

Andrew Bricker, an associate professor of English at the University of Ghent and academic coordinator for the research project Democratic Literacy and Humour, writes in an email that it’s important to recognize that, throughout his career, Fielder has always played the same altered version of himself, leaving us unsure just who he really is.

Fielder “has made the borderlands of persona and person so ambiguous, so indeterminable, so indefinable, that none of us is entirely in on the joke,” Bricker says.

Tech.title: Egypt’s Climate-Resilient ‘Super Corals’ Are Starting to Feel the Heat
Tech.content:
As coral reefs have undergone massive bleaching events across the globe, the corals of Egypt’s Red Sea have offered some hope. They’ve been unusually resilient to rising water temperatures, and if the oceans continue getting hotter, some scientists even predict that Egypt’s northern reefs could become the world’s last-remaining corals.

That’s what Mahmoud Hanafy, a professor of marine biology at Suez Canal University and consultant for the Hurghada Environmental Protection and Conservation Association (HEPCA), has previously predicted. But in the summers of 2023 and 2024, heat waves strained Red Sea coral ecosystems. A HEPCA survey led by Hanafy found bleaching throughout the Red Sea corals in 2024. In the northern areas, less than a tenth of coral colonies surveyed were affected, but further south, bleaching took out half the corals.

Scientists are racing to piece together what these events mean for reefs long described as “super coral” for their unparalleled hardiness. But now the question is not just how much heat they can withstand, but what has protected them until recently—and whether that protection will hold.

In overly warm waters, the algae nestled amongst the corals’ polyps begin to produce toxic substances. As a defense mechanism, the corals eject the algae. This is what is referred to as coral bleaching, and because these microscopic organisms are corals’ primary food source, bleaching events leave corals to starve.

That’s among other negative impacts hot seas may be having on corals, which is an issue not just for the corals, but all the other life among the reefs. According to the United Nations Environment Program, reefs cover less than 1 percent of the seafloor yet support at least 25 percent of marine species—some that are only just now being discovered.

For many years, northern Red Sea reefs remained quite stable as temperatures rose, while other coral ecosystems suffered bleaching. Eslam Osman, a marine ecologist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), points to the Egyptian corals’ evolutionary history as a likely explanation for their heat tolerance.

Corals are believed to have spread into the Red Sea through the Bab al-Mandab Straight, which lies at the southern point of the sea between modern-day Djibouti and Yemen. Crossing through these especially warm waters acted as a natural filter, Osman posits. Heat-tolerant species and genotypes survived, and their offspring spread northwards into cooler waters.

Tech.title: iPhone Duo Preorders Sell Out in Minutes: Backordered Until January
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, is a hot ticket.

Preorders for the iPhone Duo began on Friday at 5 a.m. PT, on Apple’s website, the Apple Store app and elsewhere. Although the phone has an Oct. 23 release date, as of now models preordered through Apple won’t ship until the last week of January. The availability at mobile carriers like AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile is more variable. You can also try to buy one in stores on Oct. 23.

CNET Senior Tech Reporter Abrar Al Heeti got to handle the iPhone Duo briefly ahead of preorders, and described it as essentially a compact iPhone that can double as an iPad Mini, well suited for consuming media. Beyond that, she wrote, “It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on.”

The 7.6-inch screen when opened is the largest iPhone display screen yet (there’s also a 5.4-inch outer display). The Duo is also equipped with two 48-megapixel cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide one. It’s geared for multitasking, with Apple Pencil support and drag-and-drop functionality similar to an iPad.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, but trade-in offers and Apple’s Upgrade program could lower how much you pay out of pocket.

Apple is years late to the folding phone market, though that might not matter much to those already in the iPhone ecosystem. The bigger question is whether the iPhone Duo will be tempting to those inclined to buy Android phones, where the latest hinged options include the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 and Galaxy Flip 8 and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Tech.title: Everything You Should Know About Mail Categories on Your iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro (left) and iPhone 17 Pro Patrick Holland/CNET

Finding a particular message can be difficult if you get a lot of emails. If you want to check on the status of a package, scrolling through newsletters and random ads can be irksome. Luckily, Apple introduced Categories for the mail app when the tech company released iOS 18.2 in 2025.

“The Mail app automatically sorts your email messages into categories to help you find and manage messages more quickly,” Apple wrote online.

Categories are on by default, but if you don’t like how it works in Mail, no worries. Apple gives you a few options to either ignore Categories or revert your app to look like it did before the iOS 18.2 update.

More from CNET

Here’s what you need to know about Mail Categories and how to turn the feature off so your app looks like it did before the update.

How Mail Categories work

Mail Categories are similar to categories you would find in other email services, like Gmail. The app filters your emails into one of four categories: Primary, Transactions, Updates and Promotions.

Emails with receipts, as well as order and delivery information, fill the Transactions category, and news, social and other subscription emails go to Updates. Emails with special offers and deals go to Promotions, as you might imagine.

I ignore most of the deals in my email. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

The Primary category is more difficult to pin down. Apple says in the app that Primary is for “Messages that matter most.” I’ve used the redesigned app since it launched in beta, and during that time my Primary category was filled with emails from my wife, customer service and even refund information. It’s a little bit of a catch-all category.

How to change an email’s category

Categories aren’t perfect so sometimes an email lands where it probably shouldn’t, like an ad in the Transactions category instead of the Promotions. There is a way to change an email’s category for any future messages you might receive from that sender. Here’s how.

1. Tap Mail.

2. Tap the Transactions, Updates or Promotions tab then tap a message.

3. Tap the three dots (…) in the top right corner.

4. Tap Categorize Sender.

The Promotions category feels right for this email. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Then you can manually categorize messages from a given sender to another category. You can also recategorize an email from Promotions to Deals and then back to Promotions. The only emails that can’t be recategorized are those in Primary — which can be annoying.

Once, I ordered tickets for a show at a local theater, and the email was filtered to Promotions. I moved the email with those tickets to Primary, but now all emails from that theater — including deals and sales — go to my Primary category. Not being able to change that categorization back is annoying.

How to disable Mail Categories

If you don’t like Mail Categories, you have a few options to see all your mail at once. The easiest way is to swipe the categories bar near the top of Mail to the left to reveal the option All Mail. Swiping left to view this option automatically selects All Mail. Now all your mail will be displayed from top to bottom as each message comes in, but you will still see the Categories tabs across the top of the app.

You can also remove Categories altogether so the app looks like it did before the update. Here’s how.

1. Tap Mail.

2. Tap the three dots (…) in the top right corner of the app.

3. Tap Show Categories.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Now your emails will populate in Mail from top to bottom as they arrive in your inbox.

For more iOS news, here’s what you should know about iOS 26 as well as iOS 27.

Tech.title: The Unusual Item I Use to Degrease a Pan Before Washing It
Tech.content:
My mother kept a large jar under the sink to store rendered fat or used oil from bacon, burgers, fried chicken and the like; its distinct layers represented the geologic eras of family dinners from previous months. Once full, we would presumably discard it in the trash.

This was before we recycled everything, and before we knew food waste was one of the largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Surely large jars of cooking grease set out on the curb with other refuse isn’t exactly a winning move on either the recycling or food-waste front.

The 3 Best Frying Pans, Tested by CNET See at CNET

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of many things, excess cooking grease still presents a regular quandary. It’s not exactly cooperative to slither inside biodegradable food-waste bags, if you’re fortunate enough to live somewhere that collects food waste. You also can’t toss it into your countertop composter without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

More from CNET

Should you ever pour excess oil down the sink?

Ask a plumber; oil is one of the worst things you can pour down the drain. Alina Bradford/CNET

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

CNET

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

This excess grease hack is the best thing since sliced bread

There isn’t an obvious way to discard a pan full of hot grease. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame as someone fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

How and when to use the bread method for soaking up grease

A piece of bread that’s past its prime makes an excellent oil sponge. Pamela Vachon/CNET

If it’s not obvious, this is also an excellent way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

An oily sauce or stew benefits from being sopped gently with a slice of bread. Pamela Vachon/CNET

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Oil-soaked bread can be composted, but with caution

Oil-soaked bread can go in the compost bin under certain conditions. Jenny Dettrick/Getty Images

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

Tech.title: Does Verizon’s Simplicity Phone Plan Live up to Its Name? We Compare It to MyPlan
Tech.content:
Verizon’s new Simplicity plan runs $45 a month with autopay. Here’s what’s included, what costs extra and the one thing to know before switching from myPlan. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

If you’re looking to switch to Verizon for phone service, or you’re a customer evaluating the company’s other plans, the new Simplicity offering has a lot going for it. Introduced alongside the Verizon Shine loyalty program, Simplicity is a streamlined unlimited phone plan with a key improvement over the regular entry-level unlimited plan (which is still available along with the other MyPlan options).

Simplicity runs $45 a month per line with autopay, or $30 for new customers switching to Verizon, and includes access to 5G Ultra Wideband with no network tiers and 10GB of mobile hotspot. Optional add-on bundles cover streaming services, additional hotspot and travel features. But before switching from an existing myPlan, there’s one thing worth knowing: If you have multiple lines on an account, every line must also switch to Simplicity.

The Simplicity plan costs $45 per line, but switchers who bring their number and an unlocked phone to Verizon pay $30 per month. For that, you get unlimited data, roaming in Canada and Mexico, 10GB of fast mobile hotspot data, and satellite texting.

More from CNET

That $45 rate is $20 less than Verizon’s entry-level Unlimited Welcome plan for a single line, and has a key difference. Verizon differentiates Unlimited Welcome from its other tiers by capping 5G speeds. Only the Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Ultimate plans enable the fastest 5G Ultra Wideband speeds. The Simplicity Plan gets faster data in areas where 5G UW is available.

Verizon is pitching the Simplicity plan as a simpler option — it includes only connectivity, and customers can add optional perks such as streaming or cloud storage services on top for additional cost. The company is also offering customized bundles, such as a For Movie and Show Lovers bundle that includes Disney Plus, Hulu, ESPN Plus (with ads), Netflix and HBO Max (with ads).

Verizon’s other plans are structured like a la carte extras: You pick a phone and data package, then optionally add perks one by one.

As for getting a new phone with the Simplicity plan, Verizon offers device payment plans in durations of 12, 24, 36 and 48 months.

Simplicity also turns out to be slightly more complicated, at least in its naming. If you want to upgrade your phone every year, you can opt for the Simplicity Plus or Simplicity Pro options, which aren’t different plans — they’re named after the price of the model you want. For example, top-tier phones like the iPhone 18 Pro or Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra would fall under the Simplicity Pro label. If you purchase a budget phone with the plan, it’s just Simplicity with no option to upgrade to a new phone each year.

In addition to the Simplicity plan, Verizon has introduced a new Verizon One mobile and home internet bundle. Available to new customers, it costs $70 per month, taxes and fees included. Comparing that to what I can get in my area of Seattle, the 5G Home internet plan at 100 Mbps costs $35 a month when paired with a Verizon mobile plan. That plus the Unlimited Welcome plan, at $65 for a single line, adds up to $100 a month, plus taxes and fees.

The mobile specs are the same as the Simplicity plan. The home internet speed depends on what’s available in your area; if Fios is an option, for example, the plan would start at 500 Mbps. Customers can upgrade to higher speeds for an additional cost.

Tech.title: Did AI Just Erase an Entire Swedish TV Show?
Tech.content:
Fans of TV4’s international edition of The Challenge, which features Swedish celebrities competing in physical and mental contests, will have to wait for another season. An AI agent reportedly deleted edited episodes of the show, and a TV4 backup system failure wiped out hundreds of hours of work.

The Swedish series was due to return on Nov. 22, but has been delayed indefinitely, TV4 said in a statement.

“We have to recut it from scratch. All the raw material is still there, and all that,” program director Mia Lindqvist said on the network’s website.

More from CNET

According to translated articles, the network denies an Aftonbladet report that an AI agent deleted the episodes. However, while TV4’s Lindqvist told the newspaper that an AI agent didn’t act independently, she did not deny that AI was involved in the mishap. Still, she blamed the failed backup system.

“The big problem is that (production company) Mastiff’s backup didn’t work,” she said.

A representative for TV4 didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The program features stars of other Swedish reality programs, such as the country’s version of The Bachelor and Farmen, a reality show about (wait for it…) contestants on a farm. The Challenge: Sweden first aired in 2023.

AI is increasingly a part of editing and production workflows across movies and television, with entertainment giants, including Netflix, leaning on the technology to produce content more quickly and at lower cost.

If an AI agent were somehow responsible, that would seem to have negated any of AI’s time-saving benefits for The Challenge: Sweden and its production team, who now have to spend time rebuilding the episode edits that were lost.

Tech.title: World Timekeepers Decide to Kill the Leap Second
Tech.content:
Human timekeeping rests on two main clocks, and they don’t always run at the same speed. For decades, the solution was the leap second, a minor adjustment added to international time to keep atomic accuracy aligned with the Earth’s natural motion. But on Thursday, the General Conference on Weights and Measures, or the CGPM (abbreviated from its French name), voted to abolish the leap second, closing a long-standing chapter in global time sync.

Most modern clocks rely on Coordinated Universal Time, a hybrid system caught between atomic time, which flows at a near-perfectly constant rate, and astronomical time, which fluctuates as the Earth’s rotation speeds up and slows down. To bridge the gap, UTC periodically inserted a leap second to keep pace with the planet. But reconciling physical planetary shifts with precise digital systems ultimately created more technical disruptions than it solved.

Breaking time

Computers are sensitive when it comes to timekeeping. The last few times we added a leap second to UTC — in 2012, 2015 and 2016 – some computer systems couldn’t handle it. Of the three instances, 2012 was the worst, as adding a leap second caused issues that crashed websites and software platforms, such as Reddit, LinkedIn and Mozilla.

More from CNET

The speed of Earth’s rotation experiences small changes all the time. While we can’t predict exactly how fast Earth will rotate in the future, the conference wrote that there’s a 30% chance we’ll have to add a negative leap second by 2035 to keep UTC aligned with rotational time.

If adding a regular leap second was trouble, imagine what adding a negative leap second could do. The conference doesn’t want to risk finding out. So, potential future computer anomalies caused by UTC changes are a major reason why the leap second is going away.

“Industrial users and the synchronization needs of national critical infrastructures, for example, transportation, energy distribution, telecommunication, and space projects, require UTC to be continuous without any future adjustment,” the group’s resolution reads.

Moving forward

The official death of the leap second will be May 20, 2027, when continuous UTC becomes effective. A continuous UTC means that no more leap seconds, negative or otherwise, will be added to UTC going forward. This also means that UTC and rotational time will begin to drift apart.

The CGPM noted that allowing time measurements to differ by up to an hour will keep UTC stable for several centuries.

This means in the future, when it’s noon, the sun might not be at its highest in the sky. But, considering we’ve only added 27 leap seconds since the concept was introduced in 1972, any changes that occur within our lifetimes will probably be very small.

Tech.title: New Amazon Bee Personal AI Devices Will Listen and Record You
Tech.content:
Trying to remember things yourself is so yesterday — or so AI-wearable makers want you to believe. Amazon on Thursday announced two new products, the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, which use AI to record conversations and then process them into “summaries, to-dos, reminders and insights.”

The Frontier can be worn on your wrist or your clothes, and the Eclipse attaches magnetically to the back of your phone. They are both from Amazon Bee, which is the company’s lineup of AI-powered personal assistant devices and software. Amazon acquired AI-wearable company Bee in July 2025.

There are several ways you might use the devices. Maybe you’re talking with a friend at the coffee shop about details you’ll want to remember later. The Bee Frontier — on your wrist or clipped to your clothes — can record the conversation and give you a transcript or summary, much like AI tools like Gemini can do during a business meeting. The Bee Eclipse, attached to the back of your phone, can record your phone calls and give you transcripts and summaries of your calls.

More from CNET

Just make sure you ask your conversation partners if they mind being recorded.

Amazon says you can also review memories to remember conversation details, and Bee can recommend personalized goals and actions, depending on themes or trends it picks up on.

“The more you use Bee, the smarter it becomes, learning your unique patterns, preferences and relationships, building a progressively smarter understanding of your world without demanding attention,” an Amazon spokesperson told CNET via email.

You can view all the output in the Bee mobile or desktop app.

The Bee Frontier costs $75, and the Bee Eclipse will cost $100, though the Eclipse is not yet available. Users can pick between two tiers of service: The free one allows you to get conversation summaries and recaps for up to 14 days, while the Bee Pro subscription costs $12 per month, which gets you a personal chat assistant and provides unlimited memory, integrations with Amazon, Alexa Plus and third-party apps and suggests to-do lists.

The Amazon Bee Frontier and Eclipse come in various colors. Amazon

Amazon Bee Frontier goes on wrists or clothes

The Frontier can be worn on the wrist or attached to your clothes. It’s made out of ultrasoft silicone and comes in three colors — lavender, sage and onyx. A fully charged battery can last up to seven days and uses USB-C charging. The device has dual microphones and advanced noise filtering for crowded and loud places.

Audio recording begins by pressing a button, and a light goes on to show that it’s recording. You can also configure it to stop if there has not been sound for a certain period.

Amazon Bee Eclipse attaches to phones

The size of a credit card, the Eclipse can magnetically attach to the back of a phone and comes in four colors — silver, midnight, honey and blush. A fully charged battery can last three weeks and maybe more, according to Amazon.

You begin and stop recording with the Eclipse by pressing a button, and an LED light goes on to indicate that recording is in progress.

Connecting with Alexa Plus and apps

Amazon said the Bee Frontier and Eclipse can connect to Alexa Plus, Amazon’s new AI-powered assistant, and also Amazon.com. So, instead of getting conversation summaries, insights and to-dos by looking at the Bee app on your phone, you could just ask Alexa Plus to read them to you.

When connected to Amazon, the Bee device can present shopping recommendations on the Amazon home page or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. For example, say your friend recommends a certain book while talking to you. The Frontier or Eclipse will hear that, locate it on Amazon and show that listing to you.

You can also link the Frontier and Eclipse to other apps, such as Gmail, Microsoft Outlook and Google Calendar. Amazon said Bee devices can draft emails and create calendar invites based on recorded conversations. Bee devices can also connect to your Apple HealthKit “to build a more complete picture of your wellness,” Amazon said.

What about data privacy?

Amazon said it does not store recorded audio, and you can neither access nor share it. You’ll be prompted to get permission from callers when those calls are being recorded, but it is not mandatory — the recording will still happen.

Expect the AI accessories market to grow. “Who doesn’t want to stop forgetting names and dinner plans?” asks Jon Rettinger, a tech tester with more than 1.66 million subscribers to his YouTube channel. But Rettinger said that invasion of privacy could be an issue, especially for people being recorded by someone using the Bee Frontier and Eclipse.

There are 12 states in the US where it is legally required that callers be notified that they are being recorded, known as “all-party consent.”

“The people around you never agreed to any of it, and a little light on your wrist isn’t much of a warning,” Rettinger told CNET. “In California, you legally need everyone’s consent to record a private conversation, and I’d guess most people buying these have no clue. For a work meeting where everybody knows it’s on, great. Wearing it all day is a different story.”

Amazon says Bee Private Compute — a security system built into both devices — processes conversations inside a secure and isolated environment “where no one, including Amazon, can access your data.”

After audio is recorded and processed into insights in real time, it is deleted, Amazon said. No one can get to your insights data unless you share it, and conversation transcripts are encrypted and are not accessible unless you choose to share them.

You can delete transcripts and summaries whenever you want in the app.

Tech.title: Supreme Court Weighs Major Video Privacy Case
Tech.content:
It’s usually legal for an American company to gather your personal data and use it to target you with an , and many online companies rely on this to make money. But a data privacy case now before the US Supreme Court may upend the longstanding practice of personal data collection for use in targeted ads.

The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, stems from a 2022 class action lawsuit filed by Michael Salazar. At issue is a free digital newsletter Salazar signed up for, which was published by 247Sports.com, a college sports news website owned by Paramount Global.

The website included a tracker that shared Salazar’s video viewing history with Facebook without his consent. Salazar says that Paramount did this illegally. But the federal law that Salazar says Paramount violated is a 1988 Reagan-era act governing videotape rentals.

More from CNET

Home video leak

In 1987, President Ronald Reagan nominated Robert Bork for a seat on the Supreme Court, though the nomination was famously rejected by the Senate. During Bork’s confirmation hearings, a writer for the alt-weekly Washington City Paper convinced the manager at a video rental store to slip him Bork’s video-rental history, which the paper published along with commentary on Bork’s film choices.

While Bork’s rental history was fairly boring, the story and its fallout eventually led Congress to pass the Video Privacy Protection Act. The law was created for analog media, but Salazar’s team argues that it also applies to digital media, such as website content. Essentially, if it’s illegal for a video rental store to share your customer information, why are tech companies allowed to do it?

“The Supreme Court’s decision in Salazar v. Paramount Global will affect the privacy rights of millions of people across the country,” Salazar’s lawyer, Joshua I. Hammack, told CNET via email. “Ordinary consumers might be shocked to learn how much of their online activity is tracked, disclosed, and sold. As I argued to the Supreme Court, the Video Protection Privacy Act was designed to give Americans control over our private information, even as companies like Paramount seek new ways to monetize it.”

Defining a consumer

Paramount’s argument centers on how a “consumer” is defined in the Video Privacy Protection Act, with the company asserting that the definition doesn’t include people who subscribed to a free digital newsletter. This was the reason the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the lawsuit.

“The Sixth Circuit correctly rejected that effort,” a case document filed by Paramount reads. “The court of appeals dismissed Salazar’s complaint against 247Sports on the grounds that Salazar is not a ‘consumer’ because he did not ‘rent, purchase, or subscribe’ to the delivery of any ‘video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.’”

The National Retail Federation, Retail Litigation Center, Motion Picture Association, Entertainment Software Association, Meta and the US Chamber of Commerce have all written the court in support of Paramount’s position.

A representative for Paramount Global didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Why do I care who has my data?

Neil Richards, Koch Distinguished Professor and director of the Cordell Institute at the University of Washington School of Law, believes the Video Protection Privacy Act applies to this case and should be enforced.

“Regulating surveillance-based ads, whether by banning them, by giving people meaningful choice to opt out entirely, or through interpretations of existing laws like the VPPA, would be the single best thing we could do for the privacy protections of the average internet user,” Richards told CNET via email.

Although the act was enacted back when Blockbuster Video stores blanketed the country, Richards said the law was intended for future use.

“Congress intentionally drafted the law in a far-sighted way to protect the activity of private video-watching, regardless of the technologies or formats used to watch,” Richards said. “A win for Salazar would be a much-needed win for internet privacy and a much-needed pushback to the greed of surveillance tech companies.”

What could change with data tracking

Even if Salazar wins, any restrictions on tracking could be limited, as the case is specifically about whether it’s illegal to share someone’s digital video-watching history.

“I think that video content probably isn’t actually influencing that many ads.” Justin Brookman, the director of technology policy for Consumer Reports, told CNET over the phone. “Most targeted ads are like retargeted ads based on, ‘you looked at this product, and therefore the product’s going to follow you around.’”

Applying the act here probably won’t sink online targeted ads, Brookman says, even if the law is interpreted fairly broadly. But Brookman says he hopes the case culminates in new privacy protections for internet users, as long as those new protections don’t place the burden on internet users.

“I think just a prohibition on sharing [personal data] would be a better result than forcing people through a million consent screens in every site they go to,” Brookman said.

A chilling effect

Tracking and sharing the histories of the videos people watch could negatively affect internet users’ behavior, according to Eric Null, director of the privacy and data project at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

“Watching videos is an expressive activity, and having those videos tracked, shared, and sold to third parties for various and potentially nefarious purposes will chill that expression,” Null said in an email to CNET.

“The VPPA does cover free online pre-recorded videos, but the statute nonetheless has significant limitations in its scope that can only be rectified by updating our privacy laws,” he said. “We could, of course, do so through a comprehensive privacy law that includes protections for video viewing.”

A Supreme Court ruling is expected in 2027.
